entries.shortExplanation: 먹다 means "to eat" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 먹다 (meokda) means "to eat". Start from the polite form 먹어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 먹다. A strong first sentence is 점심을 먹어요 ("eat lunch."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 먹다 also becomes 먹고 싶어요 (want), 먹을 수 있어요 (can), and 못 먹어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 먹어요. Then practice 안 먹어요 vs 못 먹어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

For everyday description, reach for the ㄴ/은 form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㅂ → 우
conjugationTips.body: 어렵다 is a ㅂ-irregular word. Before a vowel ending the final ㅂ turns into 우, so the polite form is 어려워요 — not a literal ㅂ + 어요. The same change gives the noun-describing form (맵다 → 매운, 쉽다 → 쉬운). Anchor on 어려워요 and build the rest from it.

entries.shortExplanation: 당황하다 means "to be flustered" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 당황하다 (danghwanghada) means "to be flustered". Start from the polite form 당황해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 당황하다. A strong first sentence is 당황하지 마 ("Don't panic / Keep your cool"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 당황하다 also becomes 당황하고 싶어 (want), 당황할 수 있어 (can), and 당황 못 해 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 당황해요. Then practice 당황 안 해 vs 당황 못 해, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.
survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.note: Said when someone freezes up or gets caught off guard; 하지 마 is the standard casual 'don't'.

examples.en: They suddenly asked me in English so I totally froze.
examples.note: 완전 ('totally') is the everyday intensifier here; 갑자기 = 'all of a sudden'.

examples.en: My card got declined and I panicked at the checkout.
examples.note: 계산대 = the cashier/checkout counter; ~아서/어서 links cause ('because X, I got flustered').

examples.en: I totally panicked because I called the wrong name.
examples.note: ~아서/어서 당황하다 = panic because of something; everyday slip-up situation.

entries.nuance: 당황하다 = to be momentarily flustered, thrown off, caught off guard — the perfect word for a 'my brain went blank' instant, NOT prolonged panic or dread. The Sino-Korean root is 唐慌: 唐 'abrupt/sudden' + 慌 'flurried, panicked', so it literally paints a sudden flurry of mind. Compare its neighbors: 긴장하다 (緊張) is the nervous tension you feel BEFORE an event (a held breath), while 당황하다 is the scramble in the MOMENT something unexpected hits. 놀라다 is plain 'be startled/surprised'; 당황하다 adds the 'and now I don't know what to do' confusion on top. The big English-speaker pitfall: don't say 당황돼 — unlike 걱정되다 or 긴장되다, 당황하다 already encodes the felt experience and is not normally built with 되다, so use 당황해 / 당황했어. Also keep the adjective 당황스럽다 ('the situation is bewildering') separate from the verb 당황하다 ('I got flustered').
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 당황하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 당황해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 당황돼 / 당황되다 — unlike 걱정되다 or 긴장되다, 당황하다 is not normally paired with 되다; use 당황해 / 당황했어 for the felt reaction.
Spacing the negative as 안 당황해 — because 당황 is a noun + 하다, the natural casual negative is 당황 안 해 (noun + 안 + 해).

lesson.canDo: Use 당황해요 in a real beginner sentence, then change it into want, can, cannot, and have-to forms without losing the basic meaning.
studyFlow: Say 당황해요 first. This is the safest spoken form for most beginner situations.
Add one useful frame: 당황하지 마. Read the Hangul first, then check the romanization.
Practice the contrast between 당황 안 해 and 당황 못 해.
Open one linked pattern and come back to this card to see the same grammar in a verb form.
lesson.teacherNote: Do not ask a beginner to memorize all 15 forms at once. Teach 당황해요 first, then add one communicative need: desire (당황하고 싶어), possibility (당황할 수 있어), or limitation (당황 못 해).
lesson.pronunciationTip: 당황하다 is written danghwanghada. In real sentences, compare the audio with the romanization because Korean sound changes can cross syllable blocks.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 당황해요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 당황하다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 당황하지 마. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 당황 안 해 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 당황 못 해 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 당황해요 feels easy, practice 당황하고 싶어, 당황할 수 있어, and 당황해야 돼. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

classroomScript: Teacher says: 당황해요. Learner repeats three times.
Teacher asks a yes/no question with 당황하지 마. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 당황 안 해, then 당황 못 해.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 당황하다 becomes 당황할 수 있어 ("can") and 당황할 거야 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 당황하다 = to be momentarily flustered, thrown off, caught off guard — the perfect word for a 'my brain went blank' instant, NOT prolonged panic or dread.

Compare its neighbors: 긴장하다 (緊張) is the nervous tension you feel BEFORE an event (a held breath), while 당황하다 is the scramble in the MOMENT something unexpected hits. 놀라다 is plain 'be startled/surprised'; 당황하다 adds the 'and now I don't know what to do' confusion on top.
The Sino-Korean root is 唐慌: 唐 'abrupt/sudden' + 慌 'flurried, panicked', so it literally paints a sudden flurry of mind.

Don't say 당황돼 — unlike 걱정되다 or 긴장되다, 당황하다 already encodes the felt experience and is not normally built with 되다, so use 당황해 / 당황했어. Also keep the adjective 당황스럽다 ('the situation is bewildering') separate from the verb 당황하다 ('I got flustered').

entries.shortExplanation: 질투하다 means "to be jealous" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to be jealous" in Korean is 질투하다 (jiltuhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 질투해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 질투하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 질투하는 거야? ("Are you jealous?") — then reshape the same stem into 질투하고 싶어 (desire), 질투할 수 있어 (ability), and 질투 못 해 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 질투해요. Then practice 질투 안 해 vs 질투 못 해, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

examples.en: My boyfriend has a lot of female friends so I get a bit jealous.
examples.note: 남친 = 남자친구 (boyfriend), 여사친 = 여자 사람 친구 (female friend) — essential dating slang.

examples.ko: 친구가 나보다 잘돼서 질투하는 내가 너무 싫어.
examples.romanization: chinguga naboda jaldwaeseo jiltuhaneun naega neomu sireo.
examples.en: I hate that I'm jealous of my friend doing better than me.
examples.note: 잘되다 = 'to go well / succeed'; 나보다 = 'than me'. Honest self-talk.

examples.ko: 걔 인스타 보면 가끔 질투 나.
examples.romanization: gyae inseuta bomyeon gakkeum jiltu na.
examples.en: When I see their Instagram I sometimes get jealous.
examples.note: 질투(가) 나다 is more natural than 질투하다 for a passing twinge; 걔 = 'that person (casual)'.

entries.nuance: 질투하다 carries a sharp, possessive jealousy — the romantic or competitive sting of 'they have what I want and it bothers me'. The hanja is 嫉妬, where BOTH characters (嫉 and 妬) literally mean envy/jealousy, doubling the intensity. The crucial dividing line for English speakers: English 'jealous' is used loosely for mild envy, but Korean splits it. 부럽다 = harmless, friendly envy ('lucky you, I wish I had that') and is what you say ~90% of the time; saying 부러워 warms a conversation. 질투하다 / 질투 나다 is the bitter, edged version, and accusing a friend of 질투해 can genuinely sting. Also note register: to report the feeling, 질투(가) 나 ('I feel jealous') sounds more natural and less self-incriminating than the bald 질투해. Pitfall: never reach for 질투하다 when you just mean 'how nice for you' — that is 부럽다, full stop.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 질투하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 질투해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 질투하다 where English 'jealous' only means envious — 'You went to Jeju? 부럽다!' not 질투해.
Saying 나는 너를 질투해 to mean light envy of a friend — to an actual friend this sounds accusatory; soften to 너 진짜 부럽다 or 질투 나려 그래.

entries.nuance: 포기하다 = to give up, abandon, or relinquish a goal, plan, claim, or even a person. The hanja 抛棄 is vivid: 抛 'to throw/hurl away' + 棄 'to discard, abandon', so the image is hurling something aside and walking off — a decisive letting-go, not a gentle fade. Contrast 포기하다 (stop pursuing a goal entirely) with 그만두다 (stop/quit an ongoing activity — a job, a habit) and with 단념하다 (a more bookish 'resign oneself to abandoning hope'); in speech 포기하다 is the everyday choice. Grammar: it pairs with 을/를 (목표를 포기하다) or with 는 거 / 는 걸 (사는 걸 포기하다 = 'give up on buying'). Culturally the word is loaded: N포세대, the 'give-up generation', names young Koreans said to have surrendered dating, marriage, and kids to economic pressure. English-speaker pitfall: the negative is 포기 안 해 / 포기 못 해 (noun + 안/못 + 해), NOT 안 포기해.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 포기하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 포기해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spacing the negative wrong — it's 포기 안 해 / 포기 못 해 (noun + 안/못 + 해), not 안 포기해.
Saying 일을 포기했어 to mean 'I quit my job' — for quitting an activity/job use 그만뒀어 (그만두다); 포기하다 is for giving up on a goal or outcome.

entries.nuance: 도전하다 = to take something on, rise to a challenge, brave a new or daunting endeavor — overwhelmingly positive and aspirational (a job change, a new hobby, scary spicy food, a hard exam). The hanja 挑戰 literally means 挑 'provoke, stir up' + 戰 'battle', i.e. 'to pick a fight', and that combative root explains both senses: figuratively you 'do battle' with a goal. Particle pitfall for English speakers: it takes 에, not 을/를 — 마라톤에 도전하다 ('take on the marathon'), 시험에 도전하다. Contrast it with 노력하다 (sustained, grinding effort over time) and 시도하다 (a neutral, often one-off 'attempt'): 도전하다 specifically frames the target as bold or intimidating, with a brave-the-unknown flavor. Note: it does NOT mean confronting a person in an argument — 'to challenge someone' in that sense is 이의를 제기하다 or 도전장을 내밀다, not plain 도전하다. The everyday encouragement is 도전해 봐.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 도전하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 도전해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 을/를 instead of 에 — it's 마라톤에 도전하다 ('take on the marathon'), not 마라톤을 도전하다.
Using 도전하다 to mean 'challenge a claim/person' — to dispute something, say 이의를 제기하다; 도전하다 is for taking on a goal or feat, not arguing back.

entries.shortExplanation: 노력하다 means "to make an effort" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to make an effort" in Korean is 노력하다 (noryeokhada). Grow outward from one concrete line — 노력할게 ("I'll try (my best)") — then reshape the same stem into 노력하고 싶어 (desire), 노력할 수 있어 (ability), and 노력 못 해 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

entries.nuance: 노력하다 = to make an effort, try hard, put sustained work toward a goal. The hanja 努力 spells out the meaning: 努 'to exert oneself, strain' + 力 'strength/power' — literally 'to exert one's strength', a grind-it-out word. Distinguish three look-alikes English flattens into 'try': 노력하다 = ongoing, earnest effort over time; 도전하다 = boldly taking on a fresh challenge; 시도하다 = a neutral one-off attempt. So 'I'll try harder' is 더 노력할게, never 더 도전할게. Its signature frame is ~(으)려고 노력하다 = 'try to (do)', as in 일찍 일어나려고 노력해. Culturally, effort itself is praised in Korea — 노력파 ('the hardworking type') is a compliment, and 노력할게 is a warm, sincere thing to promise. English-speaker pitfall: 노력하다 means putting in effort, not merely 'attempting once'; for 'let me try this button', that's 한번 해 볼게, not 노력할게.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 노력하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 노력해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing with 도전하다: 노력하다 = sustained effort, 도전하다 = taking on a fresh challenge. 'I'll try harder' is 더 노력할게, not 더 도전할게.
Using 노력하다 for a single quick attempt ('let me try clicking this') — that's 한번 해 볼게 / 시도해 볼게; 노력하다 implies repeated, ongoing effort.

entries.nuance: 버티다 = to hold out, hang on, withstand, or scrape through a hard stretch — often financially or under pressure (a brutal job, no money, exam season). The line between them: 견디다 leans toward passively 'enduring/bearing' pain or hardship, while 버티다 adds an active 'dig-in-your-heels and refuse to collapse' stance — holding a position against a force. So young Koreans joke 월급날까지 버틴다 ('surviving till payday') and 일단 버텨 ('just hang in there for now'). entries.nuance: 위로하다 = to comfort or console someone in pain, grief, or loss. The hanja 慰勞 is telling: 慰 'to soothe, console' + 勞 'toil, weariness', i.e. to soothe another's hardship — so the word carries real emotional weight and suits sorrow, bereavement, and exhaustion, not light cheering-up. Using 위로하다 to root for someone before a challenge — that's 응원하다; 위로하다 is for someone already hurting or grieving.

entries.nuance: 응원하다 = to cheer on, root for, and actively support — both literally (yelling for a sports team, 응원단 = a cheering squad) and emotionally (backing a friend's goals). conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 응원하다 becomes 응원할 수 있어 ("can") and 응원할 거야 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 응원하다 = to cheer on, root for, and actively support — both literally (yelling for a sports team, 응원단 = a cheering squad) and emotionally (backing a friend's goals). Telling someone 항상 응원할게 ('I'll always be rooting for you') is one of the warmest, most natural send-offs in Korean.

The key contrast is with 위로하다: 응원하다 looks FORWARD and is upbeat — you cheer someone on toward a challenge or future ('you've got this!') — whereas 위로하다 looks BACK at pain to console it. So 응원해 / 응원할게 is lighter and brighter than 위로해. It often takes the benefactive 응원해 줘 when you ask others for support.
The hanja 應援 says it well: 應 'to respond' + 援 'to aid, rescue', i.e. to answer someone's effort with support.
Don't reach for 응원하다 when someone is grieving or hurting — that calls for 위로하다 (comfort), not a pep-talk cheer.

entries.english: to make sure to eat / eat properly
entries.shortExplanation: 챙겨 먹다 means "to make sure to eat / eat properly" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 챙겨 먹다 (chaenggyeo meokda) = "to make sure to eat / eat properly". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 챙겨 먹어요 plus one useful sentence like 밥 잘 챙겨 먹어. ("Make sure you eat well."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 챙겨 먹고 싶어요 for what you want, 챙겨 먹을 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 챙겨 먹어요 for what you can't. usagePhrases.note: The classic caring sign-off to someone close; 잘 ('well/properly') almost always rides along.

examples.en: I always make sure to eat breakfast.
examples.note: Simplest frame: object + 챙겨 먹어요. 꼭 = 'without fail'.

examples.ko: 혼자 살면 끼니 챙겨 먹기 힘들어요.
examples.romanization: honja salmyeon kkini chaenggyeo meokgi himdeureoyo.
examples.en: When you live alone, it's hard to eat proper meals.
examples.note: ~기 힘들다 = 'it's hard to ~'; 끼니 챙겨 먹기 is the relatable struggle of 자취 (living alone).

examples.ko: 요즘 일이 많아서 밥을 잘 못 챙겨 먹었어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum iri manaseo babeul jal mot chaenggyeo meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: I've been so busy lately I haven't been eating properly.
examples.note: Real-life excuse: 못 goes before the whole phrase (못 챙겨 먹다 = 'fail to manage to eat').

entries.nuance: 챙겨 먹다 is a compound — 챙기다 ('to look after, gather up, pack') in its connective form (챙기 + 어 → 챙겨) plus 먹다 — so it literally means 'look-after-and-eat', i.e. make a point of eating instead of skipping. The dividing line from plain 먹다 is intention: 먹다 just reports that eating happens, while 챙겨 먹다 stresses the care of not missing a meal (끼니, 아침, 약, 영양제 all collocate). Its warmest use is 밥 잘 챙겨 먹어 — a parent's or partner's way of saying 'take care of yourself', far more natural than the stiff textbook 식사를 잘 하세요. Watch the conjugation: it rides on 챙기다 (regular ㅣ-stem), so the 요-form is 챙겨 먹어요, never 챙기어 먹어요. The English-speaker pitfall is using bare 먹다 for the caring nuance — 밥 먹었어? only asks the fact, whereas 밥 잘 챙겨 먹고 있어? carries the affection.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 챙겨 먹다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 챙겨 먹어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying the stiff 식사를 잘 하세요 to show you care — for warmth Koreans say 밥 잘 챙겨 먹어 / 끼니 잘 챙겨 먹어요.
Writing the polite form as 챙기어 먹어요 — 챙기다 is a regular ㅣ-stem, so 챙기 + 어 contracts to 챙겨, giving 챙겨 먹어요.
Misplacing 못 as 챙겨 못 먹어요 — the negation wraps the whole phrase: 못 챙겨 먹어요 ('can't manage to eat properly').

entries.english: to submit/file (an application), to register a request
entries.shortExplanation: 접수하다 means "to submit/file (an application), to register a request" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 접수하다 (jeopsuhada) means "to submit/file (an application), to register a request". Start from the polite form 접수해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 접수하다. A strong first sentence is 서류를 접수하다 ("to file/submit documents"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 접수하다 also becomes 접수하고 싶어요 (want), 접수할 수 있어요 (can), and 접수할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I submit/file (an application), to register a request.

usagePhrases.note: Often used at a counter (창구) — you hand in paperwork and it formally enters the system.

examples.en: Please submit the application form on the first floor.
examples.note: Typical instruction at a 주민센터; 접수해 주세요 is the polite request form.

examples.en: It has to be filed by today for it to be processed.
examples.note: Notice the two-step pair: 접수 (intake) comes first, 처리 (processing) follows.

examples.en: I filed it online but the reference number isn't showing.
examples.note: Real help-desk situation; 접수번호 = the receipt/tracking number you get.

entries.nuance: 접수하다 (接受하다, 接 'receive' + 受 'accept') means to formally lodge something so it enters an official system — an application, complaint, or request. The tricky part is that it works BOTH ways: from your side it is 'submit/file,' but from the staff's side it means 'to receive/accept,' which is why 접수 on a sign marks the intake counter, not the act of submitting. Compare 제출하다 ('to hand in/submit a single document') and 신청하다 ('to apply/request'): 제출하다 just stresses physically turning paper in, 신청하다 stresses the request itself, while 접수하다 stresses the moment it is officially logged. The English-speaker pitfall is choosing the wrong member of the 접- family: 접수하다 (file a request) looks almost identical to 접속하다 (to log in / connect online), so learners type the wrong one constantly.

Use 접수해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse 접수하다 (file/lodge a request) with 접속하다 (to log in / connect online) — same first syllable, unrelated meanings.
Saying 접수했어요 to mean 'they processed/finished it' is wrong; 접수 only means it was received and logged. Use 처리됐어요 for 'it was processed/done.'

entries.shortExplanation: 작성하다 means "to fill out/write up (a form or document)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to fill out/write up (a form or document)" in Korean is 작성하다 (jakseonghada). usagePhrases.note: The default verb for completing any form, contract, or report.

examples.en: Please fill in this box in Korean.
examples.note: 칸 = a single box/field on a form; very common counter instruction.

examples.en: Read it carefully before drawing up the contract.
examples.note: -기 전에 = 'before doing'; 계약서 = contract, key for housing/jobs.

examples.romanization: jiwon donggireul eotteoke jakseonghaeya halji moreugesseoyo.

examples.note: Real job-application worry; 지원 동기 = motivation/cover-letter section.

entries.nuance: 작성하다 (作成하다, 作 'make' + 成 'complete') is the standard, slightly formal verb for filling out or composing a structured document — forms, contracts, reports, official emails. The sharp contrast is with 쓰다 ('to write'): 쓰다 is the broad physical act of writing anything (a love letter, a quick note, a single word), whereas 작성하다 implies there is a template, format, or official purpose you are completing. So '편지를 쓰다' (write a letter) is natural but '편지를 작성하다' sounds stiffly bureaucratic, while '보고서를 작성하다' (write up a report) is exactly right. It collocates with 신청서, 계약서, 보고서, 이력서, 양식. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 쓰다 everywhere because English 'write' covers both — at offices and work you should default to 작성하다 the moment a form or formal document is involved.

Use 작성해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
For a quick handwritten note use 쓰다; '메모를 작성하다' sounds overly stiff for something casual.
Don't say '작성하다' for creative writing like a poem or diary — that's 쓰다. 작성하다 needs a structured/official document.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 작성하다 becomes 작성할 수 있어요 ("can") and 작성할 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: 작성하다 is the standard, slightly formal verb for filling out or composing a structured document — forms, contracts, reports, official emails. It collocates with 신청서, 계약서, 보고서, 이력서, 양식.
作成하다: 作 'make' + 成 'complete'.

The sharp contrast is with 쓰다 ('to write'): 쓰다 is the broad physical act of writing anything (a love letter, a quick note, a single word), whereas 작성하다 implies there is a template, format, or official purpose you are completing. So '편지를 쓰다' (write a letter) is natural but '편지를 작성하다' sounds stiffly bureaucratic, while '보고서를 작성하다' (write up a report) is exactly right.

entries.shortExplanation: 발급받다 means "to be issued / to get issued (a document or card)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 발급받다 (balgeupbatda) = "to be issued / to get issued (a document or card)". entries.nuance: 발급받다 (發給받다: 發 'issue out' + 給 'give,' plus native 받다 'to receive') is a compound that bakes the direction into the verb — it is specifically YOU receiving an officially issued document. For residents it is everywhere: ID cards, bank cards, certificates, visas, even certificates of employment. Near-synonyms: 받다 alone just means 'receive' (too generic for officialdom), and 떼다 is a casual colloquial verb Koreans use for pulling a certificate ('등본 한 통 떼다'). The English-speaker pitfall is dropping 받다 and saying 발급하다 about yourself; in English 'I issued my card' is impossible anyway, and Korean is equally strict — you 발급받다.

Use 발급받아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't say 발급하다 about yourself — that's what the issuing office does. You 발급받다 (receive issuance).
Don't mix up the prefixes: 재발급 = reissue (lost item), but 발급 alone = first-time issue. Saying 재발급 for a brand-new card is wrong.

entries.shortExplanation: 등록하다 means "to register / to enroll" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 등록하다 (deungnokhada) means "to register / to enroll". Start from the polite form 등록해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 등록하다. A strong first sentence is 회원으로 등록하다 ("to register as a member"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 등록하다 also becomes 등록하고 싶어요 (want), 등록할 수 있어요 (can), and 등록할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 등록해요. Then practice 등록 안 해요 vs 등록할 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

usagePhrases.note: Note 으로 ('as'): you register in the capacity of a member.

examples.note: -아야 …할 수 있어요 = 'only if you do, you can'; biometric access.

examples.ko: 수강 신청은 다음 주에 등록하면 돼요.
examples.romanization: sugang sincheongeun daeum jue deungnokamyeon dwaeyo.

examples.note: -(으)면 돼요 = 'it's enough to / you just need to'; 수강 신청 = course sign-up.

examples.note: Data-into-a-system sense; 에 marks where it's registered.

entries.nuance: 등록하다 (登錄하다, 登 'enter/ascend' + 錄 'record') literally means 'to enter onto the record/register,' which is exactly its feel: putting a person, class, device, or data point onto an official list. The key contrast is with 가입하다 ('to join a service/club/insurance'): 가입하다 is about BECOMING A MEMBER of a body, while 등록하다 is about RECORDING something into a system — and they even take different particles (보험에 가입하다 vs. 시스템에 등록하다 / 회원으로 등록하다). Also distinguish 신청하다 ('apply/request'), which is the asking step before you are actually 등록된 (registered). The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'register' and 'sign up' feel interchangeable, so learners say 등록하다 for subscribing to a streaming service where Koreans would say 가입하다. If the result is a membership, prefer 가입하다; if the result is your data on a list, use 등록하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 등록하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 등록해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
등록하다 vs 가입하다: 가입하다 is joining a service/club/insurance; 등록하다 is recording data or enrolling. Don't use 등록하다 for 'subscribe to a service.'
Watch the particle: 'register AS a member' is 회원으로 등록하다, not 회원을 등록하다.

entries.explanation: "to extend / to renew (a period)" in Korean is 연장하다 (yeonjanghada). The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

examples.en: I have to go to immigration to extend my period of stay.
examples.note: -(으)러 가다 = 'go in order to'; 체류 기간 = period of stay.

examples.ko: 도서관 책 대출을 한 번 더 연장할 수 있어요.

examples.note: 대출 = loan/borrowing; 한 번 더 = one more time.

examples.romanization: magameul iteulman yeonjanghae jusimyeon an doelkkayo?

examples.note: -주시면 안 될까요? = very soft, deferential workplace request.

entries.nuance: 연장하다 (延長하다, 延 'prolong' + 長 'long') means to make an existing time span longer — a visa, contract, loan, deadline, or operating hours. The crucial near-synonym is 갱신하다 (更新하다, 'renew/update'): 연장하다 stresses simply ADDING MORE TIME to the same arrangement, whereas 갱신하다 stresses ISSUING A FRESH TERM/version (you 갱신하다 a driver's license or passport, getting a new document). For visas you'll genuinely hear both, but everyday spoken Korean leans on 연장하다. Don't confuse it with 연기하다 ('to postpone/delay'), which moves an event to a later date rather than lengthening a period — '회의를 연기하다' (delay the meeting) ≠ '회의 시간을 연장하다' (run the meeting longer). The English-speaker pitfall: English 'extend' and 'renew' blur together, and the look-alike 연락 (contact) trips people up, so pick 연장 for 'more time,' 갱신 for 'new term.'

Use 연장해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse 연장 (extend a duration) with 연락 (contact) — similar shape, different word.
연장하다 (lengthen a period) is not 연기하다 (postpone an event). To push a meeting to next week, use 연기하다, not 연장하다.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 연장하다 becomes 연장할 수 있어요 ("can") and 연장할 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: 연장하다 means to make an existing time span longer — a visa, contract, loan, deadline, or operating hours.
延長하다: 延 'prolong' + 長 'long.'

The crucial near-synonym is 갱신하다 ('renew/update'): 연장하다 stresses simply ADDING MORE TIME to the same arrangement, whereas 갱신하다 stresses ISSUING A FRESH TERM/version (you 갱신하다 a driver's license or passport, getting a new document). English 'extend' and 'renew' blur together, and the look-alike 연락 (contact) trips people up, so pick 연장 for 'more time,' 갱신 for 'new term.'

entries.nuance: 납부하다 (納付하다, 納 'pay in/deliver' + 付 'hand over') is the formal verb for paying money OWED TO AN INSTITUTION — taxes, public utilities, insurance premiums, fines, tuition. entries.shortExplanation: 처리하다 means "to process / to handle / to deal with" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 처리하다 (cheorihada) means "to process / to handle / to deal with". Start from the polite form 처리해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 처리하다. examples.note: Passive 처리되다 in official notices; pairs with 접수되다.

examples.note: 불만 = complaint; -아야 해요 = obligation.

entries.nuance: 처리하다 (處理하다, 處 'manage/place' + 理 'put in order') is a workhorse meaning to process, handle, or take care of a task, request, or problem, and the passive 처리되다 ('be processed') saturates official status messages. The register is neutral-professional, ideal for office work and paperwork. Watch three near-neighbors: 해결하다 ('to solve/resolve') implies fully fixing a problem so it's gone, whereas 처리하다 can just mean 'deal with / move it along the pipeline' without a happy ending; 다루다 means 'to handle/treat' in the sense of how you manage a topic or object; and bare 하다 ('do') cannot stand in for 'take care of a matter.' The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that bare-하다 trap: 'I'll do this issue' translated literally as '이 문제를 할게요' is wrong — you must say 처리할게요. Reach for 처리하다 whenever English would say 'handle,' 'take care of,' or 'process.'

Use 처리해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Learners overuse 하다 alone; '이 문제를 할게요' is wrong. Use 처리하다 to mean 'handle/take care of' a matter.
처리하다 (deal with/move along) isn't always 해결하다 (fully solve). If the issue is actually resolved, say 해결됐어요, not just 처리됐어요.

entries.explanation: "to inquire / to ask (formally)" in Korean is 문의하다 (munuihada). examples.en: I inquired with immigration about visa matters.

entries.nuance: 문의하다 (問議하다, 問 'ask' + 議 'discuss/consult') is the formal, polite verb for making an inquiry to a business or institution — by phone, email, or in person — and it appears on every company's contact page. The sharp contrast is with 물어보다 ('to ask'), the everyday native verb you use with friends, classmates, or a stranger on the street; 물어보다 between you and a company sounds too casual, while 문의하다 between two friends sounds absurdly stiff, like saying 'I should like to make an inquiry' to your roommate. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'ask' is one word for every register, so learners either over-formalize among friends or under-formalize toward institutions; match 문의하다 to organizations and 물어보다 to people.

entries.nuance: 서명하다 (署名하다, 署 'sign/inscribe' + 名 'name') means to write your name on a document as a signature, and the surface you sign takes 에 (계약서에 서명하다). Two contrasts are essential. entries.nuance: 출력하다 (出力하다, 出 'come out' + 力 'force/power') literally means 'output,' and in computing it broadly opposes 입력하다 (入力, 'input/type in'). In daily admin and office life, however, it almost always means specifically 'to print out' from a computer, and that is how you'll see it on kiosks and printer menus. The register contrast is with 프린트하다, the casual English-loan equivalent people say in conversation ('이거 프린트해 줘'); 출력하다 is the cleaner, more formal/technical choice for instructions and signage. The English-speaker pitfall is the in/out pair: 출력 (out) and 입력 (in) share the 력 base and look similar, so beginners mix up 'print/output' with 'type/input' — anchor it with 출 = 'exit/out,' the same 출 as in 출구 (exit).

entries.nuance: 다치다 is the everyday verb for getting physically injured — bumps, cuts, sprains, breaks — and crucially the injured body part takes 을/를, not 이/가 (무릎을 다쳤어요, not 무릎이). Although it translates as 'to hurt', it behaves like an intransitive 'to GET hurt' aimed at yourself, so you cannot use it to mean 'I hurt someone else' — that is 다치게 하다 or 상처를 입히다. The nearest neighbor is 아프다, and the dividing line matters: 다치다 is the one-time event of getting injured (넘어져서 다쳤어요), while 아프다 is the lingering pain or sickness that follows (지금도 아파요). It pairs habitually with 크게 다치다 (badly hurt), 살짝/조금 다치다 (slightly hurt), and 다친 데 (the injured spot). At a hospital, 다치다 plus the exact body part (발목, 허리, 손목) gets you to the right department fast.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 다치다 as a complete polite sentence.

Using 아프다 when you mean an injury — 아프다 is 'it hurts / I'm sick' (a state), but 다치다 is the act of getting injured (an event). Say '넘어져서 다쳤어요' for the injury, then '지금도 아파요' for the pain that remains.
Marking the body part with 이/가 — it's 무릎을 다쳤어요 (object 을), not 무릎이 다쳤어요. The body part is what you injure, so it takes 을/를.
Trying to say 'I hurt my friend' with 다치다 — 친구를 다쳤어요 is wrong because 다치다 is about getting hurt yourself. Use 친구를 다치게 했어요 ('I caused my friend to get hurt').

entries.shortExplanation: 낫다 means "to heal / to get better" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to heal / to get better" in Korean is 낫다 (natda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 나아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 낫다 for study notes. usagePhrases.en: I do not heal / to get better.
I want to heal / to get better.
I can heal / to get better.
I have to heal / to get better.

usagePhrases.note: THE phrase to send a sick coworker or friend; the honorific 나으세요 is warmer and more polite than 빨리 나아요.

examples.en: My cold got better.
examples.note: Core pattern: the illness is the SUBJECT (감기가) — you don't heal something, the sickness heals on its own.

examples.en: I took the medicine and the cold got better quickly.
examples.note: ㅅ-irregular in action: 낫 + 았어요 → 나았어요 (the ㅅ drops). 금방 = 'in no time'. Don't write 낳았어요 (gave birth).

examples.ko: 푹 쉬면 곧 나을 거예요, 너무 무리하지 마세요.
examples.romanization: puk swimyeon gon naeul geoyeyo, neomu murihaji maseyo.
examples.en: If you rest well you'll soon get better, so don't overdo it.
examples.note: 푹 쉬다 = 'to rest fully'; the classic comforting send-off pairing 나을 거예요 with 무리하지 마세요.

entries.nuance: 낫다 means an illness or wound heals, and it is a ㅅ-irregular verb: the ㅅ disappears before a vowel (나아요, 나았어요, 나을, 나으세요) but stays before a consonant (낫습니다, 낫고, 낫지). It is intransitive — the cold or the cut is the subject (감기가 나았어요, 상처가 나았어요) — so you never 'heal something' with it; for that you'd use 치료하다 (to treat) or 고치다 (to cure/fix). The big trap for everyone, native and learner alike, is the homophone cluster: 낫다 'heal', 낳다 'give birth', and 났다 (from 나다, 'broke out/occurred') all sound like [낟따] but mean totally different things, so 나았어요 (got better) must never be spelled 낳았어요 (gave birth). Note 낫다 also has a second meaning, 'to be better/preferable' (이게 더 나아요 = this one's better), which shares the exact same conjugation. It collocates with 빨리/금방/곧 낫다 (heal fast/soon) and 다 낫다 (fully heal).

Use 나아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

Keeping the ㅅ before a vowel — it's 나아요/나았어요/나을, NOT 낫아요/낫았어요. The ㅅ only survives before consonants (낫습니다, 낫고).
Making it transitive like English 'heal it' — 감기를 나았어요 is wrong; the illness is the subject, so it's 감기가 나았어요. To 'cure' something actively, use 치료하다 or 고치다.
notes: ㅅ: memorize 나아 and 나아요 together.

entries.nuance: 긁다 is the physical act of scratching with fingernails or an object, and the itchy spot or body part takes 을/를 (등을 긁다). Its inseparable partner is the adjective 가렵다 ('to be itchy'): 가려워서 긁어요 ('it itches so I scratch') is the default chain, and the key learner distinction is exactly this — 가렵다 is the SENSATION (a descriptive adjective, 'it itches'), while 긁다 is the ACTION you take in response (a verb, 'I scratch'). Don't confuse 긁다 with the look-alike 긋다 ('to draw a line / strike a match'), a different verb entirely. Beyond skin, 긁다 has lively idioms: 복권을 긁다 (scratch a lottery ticket), 카드를 긁다 (swipe/charge a card), and 신경을 긁다 ('to get on someone's nerves', literally 'scratch the nerves'). In a medical context the negative command 긁지 마세요 ('don't scratch') is what you'll hear most.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 긁다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 긁어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

Saying 가려워요 to mean 'I scratch' — 가렵다 is an adjective ('it's itchy'), so it cannot describe the action. Use 긁다 for scratching: 손으로 긁어요.
Confusing 긁다 with 긋다 ('to draw a line') because they look similar — they are unrelated verbs. Scratching an itch is always 긁다.

entries.explanation: "to shiver / to tremble" in Korean is 떨다 (tteolda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 떨어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 떨다 for study notes. Compare with neighbors: 흔들리다 is 'to sway/wobble' (a tree, a building), while 떨다/떨리다 is fine, fast trembling of the body. To sound native, glue on mimetic adverbs — 덜덜 (hard, cold/fear shiver) and 으슬으슬 (the chilly shiver of an oncoming fever). Note the unrelated idiom 엄살 떨다 / 수선 떨다, where 떨다 means 'to make a fuss'.

usagePhrases.en: I dozed off during the meeting
usagePhrases.note: A relatable confession; 회의 중에 = 'in the middle of the meeting', the prototypical wrong place to nod off.

examples.en: I dozed off in class.
examples.note: Basic frame; 졸다 is intransitive and usually pinned to a place/time you shouldn't sleep (수업 시간에 = during class).

examples.ko: 점심 먹고 나서 자꾸 졸려서 결국 졸았어요.
examples.romanization: jeomsim meokgo naseo jakku jollyeoseo gyeolguk jorasseoyo.
examples.en: After lunch I kept getting sleepy and ended up dozing off.
examples.note: Shows the pair clearly: 졸리다 = 'to feel sleepy' (feeling) leads to 졸다 = 'to nod off' (act); 결국 = 'in the end'.

examples.ko: 지하철에서 깜빡 졸다가 내릴 역을 지나쳤어요.
examples.romanization: jihacheoreseo kkamppak joldaga naeril yeogeul jinachyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I dozed off for a moment on the subway and missed the stop I was supposed to get off at.
examples.note: Quintessential Seoul-commuter story; V-다가 = mid-action interruption, 지나치다 = to pass by/overshoot.

entries.nuance: 졸다 means to nod off or drift into a light doze — typically somewhere you're not supposed to, like a meeting, class, or the subway — and it is a ㄹ-stem verb, so the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ: formal 좁니다 (not 졸습니다). The crucial learner distinction is between 졸다 and 졸리다: 졸리다 is the adjective-like state 'to feel sleepy' (졸려요 = 'I'm drowsy', the sensation), whereas 졸다 is the verb for actually drifting off (졸았어요 = 'I nodded off', the act). It's also distinct from 자다 ('to sleep' properly, lying down for real) — 졸다 is brief, upright, involuntary micro-sleep, while 자다 is full intentional sleep. There's no Sino-Korean root; it's native Korean. It collocates with 깜빡 졸다 (doze off for a second) and feeds the compound noun 졸음 ('drowsiness'), which builds 졸음운전 (drowsy driving), plastered on every Korean highway warning sign.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 졸다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 졸아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 졸려요 when you mean you actually nodded off — 졸리다 is the feeling 'I'm sleepy', but the act of dozing off is 졸다 (졸았어요). Don't report the nap with the sensation word.
Using 자다 for nodding off in a meeting — 자다 is real, intentional sleep lying down; the brief involuntary head-bob is 졸다. '회의 중에 잤어요' sounds like you full-on slept on purpose.
Forgetting the ㄹ drops in the formal form — it's 좁니다, not 졸습니다. ㄹ-stems lose the ㄹ before the ㅂ of -ㅂ니다.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 졸아 and 졸아요 together.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 졸아요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 졸다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 회의 중에 졸았어요. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 안 졸아요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 졸 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 졸아요 feels easy, practice 졸고 싶어요, 졸 수 있어요, and 졸아야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

classroomScript: Teacher says: 졸아요. Learner repeats three times.
Teacher asks a yes/no question with 회의 중에 졸았어요. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 안 졸아요, then 졸 수 없어요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 졸다 becomes 졸 수 있어요 ("can") and 졸 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.body: 졸다 has an irregular stem (ㄹ). Memorize its polite form 졸아요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

entries.shortExplanation: 토하다 means "to vomit" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 토하다 (tohada) means "to vomit". Start from the polite form 토해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 토하다. A strong first sentence is 토할 것 같아요 ("I feel like I'm going to throw up"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 토하다 also becomes 토하고 싶어요 (want), 토할 수 있어요 (can), and 토할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: A crucial phrase for food poisoning, a hangover, or motion sickness; V-(으)ㄹ 것 같다 hedges 'I feel like I might'.

examples.en: I think I'm going to throw up.
examples.note: The bare warning you give while it's still coming on; learn this one cold for emergencies.

examples.en: I got carsick on the bus and almost threw up.
examples.note: 차멀미 = motion/car sickness; V-(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 = 'almost did (but didn't)', a very common near-miss pattern.

examples.ko: 상한 걸 먹었는지 어젯밤부터 계속 토하고 설사도 해요.
examples.romanization: sanghan geol meogeonneunji eojetbambuteo gyesok tohago seolsado haeyo.
examples.en: I think I ate something spoiled — since last night I keep vomiting and have diarrhea too.
examples.note: Full food-poisoning report; 상하다 = to go bad, -았는지 = 'whether/maybe', 설사하다 = to have diarrhea. Clinic-ready.

entries.nuance: 토하다 is the direct, neutral verb for vomiting (Sino-Korean 吐 'spit out/vomit' + 하다, so literally 'to do a 吐'), and it's perfectly fine to use at a clinic or pharmacy. While it's already on the way up, you hedge with 토할 것 같아요 ('I feel like I might throw up'). Mind the register and the synonyms: the everyday softer alternative is 게우다, and for mere nausea where nothing has come out yet, Koreans say 속이 안 좋다 ('my stomach is off') or 메스껍다 / 메슥거리다 ('to feel queasy') — these describe the queasy sensation, not the act, so don't say 토해요 unless you actually vomited. (There's also the very blunt slang 게워내다/'우웩'; 토하다 itself is the safe standard.) For a doctor, pairing 토하다 with 설사하다 (diarrhea) and 열이 나다 (fever) paints the classic 식중독 (food poisoning) picture. Note the object marker: what you throw up takes 을/를 (먹은 걸 다 토했어요).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 토하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 토해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Overusing 토하다 for mild nausea — if you only feel queasy but haven't actually vomited, say 속이 안 좋아요 or 메스꺼워요, not 토해요. 토하다 means the vomiting actually happened.
Saying 토하고 싶어요 to mean 'I feel nauseous' — that literally means 'I want to vomit' (a desire), which sounds odd. Use 토할 것 같아요 ('I feel like I'm going to') for the urge.
Forgetting 토하다 is built on 하다 — the negative is 안 토해요 / 토하지 않아요 and the past is 토했어요, conjugating like every other 하다 verb (해요 → 토해요).

entries.english: to be sick with / to suffer from
entries.shortExplanation: 앓다 means "to be sick with / to suffer from" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to be sick with / to suffer from" in Korean is 앓다 (alta). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 앓아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 앓다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 며칠 동안 감기를 앓았어요 ("I was down with a cold for a few days") — then reshape the same stem into 앓고 싶어요 (desire), 앓을 수 있어요 (ability), and 앓을 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 앓아요. Then practice 안 앓아요 vs 앓을 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

usagePhrases.en: I be sick with / to suffer from.
I do not be sick with / to suffer from.
I want to be sick with / to suffer from.
I can be sick with / to suffer from.
I have to be sick with / to suffer from.
I was down with a cold for a few days
usagePhrases.note: 앓다 takes the illness as object (감기를); it sounds heavier and more drawn-out than just 아팠어요.

examples.en: I was sick with a cold.
examples.note: Core pattern: the illness is the OBJECT (감기를 앓다), unlike 아프다 which never takes an illness as object.

examples.ko: 독감을 심하게 앓아서 일주일 동안 회사를 못 갔어요.
examples.romanization: dokgameul simhage araseo iljuil dongan hoesareul mot gasseoyo.
examples.en: I had a bad case of the flu and couldn't go to work for a week.
examples.note: 독감 = influenza (worse than 감기); 심하게 = severely. The -아서 chains the heavy illness to its consequence.

examples.ko: 할머니께서는 오래 병을 앓으셨지만 끝까지 의연하셨어요.
examples.romanization: halmeonikkeseoneun orae byeongeul areusyeotjiman kkeutkkaji uiyeonhasyeosseoyo.
examples.en: My grandmother suffered from an illness for a long time but stayed composed to the end.
examples.note: Honorific -(으)시- for an elder (앓으셨다); 병을 앓다 = to suffer from a disease, a respectful, literary register.

entries.nuance: 앓다 means to be laid low by, or suffer through, an illness over a stretch of time, and the defining grammar point is that it takes the sickness as a DIRECT OBJECT — 감기를 앓다, 독감을 앓다, 병을 앓다 — which is exactly where it parts ways with 아프다. The contrast is sharp: 아프다 is an adjective that just states something hurts or you're unwell (머리가 아파요, 몸이 아파요), whereas 앓다 is a verb meaning you actively 'go through' a named illness for a period. 앓다 also carries a heavier, more drawn-out, somewhat literary tone, so it readily extends to chronic disease and even emotional pain (마음의 병을 앓다 = 'to suffer a sickness of the heart'). The reduplicated 끙끙 앓다 paints someone groaning or quietly agonizing — over illness OR worries. Register-wise, in casual daily speech people far more often say 아팠어요; 앓다 sounds a notch more serious. It's native Korean (no hanja root). Note the modern slang 앓다 → '앓는 소리(를) 하다' meaning to whine/complain.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 앓다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 앓아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using the subject marker like 아프다 does — it's 감기를 앓다 (object 를), not 감기가 앓다. The illness is what you 'suffer through', so it takes 을/를.
Reaching for 앓다 in light, casual talk — for an everyday 'I felt sick / I was unwell', 아팠어요 is far more natural. 앓다 sounds heavy and literary, fitting flu, chronic disease, or written notes.
Trying to make 앓다 mean a single spot hurting — you can't say 머리를 앓아요 for 'my head hurts'; that's 머리가 아파요. 앓다 is for going through a whole illness (병을 앓다), not localized pain.

entries.shortExplanation: 회복하다 means "to recover" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 회복하다 (hoebokhada) = "to recover". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 회복해요 plus one useful sentence like 건강을 회복했어요 ("I've recovered my health"). entries.nuance: 삼키다 is the verb for swallowing — food, drink, pills, or saliva — and what goes down takes 을/를 (약을 삼키다, 침을 삼키다). It's genuinely practical at a pharmacy or clinic: 약을 삼키기 힘들어요 ('hard to swallow pills') or 침 삼킬 때 목이 아파요 ('it hurts when I swallow') pinpoint throat problems precisely. The crucial sequence partner is 씹다 ('to chew'): you 씹다 first, then 삼키다 — '씹어서 삼켜요' puts them in order — so don't use one for the other. Distinguish it also from 마시다 ('to drink/gulp a liquid continuously'); 삼키다 is the single act of sending something down the throat. It's a native Korean word (no hanja). Figuratively, 삼키다 is rich and very common: 눈물을 삼키다 (swallow one's tears), 화를 삼키다 (swallow one's anger), 비명을 삼키다 (stifle a scream) — all meaning to hold an emotion back. Safety warnings use it too: 통째로 삼키지 마세요 ('don't swallow it whole').
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 삼키다 as a complete polite sentence.

Using 마시다 for swallowing a pill — 마시다 is 'to drink' a liquid; sending a tablet down is 약을 삼키다. Say 약을 물이랑 같이 삼켜요, not 약을 마셔요.

entries.explanation: "to break down / to malfunction" in Korean is 고장나다 (gojangnada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 고장나요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 고장나다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 보일러가 고장났어요 ("The boiler broke down") — then reshape the same stem into 고장나고 싶다 (desire), 고장날 수 있어요 (ability), and 고장날 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

entries.nuance: 고장나다 is built from the Sino-Korean noun 고장 (故障, 'breakdown/fault') plus native 나다 ('to occur'), so it literally means 'a fault arises' — which is why it is intransitive: the machine breaks on its own and takes 이/가, never 을/를 (보일러가 고장났어요, not 보일러를). Use it for things with a mechanism — appliances, electronics, cars, elevators — not for soft objects that simply tear or wear out (옷이 찢어지다, 신발이 닳다). The near-synonym 망가지다 is broader and casual ('get wrecked/ruined') and can cover a smashed toy or a crumpled box, whereas 고장나다 specifically implies the function stopped working. The English-speaker trap: English lets a person 'break' something, but you cannot make 고장나다 transitive — to say a PERSON broke it, switch to 고장 내다 or 망가뜨리다 (동생이 리모컨을 고장 냈어요).

Using 고장나다 for a person breaking something on purpose — 'I broke the door' is 문을 고장 냈어요 or 문을 부쉈어요, since 고장나다 cannot take a doer.
Stretching it to torn clothes or a ripped bag — those are 찢어지다, not 고장나다, which needs a working mechanism to fail.

After that the endings carry the meaning — 수리하고 싶어요 for what you want, 수리할 수 있어요 for what you can, 수리할 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests.

entries.nuance: 수리하다 comes from 수리 (修理, 'mend-manage') and is the formal, on-the-invoice word for repair — you see it on signs, receipts, and in 수리비 (repair cost) and 수리 기사 (repair technician). Its everyday near-synonym 고치다 is native Korean and warmer: a friend 고쳐 줄게 ('I'll fix it for you'), but a service center 수리합니다. The dividing line is register and scale: 고치다 covers a quick DIY tweak or even fixing a habit (버릇을 고치다), while 수리하다 implies a professional working on machinery, a car, or a building, and it stays strictly physical. The English-speaker trap: 'fix' in English also means to fix a plan, a date, or a relationship — none of those take 수리하다. A relationship or a problem is 관계를 회복하다 / 문제를 해결하다, and setting a date is 날짜를 정하다, so reserve 수리하다 for objects that physically broke.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 수리하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 수리해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 수리하다 for fixing a relationship, a habit, or a plan — that is 해결하다/회복하다/고치다; 수리하다 only applies to physical objects and equipment.
Treating it as intransitive like 고장나다 — you must say 무엇을 수리하다 (보일러를 수리해요); the broken thing is the object you act on, so it takes 을/를.
Saying just 수리해 to a stranger technician — add 주세요 (수리해 주세요); the bare 해 form is reserved for close, casual relationships.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 수리해 주세요. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 수리하지 않다 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 수리할 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 수리해요 feels easy, practice 수리하고 싶어요, 수리할 수 있어요, and 수리해야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will

entries.explanation: 설치하다 (seolchihada) means "to install / to set up". Start from the polite form 설치해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 설치하다. A strong first sentence is 설치해 주세요 ("Please install it"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 설치하다 also becomes 설치하고 싶어요 (want), 설치할 수 있어요 (can), and 설치할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 설치하다 is from 설치 (設置, 'set up-place') and means putting equipment in and making it ready to run — air conditioners, shelves, a washing machine, CCTV — as well as installing software and apps. The dividing line against the plain native verb 놓다 ('put/place') is readiness: 놓다 just sets an object somewhere, while 설치하다 implies mounting, wiring, or configuring it into working order. Watch the sibling word 설정하다 (設定, 'configure'): you 설치 the app or the router first, then 설정 the options inside it — English 'set up' blurs these two, but Korean keeps them apart. The other English-speaker trap is 'uninstall': there is no 설치 취소; Koreans say 삭제하다 ('delete') or 지우다 for software and 철거하다/떼다 for physically removing fixtures, so don't try to negate 설치하다 to undo it.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 설치하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 설치해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 설치하다 (install) with 설정하다 (configure settings) — you 설치 the app, then 설정 the options; using one for the other reverses the order of the task.
Inventing 설치 취소 for 'uninstall' — that is not used; say 삭제하다/지우다 for apps or 철거하다 for physical fixtures.
Using 놓다 when you mean a real installation — 에어컨을 놓다 sounds like you just set the unit on the floor, not that it was mounted and wired to work.

entries.shortExplanation: 정리하다 means "to tidy up / to organize" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to tidy up / to organize" in Korean is 정리하다 (jeongnihada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 정리해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 정리하다 for study notes. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

entries.nuance: 정리하다 is from 정리 (整理, 'arrange-manage') and means putting things into order so a space (or even a thought) looks settled and neat. Compare three neighbors learners blur: 치우다 emphasizes clearing things AWAY/out of sight, 청소하다 (淸掃) is removing dirt by sweeping/wiping/vacuuming, and 정리하다 is arranging what stays into proper order. So you can have a 정리된 (well-arranged) desk that is still dusty, because 정리 is about order, not cleanliness. A real strength of 정리하다 is that it also takes abstract objects: 생각을 정리하다 (collect your thoughts), 일정을 정리하다 (sort out a schedule), 관계를 정리하다 (end/wrap up a relationship). The English-speaker trap is mapping 'clean up' straight onto 정리하다 — if you mean wiping grime or mopping, that is 청소하다/닦다, not 정리하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 정리하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 정리해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 정리하다 when you mean removing dirt — wiping or mopping grime is 청소하다 or 닦다; 정리하다 is about arranging, not cleaning surfaces.
Confusing it with 치우다 — 정리하다 puts things in order in place, while 치우다 clears them away; '치워!' (get it out of here) is harsher than '정리해'.
Assuming it is physical-only — 정리하다 also covers 생각/일정/관계, so 'I need to sort out my schedule' is 일정을 정리해야 돼요, not a cleaning verb.

entries.nuance: 잠그다 follows the ㅡ (으-탈락) irregular: the stem vowel 으 disappears before an 아/어 ending, and because the remaining stem vowel ㅏ is 'bright', it joins with 아 — so 잠그 + 아 → 잠가요 and 잠그 + 았 → 잠갔어요 (the 요-form is your anchor: hear 잠가요 and the past, negative, and request forms all fall out). Beyond doors and padlocks it is the standard verb for shutting off water taps and gas valves (수도/가스를 잠그다), which English splits into 'lock' vs 'turn off' but Korean unifies under one image of sealing something closed. Its opposites split too: 열다 (open a door) versus 풀다 (unlock/undo a lock or release). The English-speaker trap is the conjugation: learners regularize it to 잠궈요/잠궜어요, but those are non-standard — the 으 simply drops and ㅏ stays.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 잠그다 as a complete polite sentence.

Writing 잠궈요/잠궜어요 — the correct forms are 잠가요/잠갔어요, because after the 으 drops the stem keeps ㅏ and takes the 아 ending, not 워.
Using 끄다 (switch off a device) for a water tap — a faucet or gas valve is 잠그다, while 끄다 is for lights, TVs, and powered machines.
Saying 문을 닫다 when you mean lock — 닫다 only shuts the door; to actually engage the lock you need 잠그다.

entries.nuance: 새다 is intransitive — the liquid, gas, or light is the subject that escapes, so it always takes 이/가 (물이 새다, 가스가 새다, 불빛이 새다), never 을/를; nothing is leaking on purpose. Phonologically the stem vowel ㅐ does not add an extra vowel, it just fuses with the ending: 새 + 었 → 샜어요, 새 + 어요 → 새요. Be careful of the homophone 새다 meaning 'to stay up all night' (밤을 새다 / 밤새다) — that one takes the object 밤, while the leak sense never does, so the particle tells them apart. Compare 흐르다 ('to flow'), which describes liquid moving along a path normally (강물이 흐르다); 새다 specifically means escaping out through a crack, seam, or hole where it should not. The English-speaker trap is treating 'leak' as something you do to an object — in Korean the leaking substance is the grammatical subject.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 새다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 새요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 물을 새요 — leaks take 이/가 (물이 새요), never 을/를, because the leaking water is the subject, not a thing being acted on.
Mixing it up with 흘리다 ('spill/let flow') — you 흘리다 something on purpose or by accident, but a pipe 새다 on its own; 'the pipe is leaking' is 파이프에서 물이 새요.
Confusing the homophone — 밤을 새다 means staying up all night; a leak never takes 밤 or any object, so keep the particle 이/가.

entries.nuance: 널다 is a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ-탈락) verb: the final ㄹ drops before endings beginning with ㄴ, ㅂ, or ㅅ, giving 넙니다 (formal), 너세요 (honorific request), and 너는 빨래 (the laundry being hung) — but it stays before vowel endings, so 너 + 어요 keeps it as 널어요. Its meaning is narrow and physical: spreading out WET laundry on a line, rack, or rail so it air-dries; the partner verb for taking the dry wash back down is 걷다 (빨래를 걷다). Don't confuse it with 말리다 ('to dry something'), which names the result/cause of drying (머리를 말리다 = dry your hair), or with 매달다 ('to hang up by suspending', like a picture or a sign) — 널다 implies laying cloth over something to dry, not hanging an object as decoration. The English-speaker trap is keeping the ㄹ in the formal/honorific forms by analogy with regular verbs.

Using 널다 to hang a picture or coat — that is 걸다 (그림을 걸다, 옷을 걸다); 널다 is specifically spreading wet laundry out to dry.
Mixing it with 말리다 — 말리다 is 'to dry (something)'; you 널어서 말리다, hang it out so that it dries, so the two verbs are not interchangeable.

entries.explanation: 데우다 (deuda) = "to heat up / to warm up (food)". entries.nuance: 데우다 is the transitive 'warm something up' verb, used above all for food and drinks that are already cooked but went cold — leftover rice, soup, milk, a packed meal. Keep three look-alikes apart: 데우다 is the ACTION of heating, 따뜻하다 is an adjective for the resulting STATE ('it's warm'), and 덥다 is an adjective for the weather or your body feeling hot — so '국이 따뜻해요' (the soup is warm) is the result of '국을 데웠어요' (I heated the soup). For raising the food's heat further you choose by method: 끓이다 (boil), 굽다 (grill/roast), 볶다 (stir-fry), 요리하다 (cook generally); 데우다 only brings something back up to a comfortable temperature, it does not cook from raw. The big English-speaker trap is the near-homophone 데다 ('to get burned': 손을 데다 = I burned my hand) — drop one syllable and you change 'heat the food' into 'scald yourself'.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 데우다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 데워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Mixing up 데우다 (heat food) with 데다 (get burned) — 손을 데다 means you burned your hand; the two differ by a single syllable so keep them straight.
Using 데우다 with an adjective slot — '음식이 데워요' is wrong for 'the food is warm'; the state is 음식이 따뜻해요, while 데우다 needs an object you heat (음식을 데워요).
Reaching for 데우다 to cook raw ingredients — raw meat or eggs are 굽다/끓이다/요리하다; 데우다 only reheats something already cooked.

entries.nuance: 비우다 is the causative/transitive partner of the adjective-like verb 비다 ('to be empty'): 비다 describes the state (방이 비었어요 = the room is empty), and you 비우다 something to MAKE it empty (방을 비웠어요 = I emptied the room). So the doer takes the thing as object with 을/를 — a bin, a glass, a fridge, a room. It carries two everyday spins beyond literal emptying: 집을 비우다 / 자리를 비우다 = to be away from home or step away from your seat, and the figurative 마음을 비우다 = to let go of expectations and clear your mind. Its direct opposite is 채우다 ('to fill'). The English-speaker trap is collapsing 'empty the trash' and 'throw away the trash' into one verb: you 비우다 the CONTAINER and 버리다 the CONTENTS — 쓰레기통을 비워서 쓰레기를 버리다 (empty the bin, then throw the trash out), and saying 쓰레기를 비우다 sounds off.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 비우다 as a complete polite sentence.

Reading 집을 비우다 only literally — it usually means 'be away from home', so '며칠 집을 비워요' means you'll be out for a few days, not that the house is gutted.

entries.nuance: 갈다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb (ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ: 갑니다, 가세요, 가는), and in the home sense it means swapping a used-up or worn part for a fresh one — bulbs, filters, batteries, wiper blades, bedsheets (이불을 갈다). Two cautions. First, this 갈다 is a perfect homograph of two other verbs: 갈다 'to grind/whet' (커피를 갈다, 칼을 갈다 = grind coffee, sharpen a knife) and 갈다 'to plough' (밭을 갈다); only context separates them, since the conjugation is identical. Second, distinguish it from 바꾸다 ('to change/exchange'), which is broader and works for swapping anything including abstract things (계획을 바꾸다 = change the plan, 돈을 바꾸다 = exchange money); 갈다 specifically implies replacing a consumable component with an equivalent new one. The English-speaker trap is the ㄹ-irregular: learners write 갈습니다, but the formal form is 갑니다 because ㄹ drops before the ㅂ ending.

Using 갈다 for changing a plan or appointment — that is 바꾸다 (계획을 바꾸다); 갈다 is for swapping worn physical parts like filters and bulbs.
Confusing the home sense with 갈다 'grind/sharpen' — 칼을 갈다 means sharpen a knife, so rely on context, and prefer clear objects like 필터/전구 for the 'replace' meaning.

entries.nuance: 뽑다 means pulling something out from where it is set or embedded — a plug from an outlet, but also withdrawing cash from an ATM (돈을 뽑다), plucking a hair, pulling a weed, drawing a number in a lottery, or even selecting/recruiting a person (대표를 뽑다 = pick a representative). Its exact opposite is 꽂다 (to insert/plug in upright). The near-synonym to watch is 빼다 ('to take out/remove/subtract'): both can translate as 'take out', but 뽑다 implies a firm pull against resistance (something was inserted and you yank it free), while 빼다 is gentler removal or extraction (이를 빼다 = have a tooth pulled, 힘을 빼다 = relax/ease off). For plugs and ATM cash specifically, 뽑다 is the idiomatic choice. The English-speaker trap is over-relying on 빼다 for everything 'take out' — for a plug, 코드를 뽑다 sounds far more natural than 코드를 빼다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 뽑다 becomes 뽑을 수 있어요 ("can") and 뽑을 거예요 ("will"). Its exact opposite is 꽂다 (to insert/plug in upright). entries.nuance: 꽂다 means inserting something so it stands or stays fixed in place — a plug into an outlet, a USB stick into a port, flowers into a vase, a book into a shelf (hence 책꽂이, 'bookshelf'). It is the natural opposite of 뽑다 (pull out), and it takes the destination particle 에: 콘센트에 꽂다 (into the outlet), versus 뽑다 which takes the source particle 에서. Distinguish it from the broader 넣다 ('to put in/insert'), which just means placing something inside a space (가방에 넣다 = put it in the bag) without the sense of standing it upright or seating it firmly; 꽂다 specifically implies a snug, upright insertion. Two spelling cautions: keep the ㅈ batchim (꽂아요, 꽂습니다 — not 꼽다, which is heard colloquially but is non-standard for this meaning), and don't let the verb 꽂다 blur with the noun 꽃 ('flower'), which sounds nearly the same but is a different word. The English-speaker trap is using 넣다 for plugging in — a plug 'goes into' the outlet, but the idiomatic verb is 꽂다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 꽂다 as a complete polite sentence.

Spelling it 꼽다 — the standard verb is 꽂다 (꽂아요/꽂았어요); 꼽다 is heard colloquially but is not the correct written form for inserting.
Using 넣다 for plugging in — 넣다 just puts something inside a space, while 꽂다 means a firm upright insertion, so a plug or USB is 꽂다.
Choosing the wrong particle — it is 콘센트에 꽂다 (destination 에), the mirror of 콘센트에서 뽑다 (source 에서); swapping the particles breaks the in/out direction.

entries.nuance: 전하다 (Sino-Korean 傳, 'transmit/hand down') means relaying something from a sender to a receiver: a message, regards, an item, news, or even a feeling, so the receiver takes 에게/한테 or honorific 께 while the thing passed takes 을/를. The nearest rival is 말하다, but 말하다 is you simply saying something yourself, whereas 전하다 stresses that you are the go-between carrying someone else's words or goods to a third party — '사장님이 잘했다고 전하래요' (the boss told me to tell you 'well done'). The big English-speaker trap is hearing 전 and thinking 전화하다 ('to make a phone call'): they share the 전 syllable but are unrelated, so '전해 주세요' is 'please relay it', not 'please call them'.

The receiver of the message takes 에게/한테/께, not 을/를: '친구에게 전해 주세요', and the message itself is what takes 을/를.

A strong first sentence is 부모님을 설득했어요. ("I persuaded my parents."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 설득하다 also becomes 설득하고 싶어요 (want), 설득할 수 있어요 (can), and 못 설득해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 설득하다 (Sino-Korean 說得, literally 'speak-and-gain', i.e. win someone over by talking) means to bring a reluctant person around to your view through reasoning, and crucially the person persuaded takes the object marker 을/를, not 에게 — 친구를 설득하다, never 친구에게 설득하다. Contrast it with 권하다 ('to recommend/urge'): 권하다 is gently offering a suggestion ('커피 한 잔 권하다'), whereas 설득하다 implies active back-and-forth against initial resistance, so it is stronger and more deliberate than just 말하다 or 권하다. The noun 설득 and adjective phrase 설득력이 있다 ('be persuasive') are common. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: because English says 'persuade TO someone' feels wrong but learners still copy 에게 from verbs like 말하다, producing the ungrammatical 사람에게 설득하다. Also note 설득하다 is persuading someone to your side, not convincing yourself — for 'I'm convinced' you would say 납득이 됐어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 설득하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 설득해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
The person persuaded takes 을/를 (사람을 설득하다), never 에게; the 에게 from verbs like 말하다 does not carry over.
Do not use 설득하다 for a light suggestion — that is 권하다; 설득하다 implies overcoming the other person's resistance.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 설득하다 becomes 설득할 수 있어요 ("can") and 설득할 거예요 ("will"). entries.shortExplanation: 거절하다 means "to refuse / decline" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to refuse / decline" in Korean is 거절하다 (geojeolha-da). entries.nuance: 거절하다 (Sino-Korean 拒絶, 'block-and-sever') is the standard verb for declining a request, offer, or invitation, and the thing refused — 부탁, 제안, 초대 — takes 을/를. Compare it with the harsher 거부하다 (拒否, 'block-and-deny'): 거부하다 is a flat, often institutional rejection ('출석을 거부하다', 'refuse to comply'), while 거절하다 is the ordinary interpersonal 'no thanks'. Because directly refusing can feel rude in Korean social life, 거절하다 is habitually cushioned with 죄송하지만 ('sorry, but…'), 정중하게 ('politely'), or 어렵겠어요 ('that would be difficult'); the bare verb can sound cold. A frequent English-speaker slip is reaching for 거절하다 to mean 'reject a person' romantically — that is 차다 (dump) or 까이다 (get rejected), not 거절하다, which targets the request, not the human. Also do not confuse it with 사양하다, a humble 'I'll pass' used to politely decline an offer of food or a gift.

Use 거절해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Do not confuse 거절하다 (decline a request/offer) with the stronger 거부하다, which feels like a flat, often official rejection.
거절하다 takes the offer as its object (제안을 거절하다); to 'reject' a person romantically Koreans say 차다 / 까이다, not 거절하다.

entries.shortExplanation: 혼내다 means "to scold / tell off" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 혼내다 (honnae-da) = "to scold / tell off". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 혼내요 plus one useful sentence like 동생을 혼냈어요. ("I scolded my younger sibling."). Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

entries.nuance: 혼내다 means an older or higher-status person verbally disciplining someone beneath them — a parent a child, a teacher a pupil, a boss a junior — so the person scolded takes 을/를. The essential pair to learn is the active 혼내다 ('I scold') versus 혼나다 ('I get scolded'); '나 혼났어' ('I got chewed out') is something even adults say casually about a partner or boss. Distinguish it from 야단치다 (very close, slightly more old-fashioned/strong, often a parent shouting) and from 화내다, which is just 'to get angry / show anger' with no teaching aim — you can 화내다 at a stranger, but you only 혼내다 someone you have authority over. The English-speaker pitfall is direction: learners say '저는 부장님을 혼났어요' meaning to report being scolded, but that wrongly makes them the scolder; you must flip to 혼나다 — '부장님한테 혼났어요'. Keep 혼내다 (do the scolding) and 혼나다 (receive it) firmly apart.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 혼내다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 혼내요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Use 혼내다 when you do the scolding and 혼나다 when you are scolded; '팀장님한테 혼났어요' (I got told off), not '팀장님을 혼냈어요'.
Do not swap 혼내다 for 화내다: 화내다 is simply showing anger (even at a stranger), while 혼내다 implies authority and a corrective purpose.

entries.nuance: 따지다 (native Korean, no hanja) has two distinct flavors that share the idea of 'pinning down the truth point by point'. One is confrontational: marching up to someone to demand an explanation for a wrong, where the person/place takes 에게/한테 and the tone is combative — you feel wronged and want answers ('왜 그랬냐고 따졌어'). The other is cool and analytical: scrutinizing or weighing details (조건을 따지다, 가격을 따지다, 손익을 따지다), often with 따져 보다. Compare 물어보다, which is a neutral 'ask a question' with no accusation — switching from 따지다 to 물어보다 instantly removes the hostility. entries.nuance: 우기다 (native Korean) means to keep insisting you are right even when you are probably wrong, so it always carries a negative, hard-headed tone — picture someone digging in past the point of reason. The key contrast is with the neutral 주장하다 (主張하다, 'to assert/claim'): 주장하다 is dignified and can be perfectly reasonable ('전문가들은 ~라고 주장한다'), whereas 우기다 paints the speaker as obstinate and likely mistaken — you would never use 우기다 in a formal report about your own well-founded position. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 우기다 as a plain synonym for 'insist': in English you can insist correctly and politely, but choosing 우기다 always smuggles in the judgment 'and you're being unreasonable', so for a calm, valid claim switch to 주장하다 or 강조하다.

entries.nuance: 떠들다 means making a loud, rowdy racket by talking, chattering, or carrying on, and it is almost always framed as something you should NOT do in a quiet place (library, classroom, late at night). entries.nuance: 속이다 is the causative of 속다 ('to be fooled'), so literally 'to make (someone) be deceived' — to lead a person to believe something false, with the victim taking 을/를 and the falsified fact also often as object (나이를 속이다, 가격을 속이다). The companion verb 속다 / 속았어 ('I got fooled') is just as common in speech, and the two form an essential active/passive pair. Compare 거짓말하다 ('to tell a lie'): 거짓말하다 names the act of uttering a falsehood ('나한테 거짓말했어'), while 속이다 stresses the effect of successfully misleading someone — you can 거짓말하다 and fail, but 속이다 implies the deception landed. Keep 속이다 (deceive someone) apart from 속다 (be deceived).

Do not blur 속이다 with 거짓말하다: 거짓말하다 is uttering a lie, while 속이다 implies the lie actually misled the victim.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 속이다 becomes 속일 수 있어요 ("can") and 속일 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 속이다 is the causative of 속다 ('to be fooled'), so literally 'to make (someone) be deceived' — to lead a person to believe something false, with the victim taking 을/를 and the falsified fact also often as object (나이를 속이다, 가격을 속이다).

Compare 거짓말하다 ('to tell a lie'): 거짓말하다 names the act of uttering a falsehood ('나한테 거짓말했어'), while 속이다 stresses the effect of successfully misleading someone — you can 거짓말하다 and fail, but 속이다 implies the deception landed.

속이다 is the causative of 속다. The companion verb 속다 / 속았어 ('I got fooled') is just as common in speech, and the two form an essential active/passive pair. Keep 속이다 (deceive someone) apart from 속다 (be deceived).

The English-speaker pitfall is direction, exactly as with 혼내다: learners say '제가 속였어요' to mean 'I got tricked', but that says you did the tricking; flip to the intransitive — '제가 속았어요' ('I was deceived').

entries.nuance: 놀리다 means making fun of someone, with the target taking 을/를 and the trait teased about taking (으)로 (외모로 놀리다, 사투리로 놀리다). Its emotional range is wide: from affectionate ribbing between close friends to genuinely hurtful mockery, so tone and relationship decide whether it lands as 장난 (a joke) or 상처 (a wound). Watch out for two look-alike traps. First, this 놀리다 (tease) is homonymous with a separate verb 놀리다 meaning 'to leave idle / keep unused' (손을 놀리다 'work the hands', 공장을 놀리다 'idle a factory') — same spelling, unrelated meaning, told apart only by context. Second, English speakers constantly mix 놀리다 (tease) with 놀다 (play, hang out); they share the 놀- root but '친구랑 놀았어요' is 'I hung out with a friend', whereas '친구를 놀렸어요' is 'I teased a friend'. The object particle differs too: 랑/하고 for 놀다 versus 을/를 for 놀리다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 놀리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 놀려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Do not confuse 놀리다 (tease) with 놀다 (play / hang out): '친구랑 놀았어요' = hung out, but '친구를 놀렸어요' = teased.
To say what you tease someone about, use (으)로: '외모로 놀리다' (tease about looks), not 외모를 놀리다.

entries.nuance: 털어놓다 is a compound of 털다 ('to shake/dust out', as you shake out a dusty cloth) plus 놓다 ('to set down'), giving the vivid image of shaking everything out of your chest and laying it on the table — i.e. unburdening worries, secrets, or true feelings you have bottled up, with the listener taking 에게/한테. Because the second element is 놓다, the present and past contract in speech (놓아요 becomes 놔요), giving 털어놔요 and 털어놨어요, while the formal keeps the full stem as 털어놓습니다. Compare 고백하다, which is confessing a specific fact or romantic feeling, whereas 털어놓다 is the broader emotional unburdening of accumulated 고민 to a confidant. The English-speaker pitfall is the contraction: learners over-regularize and write 털어놓았어요 / 털어놓아요, but natural speech is 털어놨어요 / 털어놔요 — and note the imperative drops back to 털어놓으세요 (no contraction before 으). Pair it with 고민, 속마음, 비밀.

Use 털어놓다 for unburdening accumulated worries to someone; for declaring a specific fact or romantic feeling, that is 고백하다.
