entries.nuance: 고백하다 (Sino-Korean 告白, literally 'tell-plainly', i.e. lay bare) most often means confessing romantic feelings — '좋아한다고 고백하다' — which in Korean dating culture, especially for people in their 20s-30s, is a defined, weighty moment that frequently marks the official start (사귀다) of a relationship; you 고백하다 first, and if accepted, you are now dating. It also covers admitting a hidden truth or fault, like a heartfelt confession of wrongdoing. The person confessed to takes 에게/한테. Contrast it with 사과하다 ('to apologize', 謝過, expressing regret for a wrong) and with 자백하다 ('to confess to a crime', as to police) — 고백하다 is the warm, personal baring of the heart, not a legal admission or an apology. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'confess' as one word: in English you 'confess your love' and 'confess to the crime' alike, but Korean reserves 고백하다 for heartfelt romantic/personal disclosure and uses 자백하다 for criminal confession; choosing 고백하다 with the police sounds oddly intimate.

Use 고백해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
For romantic confessions use 고백하다; 사과하다 means 'to apologize' (express regret for a wrong) and is a different act entirely.
Do not use 고백하다 for confessing a crime to authorities — that is 자백하다; 고백하다 is the warm, personal baring of feelings or a fault.

entries.nuance: 삶다 means to cook a solid food by fully submerging it in boiling water — eggs, noodles, potatoes, greens, even towels for sanitizing. The stem vowel ㅏ is bright, so endings take 아: 삶아요, 삶았어요 (never 삶어요), and the ㄻ batchim is pronounced [삼], giving [삼따]/[살마]. The crucial, constantly-confused boundary is 삶다 vs 끓이다: 삶다 = put a solid INTO water to cook the solid (계란을 삶다); 끓이다 = boil the LIQUID itself or make a brothy dish (물을 끓이다, 찌개를 끓이다). English 'boil' covers both, which is exactly why learners misfire — they say 계란을 끓이다 (literally 'bring the egg to a boil') when they mean 계란을 삶다. Compare also 데치다, which is only a quick few-second blanch, whereas 삶다 is full cooking-through.

Confusing it with 데치다. 삶다 cooks food fully through; 데치다 is only a brief blanch of a few seconds.

entries.shortExplanation: 끓이다 means "to boil (a liquid) / to make (soup, stew, ramyeon)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

entries.nuance: 끓이다 is the causative/transitive partner of 끓다 ('to be boiling'): you 끓이다 a liquid so that it 끓다. As a ㅣ-stem it contracts ㅣ + 어 → ㅕ, giving 끓여요/끓였어요 (not 끓이어요). entries.nuance: 데치다 is a regular ㅣ-stem verb (데쳐요/데쳤어요, ㅣ + 어 → ㅕ) meaning a quick blanch: dropping vegetables (or sometimes squid, bean sprouts) into already-boiling water for just a handful of seconds to soften them and set their color, then immediately draining. It is the gateway move of Korean 나물 banchan: 데치다 then 무치다 (season). The pitfall that trips English speakers is the near-twin 데우다 ('to reheat/warm up already-cooked food'): same friendly 데- start, totally different job — 국을 데우다 reheats yesterday's soup, while 시금치를 데치다 blanches raw spinach. Mixing them up makes a recipe nonsensical, so anchor 데치다 = raw → boiling water → quick dunk.

examples.en: I'm seasoning the spinach.
examples.note: Bare frame; the contraction is 무쳐요 (무치 + 어 → 무쳐), never 무치어요.

examples.note: 참기름에 무치다 is the quintessential namul finish; past 무쳤어요.

entries.nuance: 무치다 is the hands-on tossing that FINISHES most Korean banchan: you blanch (데치다) a vegetable, then 무치다 it with 양념 — sesame oil, garlic, soy or gochujang — until every strand is evenly coated, traditionally squeezing it 조물조물 by hand. As a ㅣ-stem it contracts to 무쳐요/무쳤어요. The noun 무침 labels a whole menu category of cold seasoned dishes (오이무침, 골뱅이무침, 무생채). The contrast learners MUST keep straight is 무치다 vs 비비다: 무치다 means DRESSING/coating a single ingredient with seasoning so it absorbs the flavor (a side dish), whereas 비비다 means STIRRING many components together into one mixed dish (비빔밥, 비빔국수). They feel similar in English ('mix/toss'), but a Korean would never say 밥을 무치다 for bibimbap or 나물을 비비다 for seasoned spinach. Anchor it: 무치다 = season one thing; 비비다 = stir everything together.

Confusing 무치다 with 비비다. 무치다 = dress/season one ingredient (나물을 무치다); 비비다 = stir several things together (밥을 비비다).
Spelling it 뭍이다 or 무티다. The verb is 무치다, conjugated 무쳐요/무쳤어요.
Using the wrong particle for the seasoning: it's 참기름에 무치다 (에 = with/in the seasoning), not 참기름을 무치다.

entries.english: to slice / to cut (food, on a board)
entries.shortExplanation: 썰다 means "to slice / to cut (food, on a board)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 썰다 (sseolda) means "to slice / to cut (food, on a board)". Start from the polite form 썰어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 썰다. examples.en: I'm slicing onions.
examples.note: Bare frame; the ㄹ stays before the vowel ending → 썰어요, not 써요.

examples.en: I cut the meat into bite-sized pieces.
examples.note: 썰었어요 keeps the ㄹ before 었; 한입 크기로 = into bite-size. …(으)로 marks the resulting shape.

examples.en: Shall I slice the green onion?
examples.note: 썰까요? — the ㄹ DROPS before the ㄲ of 까, so it's 썰까 (not 썰을까).

entries.nuance: 썰다 is a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ-dropping) verb: the stem ㄹ vanishes before endings starting with ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ and before the ㄹ of -(으)ㄹ, giving 썹니다, 써세요, 썰 거예요, 썰까요? — but the ㄹ STAYS before vowel endings, so 썰어요/썰었어요. The dividing line: 자르다 = cut/sever anything into pieces (broad); 썰다 = rhythmically slice food with a knife on a board (specific). Learn it bundled with the cutting adverbs you'll meet in every recipe — 얇게, 채 썰다 (julienne), 어슷하게, 송송, 깍둑썰다 — because Korean encodes the cut SHAPE in these adverbs rather than in the verb. The English-speaker trap is leaning on 자르다 for all cutting; for food prep, 썰다 is what sounds like a cook.

Keeping the ㄹ before ㅂ/ㅅ endings. It drops: 썹니다 and 써세요, not 썰습니다/썰으세요.
Adding 을 in the future/proposal. The ㄹ-stem just takes ㄹ: 썰 거예요, 썰까요? — not 썰을 거예요/썰을까요.
Using 자르다 for everything in the kitchen. Slicing food on a board is more naturally 썰다; save 자르다 for paper, hair, rope.

entries.nuance: 비비다 means mixing by stirring and tossing many things together until evenly combined — it is literally the root of 비빔밥 and 비빔국수 (비빔 = the noun 'mixing'). English 'mix/toss' covers both, so beginners blur them — but 밥을 무치다 or 나물을 비비다 both sound wrong to a Korean. Beyond food, the same verb means physically rubbing two surfaces (눈을 비비다 'rub your eyes', 손을 비비다 'rub your hands', often in a pleading gesture), which is a handy everyday extension. Anchor it: at the table, 비비다 = stir it all together and eat.

entries.english: to cool (something) down / to let cool
entries.shortExplanation: 식히다 means "to cool (something) down / to let cool" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 식히다 (sikhida) means "to cool (something) down / to let cool". Start from the polite form 식혀요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 식히다. examples.note: Bare frame; the contraction is 식혀요 (식히 + 어 → 식혀), never 식히어요. 좀 softens it to a request.

entries.nuance: 식히다 is the causative/transitive partner of intransitive 식다: 식다 means food cools off BY ITSELF (국이 식다 'the soup goes cold'), while 식히다 means YOU actively cool it — blowing on it, fanning it, leaving it out. entries.nuance: 피하다 means to actively avoid, dodge, or steer clear of something — a person, a situation, bad weather, or a time of day — and the workhorse construction is N을/를 피해서 ('avoiding N'), perfect for dodging rush hour (출퇴근 시간을 피해서), crowds, or the heat. It is Sino-Korean: 避(피, 'avoid/evade') + 하다, literally 'to do avoidance', which is why it can feel slightly more deliberate than a casual sidestep. The key contrast is with 빠지다 and 거르다 (to skip/miss out on something, e.g. 회의에 빠지다 'skip the meeting', 식사를 거르다 'skip a meal') and with 막다 (to block something from happening to you): 피하다 is you moving yourself out of harm's way, not blocking it. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'avoid' onto 'skip an event' — saying 회의를 피했어요 to mean 'I skipped the meeting' actually implies you dodged it on purpose, which sounds evasive; for an innocent absence use 빠지다.

It's transitive: include the thing avoided — 비를 피하다, 사람을 피하다, not bare 피하다.
Don't say '피하해요' — 하다 verbs contract to 해요, so the polite form is 피해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 넘기다 means "to turn over, to flip, to hand over" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 넘기다 (neomgida) means "to turn over, to flip, to hand over". Start from the polite form 넘겨요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 넘기다. entries.nuance: 넘기다 is the causative/transitive partner of 넘다 ('to cross over a line/peak'): you make something go over or past, so it spans turning pages (장을 넘기다), swiping a screen (옆으로 넘기다), handing work or objects off to someone (담당자에게 넘기다), and getting through a tough stretch of time (시기를 넘기다, 고비를 넘기다). Watch two look-alikes: 넘다 is intransitive ('cross over' — 선을 넘다), and 넘어지다 means 'to topple/trip and fall', which has nothing to do with handing over. When the recipient is a person, mark them with 에게/한테 (담당자에게 넘기다); when it is a page or screen, mark the direction with -(으)로 (다음 장으로 넘기다). The English-speaker pitfall is hearing 넘어지다 and 넘기다 as the same root and producing '넘어겼어요' — keep them separate.

Use 넘겨요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse it with 넘어지다 (to trip and fall over) — 넘기다 means to flip or hand something over, not to topple.
When handing something to a person, mark the recipient with 에게/한테: 담당자에게 넘기다, not '담당자를 넘기다'.
For carefully placing an object into someone's hand, 건네다 is more precise; 넘기다 stresses passing it on/off rather than the gentle handover.

The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

entries.nuance: 들어올리다 is a compound of 들다 ('to hold/lift in the hand') + 올리다 ('to raise'), and the whole point of the compound is to foreground the UPWARD motion — getting a heavy box, a barbell, or a child up off a surface. The contrast with plain 들다 is the dividing line learners most need: 가방을 들다 just means to hold/carry a bag (it may already be in the air), whereas 가방을 들어올리다 specifically pictures the act of heaving it up. It also differs from 올리다 alone, which can raise something already in hand (선반에 올리다 'put it up on a shelf') without the lifting-from-below nuance. Collocations cluster around weight and effort: 번쩍 들어올리다 (hoist in one motion), 끝까지 들어올리다 (lift all the way up), 다리로 들어올리다 (lift with the legs). The English-speaker pitfall is over-using it as a blanket translation of 'lift/carry' — for simply toting a bag around, 들다 is far more natural, and reserving 들어올리다 for the genuine raising action keeps your Korean from sounding heavy-handed.

Use 들어올려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't over-use it where plain 들다 works: 가방을 들다 ('carry a bag') is natural; 들어올리다 is for when the upward heave itself is the point.
Don't reach for 올리다 alone when you mean lifting from the ground up — 올리다 can mean 'place up on' (선반에 올리다); the 들어- adds the lifting-from-below sense.
Keep it as one word, 들어올리다 — the spaced form 들어 올리다 is also seen, but be consistent.

entries.nuance: 내려놓다 combines 내리다 ('to bring down') + 놓다 ('to place'), so it means to lower something from your hands and set it on a surface — the natural opposite of 들어올리다. Its sharpest contrast is with bare 놓다 and 두다: 놓다 just means 'place/let go of' (책상에 놓다) and 두다 means 'leave/keep something somewhere' (그냥 둬요 'just leave it'), while 내려놓다 specifically adds the downward motion of unloading something you were holding up. Koreans use it with quiet beauty in the figurative sense 마음을 내려놓다 / 걱정을 내려놓다 — to let go of stress or attachment, exactly like the English 'put down a burden.' On conjugation: 놓 is a regular ㅎ-final stem, so before -아요 it contracts (내려놓아요 → 내려놔요, past 내려놨어요), but before -(으)세요 the ㅎ stays and you say 내려놓으세요. The English-speaker pitfall is producing '내려놔세요' by over-applying the contraction to the imperative — the polite command keeps the full stem: 내려놓으세요.

Don't substitute bare 놓다 or 두다 when you mean lowering something you held up — 내려놓다 adds the downward unloading motion that 놓다/두다 lack.

entries.english: to flip over, to turn inside out
entries.shortExplanation: 뒤집다 means "to flip over, to turn inside out" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 뒤집다 (dwijipda) means "to flip over, to turn inside out". Start from the polite form 뒤집어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 뒤집다. Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 뒤집다 means to turn something to its other side or inside out — flipping grilling meat (고기를 뒤집다), turning clothes for the wash (옷을 뒤집다), or, figuratively, overturning a situation, mood, or verdict (사건을 뒤집다). A critical conjugation warning: although the stem ends in ㅂ, this is a REGULAR verb, NOT a ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ stays put — 뒤집어요, 뒤집습니다, 뒤집었어요 — and you must never soften it to '뒤지워요'. The transitivity contrast matters too: 뒤집다 is what YOU do to an object, while its passive 뒤집히다 is for something that flips or capsizes on its own (배가 뒤집혔어요 'the boat capsized'); and to knock something over face-down you might use 엎다 (그릇을 엎다 'tip the bowl over'). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: assuming every ㅂ-final stem is irregular (it is not here), and using the active 뒤집다 for things that turn over by themselves when the passive 뒤집히다 is required.

Use 뒤집어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
This is NOT a ㅂ-irregular: it conjugates 뒤집어요 / 뒤집습니다 / 뒤집었어요 — the ㅂ never changes to 우, so '뒤지워요' is wrong.
뒤집다 is transitive (you flip it); for something that flips or capsizes on its own, use the passive 뒤집히다 (배가 뒤집히다).
Don't confuse it with 엎다 ('tip/knock over face-down') — 뒤집다 turns to the other side, 엎다 spills it over.

entries.shortExplanation: 기대다 means "to lean on, to rely on" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to lean on, to rely on" in Korean is 기대다 (gidaeda). entries.nuance: 누르다 is the go-to verb for pressing or pushing down — elevator buttons, doorbells, app icons, keypad keys, the 'like' button — and modern Korean life is so full of buttons that nailing it instantly sounds fluent. It is a textbook 르-irregular verb: before a vowel ending, the 르 transforms and an extra ㄹ appears, so the stem becomes 눌ㄹ-, giving 눌러요 and past 눌렀어요, while consonant endings stay regular (누릅니다, 누르고, 누르지 마세요). The meaning contrast to lock in is with 밀다 and 당기다: 누르다 is pressing DOWN on a surface or button, 밀다 is pushing a door/object away from you (문을 밀다 'push the door'), and 당기다 is pulling it toward you (문을 당기다) — so a door says 미세요/당기세요, never 누르세요, but a doorbell beside it says 누르세요. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: writing the un-irregular '누르어요' instead of 눌러요, and over-extending 'press/push' to doors, where Korean insists on 밀다 rather than 누르다.

entries.shortExplanation: 비키다 means "to step aside, to get out of the way" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 비키다 (bikida) means "to step aside, to get out of the way". Start from the polite form 비켜요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 비키다. entries.nuance: 비키다 means to step aside or move your own body out of someone's way, which makes it intransitive — you shift yourself, you do not move an object. The contrast to fix is with 치우다 and 옮기다, which are transitive: if a box is blocking the hall, a person 비켜요 (steps aside) but you 치워요 / 옮겨요 the box (clear/move it). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'move out of the way' as transitive and trying to 비키다 an object, or — worse — using bare 비켜 with strangers and sounding aggressive without realizing it.

structuredNuance.t: 비키다 means to step aside or move your own body out of someone's way, which makes it intransitive — you shift yourself, you do not move an object. The polite requests 비켜 주세요 and 비켜 주시겠어요? are survival phrases for crowded subways, sidewalks, and elevator doors. Register caution is essential: a bare, curt 비켜! is genuinely rude, the equivalent of barking 'Move it!' or 'Out of my way!', so unless you intend to be sharp you must cushion it with 주세요 or the very polite 주시겠어요.
The contrast to fix is with 치우다 and 옮기다, which are transitive: if a box is blocking the hall, a person 비켜요 (steps aside) but you 치워요 / 옮겨요 the box (clear/move it).
The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'move out of the way' as transitive and trying to 비키다 an object, or — worse — using bare 비켜 with strangers and sounding aggressive without realizing it.

entries.shortExplanation: 깨닫다 means "to realize" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to realize" in Korean is 깨닫다 (kkaedatda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 깨달아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 깨닫다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 뒤늦게 깨달았어요 ("I realized too late") — then reshape the same stem into 깨닫고 싶어요 (desire), 깨달을 수 있어요 (ability), and 깨달을 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 깨달아요. Then practice 깨닫지 않아요 vs 깨달을 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

examples.romanization: hanguge salmyeonseo maeun geol jal meongneundaneun geol kkaedarasseoyo.
examples.en: Living in Korea, I realized I'm actually fine with spicy food.

examples.romanization: silsuhaetdaneun geol geujeya kkaedatgo baro sagwahaesseoyo.

entries.nuance: 깨닫다 is a sudden dawning of understanding — the instant a fact or truth clicks into place, often something you feel you should have grasped sooner. Contrast it with 이해하다 (to comprehend), which is the gradual, effortful process of 'getting it'; 깨닫다 is the flash of insight that ends that process, and with 알다 (to know) which is the steady resulting state. It pairs habitually with 문득/뒤늦게/새삼 and the chunk V-(으)ㄴ 걸 깨닫다. The big English-speaker trap is the ㄷ irregular: in the 요-form the stem ㄷ turns to ㄹ before a vowel (깨달아요, 깨달았어요, 깨달으세요), but stays ㄷ before a consonant (깨닫고, 깨닫지). Learners overgeneralize and write 깨닫아요, which is simply wrong — anchor the whole verb on the correct 깨달아요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 깨닫다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 깨달아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
깨닫아요 (wrong) → 깨달아요
The ㄷ-irregular stem changes ㄷ to ㄹ before the vowel of -아요, so 깨닫 + 아요 becomes 깨달아요, never 깨닫아요.
깨달고 / 깨달지 (wrong) → 깨닫고 / 깨닫지
Before a consonant the ㄷ does NOT change. Many learners over-apply the ㄹ; keep ㄷ in 깨닫고, 깨닫지, 깨닫습니다.
Using 깨닫다 for slowly comprehending a lesson
For working through and understanding material use 이해하다; 깨닫다 is the sudden click, not the gradual grasp.
notes: ㄷ: memorize 깨달아 and 깨달아요 together.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 깨달아요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 깨닫다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 뒤늦게 깨달았어요. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 깨닫지 않아요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 깨달을 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 깨달아요 feels easy, practice 깨닫고 싶어요, 깨달을 수 있어요, and 깨달아야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

Learner changes the sentence to 깨닫지 않아요, then 깨달을 수 없어요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

entries.shortExplanation: 떠오르다 means "to come to mind" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 떠오르다 (tteooreuda) = "to come to mind". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 떠올라요 plus one useful sentence like 갑자기 떠올랐어요 ("It suddenly came to mind"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 떠오르고 싶어요 for what you want, 떠오를 수 있어요 for what you can, 떠오를 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 떠올라요. Then practice 떠오르지 않아요 vs 떠오를 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

examples.note: 이름이 안 떠오르다 = a name won't surface; the natural way to say 'it's on the tip of my tongue'

examples.en: When I hear this song, my hometown comes to mind.

examples.en: A good idea came to me during the meeting.
examples.note: 떠올랐어요 shows the 르 irregular: 르 → ㄹㄹ, so 떠오르 + 았 → 떠올랐

entries.nuance: 떠오르다 literally means 'to float/rise up' (which is why it also describes the sun rising), and figuratively a thought, memory, name, or idea rises up into your mind on its own — it is intransitive, so the idea is the subject: 생각이 떠올라요. The crucial contrast is with its transitive twin 떠올리다 (to call something to mind on purpose): 떠오르다 happens TO you, 떠올리다 is something you DO. It also differs from 생각나다 (to come to mind), which is close but plainer and more about simple recall, whereas 떠오르다 has a vivid 'surfacing/floating up' image and fits fresh ideas. The English-speaker pitfall is particle choice: because 'I think of an idea' has an object in English, learners say 생각을 떠올라요, but the intransitive 떠오르다 demands 생각이 떠올라요. Watch the 르 irregular too: 떠오르 + 았 → 떠올랐어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 떠오르다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 떠올라요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
생각을 떠올라요 (wrong) → 생각이 떠올라요
떠오르다 is intransitive: the thought is the subject, so it takes 이/가. Use the transitive 떠올리다 if you want an 을/를 object.
떠오르았어요 (wrong) → 떠올랐어요
This is a 르-irregular verb. The 르 doubles to ㄹㄹ before -았/-어, giving 떠올랐어요, not 떠오르았어요.
Confusing it with 떠올리다
떠오르다 = it surfaces by itself; 떠올리다 = you deliberately summon it. The particle (이 vs 을) tells you which one you need.
notes: 르: memorize 떠올라 and 떠올라요 together.

entries.shortExplanation: 헷갈리다 means "to get confused" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 헷갈리다 (hetgallida) means "to get confused". Start from the polite form 헷갈려요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 헷갈리다. A strong first sentence is 좀 헷갈려요 ("I'm a bit mixed up"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 헷갈리다 also becomes 헷갈리고 싶어요 (want), 헷갈릴 수 있어요 (can), and 헷갈릴 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 헷갈려요. Then practice 헷갈리지 않아요 vs 헷갈릴 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

usagePhrases.note: the go-to phrase when two things blur together; softer and more specific than 모르겠어요

examples.en: I always mix up left and right.
examples.note: A랑 B가 헷갈리다 = mix up A and B; the two confusable things take 이/가, not 을/를

examples.en: There were so many exits that I got turned around.
examples.note: 길이 헷갈리다 = lose track of the way; perfect for getting lost in a big station

examples.ko: 이 두 단어는 발음이 비슷해서 자꾸 헷갈려요.
examples.romanization: i du daneoneun bareumi biseutaeseo jakku hetgallyeoyo.
examples.en: These two words sound alike, so I keep confusing them.
examples.note: 자꾸 헷갈리다 = keep getting mixed up; 자꾸 stresses the repeated slip

entries.nuance: 헷갈리다 is the everyday word for two or more things blurring together so you can't keep them straight — left vs. right, two similar names, which subway exit. The key contrast is with 모르겠다 (I don't know): with 모르겠다 you simply lack the information, but with 헷갈리다 you actually have it and are just getting two things crossed — you're tangled, not clueless. It's also lighter than 혼란스럽다 (to be in turmoil/disoriented), which is a heavier, almost emotional confusion. Grammatically it behaves like a feeling verb: both the experiencer (저는) and the confusing thing (이게/발음이) commonly take 이/가, and the confusable pair links with -랑/-하고. The main English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 모르겠어요 ('I don't know') when you really mean 'I keep getting these mixed up' — that's exactly 헷갈려요. Also beware the spelling: it is 헷, not 햇.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 헷갈리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 헷갈려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
햇갈리다 (wrong) → 헷갈리다
The first syllable is 헷 with ㅔ, not 햇 with ㅐ. This misspelling is extremely common even among natives, so fix it early.
Saying 모르겠어요 when you mean you're mixing two things up
모르겠어요 = you lack the knowledge; 헷갈려요 = you have it but keep crossing two similar items. They are not interchangeable.
왼쪽을 오른쪽을 헷갈려요 (wrong) → 왼쪽이랑 오른쪽이 헷갈려요
The confused items take 이/가 and are joined with -랑/-하고, not stacked with 을/를.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 헷갈리다 becomes 헷갈릴 수 있어요 ("can") and 헷갈릴 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 헷갈리다 is the everyday word for two or more things blurring together so you can't keep them straight — left vs. right, two similar names, which subway exit. Beware the spelling: it is 헷, not 햇.

The key contrast is with 모르겠다 (I don't know): with 모르겠다 you simply lack the information, but with 헷갈리다 you actually have it and are just getting two things crossed — you're tangled, not clueless. It's also lighter than 혼란스럽다 (to be in turmoil/disoriented), which is a heavier, almost emotional confusion.
Grammatically it behaves like a feeling verb: both the experiencer (저는) and the confusing thing (이게/발음이) commonly take 이/가, and the confusable pair links with -랑/-하고.
The main pitfall is reaching for 모르겠어요 ('I don't know') when you really mean 'I keep getting these mixed up' — that's exactly 헷갈려요.

entries.explanation: "to hesitate" in Korean is 망설이다 (mangseorida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 망설여요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 망설이다 for study notes. usagePhrases.note: encouraging someone to just go for it; very common in shops and pep talks

entries.nuance: 망설이다 is to hesitate because you cannot commit to a choice — you waver, stall, and hold back at the threshold of acting. Its closest neighbor is 고민하다 (Sino-Korean 苦悶, 'bitter anguish'), but the dividing line is sharp: 고민하다 is the active mental labor of mulling a problem over, while 망설이다 is the stuck, hovering feeling right before you act, and it pairs constantly with -(으)ㄹ까 말까 (whether or not to). It also differs from 주저하다 (a stiffer, more written 'to be reluctant/hold back'); 망설이다 is the warmer, spoken everyday word. A useful collocation is 망설임 없이 (without hesitation) and 망설이다가 (hesitate, and as a result…). The English-speaker pitfall is using 망설이다 as a catch-all for 'worry' or 'think about it' — if you're chewing over a problem, that's 고민하다; 망설이다 specifically means you can't bring yourself to decide or move.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 망설이다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 망설여요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 망설이다 to mean general worrying/thinking it over
For mulling a problem use 고민하다. 망설이다 is specifically the inability to commit to an action, not broad worry.
살까 말까 고민할게요 vs 망설일게요 mixed up
If you're weighing pros and cons, 고민하다 fits; if you're frozen and can't act, 망설이다 fits. Don't treat them as identical.
망설리다 (wrong) → 망설이다
There is no extra ㄹ. The stem is 망설이-, giving 망설여요/망설였어요, not 망설려요.

entries.nuance: 판단하다 (Sino-Korean 判斷, 'judge/decide' + 'sever' — literally to cut through and rule on something) means to assess a situation with reason and arrive at a conclusion; it is analytical, not emotional. The sharp contrast is with 결정하다 (決定, to decide on a choice): 판단하다 is the reasoning and weighing of evidence, and 결정하다 is the act of settling on the resulting option — you 판단 the facts, then make a 결정. It also differs from 평가하다 (評價, to evaluate/rate quality). Unlike English 'judge,' 판단하다 normally carries no 'being judgmental' overtone; to get that critical sense, Koreans add 함부로 판단하다 (judge rashly) or 겉모습만 보고 판단하다 (judge by looks alone). It collocates with 상황을 판단하다, 스스로 판단하다, and 판단하기 어렵다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 판단하다 where you simply chose between options (that's 결정하다), or importing the negative 'don't judge me' tone that the bare verb does not have.

Use 판단해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

판단하다 is the reasoning/assessment; 결정하다 is locking in the decision that results. Say 메뉴를 결정했어요, not 메뉴를 판단했어요.
Assuming 판단하다 means 'be judgmental'
The plain verb is neutral and analytical. For the critical English sense, add 함부로 (rashly): 함부로 판단하지 마세요.
판단하다 with 에 instead of 을/를 for the object
It takes 을/를: 상황을 판단하다. Don't say 상황에 판단하다.

entries.explanation: 예상하다 (yesanghada) means "to expect". Start from the polite form 예상해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 예상하다. A strong first sentence is 예상했던 대로예요 ("It's just as I expected"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

examples.note: 예상하고 있다 = to be anticipating (ongoing); 어느 정도 = to some degree

entries.nuance: 예상하다 (Sino-Korean 豫想, 'beforehand' + 'think' — to think ahead) means to anticipate or predict an outcome from reasoning: what you calculate will happen. It is emotionally neutral, which is exactly where it splits from 기대하다 (期待, to look forward to / hope for): you can 예상하다 a bad result, but you would never 기대하다 one, because 기대 carries positive hope. It also differs from 예측하다 (豫測, to forecast), which is more technical/measured (weather, data, trends), whereas 예상하다 is the everyday 'I figured this would happen.' It collocates with -(으)ㄹ 거라고 예상하다, 예상보다, and 예상이 빗나가다. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'expect' covers both neutral prediction AND hopeful looking-forward; in Korean those split, so 'I'm expecting good news (hoping)' is 기대하고 있어요, while 'I expect it'll rain (forecast)' is 비가 올 거라고 예상해요. Picking the wrong one makes you sound oddly hopeful about bad outcomes.

Use 예상해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

예상하다 is a neutral forecast; 기대하다 means you're hoping for / looking forward to it. 'I expect good news' = 기대하고 있어요.
예상해 instead of the natural 예상돼/예상이 가다 for 'it's expected'
When the outcome predicts itself, Korean often uses the passive 예상되다: 큰 변화가 예상돼요 (a big change is expected).
예상에 instead of 예상보다 for comparison
'Better than expected' is 예상보다 좋았어요, using 보다 (than), not 예상에.

Sino-Korean 豫想, 'beforehand' + 'think' — to think ahead. Its neighbors are 기대하다 (期待) and 예측하다 (豫測).

English 'expect' covers both neutral prediction AND hopeful looking-forward; in Korean those split, so 'I'm expecting good news (hoping)' is 기대하고 있어요, while 'I expect it'll rain (forecast)' is 비가 올 거라고 예상해요. Picking the wrong one makes you sound oddly hopeful about bad outcomes.

usagePhrases.note: the polite, blame-free way to admit you misremembered or mixed something up

examples.en: I mistakenly thought today was Saturday.
examples.note: N인 줄 착각하다 = wrongly believe it's N; the key pattern for a false impression

examples.en: Sorry, I mistook you for someone else.
examples.note: A를 B로 착각하다 = mistake A for B; 으로/로 marks who you confused them with

examples.en: I thought the appointment was tomorrow, but I was mistaken.
examples.note: 착각이었어요 = it was a mix-up (noun form); a natural way to wrap up admitting an error

entries.nuance: 착각하다 (Sino-Korean 錯覺, 'mistaken' + 'perception' — literally a misperception) means to hold a wrong belief or impression: you were sure of something — the date, a person's identity, what someone meant — that turned out to be false. It also differs from 오해하다 (誤解, to misunderstand), which is specifically misreading someone's words or intentions, whereas 착각 covers any mistaken impression including facts and identities. It collocates with N인 줄 착각하다, A를 B로 착각하다, and the noun 착각이었어요. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'I made a mistake' as 실수했어요 when you actually mis-thought something — if you got a fact wrong in your mind, it's 착각했어요, not 실수했어요. Use 착각해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 실수하다 when you mean a wrong belief → 착각하다
실수하다 is a careless action-mistake; 착각하다 is thinking something false. 'I thought it was today (but wasn't)' = 착각했어요.

오해하다 is misreading a person's intent/words; 착각하다 is any mistaken impression, including plain facts. They overlap but aren't identical.
다른 사람을 착각했어요 (wrong) → 다른 사람으로 착각했어요

usagePhrases.note: a direct way to ask if someone suspects you; the person doubted takes 을/를

examples.note: N인 줄 알고 의심하다 = suspect it's N; very practical for spam calls and shady offers

examples.romanization: jeoneun geu saram mareul uisimhaji anayo.
examples.en: I don't doubt what that person said.
examples.note: N을/를 의심하다 takes a direct object; here it's 말 (what was said)

examples.en: Don't doubt yourself so much.
examples.note: 자기 자신을 의심하다 = doubt oneself; a kind, encouraging thing to say

entries.nuance: 의심하다 (Sino-Korean 疑心, 'doubt' + 'heart/mind' — a doubting heart) means to be suspicious of, or to doubt the truth, honesty, or safety of someone or something. It is transitive (object + 을/를) and runs from light skepticism about a claim to actively suspecting a person of wrongdoing. The contrast that matters: it is stronger and more pointed than simply being unsure (모르겠다 / 확실하지 않다) — 의심하다 means you positively suspect something is OFF, which is why aiming it at a person can sound accusatory (저를 의심해요? = 'You suspect me?'). It also differs from 믿지 않다 (to not believe), which is flat disbelief, whereas 의심하다 is the active, probing suspicion that something is wrong. It collocates with 눈을 의심하다 (doubt one's eyes), 의심할 여지가 없다, and 의심의 눈으로 보다. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping the object marker — because 의심하다 is transitive you must say 사람을 의심하다 (suspect a person), never 사람이 의심하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 의심하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 의심해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
사람이 의심하다 (wrong) → 사람을 의심하다
의심하다 is transitive, so the person or thing doubted takes 을/를. 사람이 의심하다 would mean 'the person suspects (someone).'
Using 의심하다 for mild uncertainty
If you simply aren't sure, use 확실하지 않다 or 모르겠다. 의심하다 implies active suspicion that something is wrong, and can sound accusatory.
의심하다 vs 믿지 않다 confused
믿지 않다 = flatly not believing; 의심하다 = actively suspecting it's false or dishonest. Choose 의심하다 only when you mean real suspicion.

entries.explanation: 짐작하다 (jimjakhada) means "to guess". Start from the polite form 짐작해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 짐작하다. Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

examples.romanization: pyojeongman bwado museun irinji jimjakal su isseoyo.
examples.en: I can guess what's going on just from your face.

examples.note: 짐작도 안 가다 = can't even guess; the 도…안 form pushes it to 'not at all'

entries.nuance: 짐작하다 is to make an educated guess — to infer or surmise something from limited clues rather than know it outright; you're reading the signs. The sharp contrast is with 찍다 (literally 'to stab/dot,' the slang for picking a multiple-choice answer at random): 짐작하다 is reasoned inference, 찍다 is a blind stab with no basis. It also differs from 추측하다 (Sino-Korean 推測, to conjecture), which is a touch more formal/logical, whereas 짐작하다 is the warm, everyday word and lives especially in the idiom 짐작이 가다 ('a guess comes to me' = I can imagine / I have a hunch), far more common in speech than the plain 짐작하다. It collocates with 대충 짐작이 가다, 짐작했던 대로, and the negative 짐작도 안 가다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 짐작하다 for a pure random guess on a quiz — that situation needs 찍다; reserve 짐작하다 for when you're actually inferring from evidence, and prefer 짐작이 가요 over 짐작해요 in conversation.

In speech the idiom 짐작이 가다 is far more natural for 'I can imagine / I have a hunch': 대충 짐작이 가요.

usagePhrases.note: 떠올려 보다 = try to bring to mind; a gentle prompt to jog someone's memory

examples.en: I tried to bring back the memory of that time.

examples.romanization: i sajineul bomyeon yennal saenggageul tteoollige dwaeyo.
examples.en: Looking at this photo makes me recall the old days.

entries.nuance: 떠올리다 is the transitive partner of 떠오르다 (it's the causative 'make it float up'): YOU deliberately call a memory, image, or idea to mind — 기억을 떠올리다 means you do the recalling, with the object marked 을/를. The all-important contrast is exactly with 떠오르다, where the thought surfaces on its own (기억이 떠올라요, marked 이/가): 떠올리다 = active effort, 떠오르다 = it happens to you, and the particle is your tell. It also differs from 기억하다 (記憶, plain 'to remember / retain in memory'): 떠올리다 is the vivid act of conjuring up an image or scene in the moment, while 기억하다 is the steady storage/retention of information. It collocates with 기억을/얼굴을/생각을 떠올리다 and 떠올려 보다. The English-speaker pitfall is swapping it with 떠오르다 because English 'X comes to mind' and 'I bring X to mind' aren't clearly split — in Korean the particle decides: 생각을 떠올리다 (you recall) vs 생각이 떠오르다 (it pops up).

Use 떠올려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

For something surfacing on its own, the natural verb is simply 떠오르다, not a passive of 떠올리다.

entries.nuance: 알아차리다 (built from 알다 'know' + 차리다 'gather/pull together one's senses') is to notice or catch on — to suddenly become aware of something through perception: a shift in mood, a mistake, someone's hidden intention. It's about detection, not analysis; you sense it and it registers in an instant. The sharp contrast is with 깨닫다 (to realize a fact or truth, often deeper and more reflective): 알아차리다 is the quick 'oh, I noticed that,' while 깨닫다 is the weightier 'I came to understand.' It also outpaces plain 알다 (to know), which is the ongoing state of knowing, not the moment of catching on. It pairs with 눈치 (social awareness) — 눈치를 알아차리다 / 눈치채다 — and with 바로/금방 알아차리다 and 못 알아차리다. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as plain 알다: 'I knew' is 알았어요, but 'I noticed/caught on' is specifically 알아차렸어요, the flash of detection rather than the steady knowing.

알아차리다 = quick sensory noticing (the mood, a mistake); 깨닫다 = deeper realization of a truth. Don't use them interchangeably.
안 알아차렸어요 vs 못 알아차렸어요
For failing to notice, 못 (couldn't/didn't catch) is far more natural than 안: 아무도 못 알아차렸어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 되돌아보다 means "to look back on" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 되돌아보다 (doedoraboda) means "to look back on". Start from the polite form 되돌아봐요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 되돌아보다. A strong first sentence is 지난 한 해를 되돌아봤어요 ("I looked back on the past year"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 되돌아보다 also becomes 되돌아보고 싶어요 (want), 되돌아볼 수 있어요 (can), and 되돌아볼 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 되돌아보다 is to reflect on or look back over the past — your year, your choices, a relationship — usually to draw a lesson or feeling from it. The 되- prefix adds a 'back, again' nuance, so it's more reflective and complete than plain 돌아보다 (to turn and look around, which can be literal). The sharp contrast is with 후회하다 (後悔, to regret): 되돌아보다 is the calm, even-handed act of reviewing the past, which may lead to a lesson but isn't inherently negative, whereas 후회하다 is specifically wishing you'd done otherwise. It also differs from 반성하다 (反省, to self-reflect with remorse over a fault), which carries 'I did wrong and resolve to fix it'; 되돌아보다 is broader and gentler. It collocates with 지난 한 해를 되돌아보다, 삶을/지나온 길을 되돌아보다, and 되돌아볼 필요가 있다. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for physically turning your head to look behind — that's 돌아보다 or 뒤를 돌아보다; 되돌아보다 is overwhelmingly about reflecting on the past.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 되돌아보다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 되돌아봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 되돌아보다 for physically turning to look behind → 돌아보다
For literally glancing back over your shoulder, say 뒤를 돌아보다. 되돌아보다 is almost always figurative reflection on the past.
되돌아보다 vs 후회하다 confused
되돌아보다 is neutral review of the past; 후회하다 is specifically regretting it. You can 되돌아보다 happy memories, but you wouldn't 후회하다 them.
되돌아보다 vs 반성하다
반성하다 (反省) implies remorse over a fault and resolve to improve; 되돌아보다 is broader, gentler reflection without the built-in guilt.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 되돌아보다 becomes 되돌아볼 수 있어요 ("can") and 되돌아볼 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 되돌아보다 is to reflect on or look back over the past — your year, your choices, a relationship — usually to draw a lesson or feeling from it. It collocates with 지난 한 해를 되돌아보다, 삶을/지나온 길을 되돌아보다, and 되돌아볼 필요가 있다.

The sharp contrast is with 후회하다 (to regret): 되돌아보다 is the calm, even-handed act of reviewing the past, which may lead to a lesson but isn't inherently negative, whereas 후회하다 is specifically wishing you'd done otherwise. It also differs from 반성하다 (to self-reflect with remorse over a fault), which carries 'I did wrong and resolve to fix it'; 되돌아보다 is broader and gentler.
The 되- prefix adds a 'back, again' nuance, so it's more reflective and complete than plain 돌아보다 (to turn and look around, which can be literal). Its neighbors are 후회하다 (後悔) and 반성하다 (反省).
The pitfall is using it for physically turning your head to look behind — that's 돌아보다 or 뒤를 돌아보다; 되돌아보다 is overwhelmingly about reflecting on the past.

entries.shortExplanation: 바뀌다 means "to change, to be switched" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to change, to be switched" in Korean is 바뀌다 (bakkwida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 바뀌어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 바뀌다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 비밀번호가 바뀌었어요. ("The password changed.") — then reshape the same stem into 바뀌고 싶어요 (desire), 바뀔 수 있어요 (ability), and 바뀔 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 바뀌어요. Then practice 안 바뀌어요 vs 바뀔 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.
survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.en: I do not change, to be switched.
I want to change, to be switched.
I can change, to be switched.
I have to change, to be switched.

usagePhrases.note: 바뀌다 = something gets switched/replaced by something else. The thing that changes takes 이/가, never 을/를.

examples.en: The meeting time got changed to 3 o'clock.
examples.note: Super common at work — schedules and times 'get changed' on you; note 3시로 with (으)로.

examples.en: Oh, the shop's name changed.
examples.note: ~네요 adds a 'huh, I just noticed' tone — natural the moment you spot a change.

examples.en: The plan might change again.
examples.note: 또 (again) + 바뀌다 is the everyday way to warn that things aren't fixed yet.

entries.nuance: 바뀌다 is the intransitive twin of 바꾸다: the thing that changes is itself the subject (이/가) and nobody is named as the doer, so it covers things getting switched, replaced, or mixed up on their own. The dividing line vs 변하다 is key — 변하다 means a thing's inner nature transforms (사람이 변했다 = he's become a different person), while 바뀌다 means one item is swapped out for another (번호가 바뀌었다 = the number was replaced). Use 바꾸다 when YOU actively swap something (번호를 바꿨어요) and 바뀌다 when it simply ends up different (번호가 바뀌었어요). The 요-form is 바뀌어요 because the stem ends in the vowel 위, which won't contract — so spelling matters: it's 바뀌-, and the polite past is 바뀌었어요, never the wrong 바껴요/바꼈어요 that English speakers reach for by analogy.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 바뀌다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 바뀌어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 바뀌다 transitively — '번호를 바뀌었어요' is wrong because 바뀌다 has no object. If YOU did it, use 바꾸다: 번호를 바꿨어요.
Don't write the polite form as 바껴요 or the past as 바꼈어요; the 바뀌- stem keeps its 위 and gives 바뀌어요 / 바뀌었어요.
Don't blur 바뀌다 and 변하다: 마음이 바뀌었어요 = I changed my mind (switched decisions), but 마음이 변했어요 = my feelings have transformed (e.g., fallen out of love).

lesson.canDo: Use 바뀌어요 in a real beginner sentence, then change it into want, can, cannot, and have-to forms without losing the basic meaning.
studyFlow: Say 바뀌어요 first. This is the safest spoken form for most beginner situations.
Add one useful frame: 비밀번호가 바뀌었어요.. Read the Hangul first, then check the romanization.
Practice the contrast between 안 바뀌어요 and 바뀔 수 없어요.

lesson.teacherNote: Do not ask a beginner to memorize all 15 forms at once. Teach 바뀌어요 first, then add one communicative need: desire (바뀌고 싶어요), possibility (바뀔 수 있어요), or limitation (바뀔 수 없어요).
lesson.pronunciationTip: 바뀌다 is written bakkwida. In real sentences, compare the audio with the romanization because Korean sound changes can cross syllable blocks.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 바뀌어요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 바뀌다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 비밀번호가 바뀌었어요.. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 안 바뀌어요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 바뀔 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 바뀌어요 feels easy, practice 바뀌고 싶어요, 바뀔 수 있어요, and 바뀌어야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

classroomScript: Teacher says: 바뀌어요. Learner repeats three times.
Teacher asks a yes/no question with 비밀번호가 바뀌었어요. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 안 바뀌어요, then 바뀔 수 없어요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

entries.shortExplanation: 달라지다 means "to become different, to change" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 달라지다 (dallajida) = "to become different, to change". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 달라져요 plus one useful sentence like 분위기가 완전히 달라졌어요. ("The atmosphere became completely different."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 달라지고 싶어요 for what you want, 달라질 수 있어요 for what you can, 달라질 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 달라져요. Then practice 안 달라져요 vs 달라질 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

usagePhrases.en: I do not become different, to change.
I want to become different, to change.
I can become different, to change.
I have to become different, to change.

usagePhrases.note: 달라지다 = end up noticeably different from before. Built from 다르다 (be different) + -아지다.

examples.en: Did you cut your hair? You look different.
examples.note: Great compliment-ish line — 느낌이 달라지다 = the vibe/impression changed.

examples.en: Now that I've lived here, my thinking has changed a lot.
examples.note: Use for gradual inner change — 생각이/가치관이 달라지다.

examples.en: The rules will be different starting next year.
examples.note: Common in notices about policies, fees, or schedules changing.

entries.nuance: 달라지다 spotlights the before-and-after gap: something is now clearly unlike how it used to be, which makes it the everyday verb for noticing change in a person's looks, mood, or a situation. It's the inchoative of the adjective 다르다 (to be different) — 다르 + -아지다 'become' — and that origin is the #1 pitfall: 다르다 states a static difference between two things (A는 B와 달라요 = A is different from B), while 달라지다 is the dynamic act of becoming different over time (분위기가 달라졌어요 = the mood changed). It overlaps with 변하다 and 바뀌다, but the dividing line is focus: 달라지다 = 'the result looks different now,' 변하다 = 'the inner nature transformed,' 바뀌다 = 'one thing got swapped for another.' Both 달라지다 and the thing changing take 이/가; the form 달라져요 comes from -지다 verbs taking 어 in the 요-form (지+어 → 져).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 달라지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 달라져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't confuse it with 다르다 — 다르다 is an adjective for a static difference (저는 형과 성격이 달라요), while 달라지다 is a verb for becoming different (성격이 달라졌어요).
It's intransitive, so don't attach 을/를: say 생각이 달라졌어요, not 생각을 달라졌어요. To deliberately change something, use 바꾸다.
Don't say the present as 달라요 when you mean 'is changing'; 달라요 = 'is different (now)', 달라지고 있어요 = 'is becoming different'.

entries.english: to increase, to grow, to stretch out
entries.shortExplanation: 늘어나다 means "to increase, to grow, to stretch out" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 늘어나다 (neureonada) means "to increase, to grow, to stretch out". Start from the polite form 늘어나요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 늘어나다. A strong first sentence is 요즘 일이 많이 늘어났어요. ("My workload has grown a lot lately."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 늘어나다 also becomes 늘어나고 싶어요 (want), 늘어날 수 있어요 (can), and 늘어날 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 늘어나요. Then practice 안 늘어나요 vs 늘어날 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

usagePhrases.en: I increase, to grow, to stretch out.
I do not increase, to grow, to stretch out.
I want to increase, to grow, to stretch out.
I can increase, to grow, to stretch out.
I have to increase, to grow, to stretch out.
My workload has grown a lot lately.
usagePhrases.note: 늘어나다 = an amount/number gets bigger. A touch more vivid and visual than plain 늘다.

examples.en: The foreign-resident population keeps growing.
examples.note: 점점 + 늘어나고 있어요 = 'is gradually increasing' — common in news and small talk.

examples.en: My card bill suddenly went up.
examples.note: Money talk: 지출이/요금이 늘어나다 (expenses/fees increase).

examples.en: If you practice, your vocabulary will naturally grow.
examples.note: Encouraging line about skills/knowledge increasing.

entries.nuance: 늘어나다 means a quantity, number, or length gets bigger, and it feels more concrete and visual than its plainer synonym 늘다 — picture something physically stretching or a count climbing on a screen. The contrast worth memorizing: 늘다 vs 늘어나다 are near-interchangeable for amounts, but only 늘어나다 carries the physical 'stretch out and lose shape' meaning (니트가 늘어났어요), while only 늘다 is used for a skill improving (실력이 늘다, not 늘어나다). It's intransitive — the growing thing takes 이/가 — so if YOU increase something on purpose you must switch to the transitive 늘리다 (시간을 늘리다 = extend the time). The big English-speaker trap is treating 'increase' as transitive: 'I increased my savings' is 저축을 늘렸어요 with 늘리다, but 'my savings increased' is 저축이 늘어났어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 늘어나다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 늘어나요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't pair it with 을/를 as if it were transitive — say 일이 늘어났어요, not 일을 늘어났어요. Use 늘리다 when you actively increase something.
Don't use 늘어나다 for a skill getting better; that's 늘다: 한국어가 많이 늘었어요 (not 늘어났어요).
Don't confuse 늘어나다 (to increase) with 늘어서다 (to line up in a row) or 늘어지다 (to droop/sag); they look alike but mean different things.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 늘어나다 becomes 늘어날 수 있어요 ("can") and 늘어날 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: 늘어나다 means a quantity, number, or length gets bigger, and it feels more concrete and visual than its plainer synonym 늘다 — picture something physically stretching or a count climbing on a screen.

The contrast worth memorizing: 늘다 vs 늘어나다 are near-interchangeable for amounts, but only 늘어나다 carries the physical 'stretch out and lose shape' meaning (니트가 늘어났어요), while only 늘다 is used for a skill improving (실력이 늘다, not 늘어나다).

It's intransitive — the growing thing takes 이/가 — so if YOU increase something on purpose you must switch to the transitive 늘리다 (시간을 늘리다 = extend the time). The big English-speaker trap is treating 'increase' as transitive: 'I increased my savings' is 저축을 늘렸어요 with 늘리다, but 'my savings increased' is 저축이 늘어났어요.

entries.english: to decrease, to shrink, to dwindle
entries.shortExplanation: 줄어들다 means "to decrease, to shrink, to dwindle" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to decrease, to shrink, to dwindle" in Korean is 줄어들다 (jureodeulda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 줄어들어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 줄어들다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 스트레스가 많이 줄어들었어요. ("My stress has gone down a lot.") — then reshape the same stem into 줄어들고 싶어요 (desire), 줄어들 수 있어요 (ability), and 줄어들 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 줄어들어요. Then practice 안 줄어들어요 vs 줄어들 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

usagePhrases.note: 줄어들다 = an amount/pressure gets smaller. More vivid and gradual-feeling than plain 줄다.

examples.en: Customers suddenly dropped off.
examples.note: Business small talk — 손님이/매출이 줄어들다.

examples.en: My weight is gradually going down.
examples.note: 조금씩 + 줄어들고 있어요 = 'is decreasing little by little'.

examples.en: If you move somewhere with cheaper rent, the burden will lessen.

entries.nuance: 줄어들다 means a quantity, size, or pressure shrinks, and it feels more vivid and gradual than its plainer synonym 줄다 — you can almost watch the number sliding down. It's the exact opposite of 늘어나다, and like that verb it pairs naturally with 점점/계속/조금씩 for a 'bit by bit' feel. Crucially it's a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ-탈락) stem: the final ㄹ of 들- drops before the ㅂ of -ㅂ니다 and before -(으) endings, giving 줄어듭니다 and 줄어드세요 — but it stays before vowel endings, so the 요-form is 줄어들어요 and the past is 줄어들었어요. It's intransitive, the shrinking thing taking 이/가; when YOU reduce something on purpose, switch to the transitive 줄이다 (소리를 줄이다 = turn the volume down, 양을 줄이다 = cut the portion). The classic English trap is using one word for both: 비용이 줄어들었어요 = the cost went down, but 비용을 줄였어요 = I cut the cost.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 줄어들다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 줄어들어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't write the formal form as 줄어들습니다 — the ㄹ drops before ㅂ, so it's 줄어듭니다.
Don't use it transitively: say 비용이 줄어들었어요 (the cost decreased), but 비용을 줄였어요 (I reduced the cost) with 줄이다.
Don't drop the ㄹ before a vowel ending — the past is 줄어들었어요, not 줄어었어요.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 줄어들어 and 줄어들어요 together.

entries.shortExplanation: 사라지다 means "to disappear, to vanish" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 사라지다 (sarajida) = "to disappear, to vanish". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 사라져요 plus one useful sentence like 지갑이 갑자기 사라졌어요. ("My wallet suddenly disappeared."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 사라지고 싶어요 for what you want, 사라질 수 있어요 for what you can, 사라질 수 없어요 for what you can't. I want to disappear, to vanish.
I have to disappear, to vanish.

usagePhrases.note: 사라지다 = something is gone / no longer there. The lost thing takes 이/가.

examples.en: It vanished right before my eyes.
examples.note: 눈앞에서 사라지다 = vanish from sight; 갑자기 emphasizes the suddenness.

examples.en: That cafe was gone within a year.
examples.note: Used for shops/places closing down and vanishing from the neighborhood; 1년 만에 = in just a year.

examples.en: Your worries will soon disappear.
examples.note: Comforting line — pairs an abstract subject (걱정) with the future 사라질 거예요.

entries.nuance: 사라지다 means something stops being present — it's gone from sight or from existence — and it works for objects, people, places, and even feelings like worry or pain. The synonym to weigh it against is 없어지다: both mean 'become gone,' but 사라지다 is more dramatic and visual, implying a clean, often sudden vanishing (지갑이 사라졌어요 = it mysteriously vanished), whereas 없어지다 is plainer and often just means 'ran out / ceased to exist' (돈이 없어졌어요 = the money's gone). It's strictly intransitive — there's no one 'doing' the disappearing, so the vanished thing is the subject (이/가). The form 사라져요 follows the -지다 pattern (지 + 어 → 져). The English trap is the transitive 'make it disappear': Korean has no transitive 사라지다, so you must use 없애다 (get rid of) or 지우다 (erase/delete) instead.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 사라지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 사라져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use it transitively — you can't 'disappear something'. To make something gone, use 없애다 (얼룩을 없애 주세요) or 지우다 (파일을 지웠어요).
Don't default to 사라지다 for 'I ran out of X'; that's usually 없어지다 or 떨어지다: 우유가 떨어졌어요 (we're out of milk).
Don't confuse 사라지다 (to vanish) with 사다 (to buy); they only share the first syllable.

entries.shortExplanation: 생기다 means "to come up, to arise, to form, to get" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 생기다 (saenggida) means "to come up, to arise, to form, to get". Start from the polite form 생겨요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 생기다. A strong first sentence is 갑자기 일이 생겼어요. ("Something came up suddenly."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 생기다 also becomes 생기고 싶어요 (want), 생길 수 있어요 (can), and 생길 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

I do not come up, to arise, to form, to get.
I want to come up, to arise, to form, to get.
I can come up, to arise, to form, to get.
I have to come up, to arise, to form, to get.

usagePhrases.note: 일이 생기다 = an errand/issue comes up — the #1 polite excuse for canceling plans.

examples.en: I got another pimple.
examples.note: For skin/body marks: 여드름이/멍이 생기다 ('a pimple/bruise forms').

examples.en: Did you get a boyfriend?
examples.note: Casual but super common — 애인이/여자친구가 생기다 = 'to get a partner'.

examples.en: If a problem comes up, contact me right away.
examples.note: 문제가 생기다 = a problem arises; the conditional 생기면 is everyday phrasing.

entries.nuance: 생기다 covers a surprisingly wide range tied by one idea — something comes into being on its own: a thing appearing (가게가 생기다), an event or issue arising (일이/문제가 생기다), or a person 'getting' something they didn't have (돈이/시간이/애인이 생기다). The crucial pitfall for English speakers is that even when English says 'get,' 생기다 is intransitive, so what you acquire takes 이/가, not 을/를: 시간이 생겼어요, never 시간을 생겼어요. Contrast it with two relatives: 생기다 = something newly comes to exist, while 만들어지다 = something gets made/created by a process, and 받다 = you actively receive something handed to you (선물을 받다, with 을/를). Note too the unrelated second sense 'to look (a certain way)': 잘생기다 = good-looking, 못생기다 = plain — here 생기다 describes appearance, not appearance-into-existence.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 생기다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 생겨요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't translate 'I got X' with 을/를 — it's 시간이 생겼어요 (I got time), not 시간을 생겼어요.
When canceling, '일이 생겼어요' is the natural set excuse; learners over-explain instead of using it.
Don't say 만들어요 when something just appears — 새 카페가 생겼어요 (a new cafe popped up), not 만들었어요 (which means somebody built it).

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 생기다 becomes 생길 수 있어요 ("can") and 생길 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 생기다 covers a surprisingly wide range tied by one idea — something comes into being on its own: a thing appearing (가게가 생기다), an event or issue arising (일이/문제가 생기다), or a person 'getting' something they didn't have (돈이/시간이/애인이 생기다). Note too the unrelated second sense 'to look (a certain way)': 잘생기다 = good-looking, 못생기다 = plain — here 생기다 describes appearance, not appearance-into-existence.
Contrast it with two relatives: 생기다 = something newly comes to exist, while 만들어지다 = something gets made/created by a process, and 받다 = you actively receive something handed to you (선물을 받다, with 을/를).
The crucial pitfall for English speakers is that even when English says 'get,' 생기다 is intransitive, so what you acquire takes 이/가, not 을/를: 시간이 생겼어요, never 시간을 생겼어요.

entries.english: to break down, to get ruined
entries.shortExplanation: 망가지다 means "to break down, to get ruined" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

entries.nuance: 망가지다 means something is damaged to the point it no longer works or holds its shape, and it's broader than its near-synonym 고장나다 — that word is specifically about machines/devices ceasing to function (시계가 고장났어요), whereas 망가지다 adds the nuance of physical wreckage and also stretches to objects, plans, health, and routines falling apart. So a phone that simply won't turn on is more naturally 고장났어요, but a phone with a smashed body is 망가졌어요. Use 망가져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use it transitively — say 핸드폰이 망가졌어요 (the phone broke), but 핸드폰을 망가뜨렸어요 / 망쳤어요 when YOU broke it.
For a pure machine malfunction with no visible damage, 고장났어요 is more natural; reserve 망가지다 for real wreckage or 'falling apart'.
Don't use 망가지다 for brittle things shattering — a cup that smashes is 깨졌어요, not 망가졌어요.

Don't swap it with 쓰러지다 — a fainting person is 쓰러졌어요, not 무너졌어요; 무너지다 implies breaking apart, not just toppling.
Don't use 마음이 무너지다 for mild disappointment; it's strong, for heartbreak-level moments. For 'a bit let down' use 실망했어요.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 깨지다 becomes 깨질 수 있어요 ("can") and 깨질 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 깨지다 is the verb for hard, brittle things shattering or cracking — glass, dishes, phone screens, eggs. Figuratively it covers promises, deals, records, and moods 'breaking' (약속이/기록이/분위기가 깨지다), and in casual speech 둘이 깨졌어 means a couple split up.
The key is matching the verb to the material: it contrasts with 부러지다 (long, rigid things snapping: 팔이/연필이 부러지다) and 찢어지다 (paper or fabric tearing: 종이가/옷이 찢어지다).

It's intransitive (the broken thing takes 이/가); to smash something yourself, use the transitive 깨다 (컵을 깼어요 = I broke the cup) — note the e/ae spelling difference, 깨다 vs 깨지다. The 요-form is 깨져요 (지 + 어 → 져).
English speakers habitually say 'I broke the glass' with the intransitive form; you must use 깨다 when there's an agent.

entries.english: to burst, to explode, to go off
entries.shortExplanation: 터지다 means "to burst, to explode, to go off" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to burst, to explode, to go off" in Korean is 터지다 (teojida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 터져요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 터지다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 여기는 와이파이가 잘 안 터져요. ("The Wi-Fi barely works here.") — then reshape the same stem into 터지고 싶어요 (desire), 터질 수 있어요 (ability), and 터질 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 터져요. Then practice 안 터져요 vs 터질 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.
survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.en: I burst, to explode, to go off.
I do not burst, to explode, to go off.
I want to burst, to explode, to go off.
I can burst, to explode, to go off.
I have to burst, to explode, to go off.

usagePhrases.note: 터지다 = (signal) comes through. 와이파이/인터넷/데이터가 터지다 is the everyday way to say a signal works.

examples.en: It's a basement, so my phone has no signal.
examples.note: 폰이 안 터지다 = 'no reception' — essential for cafes, subways, basements.

examples.en: My blister popped and it hurts.
examples.note: For body stuff — 물집이/혈관이 터지다.

examples.en: I suddenly burst out laughing.
examples.note: 웃음이 터지다 = laughter erupts; you can't hold it in — a fixed, very natural phrase.

entries.nuance: 터지다 literally means to burst or explode — balloons, blisters, pipes, fireworks — but two everyday uses dominate life in Korea and trip up learners. First, signal coverage: 와이파이/폰이 터지다 means the signal works, and crucially 안 터져요 = 'no reception' (not 'it doesn't explode'!). Second, emotions and events erupting: 화가/웃음이/울음이 터지다 (anger/laughter/tears burst out), and 사건이 터지다 (a scandal breaks). Compare it with the milder 깨지다 (brittle things crack) — 터지다 implies internal pressure blowing outward, while 깨지다 implies a fracture from impact. It's intransitive (the bursting thing takes 이/가); to set something off or pop it yourself, use the transitive 터뜨리다 (풍선을 터뜨리다). The 요-form is 터져요 (지 + 어 → 져).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 터지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 터져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
For phone reception, '안 터져요' means 'no signal' — don't say 안 돼요, which is vaguer and could mean many things.
Don't use it transitively — say 풍선이 터졌어요 (the balloon popped), but 풍선을 터뜨렸어요 when YOU popped it.
Don't translate 'burst out laughing' literally with 웃다; the idiom is 웃음이 터졌어요 (laughter burst out), with 웃음 as the subject.

lesson.canDo: Use 터져요 in a real beginner sentence, then change it into want, can, cannot, and have-to forms without losing the basic meaning.
studyFlow: Say 터져요 first. This is the safest spoken form for most beginner situations.
Add one useful frame: 여기는 와이파이가 잘 안 터져요.. Read the Hangul first, then check the romanization.
Practice the contrast between 안 터져요 and 터질 수 없어요.

lesson.teacherNote: Do not ask a beginner to memorize all 15 forms at once. Teach 터져요 first, then add one communicative need: desire (터지고 싶어요), possibility (터질 수 있어요), or limitation (터질 수 없어요).
lesson.pronunciationTip: 터지다 is written teojida. In real sentences, compare the audio with the romanization because Korean sound changes can cross syllable blocks.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 터져요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 터지다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 여기는 와이파이가 잘 안 터져요.. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 안 터져요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 터질 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 터져요 feels easy, practice 터지고 싶어요, 터질 수 있어요, and 터져야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

classroomScript: Teacher says: 터져요. Learner repeats three times.
Teacher asks a yes/no question with 여기는 와이파이가 잘 안 터져요. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 안 터져요, then 터질 수 없어요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

entries.explanation: 멎다 (meotda) = "to stop, to cease (rain, bleeding)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 멎어요 plus one useful sentence like 비가 멎었어요. examples.en: I'll head out once the snow stops.
examples.note: Conditional 멎으면 = 'once it stops' — natural for weather; note 멎으면 takes the 으 linker after the ㅈ-batchim.

examples.en: I was so startled my heart felt like it stopped.
examples.note: 심장이 멎다 = heart stops; the set phrase 멎는 줄 알았어요 = 'I thought it would stop'.

examples.en: The sound of rain stopped only after a long while.
examples.note: Slightly literary; 멎다 has a quieter, more natural feel than 멈추다.

entries.nuance: 멎다 means something flowing or continuous comes to a halt by itself — rain, snow, wind, bleeding, a heartbeat, breath. It overlaps with the much more common 멈추다 (to stop), but the dividing line is scope and tone: 멈추다 is the general word and works for machines, cars, and people stopping (차가 멈췄어요, 발걸음을 멈췄어요), while 멎다 is narrower, quieter, and a touch literary, reserved for natural or bodily processes ceasing on their own. So rain can be either 멎다 or 멈추다, but a car can only 멈추다, never 멎다. It's strictly intransitive and never takes an object; for stopping a vehicle or machine yourself you'd use 멈추다 or 세우다 (차를 세우다). One pronunciation note: the ㅈ-batchim means vowel endings add the 으/어 linker — hence 멎어요, 멎으면, 멎을 거예요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 멎다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 멎어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 멎다 for vehicles or machines — say 차가 멈췄어요 (the car stopped), not 차가 멎었어요.
It's intransitive, so don't add 을/를: 피가 멎었어요 (the bleeding stopped), not 피를 멎었어요. To stop something yourself, use 멈추다/세우다.
Don't drop the linking vowel — it's 멎으면 / 멎을 거예요 (with 으 after the ㅈ batchim), not 멎면 / 멎ㄹ 거예요.

entries.english: to continue, to be connected, to lead to
entries.shortExplanation: 이어지다 means "to continue, to be connected, to lead to" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 이어지다 (ieojida) means "to continue, to be connected, to lead to". Start from the polite form 이어져요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 이어지다. A strong first sentence is 이 길은 시장으로 이어져요. ("This road leads to the market."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 이어지다 also becomes 이어지고 싶어요 (want), 이어질 수 있어요 (can), and 이어질 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 이어져요. Then practice 안 이어져요 vs 이어질 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

I do not continue, to be connected, to lead to.
I want to continue, to be connected, to lead to.
I can continue, to be connected, to lead to.
I have to continue, to be connected, to lead to.
This road leads to the market.
usagePhrases.note: 이어지다 = one thing connects/continues to another. Often with ~(으)로 (leads to) or ~까지 (continues until).

examples.en: The heat will continue into next week.
examples.note: Weather forecasts love this — 폭염이/장마가 이어지다; ~까지 marks how long it runs.

examples.en: The meeting dragged on until evening.
examples.note: 이어지다 = an event runs on longer than expected, without stopping.

examples.en: The accident led to major damage.
examples.note: ~(으)로 이어지다 for a cause leading to a (often serious) result.

entries.nuance: 이어지다 means something continues without breaking, or one thing connects into another — a road leading somewhere (길이 ~로 이어지다), weather persisting (더위가 이어지다), a conversation flowing on, or a cause leading to a result (X로 이어지다). It's the intransitive partner of 잇다 (to connect/join), so when you actively link things you switch to 잇다 or the compound 이어 가다 (전통을 이어 가다 = to carry on a tradition). The synonym to weigh is 계속되다 (to continue): the two overlap for duration (회의가 이어지다/계속되다 are both fine), but only 이어지다 carries the spatial 'connects to / leads to' sense — a road 이어지다 to a place, never 계속되다 there. The connected thing takes 이/가, and for 'leads to a result' the new state takes (으)로, not 에. The 요-form is 이어져요 (지 + 어 → 져).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 이어지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 이어져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use it transitively — say 대화가 이어졌어요 (the conversation continued), but 대화를 이어 갔어요 when someone keeps it going (이어 가다).
For 'leads to a result,' use the particle (으)로: 노력이 성공으로 이어졌어요, not 성공에 이어졌어요.
Don't swap it with 계속되다 for spatial connection — a road that runs to the station is 역으로 이어져요, not 계속돼요.

entries.english: to throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves)
entries.shortExplanation: 두근거리다 means "to throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves)" in Korean is 두근거리다 (dugeungeorida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 두근거려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 두근거리다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 가슴이 두근거리다 ("for one's heart to pound") — then reshape the same stem into 두근거리고 싶어요 (desire), 두근거릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 두근거릴 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 두근거려요. Then practice 두근거리지 않아요 vs 두근거릴 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.
survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.en: I throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves).
I do not throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves).
I want to throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves).
I can throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves).
I have to throb / for one's heart to pound (with excitement or nerves).

usagePhrases.note: The default subject is 가슴(이) or 심장(이) — the heart, never the person. Say 가슴이 두근거려요, not 저는 두근거려요.

examples.en: My heart is going thump-thump.
examples.note: The simplest form: the mimetic 두근두근 + 하다. Kids and adults both say this.

examples.en: It's right before my presentation, so my heart is racing.
examples.note: 심장이 두근거리다 and 가슴이 두근거리다 are interchangeable; 가슴 sounds a touch softer and more everyday.

examples.ko: 내일 그 사람 만난다고 생각하니까 벌써 두근거려.
examples.romanization: naeil geu saram mannandago saenggakanikka beolsseo dugeungeoryeo.
examples.en: Just thinking about meeting them tomorrow, my heart's already fluttering.
examples.note: Casual 두근거려 to a close friend, with the subject 가슴 left unspoken because context makes it obvious.

entries.nuance: 두근거리다 names the physical sensation of a pounding, fluttering heartbeat, built from the mimetic 두근 ('thump') + the repetitive-motion suffix -거리다, so its grammatical subject is 가슴/심장 and the person is marked with -은/는 or a cause phrase, never as the doer. It spans the whole range from giddy anticipation to dread, so Koreans lean on partners — 설레서 두근거리다 for good nerves, 긴장돼서 두근거리다 for bad — to pin down which. Its close cousin 떨리다 also means 'tremble/be nervous' but centres on shakiness rather than the heartbeat itself, and 설레다 names the emotion while 두근거리다 names the bodily symptom of it. The English-speaker trap is treating it like 'I'm excited' and saying 저는 두근거려요; let the heart be the subject (가슴이 두근거려요), or switch to 저는 설레요 when you mean the feeling.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 두근거리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 두근거려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 저는 두근거려요 to mean 'I'm excited' — the heart is the subject, so use 가슴이 두근거려요 (or 저는 설레요 if you mean the feeling).
Imperative/propositive forms like 두근거리세요 are grammatically possible but sound odd in real life, since you can't really order someone's heart to pound.
Reaching for 두근거리다 as a generic 'be excited'; it only describes the heartbeat, so 신나다/설레다 are the words for the actual mood.

lesson.canDo: Use 두근거려요 in a real beginner sentence, then change it into want, can, cannot, and have-to forms without losing the basic meaning.
studyFlow: Say 두근거려요 first. This is the safest spoken form for most beginner situations.
Add one useful frame: 가슴이 두근거리다. Read the Hangul first, then check the romanization.
Practice the contrast between 두근거리지 않아요 and 두근거릴 수 없어요.
