lesson.teacherNote: Do not ask a beginner to memorize all 15 forms at once. Teach 두근거려요 first, then add one communicative need: desire (두근거리고 싶어요), possibility (두근거릴 수 있어요), or limitation (두근거릴 수 없어요).
lesson.pronunciationTip: 두근거리다 is written dugeungeorida. In real sentences, compare the audio with the romanization because Korean sound changes can cross syllable blocks.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 두근거려요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 두근거리다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 가슴이 두근거리다. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 두근거리지 않아요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 두근거릴 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 두근거려요 feels easy, practice 두근거리고 싶어요, 두근거릴 수 있어요, and 두근거려야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

classroomScript: Teacher says: 두근거려요. Learner repeats three times.
Teacher asks a yes/no question with 가슴이 두근거리다. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 두근거리지 않아요, then 두근거릴 수 없어요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 두근거리다 becomes 두근거릴 수 있어요 ("can") and 두근거릴 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

Its close cousin 떨리다 also means 'tremble/be nervous' but centres on shakiness rather than the heartbeat itself. 설레다 names the emotion while 두근거리다 names the bodily symptom of it.

entries.english: to miss / to long for (someone or something absent)
entries.shortExplanation: 그립다 means "to miss / to long for (someone or something absent)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 그립다 (geuripda) = "to miss / to long for (someone or something absent)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 그리워요 plus one useful sentence like 고향이 그립다 ("to miss one's hometown"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 그리워하고 싶어요 for what you want, 그리울 수 있어요 for what you can, 그리울 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 그리워요. Then practice 그립지 않아요 vs 그리울 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

usagePhrases.en: I miss / to long for (someone or something absent).
I do not miss / to long for (someone or something absent).
I want to miss / to long for (someone or something absent).
I can miss / to long for (someone or something absent).
I have to miss / to long for (someone or something absent).

usagePhrases.note: 그립다 is an adjective, so what you miss takes -이/가, not -을/를: 고향이 그리워요, never 고향을 그리워요.

examples.en: I miss my hometown.
examples.note: The base pattern: the thing missed takes -이/가, and ㅂ-irregular 그립- + -어요 gives 그리워요.

examples.ko: 한국에 산 지 일 년 됐는데 가끔 엄마 음식이 그리워요.
examples.romanization: hanguge san ji il nyeon dwaenneunde gakkeum eomma eumsigi geuriwoyo.
examples.en: It's been a year living in Korea, and sometimes I miss my mom's cooking.
examples.note: Everyday expat use; you can long for food and places, not only people.

examples.en: I missed my friend so much that I made a video call.
examples.note: 그리워서 (because I missed) drives a real action. To say someone else actively misses, you'd switch to 그리워하다.

entries.nuance: 그립다 is an adjective expressing your own felt longing, so the thing you miss is the subject (-이/가) and you cannot hang a direct object on it; to describe a third person missing something ('he misses home') Korean shifts to the verb 그리워하다, because Korean treats adjectives of feeling as reportable only from the inside. The sharp contrast to learn is 보고 싶다 vs 그립다: 보고 싶다 ('want to see') is the everyday, conversational way to say you miss a specific person and works fine for texting a friend, whereas 그립다 is more wistful, broader (it covers places, eras, tastes, not just faces), and reads as faintly literary. It's a ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ turns to 우 before vowel endings: 그립- + -어요 → 그리워요, past 그리웠어요. The classic English trap is the object particle — 'I miss my hometown' tempts you to say 고향을 그리워요, but the correct adjective frame is 고향이 그리워요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 그립다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 그리워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the object with -을/를 (고향을 그리워요) — as an adjective it needs -이/가: 고향이 그리워요.
Using 그립다 to say someone else misses something; switch to 그리워하다 (동생이 고향을 그리워해요).
Defaulting to 그립다 when texting a friend 'I miss you' — Koreans say 보고 싶어, which is warmer and more direct than the wistful 그립다.
notes: ㅂ: memorize 그리워 and 그리워요 together.

entries.english: to be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed
entries.shortExplanation: 부끄럽다 means "to be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 부끄럽다 (bukkeureopda) means "to be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed". Start from the polite form 부끄러워요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 부끄럽다. A strong first sentence is 부끄러워서 얼굴이 빨개지다 ("to blush from embarrassment"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 부끄럽다 also becomes 부끄러워하고 싶어요 (want), 부끄러울 수 있어요 (can), and 부끄러울 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 부끄러워요. Then practice 부끄럽지 않아요 vs 부끄러울 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

usagePhrases.en: I be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed.
I do not be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed.
I want to be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed.
I can be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed.
I have to be embarrassed / to be shy / to be ashamed.

usagePhrases.note: The textbook physical tell: 부끄러워서 + 얼굴이 빨개지다 ('face goes red') is the stock collocation.

examples.en: I'm a little shy.
examples.note: The base feeling about oneself; ㅂ-irregular 부끄럽- + -어요 → 부끄러워요.

examples.ko: 사람들 앞에서 한국어로 말하는 게 아직 부끄러워요.
examples.romanization: saramdeul apeseo hangugeoro malhaneun ge ajik bukkeureowoyo.
examples.en: I'm still shy about speaking Korean in front of people.
examples.note: The cause (말하는 게) takes -이/가 because this is an adjective describing your own state.

examples.en: My younger sibling is shy around strangers.
examples.note: For someone else's shyness, switch to the verb 부끄러워하다, which can take an object (낯선 사람을).

entries.nuance: 부끄럽다 covers both bashful shyness (meeting new people, being praised) and self-conscious embarrassment over a small slip, and it leans gentler, more inward and even endearing compared with 창피하다, which is sharper, louder, public mortification. The dividing line worth memorising: 부끄럽다 ≈ shy/quietly abashed and can sound cute, while 창피하다 ≈ 'I want to disappear' after a public blunder; a child hiding behind a parent is 부끄러워하는 것, not 창피해하는 것. Because it's an adjective, your own feeling and its cause take -이/가, and reporting someone else's shyness requires the verb 부끄러워하다 (third-person feelings need the -어하다 verb across this whole word family). It's a ㅂ-irregular: 부끄럽- + -어요 → 부끄러워요, past 부끄러웠어요. The related noun 부끄러움 ('shyness/shame') belongs to more formal or written registers. English speakers often grab 부끄럽다 for strong public humiliation — for that punch, reach for 창피하다 instead.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 부끄럽다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 부끄러워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 부끄럽다 for strong public humiliation; 창피하다 hits harder for 'mortified.'
Trying to say 'he is shy' with the plain adjective — use 부끄러워하다 for third-person feelings.
Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular and saying 부끄럽어요; the ㅂ becomes 우, giving 부끄러워요.
notes: ㅂ: memorize 부끄러워 and 부끄러워요 together.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 부끄럽다 becomes 부끄러울 수 있어요 ("can") and 부끄러울 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 부끄럽다 has an irregular stem (ㅂ). Memorize its polite form 부끄러워요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

structuredNuance.t: 부끄럽다 covers both bashful shyness (meeting new people, being praised) and self-conscious embarrassment over a small slip. It leans gentler, more inward and even endearing. Because it's an adjective, your own feeling and its cause take -이/가, and reporting someone else's shyness requires the verb 부끄러워하다 (third-person feelings need the -어하다 verb across this whole word family). The related noun 부끄러움 ('shyness/shame') belongs to more formal or written registers.

Compared with 창피하다, which is sharper, louder, public mortification: 부끄럽다 ≈ shy/quietly abashed and can sound cute, while 창피하다 ≈ 'I want to disappear' after a public blunder. A child hiding behind a parent is 부끄러워하는 것, not 창피해하는 것.
It's a ㅂ-irregular: 부끄럽- + -어요 → 부끄러워요, past 부끄러웠어요.
English speakers often grab 부끄럽다 for strong public humiliation — for that punch, reach for 창피하다 instead.

entries.english: to be embarrassing / to feel mortified
entries.shortExplanation: 창피하다 means "to be embarrassing / to feel mortified" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to be embarrassing / to feel mortified" in Korean is 창피하다 (changpihada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 창피해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 창피하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 창피해 죽겠다 ("to be dying of embarrassment") — then reshape the same stem into 창피해하고 싶어요 (desire), 창피할 수 있어요 (ability), and 창피할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

I do not be embarrassing / to feel mortified.
I want to be embarrassing / to feel mortified.
I can be embarrassing / to feel mortified.

usagePhrases.note: -아/어 죽겠다 ('dying of ~') is the go-to intensifier with feeling words; 창피해 죽겠어요 is extremely common.

examples.en: Ugh, this is so embarrassing.
examples.note: The blunt casual reaction. 하다-verb contracts: 창피하- + -아 → 창피해.

examples.en: Everyone was staring, so I was embarrassed.
examples.note: Past 창피했어요; the cause here is a public situation, which is typical of this word.

examples.ko: 그렇게 큰 소리로 말하면 내가 창피하잖아.
examples.romanization: geureoke keun soriro malhamyeon naega changpihajana.
examples.en: If you talk that loudly, you embarrass me.
examples.note: Used to tell someone they're embarrassing you; -잖아 adds a mild complaining, 'come on' tone.

entries.nuance: 창피하다 is the stronger, more public sibling of 부끄럽다 — the 'I want the floor to swallow me' feeling after you trip in a crowd or get scolded openly — and it describes either your own mortification (저 창피해요) or the situation that causes it (창피한 상황). It is Sino-Korean: 창피 猖披, where 猖 means 'run wild/rampage' and 披 means 'spread open, be dishevelled,' the image being clothes worn so carelessly you're exposed, hence ashamed. The three-way register map is worth holding: 부끄럽다 = gentle/shy, 창피하다 = strong public embarrassment (neutral-polite), and 쪽팔리다 = the same feeling but slangy, rough, friends-only and unfit for work or elders. As a 하다-adjective it contracts 창피하- + -아요 → 창피해요 (not 창피하아요), past 창피했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the slang 쪽팔리다 in a workplace or with seniors to sound natural — keep 창피하다 there, since 쪽팔리다 can read as crude.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 창피하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 창피해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Swapping in the slang 쪽팔리다 in formal or work situations — keep 창피하다 there.
Forgetting the contraction: 창피하- + -아요 becomes 창피해요, not 창피하아요.
Using 창피하다 for mild bashful shyness (e.g., a child meeting a guest) — that gentler feeling is 부끄럽다.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 창피해요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 창피하다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability

entries.english: to be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous
entries.shortExplanation: 황당하다 means "to be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 황당하다 (hwangdanghada) = "to be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 황당해요 plus one useful sentence like 황당한 일 ("an absurd / ridiculous incident"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 황당해하고 싶어요 for what you want, 황당할 수 있어요 for what you can, 황당할 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

I can be absurd / to be dumbfounded by something ridiculous.

usagePhrases.note: 황당한 + noun describes the baffling thing itself: 황당한 일, 황당한 상황, 황당한 변명, 황당한 소문.

examples.en: This is honestly ridiculous.
examples.note: The base reaction. 하다-verb: 황당하- + -아요 → 황당해요.

examples.ko: 갑자기 예약이 취소됐다고 해서 너무 황당했어요.
examples.romanization: gapjagi yeyagi chwisodwaetdago haeseo neomu hwangdanghaesseoyo.
examples.en: They suddenly said my reservation was canceled, so I was dumbfounded.
examples.note: Past 황당했어요; a very common customer-service mishap context.

examples.ko: 그 사람 변명이 너무 황당해서 웃음이 나왔어.
examples.romanization: geu saram byeonmyeongi neomu hwangdanghaeseo useumi nawasseo.
examples.en: His excuse was so absurd that I burst out laughing.
examples.note: 황당해서 (because it was absurd) leads to a reaction. Casual register with a friend.

entries.nuance: 황당하다 captures the 'wait, what?' feeling when something is so unexpected or illogical that it leaves you stunned — a baffling excuse, an out-of-nowhere cancellation, an absurd demand — and it covers both the ridiculous thing itself (황당한 변명) and your reaction to it (너무 황당했어요). It is Sino-Korean: 황당 荒唐, where 荒 means 'wild/overgrown/desolate' and 唐 carries an old sense of 'boastful, rambling, far-fetched,' so the literal flavour is 'wildly preposterous.' The synonym to separate it from is 어이없다: 황당하다 leans toward 'bizarre/unbelievable, doesn't compute,' while 어이없다 adds exasperation or contempt ('so dumb it's almost offensive'); a UFO story is 황당하다, but a line-cutter is more 어이없다. Don't confuse it with the near-twin 당황하다 ('to panic/be flustered'), which is about losing your own composure, not judging something as absurd. As a 하다-adjective: 황당하- + -아요 → 황당해요, past 황당했어요. The English trap is translating it as plain 'surprised' (놀라다) — 황당하다 specifically implies absurdity, not mere unexpectedness.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 황당하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 황당해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Translating it as plain 'surprised' (놀라다) — 황당하다 specifically implies the thing was absurd or nonsensical, not just unexpected.
Confusing it with 당황하다 ('to be flustered/panicked'); 황당하다 judges the situation as absurd, while 당황하다 describes you losing composure.
Overusing it for mild surprises; save it for genuinely ridiculous, illogical situations.

entries.english: to be flabbergasted / to find something absurd and senseless
entries.shortExplanation: 어이없다 means "to be flabbergasted / to find something absurd and senseless" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 어이없다 (eoieopda) means "to be flabbergasted / to find something absurd and senseless". Start from the polite form 어이없어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 어이없다. A strong first sentence is 어이가 없다 ("to be dumbfounded (full form)"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 어이없다 also becomes 어이없어하고 싶어요 (want), 어이없을 수 있어요 (can), and 어이없을 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 어이없어요. Then practice 어이없지 않아요 vs 어이없을 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

usagePhrases.note: The headword is a contraction of 어이가 없다; the 가 stays in careful speech and drops in fast speech: 어이없어.

examples.en: Wow, this is unbelievable.
examples.note: The everyday speechless reaction; the 가 of 어이가 없다 drops in casual speech.

examples.en: Someone cut in line, so I was totally flabbergasted.
examples.note: 없다-type adjective: 어이없- + -었어요 → 어이없었어요. Note -길래 = 'because (I saw/noticed).'

examples.ko: 그 말 듣고 너무 어이없어서 헛웃음이 나왔어.
examples.romanization: geu mal deutgo neomu eoieopseoseo heosuseumi nawasseo.
examples.en: After hearing that, I was so dumbfounded I let out a dry laugh.
examples.note: Pairs naturally with 헛웃음 (a hollow, dry laugh). Casual register.

entries.nuance: 어이없다 (full form 어이가 없다) is the punchy, everyday way Koreans react to something so absurd, unfair, or stupid that it stuns them into a speechless half-laugh — 어이 means roughly 'the wits/sense' you'd need to handle the situation, so 'lacking 어이' is being knocked clean out of your composure. Set beside 황당하다, it carries more exasperation or contempt: 황당하다 = 'this is bizarre/doesn't compute,' while 어이없다 = 'this is so dumb it almost offends me,' which is why it's what you mutter when someone cuts in line or hands you a nonsense excuse. It's a hair more casual than 황당하다 but still fine in polite speech (어이없어요); the truly rough register would be slang like 어처구니없다's blunt cousins or profanity. Because 없다 behaves like an adjective, a third party's reaction takes the verb 어이없어하다. The most common pitfalls are spelling and polarity: it is 어이없다 (the cute misspelling 어의없다 is wrong), and it is always negative — never use it for a pleasant surprise.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 어이없다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 어이없어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spelling or hearing it as 어의없다 — the word is 어이 (not 어의); standard spelling is 어이없다.
Using it for pleasant surprise; 어이없다 is always negative — bafflement mixed with annoyance.
Dropping into the plain adjective for someone else's reaction; a third person 'is dumbfounded' is 어이없어해요, using the -어하다 verb.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 어이없다 becomes 어이없을 수 있어요 ("can") and 어이없을 거예요 ("will"). examples.note: The base exclamation. 하다-verb: 짜릿하- + -아 → 짜릿해.

examples.en: I love that electric thrill when riding a roller coaster.
examples.note: 짜릿한 느낌/스릴 are natural collocations; casual ending with a friend.

examples.en: The moment the comeback goal went in, it was such a rush.
examples.note: Past 짜릿했어요; sports — especially a last-second turnaround — are the classic context.

entries.nuance: 짜릿하다 originally describes a literal tingling, electric sensation — a mild shock, a cold splash, a limb that's gone numb — and extends to the metaphorical thrill of exhilarating moments like a comeback win, a thrill ride, or a daring success; it's overwhelmingly positive and high-adrenaline. The synonym to contrast is 신나다: 신나다 is broad, upbeat 'fun/psyched' (a party, a good song), whereas 짜릿하다 is the sharp, spine-tingling spike of intensity, so a fun picnic is 신나다 but a buzzer-beater is 짜릿하다; it also outranks calm 재미있다 ('enjoyable'). It frequently teams up with the loanword 스릴 (짜릿한 스릴) and powers marketing copy for rides, sports, and games. As a 하다-adjective it contracts 짜릿하- + -아요 → 짜릿해요, past 짜릿했어요. Two pitfalls for English speakers: don't downgrade it to ordinary mild fun (use 재미있다/신나다 for calmer enjoyment), and watch the spelling — it has a double ㅈ (ㅉ) and a tense ㅌ, so it's 짜릿하다, not 자릿하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 짜릿하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 짜릿해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using it for ordinary mild fun; 짜릿하다 implies a sharp, intense rush, so 재미있다/신나다 fit calmer enjoyment.
Forgetting the double ㅉ and tense ㅌ in spelling: 짜릿하다, not 자릿하다.
Assuming it's only emotional — it also describes a physical tingle (cold water, a mild electric jolt, a numb limb).

entries.shortExplanation: 섭섭하다 means "to feel hurt / to feel let down by someone close" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 섭섭하다 (seopseophada) = "to feel hurt / to feel let down by someone close". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 섭섭해요 plus one useful sentence like 섭섭하게 생각하지 마세요 ("please don't take it the wrong way"). usagePhrases.note: A set phrase to reassure someone you didn't mean to slight them; 섭섭하게 생각하다 = 'to take it as a snub.'

examples.en: I'm a little hurt.
examples.note: The base feeling, kept soft with 조금. 하다-verb: 섭섭하- + -아요 → 섭섭해요.

examples.ko: 생일인데 연락도 안 해서 좀 섭섭했어요.
examples.romanization: saengirinde yeollakdo an haeseo jom seopseopaesseoyo.
examples.en: It was my birthday and you didn't even text, so I felt a bit hurt.
examples.note: Past 섭섭했어요; the classic mild-grievance use, never rising to real anger.

examples.en: Hearing you're already leaving makes me sad to see you go.
examples.note: The bittersweet-goodbye sense, not grievance at all. -네요 adds soft, freshly-felt emotion.

entries.nuance: 섭섭하다 is a uniquely Korean shade of feeling: a gentle, wistful hurt or letdown when someone close doesn't meet your emotional expectations, or the bittersweet pang of parting. The near-synonym 서운하다 sits almost on top of it — most speakers use them interchangeably — with 섭섭하다 carrying a slightly older, warmer texture and 서운하다 feeling a touch softer and more current; both are far milder than anger, so they are wrong for 화나다 ('be angry') or 짜증나다 ('be annoyed/irritated'). As a 하다-adjective it contracts 섭섭하- + -아요 → 섭섭해요, and a third person's hurt takes the verb 섭섭해하다. The key English-speaker pitfall is treating it as anger or using it about strangers — it presumes a relationship close enough to have expectations in the first place.

Use 섭섭해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Treating it as anger; 섭섭하다 is tender disappointment, so 화나다/짜증나다 are wrong for this feeling.
Using it about strangers — it implies a relationship close enough to have expectations.
Reporting someone else's hurt with the plain adjective; a third person 'feels let down' is 섭섭해해요, using the -어하다 verb.

entries.explanation: 질리다 (jillida) means "to be sick of / to get fed up with something". Start from the polite form 질려요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 질리다. A strong first sentence is 라면에 질리다 ("to be sick of ramen"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 질리다 also becomes 질리고 싶어요 (want), 질릴 수 있어요 (can), and 질릴 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

I do not be sick of / to get fed up with something.
I want to be sick of / to get fed up with something.
I can be sick of / to get fed up with something.
I have to be sick of / to get fed up with something.

usagePhrases.note: The source of your boredom takes -에 (most standard) or -이/가: 라면에 질렸어요 / 라면이 질렸어요.

examples.en: I'm sick of it now.
examples.note: The base 'fed up' statement; 이-stem 질리- + -었어요 → 질렸어요.

examples.ko: 매일 라면만 먹으니까 이제 진짜 질렸어요.
examples.romanization: maeil lamyeonman meogeunikka ije jinjja jillyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Eating only ramen every day, I'm really sick of it now.
examples.note: The source is marked with -에 (라면에) as the textbook choice; everyday over-saturation.

examples.ko: 그 말 듣고 겁에 질려서 아무 말도 못 했어요.
examples.romanization: geu mal deutgo geobe jillyeoseo amu maldo mo taesseoyo.
examples.en: Hearing that, I froze in fear and couldn't say a word.
examples.note: The other meaning entirely: 겁에 질리다 = paralyzed with fear. Context tells the two senses apart.

entries.nuance: 질리다 is the everyday verb for being so over-saturated with something — a food, a routine, a song — that you can't stand a drop more of it, the 'I'm so done with this' feeling; for this sense you mark the source with -에 (most standard) or -이/가, and the partner phrases 질릴 만큼 / 질릴 정도 mean 'to the point of being fed up.' But it has a second, scarier life: 질리다 also means to turn pale or be paralyzed with fear, as in 겁에 질리다 ('frozen with terror') and 새파랗게 질리다 ('go deathly white'), so context decides which world you're in. entries.nuance: 설레다 is the warm, fluttery thrill of looking forward to something good — the butterflies before a date, a trip, or a fresh start — and it names the emotion itself, with 마음/가슴 as the typical subject. The contrast students need is 설레다 vs 긴장되다: both quicken the heart, but 설레다 is sweet, hopeful anticipation while 긴장되다 ('get nervous/tense') is anxious pressure, so a first date can be both 설레고 긴장돼요; meanwhile 두근거리다 names the bodily pounding that 설레다 produces. The single most important accuracy point is the form: the standard dictionary verb is 설레다 (present 설레요, past 설렜어요, noun 설렘), and although you will see 설레이다 / 설레여요 / 설레임 absolutely everywhere in lyrics and posts, those are nonstandard — write 설레요 / 설렜어요 / 설렘. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that: copying the pretty but incorrect 설레임 from a caption, and mis-contracting the past as 설레었어요 instead of the natural 설렜어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 설레다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 설레요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 설레이다 / 설레여요 / 설레임 — these are nonstandard; the correct forms are 설레다 / 설레요 / 설렘.
Confusing the contraction: 설레 + 었어요 = 설렜어요, not 설레었어요 in natural speech.
Blurring it with 긴장되다; 설레다 is happy anticipation, while 긴장되다 is nervous tension — a date can be both at once.

entries.nuance: 주눅들다 (from 주눅(이) 들다, where 주눅 is the native noun for 'cowed timidity' and 들다 means 'to set in') means to feel so intimidated or self-conscious that you shrink back, lose your nerve, and can't assert yourself — a genuinely useful word for the expat experience of freezing up in Korean meetings or formal settings. Set it against 긴장하다 ('get nervous/tense'): 긴장하다 is momentary jitters before a test or speech and is neutral, whereas 주눅들다 is a deflating loss of confidence that makes you cower and stay small, often before someone or something more powerful; it's also more passive and lasting than a quick 당황하다 ('fluster'). It's built on 들다, so it follows the ㄹ-irregular pattern — the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ endings, giving 주눅듭니다 (not 주눅들습니다) — while vowel endings keep it: 주눅들어요, past 주눅들었어요. The natural cure-words are 당당하다 ('be self-assured') and the encouragement 주눅들지 마. English-speaker pitfalls: keeping the ㄹ before -ㅂ니다, and marking the cause with -을/를 instead of the correct -에 (분위기에 주눅들다).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 주눅들다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 주눅들어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Keeping the ㄹ before -ㅂ니다 (saying 주눅들습니다) — the ㄹ drops: 주눅듭니다.
Marking the cause with -을/를; use -에 (분위기에 주눅들다).
Equating it with plain 긴장하다; 주눅들다 is a deflating loss of confidence that makes you shrink, not just momentary nerves.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 주눅들어 and 주눅들어요 together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 주눅들다 becomes 주눅들 수 있어요 ("can") and 주눅들 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

entries.explanation: "to take out" in Korean is 꺼내다 (kkeonaeda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 꺼내요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 꺼내다 for study notes. entries.nuance: 꺼내다 is the default verb for taking something out of an enclosed space — a bag, pocket, fridge, drawer — so it almost always pairs with 에서 marking the place. The nearest rival is 빼다: the dividing line is that 빼다 is pulling out something fitted or stuck (a key from a lock, a tooth, a USB), while 꺼내다 is retrieving a freely-resting thing from inside. It's a plain native verb with no 한자, and the 내- piece carries an 'outward' feel (compare 내보내다 'send out'). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 빼다 because 'take out' feels like 'pull out'; the second pitfall is the figurative 얘기를 꺼내다 ('bring up a topic') — learners try 가져오다 ('bring') here, but Korean specifically 'pulls the words out,' so 꺼내다 is required.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 꺼내다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 꺼내요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 빼다 to take a wallet out of a bag — 빼다 implies a fitted or stuck object you extract (열쇠를 빼다 'pull out a key'). For retrieving from open inner space, it must be 가방에서 지갑을 꺼내다.
Saying 얘기를 가져오다 to mean 'bring up a topic' — 가져오다 is physically fetching an object. To raise a subject you 'pull it out': 그 얘기 왜 꺼냈어? (Why did you bring that up?).
Forgetting the 에서 and using 에 — it is 가방에서 꺼내다 (out of), not 가방에 꺼내다; 에 would point to a destination, the wrong direction for 'taking out.'

entries.nuance: 집다 means to pick up a small object with a precise pincer grasp — fingers, chopsticks, or tongs (집게, literally 'the picking tool,' comes straight from this verb). The contrast learners need is with 들다 (to lift/raise with the hand or arm) and 줍다 (to pick up off the ground something dropped): you 집어 a single fry, 들어 a heavy box, and 주워 a coin that fell. It's a plain native verb, no 한자. The single biggest pitfall is conjugation: because it ends in ㅂ, English speakers over-apply the ㅂ-irregular and write 지워요, but 집다 is REGULAR — like its cousins 잡다 and 좁다 it keeps the ㅂ, so the 요-form is 집어요. A second trap is using 집다 for picking up off the floor; that situation wants 줍다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 집다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 집어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Conjugating it as a ㅂ-irregular — the correct 요-form is 집어요, never 지워요. 집다, 잡다, 좁다 all keep their ㅂ, unlike true ㅂ-irregulars such as 돕다 → 도와요.
Using 집다 for picking trash up off the ground — that is 줍다 (쓰레기를 줍다). 집다 is a controlled fingertip grasp, not retrieving something that fell.
Confusing 집다 with 들다 for heavy or large things — you 집어 a coin but you must 들어 (lift) a suitcase; 집다 only works on small graspable objects.

entries.explanation: 두다 (duda) means "to put". Start from the polite form 둬요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 두다. A strong first sentence is 두고 오다 ("to leave (something) behind"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 두다 also becomes 두고 싶어요 (want), 둘 수 있어요 (can), and 둘 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 두다 means to place something somewhere and leave it resting there — the emphasis falls on the resulting stationary state, not the motion of setting it down. That is exactly how it splits from 놓다, its nearest synonym: 놓다 stresses the physical act of letting go onto a surface, whereas 두다 stresses leaving it (and often abandoning or keeping it) in place. It is also hugely productive as an auxiliary, -어 두다 meaning 'do something and keep it that way' (예약해 뒀어요 'I went ahead and booked it'). It's a plain native verb with no 한자. The grammar pitfall: 두다 is a ㅜ-stem, so 두 + 어요 contracts to 둬요 — English speakers often write the wrong 두요. The usage pitfall is reaching for 놓다 or 넣다 in 'I left it at home' sentences, where Korean firmly uses 두고 오다/나오다.

entries.nuance: 펴다 is the all-purpose verb for unfolding, spreading out, or straightening — opening a book, laying out bedding, popping an umbrella, or un-bending your back. It is the direct everyday opposite of 접다 (to fold), and that pairing is the easiest way to fix its meaning. Learners often confuse it with 펼치다, which is showier and more spatial ('to unfurl, spread wide, roll out a plan/map'): you 펴 a single newspaper at the table but 펼쳐 a huge map across the floor or 꿈을 펼치다 'pursue a dream.' It's a plain native verb with no 한자. The reliable pitfall is the past tense: the ㅕ + 었 ALWAYS contracts, so it is 폈어요, never the spelled-out 펴었어요 — English speakers who reason form-by-form tend to leave it uncontracted.

entries.nuance: 끼우다 means to insert or wedge something snugly into a slot or gap so that it fits tightly — a SIM card into a tray, a cable into a port, a bookmark between pages, a ring onto a finger. The tight, fitted feel is exactly what separates it from 넣다 (loosely 'put in') and 담다 (fill a container): you 넣어 coins loosely into a piggy bank but 끼워 a SIM that has to click into place. Its plain twin 끼다 is just as natural for wearable fits (안경을 끼다 'wear glasses,' 장갑을 끼다 'wear gloves'). It's a native verb, no 한자, and as a ㅜ-stem it contracts 끼우 + 어 = 끼워요. Pitfall: English speakers say 유심을 넣다 because 'insert' feels generic, but a fitted insertion calls for 끼우다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 끼우다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 끼워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

Forgetting the ㅜ + 어 contraction — the 요-form is 끼워요, not 끼우어요 spelled out; the past is 끼웠어요.

structuredNuance.t: 끼우다 means to insert or wedge something snugly into a slot or gap so that it fits tightly — a SIM card into a tray, a cable into a port, a bookmark between pages, a ring onto a finger. Its plain twin 끼다 is just as natural for wearable fits (안경을 끼다 'wear glasses,' 장갑을 끼다 'wear gloves').
The tight, fitted feel is exactly what separates it from 넣다 (loosely 'put in') and 담다 (fill a container): you 넣어 coins loosely into a piggy bank but 끼워 a SIM that has to click into place.
It's a native verb, no 한자.
As a ㅜ-stem it contracts 끼우 + 어 = 끼워요, with the past 끼웠어요.
English speakers say 유심을 넣다 because 'insert' feels generic, but a fitted insertion calls for 끼우다.

entries.nuance: 얹다 means to rest or lay something lightly on top of a surface — an egg on rice, a hand on a shoulder, a strawberry on a cake — so it pairs almost reflexively with 위에 ('on top of'). It is gentler and far more specific than its neighbors 놓다 (general 'set down anywhere') and 두다 (leave somewhere): 놓다 just releases an object onto a surface, but 얹다 specifically frames it as perched on top of something else, often delicately. It's a plain native verb, no 한자. The signature pitfall is spelling, because of the ㄵ cluster: when you add a vowel the sound resyllabifies to [언저], so learners wrongly write 언어요 — but the ㅈ must stay, giving 얹어요, 얹었어요, 얹어 주세요. A second trap is dropping 위에 and using a bare 에, which loses the 'on top' meaning.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 얹다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 얹어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spelling the 요-form as 언어요 — the ㄵ cluster is pronounced [언저] but written with the ㅈ intact: 얹어요, 얹었어요. Losing the ㅈ is a spelling error.
Using 놓다 when you mean 'rest on top of' — 놓다 only says you set it down somewhere; for perching one thing atop another you want 위에 얹다 (밥 위에 계란을 얹다).
Dropping 위에 and saying just 밥에 얹다 — the 'on top' nuance lives in 위에, so natural Korean keeps 밥 위에 얹다.

entries.nuance: 감싸다 means to wrap something around an object so as to cover, cushion, or protect it — a towel around wet hair, bubble wrap around dishes, a blanket around your shivering body — and it carries a distinct flavor of enveloping and shielding. That protective nuance is what separates it from the plain 싸다 ('wrap/pack,' as in wrapping a gift or packing a lunch): the 감- prefix (from 감다 'wind/coil around') adds the 'all the way around, enveloping' feeling. Figuratively it means to stand up for or shield a person — 나를 감싸 줬어요. It's a native verb (no 한자), a regular ㅏ-stem, so 감싸 + 았어요 contracts to 감쌌어요. Key pitfall: for 'take someone's side' English speakers invent 편을 감싸다, but you 감싸다 the person directly, while 'take a side' is the separate idiom 편을 들다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 감싸다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 감싸요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 편을 감싸다 for 'take someone's side' — you 감싸다 the person directly (친구가 나를 감싸 줬어요). 'Take a side' is a different idiom, 편을 들다.
Writing the past tense as 감싸았어요 — the ㅏ + 았 contracts fully to 감쌌어요.
Using the bare 싸다 when you mean protectively envelop — 싸다 is plain wrapping/packing (선물을 싸다, 도시락을 싸다); the 'wrap all around to protect' sense needs 감싸다.

entries.nuance: 뜯다 means to tear, rip, or peel something open by pulling it apart — a snack bag, a delivery box, an envelope, a protective film — usually destructively and irreversibly. The contrast learners must hold is with 풀다 (to untie/undo, reversibly): you 풀어 a ribbon, a knot, or shoelaces and could re-tie them, but you 뜯어 sealed tape or a glued flap and there's no going back. It's a plain native verb, no 한자. The headline pitfall is conjugation: because it ends in ㄷ, English speakers assume the ㄷ-irregular and write 뜰어요 — but 뜯다 is REGULAR (like 받다, 묻다 'bury', 믿다), so the ㄷ stays put: 뜯어요, 뜯었어요. Only true ㄷ-irregulars like 듣다 → 들어요 and 걷다 → 걸어요 change ㄷ to ㄹ.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 뜯다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 뜯어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Treating it as a ㄷ-irregular — the 요-form is 뜯어요, never 뜰어요. Unlike 듣다/걷다, the ㄷ in 뜯다 does not turn into ㄹ; it patterns with regular 받다, 믿다.
Using 풀다 to open sealed packaging — 풀다 is for undoing something tied or knotted (리본을 풀다). Sealed tape, bags, and boxes are 뜯다.
Saying 열다 ('open') for a snack bag or a vacuum-sealed packet — 열다 fits doors and lids; tearing into sealed packaging is 봉지를 뜯다.

entries.nuance: 쥐다 means to grip or clench — to close your hand firmly around something like a handle, a pen, or a strap, and it is the verb behind 주먹을 쥐다 'to make a fist.' What sets it apart from its neighbors is the whole-hand squeezing grasp: 집다 picks a small thing up with the fingertips (you 집어 a coin), and 잡다 is the broad 'catch/hold/grab' (you 잡아 a taxi, a hand, or a chance), but 쥐다 specifically clenches the fist tight around an object. Figuratively it implies holding power or information firmly — 주도권을 쥐다 'hold the initiative.' It's a native verb, no 한자, and as a ㅟ-stem it conjugates 쥐 + 어 = 쥐어요 (colloquially heard as 줘요), with the formal 쥡니다. Pitfall: English speakers blur 쥐다 and 집다, but you 쥐어 a railing and 집어 a single fry.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 쥐다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 쥐어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 쥐다 (clench in the whole fist) with 집다 (pick up with fingertips) — you 쥐어 a handle or strap but 집어 a coin or a piece of food.
Using 쥐다 where Korean wants the broader 잡다 — for catching a taxi, seizing a chance, or holding someone's hand it is 잡다 (택시를 잡다, 기회를 잡다); 쥐다 is specifically the tight fist-grip.
Mishandling the contraction — the 요-form is 쥐어요 (you may hear 줘요 in speech), and the formal is 쥡니다, not 쥐읍니다.

entries.explanation: "to treat / to host (with food)" in Korean is 대접하다 (daejeophada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 대접해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 대접하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 제가 대접할게요 ("Let me treat you (to a meal)") — then reshape the same stem into 대접하고 싶어요 (desire), 대접할 수 있어요 (ability), and 대접 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

I want to treat / to host (with food).

I have to treat / to host (with food).
Let me treat you (to a meal)
usagePhrases.note: Said when you want to pay and host; warmer and more formal than 제가 살게요, which is just 'I'll pay.'

examples.en: Today it's my treat.
examples.note: The everyday host line at a restaurant when you insist on paying; -ㄹ게요 signals a warm offer.

examples.en: I invited them over and hosted them with a Korean set meal.
examples.note: 한정식으로 대접하다 = host with N; the 으로 marks what you served. Implies real hosting effort.

examples.en: You shouldn't treat a customer like this.
examples.note: Shows the wider sense: 대접하다 also = how you treat people (service quality), not only feeding them.

entries.nuance: 대접하다 is Sino-Korean (待接, 待 'receive/wait on' + 接 'meet/connect'), so its core is 'receiving someone and attending to them' — usually by serving food, but also by how respectfully you treat a person. The near-synonym is 사다 ('buy a meal'): 사다 just means you pay, while 대접하다 adds hosting, effort, and respect, typically toward an elder, a guest, or a client. As a 하다-verb it conjugates regularly (대접해요, 대접했어요), and in the negative the 하다 splits off (대접 안 해요). The very common passive 대접받다 ('be treated/hosted') is as frequent as the active. English speakers wrongly stretch 대접하다 to tiny favors ('I'll get this coffee') — for casual treats say 제가 살게요 and reserve 대접하다 for proper hosting.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 대접하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 대접해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 대접하다 for a casual 'I'll grab this coffee' — for small, light treats Koreans say 제가 살게요; 대접하다 implies real hosting or respectful treatment.
Saying 대접해요 to mean only 'pay' — it bundles serving/hosting too, so 'I'll pay but you cook' doesn't fit 대접하다; use 계산하다/내다 for the bill alone.
Forgetting the passive: after being hosted, the natural thank-you is 잘 대접받았어요, not the active 잘 대접했어요 (which would mean you hosted them).

entries.shortExplanation: 거들다 means "to help out / to lend a hand" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

entries.nuance: 거들다 means to pitch in on a task that is already in progress — you are a secondary helper, not the main doer. The dividing line vs 돕다 (the general 'help') matters: 돕다 can be the primary act of helping or even rescuing, while 거들다 is lighter, side-by-side assistance ('lend a hand'), so you'd never 거들다 a drowning person. It also has a figurative sense, 말을 거들다 ('chime in, back someone up' in conversation). Crucially it is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, so the formal form is 거듭니다 (never 거들습니다), but the ㄹ stays everywhere else (거들어요, 거들 거예요, 거들지 마세요). English speakers also tend to use it for serious help, where 돕다 is correct.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 거들다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 거들어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the formal form as 거들습니다 — because of the ㄹ-irregular the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, giving 거듭니다.
Treating 거들다 as full-scale help or rescue ('please help me, I'm in trouble') — for serious help use 도와주세요/돕다; 거들다 is only light, secondary assistance.
Dropping the ㄹ where it should stay — the present is 거들어요, not 거어요; the ㄹ only disappears before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 거들어 and 거들어요 together.

entries.explanation: 양보하다 (yangbohada) means "to yield / to give way". Start from the polite form 양보해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 양보하다. A strong first sentence is 자리 좀 양보해 주세요 ("Please give up your seat"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 양보하다 also becomes 양보하고 싶어요 (want), 양보할 수 있어요 (can), and 양보 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I do not yield / to give way.
I want to yield / to give way.
I can yield / to give way.
I have to yield / to give way.

usagePhrases.note: Asking someone to offer a seat — often to an elderly or pregnant passenger on the subway.

examples.en: I'll give in this time.
examples.note: Everyday concession to keep harmony; 양보하다 here = back down, not literally hand something over.

examples.en: I gave up my seat to an elderly woman on the subway.
examples.note: Classic 양보 scene; 께 is the honorific 'to' for the older person, raising the recipient.

examples.en: It's nice if we each give a little, right?
examples.note: 한 발씩 양보하다 = 'each take a step back / compromise,' a fixed expression for meeting halfway.

entries.nuance: 양보하다 is Sino-Korean (讓步, 讓 'yield/cede' + 步 'step' — literally 'yield a step'), and it covers both physical yielding (a seat, the right of way) and figurative conceding (backing down in an argument, letting someone have their way). The key contrast is with 포기하다 ('give up entirely'): 양보하다 means you give way to another person out of courtesy and could have kept it, whereas 포기하다 means you abandon a goal altogether. Culturally the nuance is positive — yielding is considerate, not weak — which is why you see the bare noun 양보 on subway signs and in driving etiquette (양보 운전). As a 하다-verb it's regular (양보해요), splitting in the negative (양보 안 해요). Don't confuse it with 포기하다 or with simply losing.

Confusing 양보하다 (yield/concede to someone) with 포기하다 (give up a goal entirely) — you 양보하다 your seat to a person, but you 포기하다 a dream or plan.
Marking the recipient with 을/를: it's 할머니께 자리를 양보하다 — the seat takes 을/를 and the person takes 께/한테, not the other way around.
Reading 양보 as defeat — saying 내가 양보할게 is a gracious 'I'll let it go,' not an admission that you lost; the tone is courteous, not bitter.

entries.explanation: "to see someone off" in Korean is 배웅하다 (baeunghada). The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Politely telling a host not to walk you out; 나오다 = come out (to the door/gate).

examples.ko: 다음에 또 와, 하면서 배웅해 줬어요.
examples.romanization: daeume tto wa, hamyeonseo baeunghae jwosseoyo.
examples.en: They saw me off saying 'come again next time.'
examples.note: A natural parting scene after visiting someone's home; -아/어 주다 frames it as kindness done for you.

examples.ko: 친구가 떠나는 게 아쉬워서 역까지 배웅했어.
examples.romanization: chinguga tteonaneun ge aswiwoseo yeokkkaji baeunghaesseo.
examples.en: I was sad my friend was leaving, so I saw them off at the station.
examples.note: 역까지 배웅하다 = accompany a departing person as far as the station; 까지 marks the distance.

examples.ko: 할머니가 문 앞까지 나와서 배웅해 주셨어요.
examples.romanization: halmeoniga mun apkkaji nawaseo baeunghae jusyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Grandma came out to the door to see me off.
examples.note: Common Korean courtesy — older hosts walk guests out; -아/어 주시다 honors the kindness done for you.

entries.nuance: 배웅하다 means to accompany someone who is leaving — walking them to the door, the station, or the airport — and it is the exact counterpart of 마중하다 ('to go meet someone arriving'). Keep that pair straight: 배웅 is for departures, 마중 is for arrivals, and learners constantly swap them. It differs from a plain goodbye (인사하다/잘 가) because it implies physically going part of the way with the person, which signals warmth and respect; declining a host's offer ('배웅 안 나오셔도 돼요') is itself a polite gesture. As a 하다-verb it conjugates regularly (배웅해요, 배웅했어요) and splits in the negative (배웅 안 해요); the noun 배웅 also stands alone in 배웅 나가다 and 배웅 인사.

Use 배웅해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Swapping 배웅하다 (see off / departure) with 마중하다 (meet / arrival) — they are opposites; you 배웅하다 someone leaving and 마중하다 someone arriving.
Treating 배웅하다 as a mere verbal goodbye — it implies actually walking the person out or going part of the way, so just waving and saying 잘 가 is not yet 배웅.
Forcing an English 'see off' object pattern — it's 친구를 배웅하다 (person takes 을/를); don't add an extra 'off' particle or say 친구에게 배웅하다.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 배웅하다 becomes 배웅할 수 있어요 ("can") and 배웅할 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: To accompany someone who is leaving — walking them to the door, the station, or the airport. It implies physically going part of the way with the person, which signals warmth and respect; declining a host's offer ('배웅 안 나오셔도 돼요') is itself a polite gesture.

entries.shortExplanation: 어기다 means "to break / to violate (a rule or promise)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

examples.en: I broke my promise again, so my friend got angry.

entries.nuance: 어기다 is the standard verb for breaking something intangible that you are bound to keep — a promise (약속), a rule (규칙), a law (법), a signal (신호), or an appointment. Its direct antonym is 지키다 ('keep/abide by'), and the cleanest way to learn it is as that opposite: you either 지키다 or 어기다 a 약속. The crucial pitfall for English speakers is that English 'break' covers both rules and physical objects, but 어기다 only works for the intangible — a broken cup or phone is 깨다/부수다/고장 내다, never 어기다. It is a regular verb (어겨요, 어겼어요, 어기지 마세요), and in practice the natural negative command is 어기지 마세요 rather than 지키지 마세요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 어기다 as a complete polite sentence.

Mixing it up with 지키다 — they are opposites; 약속을 어기다 = break a promise, 약속을 지키다 = keep one. Saying you 어기다 a promise you meant to keep reverses your meaning.
Translating 'I broke up with my friend' as 친구를 어기다 — that's nonsense in Korean; 어기다 never takes a person as object. Use 헤어지다/절교하다 for relationships.

entries.nuance: 지키다 is a high-frequency verb covering three linked senses: keep (a promise, a secret, a time/appointment), abide by (rules, order, manners, distance), and protect/guard (a person, a home, a country). For promises and rules it is the direct antonym of 어기다, so learning the pair together fixes both. Against 보호하다 ('protect' — more formal/abstract, e.g. 환경을 보호하다), 지키다 is the everyday, hands-on 'guard/defend' and also carries the 'keep/abide by' meanings that 보호하다 lacks. The English idiom 'keep a promise' transfers, but 'keep' in the sense of physically retaining something is 가지다/두다, not 지키다. It is a regular verb (지켜요, 지켰어요); note that the literal negative 지키지 마세요 is rarely used — to tell someone not to break a rule you say 어기지 마세요.

Overextending 'keep' — 'keep the receipt / keep it in your bag' is 가지고 있다/두다, not 지키다; 지키다 is keep-a-promise/guard, not keep-an-object.
Using 지키지 마세요 to warn against rule-breaking — that literally means 'don't keep it'; the natural phrase is 어기지 마세요 ('don't break it').

examples.en: The boss is always generous to the employees.

examples.en: They say what you give to others comes back to you.
examples.note: A common saying about generosity (karma-like); 만큼 = 'as much as,' linking giving and return.

entries.nuance: 베풀다 means to give generously of yourself — kindness, help, hospitality, favors, even a feast — usually from a position of being able to give, which is why it suits a boss, an elder, or a benefactor. It is warmer and more elevated than the plain 주다 ('give'), and it pairs with abstract nouns (은혜, 호의, 친절, 인심, 도움) rather than concrete objects: 선물을 베풀다 sounds odd, while 친절을 베풀다 is natural. It is a ㄹ-irregular verb — the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, so the formal form is 베풉니다 (never 베풀습니다), but the ㄹ stays elsewhere (베풀어요, 베풀 거예요, 베풀지 마세요). The biggest English-speaker trap is reaching for it as a generic 'give'; keep it for bestowing intangible kindness.

notes: ㄹ: memorize 베풀어 and 베풀어요 together.

entries.explanation: 나누다 (nanuda) means "to share / to divide". Start from the polite form 나눠요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 나누다. examples.note: Splitting the check (n빵/더치페이); 나누다 is the verb for dividing the cost, 똑같이 = evenly.

entries.nuance: 나누다 holds two linked ideas: to divide (split a bill, cut into portions, partition) and to share (food, feelings, conversation). The 'share' sense is the warm heart of the word and surfaces in set combos like 나눠 먹다 (share food) and 이야기를/고민을 나누다 (share talk or worries) — sharing *with* someone, not a cold mathematical split. The crucial English-speaker pitfall is the digital sense of 'share': reposting a photo or link online is 공유하다, never 나누다, so 사진을 나누다 sounds wrong for social media. It is a regular verb (나눠요, 나눴어요); for splitting a restaurant bill specifically, 나누다 and the slang n빵 both work. Contrast with 쪼개다 ('split/crack into pieces'), which is more physical and lacks the 'share with someone' warmth.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 나누다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 나눠요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 나누다 for 'share a post/photo online' — for social-media reposting Koreans say 공유하다; 사진을 나누다 doesn't mean sharing on SNS.
Dropping the partner particle for conversation — it's 친구랑/친구와 이야기를 나누다 ('converse with a friend'); the co-participant takes 랑/와, not 을/를.
Reaching for 나누다 when you mean 'crack/split into pieces' — physical breaking into shards is 쪼개다/가르다; 나누다 implies portioning or sharing, often with someone.

entries.english: to attend on / to escort (an elder, honorific)
entries.shortExplanation: 모시다 means "to attend on / to escort (an elder, honorific)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to attend on / to escort (an elder, honorific)" in Korean is 모시다 (mosida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 모셔요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 모시다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 부모님을 모시고 살아요 ("I live with (and look after) my parents") — then reshape the same stem into 모시고 싶어요 (desire), 모실 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 모셔요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

examples.en: I'll show the guest to their seat.
examples.note: A fixed service phrase; 모시다 elevates the customer, so it sounds polished and respectful.

entries.nuance: 모시다 is the suppletive honorific verb for accompanying, escorting, taking, or living with someone of higher status — parents, grandparents, bosses, clients, honored guests. It replaces the plain 데리고 가다/오다 (which is reserved for peers, children, and pets) whenever respect is owed, much as 잡수시다 replaces 먹다 or 주무시다 replaces 자다. You'll hear it constantly in two settings: service speech (손님을 모시겠습니다, 자리로 모시다) and family talk (부모님을 모시고 살다). It also has a ritual sense — 제사를 모시다 / 조상을 모시다 (to hold ancestral rites). It is a regular verb (모셔요, 모셨어요). The core pitfall for English speakers is status-blindness: using 데리고 가다 for an elder sounds rude, while using 모시다 for a friend or pet sounds absurdly over-deferential.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 모시다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 모셔요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 데리고 가다 for an elder, boss, or client — it sounds rude toward someone you should honor; switch to 모시고 가다.
Using 모시다 for friends, children, or pets — it is only for people you must respect; for equals or those below you use 데리다/데리고 가다.
Forgetting it's already honorific — you don't add another honorific to the object's verb redundantly; 모시고 가다 alone correctly raises the person, so 모시고 가시다 about your own action is off.

structuredNuance.t: The suppletive honorific verb for accompanying, escorting, taking, or living with someone of higher status — parents, grandparents, bosses, clients, honored guests. You'll hear it constantly in two settings: service speech (손님을 모시겠습니다, 자리로 모시다) and family talk (부모님을 모시고 살다). It also has a ritual sense — 제사를 모시다 / 조상을 모시다 (to hold ancestral rites).
It replaces the plain 데리고 가다/오다 (which is reserved for peers, children, and pets) whenever respect is owed, much as 잡수시다 replaces 먹다 or 주무시다 replaces 자다.
It is a regular verb (모셔요, 모셨어요).
The core pitfall for English speakers is status-blindness: using 데리고 가다 for an elder sounds rude, while using 모시다 for a friend or pet sounds absurdly over-deferential.

entries.shortExplanation: 권하다 means "to recommend / to offer / to urge" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 권하다 (gwonhada) = "to recommend / to offer / to urge". entries.nuance: 권하다 is Sino-Korean (勸, 'urge/encourage') + 하다, and it spans a spectrum: recommending (a dish, a book), offering (food, a drink, a seat to someone), and urging/advising (a course of action like 금연). Against the neutral 추천하다 ('recommend' — often a product, a place, in writing or impersonally), 권하다 is more face-to-face and personal, and it carries the extra 'offer/press upon someone' meaning that 추천하다 lacks. In daily life its most culturally loaded use is 술을 권하다 — offering and sometimes insistently pressing drinks at a 회식 — where graceful refusal is its own social skill. It is a regular 하다-verb (권해요, 권했어요), and the negative can split (권 안 해요). The pitfall: don't assume 권하다 is always gentle; depending on context it can mean actively pushing something on someone.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 권하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 권해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Assuming 권하다 always means a soft suggestion — 술을 권하다 can mean actively pressing someone to drink, so read the social context before translating it as 'recommend.'
Swapping it for 추천하다 in every case — for an impersonal/written recommendation (a product, a tourist spot) 추천하다 fits; 권하다 leans personal and adds the 'offer/urge upon someone' sense.
Mishandling the recipient — it's 저한테 메뉴를 권하다 (person takes 한테/에게, thing takes 을/를); don't mark the person with 을/를.

examples.note: 정중히 사양하다 = decline courteously; the go-to phrase for refusing drinks at 회식 gracefully.

entries.nuance: 사양하다 is Sino-Korean (辭讓, 辭 'decline/take leave' + 讓 'yield') and means to decline an offer — food, a drink, a gift, an invitation — courteously and somewhat formally. The sharp contrast is with 거절하다 ('reject/refuse'): 거절하다 is firm and can sound cold or final (거절당하다 = 'be rejected'), while 사양하다 is the soft, face-saving 'I'll pass, thank you,' typically for hospitality you appreciate but don't want to accept. Because Korean politeness often scripts a first, modest refusal, the host's fixed line 사양하지 말고 드세요 ('don't be shy, eat up') is something you'll hear constantly, and knowing how to 사양하다 gracefully is genuinely useful etiquette. It is a regular 하다-verb (사양해요, 사양했어요), splitting in the negative (사양 안 해요). Pitfall: using 거절하다 for a kind meal or gift sounds harsh.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 사양하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 사양해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 거절하다 where 사양하다 fits — 거절하다 (reject) sounds firm or cold for a meal, drink, or gift; 사양하다 is the warm, polite decline.
Confusing it with 양보하다 — 사양하다 (辭讓) = decline an offer for yourself, while 양보하다 (讓步) = yield something to someone else; they share 讓 but aren't interchangeable.
Declining yet still reaching for the item — culturally 사양하다 should match your action; saying 사양할게요 while taking it sends a mixed, awkward signal.

entries.shortExplanation: 근무하다 means "to work (be on duty)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to work (be on duty)" in Korean is 근무하다 (geunmuhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 근무해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 근무하다 for study notes. entries.nuance: 근무하다 is the workplace word for 'to work / be on duty', focused on your employment and shift rather than the physical act of doing tasks. The hanja is 勤務 (勤 'diligence/service' + 務 'duty'), so it literally means 'serve one's duty' — that institutional flavor is why it dominates contracts, ID badges, and self-introductions. The sharp contrast is with 일하다: 일하다 is the everyday, hands-on 'do work' you say to friends, while 근무하다 is about being formally posted somewhere, so a soldier, a 9-to-5 office worker, or a clerk 근무한다 at a location. Habitual collocations are all fixed nouns: 주 5일 근무, 재택근무, 야간 근무, 근무 시간 (working hours), 근무 환경 (work environment). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: the workplace takes 에서 (location of an activity), so it is 회사에서 근무해요, never 회사에 근무해요 or 회사를 근무해요. Also do not reach for 근무하다 to describe doing a single chore — that is 하다 or 일하다.

Use 근무해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Wrong particle: say 회사에서 근무해요 (location of activity = 에서), not 회사에 근무해요. 에 marks static existence (있다), but 근무하다 is an activity, so it needs 에서.
Don't use 근무하다 for a one-off task like tidying your desk — 근무하다 is about being employed / on shift, not doing a specific chore; use 일하다 or just 하다 there.

entries.nuance: 맡다 is the everyday native-Korean verb for taking on a role or responsibility — a task, a project, a part, even a saved seat. It feels more personal and active than the Sino-Korean 담당하다: where 담당하다 is the official 'assigned to me' on an org chart, 맡다 is the warm, often-volunteered 'I'll take this', so 제가 맡을게요 sounds team-friendly and proactive in a meeting. Its causative partner 맡기다 ('to entrust/hand over') flips the direction: you 맡다 a job yourself, but you 맡기다 it to someone else (저한테 맡기세요). Habitual collocations: 역할을 맡다, 책임을 맡다, 업무를 맡다, 자리를 맡다.

entries.nuance: 보고하다 is the formal verb for reporting information up a hierarchy — to a boss, a client, or headquarters. The hanja 報告 is 報 'to inform/requite' + 告 'to tell/announce', a doubled 'make known' that signals officialness. In Korea's hierarchy-conscious workplaces, 보고 (the report itself) is a weighty ritual, which is why you very often switch to the humble 보고드리다 when the listener outranks you. The decisive synonym contrast is with 말하다 / 알려주다: those are neutral 'tell / let know' for peers and friends, whereas 보고하다 frames the act as an upward, accountable report. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold — English 'report' covers casual gossip ('did you hear?'), but 보고하다 does NOT, so telling a friend news is 말하다/알려주다, not 보고하다; and learners forget to elevate to 보고드리다 when reporting to a senior.

entries.nuance: 마치다 means to finish or conclude something properly — your workday, a meeting, a report, a course of study. Two contrasts a learner must hold apart. First, against 끝내다: both are transitive 'finish it', but 마치다 is more bookish and dignified (a meeting, a ceremony, a semester), while 끝내다 is the casual, hands-on 'get it done' of daily office chatter. Second, and the real pitfall, against 끝나다: 끝나다 is INTRANSITIVE ('it ends by itself') and takes no object, so 'the work ended' is 일이 끝났어요, never 일을 마쳤어요 unless you are the one actively concluding it. entries.nuance: 검토하다 means to review or examine something carefully — documents, proposals, plans, contracts — usually before approving or deciding. entries.nuance: 야근하다 is the verb every Korean office worker knows: to stay and work into the evening, past regular hours. entries.nuance: 퇴사하다 means to leave your company — to resign or quit for good. The hanja 退社 is 退 'retreat/withdraw' + 社 'company', literally 'withdraw from the company', and it is the exact mirror of 입사하다 (入社, 'enter the company'), so the two are best memorized as a set. 퇴사 is a culturally loaded, much-discussed topic among younger Korean workers, traveling with 이직 (移職, changing jobs), 인수인계 (handover), and 퇴사 통보 (notice of resignation). 퇴사하다 vs 입사하다 direction: 퇴사(退) is leaving, 입사(入) is joining. Don't reverse them — 작년에 퇴사했어요 means you LEFT last year, not started.

entries.nuance: 회의하다 means to hold or have a meeting — the daily texture of office life. The hanja 會議 is 會 'gather/assemble' + 議 'discuss/deliberate', literally 'gather-and-deliberate', which captures that it implies a real, purposeful, usually scheduled discussion rather than idle talk. In practice the bare noun 회의 surfaces even more than the verb: 회의 중이에요 (in a meeting), 회의 잡다 (set a meeting), 회의실 (meeting room), 회의록 (meeting minutes). entries.explanation: "to sulk (and turn away)" in Korean is 토라지다 (torajida). entries.nuance: 토라지다 is the specific sulk where someone feels hurt or slighted and pointedly turns cold — going quiet, looking away, giving you the silent treatment. The dividing line versus its near-synonym 삐치다 matters: 삐치다 just names the hurt-and-pouty feeling, while 토라지다 foregrounds the visible turning-away and icy withdrawal, so it sounds a touch more serious and dramatic (단단히 토라지다 = sulk hard). It is far softer and more passive than 화내다, where the person openly shouts; a person who 토라지다 withdraws rather than explodes. Register is casual and affectionate, used overwhelmingly of couples, close friends, and children — you would not say a CEO 토라졌다 in a formal report. It collocates with 등을 돌리다, 입을 삐죽 내밀다, and the recovery phrase 기분이 풀리다. English-speaker pitfall: do not reach for 'angry' and translate it as 화나다 — that loses the whole 'silent, turned-away' core; also resist adding an object with 을/를, because 토라지다 is intransitive (you 토라지다 at a state, you don't 토라지다 something).

Use 토라져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't translate it as 화내다 — 토라지다 is sulking/pouting silently and turning away, not actively shouting. If someone is loudly angry, use 화내다.
토라지다 is intransitive: say 친구가 토라졌어요, never 친구를 토라졌어요. To mark who they're sulking at, use ...한테 토라지다 (나한테 토라졌어 = he's sulking at me).
Past tense is 토라졌어요 (토라지 + 었 → 토라졌). Don't spell it 토라젔어요 or 토라졌써요.

entries.nuance: 골내다 blends sulking with irritation — a grumpy, moody upset where someone broods, gives off a sour mood, and goes half-pouting, half-cross. On the spectrum it sits between 삐치다 (lighter, just hurt feelings) and 화내다 (open anger): grumpier and more visibly cross than 삐치다, but not the explosive shouting of 화내다. Its intransitive partner is 골나다 ('to become grumpy'), exactly mirroring 화내다 / 화나다. It collocates with 혼자 (sulking alone), 골난 표정 (a sullen face), and ...한테 골내다 (be grumpy at someone). English-speaker pitfall: keep the 내다/나다 split straight — you 골내다 (actively show it) but you 골나다 (the mood arises in you); and don't confuse this 골 (temper) with the homographs 골 meaning 'brain' or the loanword 'goal'. It is colloquial, so it stays in casual speech, not formal writing.

entries.nuance: 짜증내다 is to outwardly express irritation or annoyance — snapping, a sharp tone, an exasperated huff or face. It is one of the most-used emotion verbs in daily Korean life: clearly negative and usually aimed at someone, yet lighter than full-blown 화내다 (real anger). The crucial contrast for learners is the 내다/나다 pair: 짜증나다 names the internal feeling that wells up ('나 짜증 나' = I'm annoyed / it's annoying me), while 짜증내다 names the outward act of taking it out on someone ('나한테 짜증 내지 마' = don't be snippy at me) — same root noun 짜증, different verb of expression vs arising, just like 화내다 / 화나다. It collocates with 한테 (the target), 자꾸 (repeatedly), 짜증 섞인 말투 (an irritated tone), and the noun can detach as 짜증을 내다. English-speaker pitfall: learners say 나 짜증내 to mean 'I'm annoyed', but that wrongly implies you're actively snapping at someone — use 짜증나 for the feeling. Also, the double ㅉ is a tense consonant romanized 'jj', not a plain 'j'.

Romanize the double ㅉ as 'jj' (a tense consonant), not 'j' — 짜 is not 자.
To name the target, use 한테/에게, not 을/를: 동생한테 짜증냈어 (correct), not 동생을 짜증냈어.

("The kid is throwing a fit demanding I buy a toy."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 떼쓰고 싶어요 for what you want, 떼쓸 수 있어요 for what you can, 떼쓸 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 떼써요. Then practice 떼쓰지 않아요 vs 떼쓸 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

usagePhrases.en: I do not throw a tantrum (demand stubbornly).
I want to throw a tantrum (demand stubbornly).
I can throw a tantrum (demand stubbornly).
I have to throw a tantrum (demand stubbornly).
The kid is throwing a fit demanding I buy a toy.
usagePhrases.note: The textbook scene for 떼쓰다 — a child's nagging demand; note -아/어 달라고.

examples.ko: 마트에서 과자 사 달라고 바닥에 누워서 떼썼어요.
examples.romanization: mateueseo gwaja sa dallago badage nuwoseo ttesseosseoyo.
examples.en: He lay on the floor at the mart demanding snacks.
examples.note: 떼썼어요 = past (떼쓰 + 었, the ㅡ drops). Very vivid kid behavior.

examples.en: You can't keep throwing tantrums now that you're an adult.
examples.note: Playfully scolding adult stubbornness; -까지 = 'even to the point of'.

examples.ko: 아무리 떼써도 안 되는 건 안 돼.
examples.romanization: amuri ttesseodo an doeneun geon an dwae.
examples.en: No matter how much you whine for it, no means no.
examples.note: Firm boundary-setting language with kids; 아무리 ...아/어도 = no matter how.

entries.nuance: 떼쓰다 is to insistently, unreasonably demand something — the whining, foot-stamping, floor-flopping, won't-take-no-for-an-answer behavior, prototypically a child but also said of adults acting childishly. It is built from the noun 떼 ('an unreasonable demand / a fit') plus 쓰다 ('to use/employ'), so it literally = 'to employ a fit'; the noun can stand alone as 떼를 쓰다, and the intensified 생떼를 쓰다 means an utterly baseless tantrum. Crucially it centers on stubborn demanding, not sadness or quiet sulking — that is the dividing line versus 보채다 (restless fretful whining/urging) and versus 삐치다 (wounded pouting). Conjugation follows the ㅡ-irregular: the stem 쓰- loses its ㅡ before -어, giving 써 / 써요 / 떼썼어요. It collocates almost obligatorily with -아/어 달라고 (떼쓰다) ('demand that something be done'). English-speaker pitfall: never write 떼쓰어요 — the ㅡ must drop to 떼써요; and watch the vowel, it is 떼 (ㅔ), not 때 (ㅐ).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 떼쓰다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 떼써요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
쓰다 follows the ㅡ-irregular: stem 떼쓰- + 어 → 떼써, past 떼썼어요. Don't write 떼쓰어요.
It's 떼쓰다, not 때쓰다 — the first vowel is ㅔ (떼 = a fit / an unreasonable demand), not ㅐ.
떼쓰다 is stubborn demanding, not quiet sulking — don't use it where 삐치다 (hurt pout) or 보채다 (restless fussing) is meant.
notes: ㅡ: memorize 떼써 and 떼써요 together.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 떼써요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 떼쓰다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 애가 장난감 사 달라고 떼써요.. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 떼쓰지 않아요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 떼쓸 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 떼써요 feels easy, practice 떼쓰고 싶어요, 떼쓸 수 있어요, and 떼써야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

classroomScript: Teacher says: 떼써요. Learner repeats three times.
Teacher asks a yes/no question with 애가 장난감 사 달라고 떼써요. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 떼쓰지 않아요, then 떼쓸 수 없어요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 떼쓰다 becomes 떼쓸 수 있어요 ("can") and 떼쓸 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.body: 떼쓰다 has an irregular stem (ㅡ). Memorize its polite form 떼써요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

entries.shortExplanation: 보채다 means "to fuss (and pester)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 보채다 (bochaeda) means "to fuss (and pester)". Start from the polite form 보채요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 보채다. A strong first sentence is 아기가 배고픈지 계속 보채요. ("The baby keeps fussing — maybe it's hungry."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 보채다 also becomes 보채고 싶어요 (want), 보챌 수 있어요 (can), and 보챌 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 보채요. Then practice 보채지 않아요 vs 보챌 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

examples.en: He keeps pestering me to hurry, so I can't focus.
examples.note: 보채다 of an impatient adult nagging you to rush; -니까 gives the cause.

examples.en: What's so urgent that you keep pestering me?
examples.note: Pushing back on someone's impatient nagging.

entries.nuance: 보채다 has two everyday senses that share one feel — restless, repeated fussing. First, a baby or young child fretting and crying for a need (hunger, sleep, wanting to be held: 안아 달라고 보채다). Second, a person impatiently pestering or nagging you to hurry up or give them something (빨리 가자고 보채다). The dividing line versus 떼쓰다 is the type of pressure: 떼쓰다 is a stubborn, specific, won't-budge demand ('buy me THAT toy'), whereas 보채다 leans toward restless, antsy whining and urging without a single fixed demand. It is also gentler and more sympathetic than 떼쓰다 — a fussing baby earns pity, a tantruming one earns a scolding. Conjugation: 보채- + 어 contracts (ㅐ + 어 → ㅐ) to 보채 / 보채요, past 보챘어요. It collocates with 밤새 보채다 (fuss all night), 계속/자꾸 보채다, and -아/어 달라고 보채다. English-speaker pitfall: don't write 보채어요 — the vowels contract to 보채요; and don't stretch it to mean adult 'anger' — it is fussing/pestering, never shouting.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 보채다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 보채요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
보채 + 어 contracts to 보채 (보채요), past 보챘어요 — don't write 보채어요.
Mostly for babies or impatient pestering; it does not mean adult 'anger' — don't use it where 화내다 or 짜증내다 is meant.
For a stubborn, fixed demand ('I want THAT one'), use 떼쓰다; 보채다 is the looser, restless fussing.

entries.shortExplanation: 달래다 means "to soothe (and calm down)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to soothe (and calm down)" in Korean is 달래다 (dallaeda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 달래요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 달래다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 우는 아이를 달래고 있어요. ("I'm soothing the crying child.") — then reshape the same stem into 달래고 싶어요 (desire), 달랠 수 있어요 (ability), and 달랠 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 달래요. Then practice 달래지 않아요 vs 달랠 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

usagePhrases.note: The prototypical use — calming a crying kid.

examples.en: Even soothing him with candy didn't stop the crying.
examples.note: 달래도 = even though I soothe; pairs with 울음을 그치다 (stop crying).

examples.en: I broke a sweat trying to calm down the angry customer.
examples.note: Service-job reality; -느라 = in the course of (an effortful) doing.

examples.ko: 속상한 마음을 달래려고 매운 음식을 먹었어요.
examples.romanization: soksanghan maeumeul dallaeryeogo maeun eumsigeul meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: I ate spicy food to soothe my upset feelings.
examples.note: 마음을 달래다 = to comfort/soothe one's own heart; -려고 = in order to.

entries.nuance: 달래다 is to soothe, comfort, or placate someone who is crying, upset, or angry — and, importantly, also to calm your own feelings (마음을 달래다 = comfort one's heart). It is the natural counterpart to 울다, 토라지다, 떼쓰다, 화나다: someone gets upset, and you 달래다 them back to calm. The tone is warm and caring. The dividing line versus 위로하다 (to console) is method and scope: 위로하다 consoles mainly with sympathetic words about a loss or sorrow, while 달래다 actively settles a present upset — by holding, coaxing, distracting, or placating — and works on anger and tantrums too, not just grief. Conjugation: 달래- + 어 contracts to 달래 / 달래요, past 달랬어요. It collocates with 우는 아이를 달래다, 화난 고객을 달래다, ...로 달래다 (소리로/사탕으로 달래다 = soothe with...), and 마음을 달래다. English-speaker pitfall: don't write 달래어요 — the vowels contract to 달래요; and don't confuse the verb 달래다 with its exact homophone 달래, the wild chive eaten in spring — only context separates them.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 달래다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 달래요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
달래 + 어 contracts to 달래 (달래요), past 달랬어요 — never 달래어요.
달래다 (to soothe, transitive) takes 을/를: 아이를 달래다, 마음을 달래다 — don't drop the object marker.
The verb 달래다 is unrelated to the homophone 달래 (a wild chive); context makes it clear.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 달래다 becomes 달랠 수 있어요 ("can") and 달랠 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: 달래다 is to soothe, comfort, or placate someone who is crying, upset, or angry — and, importantly, also to calm your own feelings (마음을 달래다 = comfort one's heart). It is the natural counterpart to 울다, 토라지다, 떼쓰다, 화나다: someone gets upset, and you 달래다 them back to calm. The tone is warm and caring. It collocates with 우는 아이를 달래다, 화난 고객을 달래다, ...로 달래다 (소리로/사탕으로 달래다 = soothe with...), and 마음을 달래다.

The dividing line versus 위로하다 (to console) is method and scope: 위로하다 consoles mainly with sympathetic words about a loss or sorrow, while 달래다 actively settles a present upset — by holding, coaxing, distracting, or placating — and works on anger and tantrums too, not just grief.

entries.nuance: 토닥이다 is the soft, rhythmic comforting pat — on a back, shoulder, or head — that wordlessly says 'it's okay, you did well.' It's a kindness toward someone, so it almost always takes 주다: 등을 토닥여 줬어요 — bare 토닥였어요 sounds incomplete in caring contexts.

entries.nuance: 다독이다 means to comfort and steady someone — gently patting while reassuring them so they settle, regroup, and feel supported. It is warmer and more emotionally loaded than the purely physical 토닥이다: where 토닥이다 highlights the literal pat-pat motion, 다독이다 carries the follow-through of 'pulling someone back together,' which is why it extends to rallying a group (팀을 다독여 분위기를 살리다) in a way 토닥이다 does not. Its true opposite is 다그치다 ('to press, push, urge harshly') — the same emotional axis pulled in reverse, which is why the pairing 다그치지 말고 다독여 주세요 ('don't pressure — reassure') is idiomatic. Conjugation is the 이다-stem pattern: 다독이- + 어 → the ㅣ+어 fuses to 여, giving 다독여 / 다독여요, past 다독였어요. It collocates with 다독여 주다, 다독이며 (위로하다), 마음이 놓이다, and 사기를/분위기를 살리다.
