이다-ending: 다독이 + 어 → 다독여 (ㅣ+어 fuses to 여), past 다독였어요. Not 다독이어요.
다독이다 (comfort, steady) is the near-opposite of 다그치다 (to press/push someone harshly) — don't mix them up, or you reverse your meaning.
When the comfort is purely a physical pat, 토닥이다 fits better; reach for 다독이다 when you mean reassuring and steadying someone emotionally.

entries.explanation: "to encourage" in Korean is 격려하다 (gyeongnyeohada). examples.ko: 시험 떨어진 친구를 격려해 주고 싶었어요.
examples.romanization: siheom tteoreojin chingureul gyeongnyeohae jugo sipeosseoyo.
examples.en: I wanted to encourage my friend who failed the exam.
examples.note: Pairs with 떨어지다 (to fail); -아/어 주고 싶다 = want to do (for someone).

examples.en: The coach gave a speech encouraging the players.
examples.note: 격려하다 is the go-to verb for pep talks and speeches.

examples.ko: 힘든 시기에 격려해 주셔서 정말 감사했어요.

examples.note: Polite gratitude; very natural in messages to mentors and seniors.

entries.nuance: 격려하다 is to encourage or cheer someone on with words — a pep talk, a 'you can do it,' a supportive note during a hard stretch. It is Sino-Korean: 激勵 combines 激 ('rouse, stir up') and 勵 ('urge on, exhort'), literally 'to stir up and spur on,' which is why it sounds a notch more formal and elevated than its native-feeling cousins. The dividing line versus 응원하다 (應援, 'to root for/cheer') is tone and setting: 응원하다 is energetic supporter-style cheering (a fan 응원s a team), while 격려하다 is more dignified, verbal encouragement, fitting speeches, workplaces, mentors, and 격려의 말씀 (words of encouragement) at formal events; and unlike the physical comforting of 다독이다 / 토닥이다, 격려하다 works through words. As a 하다-verb it conjugates regularly: 격려하- + 여 → 격려해 / 격려해요, past 격려했어요. It collocates with 격려해 주다, 서로 격려하다, 격려의 말씀, and 격려하는 연설. English-speaker pitfall: pronunciation — the ㄱ + ㄹ in 격려 nasalizes to [경녀] (romanized gyeongnyeo), so never say 'gyeok-lyeo'; and don't use 격려하다 for physically comforting someone — that's 다독이다 / 토닥이다.

Use 격려해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

entries.nuance: 야단치다 is to scold or tell someone off — a parent, teacher, or boss reprimanding a child or junior for doing wrong. It is built from the noun 야단 ('a fuss, an uproar, a scolding') plus 치다 ('to strike/deliver'), so it literally = 'to deliver a scolding,' which is why the noun can detach as 야단을 치다 and the receiving side surfaces as 야단을 듣다 / 야단을 맞다. It is stronger and more authority-driven than plain 화내다 (simply being angry): 야단치다 implies a power gap (older/senior reprimanding younger) and a corrective purpose, not just venting emotion. Its gentler neighbor is 타이르다 ('to admonish and reason with calmly'), which is why 야단치기보다 타이르다 ('reason rather than scold') is a natural contrast. Conjugation: 야단치- + 어 → the ㅣ+어 fuses to 쳐, giving 야단쳐 / 야단쳐요, past 야단쳤어요. It collocates with 크게 야단치다 (scold severely), 야단맞다/야단 듣다 (be scolded), and 혼나다 (get told off). It implies a senior-to-junior power gap; you don't 야단치다 your boss — between equals, 뭐라고 하다 or just 화내다 fits better.

entries.nuance: 비웃다 is to laugh at someone scornfully — to mock, sneer, ridicule, and look down on them. It is a compound of the prefix 비- (Sino-Korean 非/卑, carrying a 'belittling, disparaging' force, as in 비하 'to demean' or 비방 'to slander') plus the native verb 웃다 ('to laugh'), so it is literally 'belittling laughter,' which is exactly what separates it from neutral 웃다. The dividing line versus 놀리다 ('to tease') is intent and warmth: 놀리다 can be light, affectionate teasing between friends ('I'm just teasing you'), whereas 비웃다 is contemptuous and genuinely hurtful, with the laugher looking down on the target. It collocates with 남을/실수를/꿈을 비웃다, 대놓고 비웃다 (sneer openly), and the idiom 콧방귀를 뀌며 비웃다 (scoff and sneer). Conjugation point: 웃다 keeps its ㅅ — it is NOT a ㅅ-irregular — so the forms are 비웃어요 / 비웃었어요 / 비웃을 거예요, with the ㅅ intact. English-speaker pitfall: never drop that ㅅ (비웃어요, not 비웄어요); and don't use 비웃다 for friendly ribbing — that's 놀리다 — or you will sound far harsher and meaner than you intend.

비웃다 is scornful and mean; for light, friendly teasing use 놀리다 instead, or you'll sound much harsher than intended.
It takes a direct object with 을/를 (사람을/실수를 비웃다), not 에게/한테 — don't say 나에게 비웃지 마, say 나를 비웃지 마.

entries.nuance: 벌다 is the everyday verb for bringing in money or income through work — 돈을 벌다 is the core phrase, and 'making a living' is 먹고살다. The dividing line you must feel: 벌다 is acquiring income, 쓰다 is spending it, 모으다 is saving/accumulating it, so a salary you 벌어서 모아요 then 써요. Register is neutral and usable anywhere, but asking 얼마 벌어요? to a senior or new coworker is socially risky. Crucially 벌다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the final ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다 and -ㄴ, giving the formal 법니다, yet it survives in 벌어요. The single biggest English-speaker trap is the past modifier — 'the money I earned' is 번 돈, never 벌은 돈, because ㄹ disappears before -ㄴ.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 벌다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 벌어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 벌은 돈 for 'earned money' — because ㄹ drops before -ㄴ, the correct past modifier is 번 돈.
Saying 법니다 wrong as 벌습니다 — a ㄹ-stem takes -ㅂ니다 (not -습니다) and the ㄹ drops, so the formal form is 법니다.
Using 만들다 ('make/create') for earning money — you don't 돈을 만들다 (that implies counterfeiting); you 돈을 벌다.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 벌어 and 벌어요 together.

entries.nuance: 모으다 covers both saving money over time and gathering/pooling things or people together (돈, 동전, 사람, 자료, 회비). Against 저축하다 (the formal Sino-Korean 'to save'), 모으다 is the warm everyday word, and against 낭비하다 (waste) it is the opposite. It is a ㅡ-irregular verb: the stem ㅡ drops before -아/어, and since the preceding vowel ㅗ is bright it takes 아, so 모으 + 아요 → 모아요, past 모았어요.

entries.nuance: 아끼다 means to be sparing with a resource so as not to waste it — money, electricity, water, even time — and the set phrase 아껴 쓰다 ('use frugally') is one of the most common chunks in daily speech. The synonym line: 절약하다 is the formal Sino-Korean equivalent (절약 節約) used in writing and slogans, while 아끼다 is the warm native verb you actually say; its sharp opposite is 낭비하다 (to squander). There is also a tender second meaning — 'to treasure/cherish' a person or thing (아끼는 후배, 아끼는 옷), so 아끼다 can carry affection, not just thrift. Use 아껴요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spelling the polite form as 아끼어요 instead of contracting ㅣ + 어 to 아껴요 (past 아꼈어요).
Saying 돈에 아끼다 with the wrong particle — the resource is a direct object, so it's 돈을 아끼다.
Assuming 아끼다 only means thrift — it also means 'cherish', so 너를 아껴 means 'I treasure you', not 'I'm stingy with you'.

entries.nuance: 낭비하다 means to waste or squander a resource — money, time, energy — and always carries a clearly negative tone, so unlike English 'spend' it can never be neutral. It is Sino-Korean: 浪費 literally 'reckless(浪) expense(費)', i.e. spending that flows away wastefully, paired with the verb 하다. The synonym boundary: 쓰다 is neutral 'to spend/use', 낭비하다 is 'to spend wastefully', and its opposites are 아끼다 / 절약하다 (be frugal). Because the negative meaning is what you actually need in daily life, both the polite command and the prohibitive collapse onto 낭비하지 마세요 — a literal 낭비해 주세요 ('please waste it') sounds absurd. entries.nuance: 갚다 means to pay back what you owe — money (돈, 카드값, 대출, 빚) or, figuratively, a favor or kindness (은혜를 갚다, 신세를 갚다). Confusing 갚다 (pay back) with the noun 값 (price) — '값이 비싸다' (the price is high) has nothing to do with repaying.

entries.nuance: 맡기다 means to entrust or hand something over into someone's care — money to a bank (돈을 은행에 맡기다 = deposit), bags to a counter, laundry to a shop, or a job to a person. It is the causative counterpart of 맡다 ('to take charge of, to keep'): you 맡겨 your money to the bank, and the bank 맡아 keeps it — same root, opposite direction, which is exactly where English speakers slip. For strictly financial deposits there is the formal 예금하다, but 맡기다 is the warm everyday word and also covers physical things and tasks, which 예금하다 cannot. It conjugates regularly, stem ㅣ + 어 contracting to 여: 맡기 + 어요 → 맡겨요, past 맡겼어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 맡기다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 맡겨요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 맡기다 (entrust to others) with 맡다 (take charge oneself) — you 맡겨 your money to the bank; the bank 맡아 keeps it.

Spelling the polite form as 맡기어요 — ㅣ + 어 contracts to 여, giving 맡겨요 (past 맡겼어요).

entries.nuance: 흥정하다 is to bargain or negotiate over a price, going back and forth until both sides agree — natural at traditional markets, in secondhand deals (중고거래), and for big buys like a used car. The synonym contrast learners most need: 흥정하다 names the whole negotiating process, whereas 깎다 is the concrete act of getting the price knocked down, so you 흥정해서 깎아요 ('negotiate, and as a result get it lowered'). 흥정 is a native Korean noun (not Sino-Korean) plus 하다, distinct from the broader business word 협상하다 ('to negotiate' deals/terms). A key cultural pitfall for English speakers: fixed-price stores (정찰제) like department stores and franchises do not allow it — 흥정 안 돼요 — so haggling there is awkward, unlike at a market. As a regular 하다 verb: 흥정해요, 흥정했어요.

Using 협상하다 for market haggling — 협상하다 fits formal/business negotiation; everyday price-bargaining is 흥정하다.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 흥정하다 becomes 흥정할 수 있어요 ("can") and 흥정할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 흥정하다 is to bargain or negotiate over a price, going back and forth until both sides agree — natural at traditional markets, in secondhand deals (중고거래), and for big buys like a used car.

The synonym contrast learners most need: 흥정하다 names the whole negotiating process, whereas 깎다 is the concrete act of getting the price knocked down, so you 흥정해서 깎아요 ('negotiate, and as a result get it lowered'). It is also distinct from the broader business word 협상하다 ('to negotiate' deals/terms).
흥정 is a native Korean noun (not Sino-Korean) plus 하다, unlike the Sino-Korean business word 협상하다.
As a regular 하다 verb: 흥정해요, 흥정했어요.
A key cultural pitfall for English speakers: fixed-price stores (정찰제) like department stores and franchises do not allow it — 흥정 안 돼요 — so haggling there is awkward, unlike at a market.

entries.shortExplanation: 보태다 means "to chip in" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 보태다 (botaeda) = "to chip in". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 보태요 plus one useful sentence like 생활비에 보태다 ("to put toward living expenses"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 보태고 싶어요 for what you want, 보탤 수 있어요 for what you can, 보탤 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

entries.nuance: 보태다 means to add money or resources to make up a shortfall or supplement an amount — chipping in for a shared gift, helping with living costs, topping up someone's allowance — and its signature pattern is 'X에 보태다' (put toward X). The synonym you must distinguish is 모으다: with 보태다 each person adds their share into a pot, while 모으다 is collecting/pooling the whole total, so everyone 보태서 모아요 ('each chips in, and together it's gathered'); it also overlaps with 더하다 ('to add' in the plain/arithmetic sense), but 보태다 specifically implies helping or filling a gap. The English idiom 'chip in' transfers in meaning but not in grammar — there is no preposition; you simply mark the goal with -에. It is a regular ㅐ-stem verb, so 보태 + 어요 stays 보태요, and the past contracts to 보탰어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 보태다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 보태요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the past tense as 보태었어요 — the stem vowel ㅐ absorbs 었, giving 보탰어요.
Using 모으다 when you mean your own contribution — you 보태 your share, whereas 모으다 is pooling the whole total.
Adding an English-style preposition — say 생활비에 보태다, not 생활비를 위해 보태다, since -에 already marks the target.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 생활비에 보태다. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 안 보태요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 보탤 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 보태요 feels easy, practice 보태고 싶어요, 보탤 수 있어요, and 보태야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

entries.shortExplanation: 떼다 means "to take a cut from" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 떼다 (tteda) means "to take a cut from". Start from the polite form 떼요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 떼다. entries.nuance: 떼다 in a money context means to take a portion out — deducting tax or a fee from a larger sum (월급에서 세금을 떼다, 수수료를 떼다), with the structure 'A에서 B를 떼다' (take B out of A). The synonym boundary: 빼다 is the neutral 'subtract/remove', but 떼다 specifically implies detaching a slice off a whole, often a cut someone takes. It carries a very useful idiomatic sense too — 서류를 떼다 means to obtain or issue an official document (등본, 초본) from an office, something residents do constantly, where 발급받다 is the formal equivalent. Its literal core is 'to detach/peel off', the opposite of 붙이다 ('to stick on'). It is a regular ㅔ-stem verb: 떼 + 어요 stays 떼요, but the past contracts to 뗐어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 떼다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 떼요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the past as 떼었어요 — the ㅔ stem contracts with 었 to give 뗐어요.
Using 빼다 for the document idiom — '등본을 빼다' is wrong; you 등본을 떼다 (issue/obtain a document).
Marking the source with 을/를 instead of 에서 — it's 월급에서 세금을 떼다, where the larger sum takes 에서.

entries.shortExplanation: 부치다 means "to send (by mail)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to send (by mail)" in Korean is 부치다 (buchida). entries.nuance: 부치다 means to send something off to a distant place — a parcel or letter through the post office, or money to someone (돈을 부치다 = remit). For money it overlaps with the precise banking term 송금하다 and the broad 보내다, but 부치다 feels warmer and more everyday, especially family sending support back home, and unlike 송금하다 it also covers physical mail. The pitfall that trips every English speaker is the homophone 붙이다 ('to stick/attach'): they are pronounced identically but spelled differently and mean opposite things — 우표를 붙여서 편지를 부쳐요 ('stick on a stamp and send the letter'). It conjugates regularly, stem ㅣ + 어 contracting to 여: 부치 + 어요 → 부쳐요, past 부쳤어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 부치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 부쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Mixing up 부치다 (send/mail) with 붙이다 (stick on) — they sound identical but are opposites: 우표를 붙여서 편지를 부쳐요.
Spelling the polite form as 부치어요 — ㅣ + 어 contracts to 여, giving 부쳐요 (past 부쳤어요).
Marking the recipient of money with 을/를 — say 친구에게 돈을 부치다, where the person takes 에게/한테.

entries.nuance: 송금하다 is the precise banking word for transferring money from one account to another — used on bank apps, for paying rent, and for overseas remittances (해외 송금). It is Sino-Korean: 送金 literally 'send(送) money(金)', the verb 하다 attached. The synonym scale runs from formal to casual: 송금하다 (account-specific, on every banking screen) → 부치다 (warm, everyday, also covers mail) → 보내다 (the plain 'send money') → the slang 쏘다 ('I'll get this/pay'); pick by register. The particle pitfall for English speakers is the destination: money goes 계좌로/에게 송금하다 (to an account/person) — the recipient is never marked with 을/를, because 송금 already contains 'money'. As a regular 하다 verb: 송금해요, 송금했어요, 송금합니다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 송금하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 송금해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the recipient with the wrong particle — money goes 계좌로/에게 송금하다, never 사람을 송금하다.
Saying 돈을 송금하다 redundantly — 송금(送金) already means 'send money', so the object 돈을 is unnecessary (though tolerated).
Using slangy 쏘다 in a formal context — 쏘다 means 'treat/pay' casually among friends; for a bank transfer use 송금하다.

entries.nuance: 깎다 in a money context means to knock down or discount a price — 값을 깎다 ('lower the price'), with the seller's 깎아 주다 ('give a discount') being the phrase you hear and use most. The synonym line learners confuse: 깎다 is the concrete result of 흥정하다 (the back-and-forth negotiating), so you 흥정해서 깎아요; against 할인하다 ('to discount', the shop's official markdown), 깎다 is the personal, on-the-spot lowering you request. Outside money, the same verb means to peel/pare (과일을 깎다) and to sharpen (연필을 깎다) — one verb, three everyday senses. Despite ending in the double consonant ㄲ it is fully regular: 깎 + 아요 → 깎아요, past 깎았어요, the ㄲ kept in spelling though pronounced [까까요].
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 깎다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 깎아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Reducing the spelling to 까다/까아요 — keep the double ㄲ: 깎아요, 깎았어요 (pronounced [까까요]/[까깠어요]).
Treating 깎다 as the same as 흥정하다 — 깎다 is actually lowering the price, 흥정하다 is the negotiating that leads to it.
Confusing 깎다 with 깍다 — there is no 깍다; the headword is spelled 깎다 with the double consonant.

entries.shortExplanation: 쳐다보다 means "to stare at / look up at" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to stare at / look up at" in Korean is 쳐다보다 (chyeodaboda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 쳐다봐요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 쳐다보다 for study notes. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 쳐다봐요. Then practice 안 쳐다봐요 vs 쳐다볼 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

entries.nuance: 쳐다보다 is built from 치어다(보다) ('look upward') fused with 보다, and that upward/fixed feel survives: it means to look directly and steadily at something, frequently raising your eyes (천장을, 하늘을 쳐다보다). The dividing line from plain 보다 is intensity and duration — 보다 is any neutral 'see/look', while 쳐다보다 is a held, pointed gaze. Against 바라보다 (a calm, fond, distant gaze) it is far less warm: aimed at a person it slides easily into the uncomfortable 'why are you staring at me' zone, so 왜 쳐다봐요? sounds mildly confrontational. It conjugates as a 보다-verb: 보 + -아 contracts to 봐, giving 쳐다봐요 / past 쳐다봤어요. English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 쳐다보다 every time you'd say 'look at' — for watching TV, a movie, or a performance you want 보다, and forcing 쳐다보다 there sounds like you're glaring at the screen.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 쳐다보다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 쳐다봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 쳐다보다 for casually watching TV or a movie — that situation is 보다. 영화를 쳐다봤어요 wrongly implies you sat glaring at the film; say 영화를 봤어요.
Marking the target with 에 instead of 를. It's 저를 쳐다봐요, not 저에 쳐다봐요 — 쳐다보다 takes a direct object with 을/를.
Assuming it always sounds rude. With 천장을/하늘을 쳐다보다 it is perfectly neutral; the negative tinge only appears when the object is a person.

entries.nuance: 바라보다 (from 바라- + 보다) is to look at something usually at some distance and with a calm, often emotional or contemplative feeling — scenery, a loved one's face, the future. The key contrast is with 쳐다보다: where 쳐다보다 is a pointed, sometimes prickly stare, 바라보다 is soft and almost never aggressive, which makes it the safe verb for looking fondly or wistfully at someone (사랑스럽게 바라보다). Against 보다 (any plain 'see/look'), 바라보다 adds emotional depth and the sense of holding your eyes on something across space. It also lives a second, figurative life — 같은 곳을 바라보다, 미래를 바라보다 — meaning to share a vision or face the future. It conjugates as a regular 보다-verb: 바라보 + -아 → 바라봐요, past 바라봤어요. English-speaker pitfall: don't use 바라보다 for reading fine print or inspecting an object up close; that nearness belongs to 살펴보다 or 보다, since 바라보다 implies looking across a gap, not scrutinizing.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 바라보다 as a complete polite sentence.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 바라보다 becomes 바라볼 수 있어요 ("can") and 바라볼 거예요 ("will"). entries.nuance: 살펴보다 joins 살피다 ('to scan/watch attentively, take care') with 보다, so its core is attentive, careful looking — to review, inspect, or check something over until you understand it: documents, a room, symptoms, your surroundings. It is the everyday 'review/check over' verb and pairs habitually with 꼼꼼히 ('meticulously'). The sharp contrast is with 둘러보다: 둘러보다 is a relaxed sweep around a whole space, while 살펴보다 zooms in with intent to verify, so 가게를 둘러봤어요 (browsed the shop) and 가게를 살펴봤어요 (inspected/cased the shop) feel quite different. Versus 훑어보다 (a fast skim for the gist), 살펴보다 is slower and more thorough. As a 보다-verb it contracts 살펴보 + -아 → 살펴봐요, past 살펴봤어요. English-speaker pitfall: 'look over' in English can mean both 'skim' and 'scrutinize', but 살펴보다 only covers the careful end — if you mean a quick glance, use 훑어보다, not 살펴보다.

entries.nuance: 알아보다 fuses 알다 ('know') with 보다, and the two senses both fall out of 'look in order to know.' Sense 1 — investigate / look into / research (information, prices, options, procedures): 비자 연장 방법을 알아보다. This is one of the most useful verbs for living in Korea — 제가 알아볼게요 is how you tell someone you'll check on a matter. Sense 2 — recognize / make out (a face, handwriting, a thing): 글씨를 못 알아보겠어요. The crucial contrast is with plain 알다: 알다 is the static state 'to know', while 알아보다 is the active 'find out' or 'identify on sight' — you can 알다 a fact, but you 알아보다 to obtain it. It contracts as 알아보 + -아 → 알아봐요, past 알아봤어요; the recognition sense often appears negative as 못 알아보다. English-speaker pitfall: for 'recognize someone' don't use 알다 — 그 사람을 알아요 means you know them, while 그 사람을 알아봤어요 means you recognized them by sight.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 알아보다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 알아봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 알다 for 'recognize'. 알다 is just 'to know'; to say you recognized someone on sight, use 알아보다 — 저를 알아봤어요, not 저를 알았어요.
Saying 찾다 when you mean to research options. 찾다 is 'to search for/find', but 'I'll look into it (and weigh the choices)' is 알아볼게요, not 찾을게요.
Forgetting 못 for the can't-recognize meaning. 'I couldn't recognize the handwriting' is 글씨를 못 알아봤어요; 안 알아봤어요 would mean you chose not to look into it.

entries.nuance: 지켜보다 combines 지키다 ('to guard/keep') with 보다, so unlike a one-off look it means to watch continuously over time — to monitor, keep an eye on, or 'wait and see.' That 지키다 root gives it a flavor of care or guardianship, which is why it dominates medical advice (며칠 더 지켜봅시다 = let's observe a few more days), parenting (아이를 지켜보다), and decisions you want to postpone until things develop (상황을 지켜보다). Contrast it with 쳐다보다 and 바라보다, which are momentary looks: 지켜보다 is durative — you keep looking across a stretch of time. It also differs from 살펴보다, which is a careful inspection at one moment rather than ongoing surveillance. With the helper -아 주다 it becomes warmly protective: 지켜봐 주다 = watch over someone for their sake. It contracts 지켜보 + -아 → 지켜봐요, past 지켜봤어요. English-speaker pitfall: don't use 지켜보다 for watching a show or game for fun — that single sitting is 보다; 지켜보다 implies vigilant, time-extended monitoring.

Treating it as a quick glance. 지켜보다 is durative; for an instant look use 쳐다보다 or 보다. 한 번 지켜봤어요 sounds odd because the verb implies sustained watching.

entries.nuance: 둘러보다 is built from 두르다/둘러- ('to encircle, go around') plus 보다, so it literally means to send your eyes around a whole space — a store, a neighborhood, an exhibition — taking a broad, relaxed look. It is the natural verb for browsing: when a clerk asks 도와드릴까요?, the textbook reply is 그냥 둘러볼게요 or 둘러보는 거예요 ('I'm just looking'). The decisive contrast is with 들여다보다, its near-opposite: 둘러보다 is a wide sweep over many things, while 들여다보다 is a close peer into one thing, so 가게를 둘러보다 (browse the shop) vs 가방을 들여다보다 (peer into the bag). It also contrasts with 살펴보다, which adds careful scrutiny rather than a casual survey. As a 보다-verb it contracts 둘러보 + -아 → 둘러봐요, past 둘러봤어요. English-speaker pitfall: don't use 둘러보다 for inspecting a single item closely — surveying a whole space is its job; for examining one thing carefully, switch to 살펴보다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 둘러보다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 둘러봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

Saying 찾아보다 when you only meant to browse with no goal. 찾아보다 implies looking for something specific; 그냥 둘러볼게요 conveys aimless browsing.
Over-formalizing the browsing line. To a clerk, the idiomatic answer is 그냥 둘러볼게요 / 둘러보는 거예요; a stiff 저는 상품을 관찰하고 있습니다 sounds unnatural.

entries.shortExplanation: 들여다보다 means "to peer into / look closely at" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.

entries.nuance: 들여다보다 comes from 들이다 ('to bring/let inward') in the -여다 form plus 보다 — literally 'look inward into' — so it means a close, leaning-in look into something: a container, a screen, or, figuratively, a problem. The defining feature is up-close, focused attention, usually with your head bent toward the object. The sharp contrast is with 둘러보다: 들여다보다 narrows onto one thing from near, while 둘러보다 sweeps broadly over a space — peering into a bag vs scanning a whole store. Against 살펴보다 (careful inspection that can be at normal distance), 들여다보다 adds the physical sense of bringing your eyes right up to or inside something. Figuratively, 문제를 들여다보다 means to examine an issue in depth, much like English 'look into.' It contracts 들여다보 + -아 → 들여다봐요, past 들여다봤어요. English-speaker pitfall: don't swap it with 둘러보다 — a close look into one thing is 들여다보다, a broad look around a space is 둘러보다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 들여다보다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 들여다봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Swapping it with 둘러보다. 들여다보다 is a close look into one thing; 둘러보다 is a broad look around a space — 가게를 둘러보다 (browse) vs 가게 안을 들여다보다 (peer inside).
Using it for distant gazing. 들여다보다 implies nearness and leaning in, so for looking at a faraway view use 바라보다, not 들여다보다.
Forgetting 안/속 with containers in natural speech. Koreans usually say 냉장고 안을 들여다봤어요 (peered inside the fridge); bare 냉장고를 들여다봤어요 is less idiomatic for looking into its interior.

entries.nuance: 노려보다 derives from 노리다 ('to take aim at, target') plus 보다, and that 'taking aim' is exactly the feeling — to fix someone with an angry, hostile stare, i.e. to glare. It is strong and unambiguously negative, signaling irritation, threat, or a challenge, and pairs naturally with 눈을 부릅뜨고 ('eyes flung wide'). Compare the family: 보다 is neutral 'look', 쳐다보다 is an uncomfortable lingering stare, and 노려보다 is openly hostile — only the last carries real anger. A close casual synonym is 째려보다, which is more colloquial and often a quick, sharp dirty look, whereas 노려보다 can be a sustained, intense glare. Because 노리다 also means 'to covet/eye a target', 노려보다 occasionally edges toward 'eye something one is after', but its default is anger. It contracts 노려보 + -아 → 노려봐요, past 노려봤어요. English-speaker pitfall: never use 노려보다 where neutral English 'look at' would do — it always injects hostility, so for a plain look use 보다 and for an awkward stare use 쳐다보다.

Confusing it with 쳐다보다. 쳐다보다 can be merely uncomfortable, but 노려보다 is openly hostile — don't pick 노려보다 to describe ordinary staring.
Mixing up 노려보다 (glare) and 바라보다 (gaze fondly). They are tonal opposites; 아기를 노려봤어요 would mean you glared at a baby, the reverse of the warm 바라보다.

Its essence is speed and breadth with shallow attention, which is why it bonds with 쓱, 쭉, and 대충. The decisive contrast is with 살펴보다: 살펴보다 is slow, careful inspection, while 훑어보다 is a fast once-over, so 계약서를 훑어보다 (skim the contract) vs 계약서를 살펴보다 (go through it carefully) carry opposite levels of diligence. entries.nuance: 엿듣다 is the listening counterpart of 엿보다: the secret prefix 엿- plus 듣다 ('to hear/listen'), meaning to overhear or eavesdrop, normally on the sly. English-speaker pitfall (two): don't write 알아듣어요 — the ㄷ-irregular makes it 알아들어요; and don't substitute 이해하다 when you simply mean you caught the words, since 이해해요 claims you grasped the idea, not that you heard it.

entries.nuance: 걸리다 is a high-frequency verb that fans out into three everyday senses learners meet fast: (1) time being needed — 시간이 걸리다; (2) catching an illness — 감기에 걸리다; and (3) getting caught/busted — 경찰한테 걸리다, 거짓말이 걸리다. entries.explanation: "to go over / to exceed" in Korean is 넘다 (neomda). entries.nuance: 넘다 means to go over or pass beyond a limit — a wall, a mountain pass, a number, a clock time, or even a social boundary (선을 넘다 = 'cross the line', exactly like the English idiom). The crucial English-speaker pitfall is that the particle flips with the meaning: for physically crossing something the object takes 을/를 (산을 넘다), but for *exceeding* a number or time the figure becomes the subject with 이/가 (열 시가 넘었어요, 만 원이 넘어요), not 을/를. Keep 넘다 ('cross/exceed') apart from 건너다, which is for crossing a flat span like a street or river (길을 건너다) — 넘다 implies getting over a height or threshold, 건너다 implies going across to the other side. It is a regular consonant-stem verb: 넘 + 어요 → 넘어요. Do not confuse it with the excluded 넘어지다 ('to fall over/trip'), which looks related but describes losing your balance.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 넘다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 넘어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
For exceeding a number/time, use 이/가, not 을/를: 열 시가 넘었어요 (right) vs 열 시를 넘었어요 (wrong).
Don't mix up 넘다 (go over a height/limit) with 건너다 (cross a street/river) — 길은 건너고, 산은 넘습니다.

entries.explanation: 놓치다 (nochida) = "to miss". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 놓쳐요 plus one useful sentence like 버스를 놓쳤어요 ("I missed the bus"). Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: 놓치다 = fail to catch a bus/train/flight; the thing missed takes 을/를.

examples.en: I just missed the bus
examples.note: The most typical use, for transport you failed to catch.

examples.en: I was late because I missed the subway

examples.note: Opportunities use 놓치다 too; -면 안 되다 gives the 'mustn't' warning.

entries.nuance: 놓치다 is for missing something you were actively trying to catch or hold — a bus, a train, a flight, a chance, or even the thread of a conversation (요점을 놓치다 = 'miss the point') — and it always takes a 을/를 object. Its make-up shows the meaning: 놓다 ('to let go/release') + 치다, so it literally pictures something slipping out of your grasp. The single biggest English-speaker pitfall is using it for missing a *person*: English 'I miss you' is NOT 놓치다 — that is 보고 싶다 ('want to see'), so 엄마가 보고 싶어요, never 엄마를 놓쳐요. Contrast 놓치다 ('fail to catch what was within reach') with 지나가다/지나치다 ('let pass / pass by'): you 놓치다 a bus you ran for, but a chance that quietly 지나가다 simply went by. It is a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 놓치 + 어 → 놓쳐요, and it frequently appears alongside 늦다 ('be late').
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 놓치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 놓쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
To say you miss a PERSON, use 보고 싶다, not 놓치다 — 놓치다 is only for missing a bus, train, chance, etc.
Don't drop the object marker: it's 버스를 놓쳤어요, since 놓치다 is transitive and needs a 을/를 object.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 나오다 becomes 나올 수 있어요 ("can") and 나올 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 나오다 is 'come out' — emerging toward the speaker or out of an enclosed place. Beyond the literal, it's everywhere for water/gas running (물이 안 나와요), food being served (음식이 나왔어요), people leaving work (회사에서 나오다), and appearing in media (TV에 나오다).

Because Korean bakes direction into the verb, it pairs with 나가다 ('go out', away from the speaker): the very same English 'come/go out' splits depending on where you stand, so a waiter bringing food says 음식이 나와요, but you stepping outside say 밖에 나가요.
It's built transparently from 나 ('out') + 오다 ('come').
The conjugation pitfall: the stem ends in 오, and 오 + 아 contracts to 와, giving 나와요 and past 나왔어요 (not 나오아요).
The directional pitfall is the big one — don't default to 나오다 for every 'go out'; if the motion is away from you, it must be 나가다.

entries.shortExplanation: 넣다 means "to put in" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 넣다 (neota) means "to put in". Start from the polite form 넣어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 넣다. A strong first sentence is 설탕을 넣어요 ("I put in sugar"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 넣다 also becomes 넣고 싶어요 (want), 넣을 수 있어요 (can), and 넣을 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 넣어요. Then practice 안 넣어요 vs 넣을 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

examples.note: Everyday food/drink use; 에 marks what you put it into.

entries.nuance: 넣다 means to put or insert something into a place or container, so it is a two-slot verb: it needs both the thing (을/를) and the destination (에) — 가방에 책을 넣어요. From that core it stretches to filling in forms (이름을 넣다), depositing money (통장에 돈을 넣다), and adding ingredients while cooking. The pronunciation/spelling pitfall for English speakers is the stem-final ㅎ: unlike ㅎ-irregular *adjectives* (빨갛다 → 빨개요), verbs ending in ㅎ are perfectly regular and keep the ㅎ in writing, so it's 넣 + 어요 → 넣어요 and past 넣었어요 (never 너어요 / 너었어요), even though the ㅎ is barely heard. Mind the particle, too: the destination is 에 (the static location 'into'), not 에서 (which marks a source) — that 에 vs 에서 split is exactly what separates 넣다 ('put into', 에) from its opposite 빼다 ('take out from', 에서).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 넣다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 넣어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
넣다 is a regular verb — keep the ㅎ in writing: the past is 넣었어요, not 너었어요.
Use 에 for the destination, not 에서: 가방에 넣다 (put into the bag), since 에서 marks a source, not a goal.

lesson.canDo: Use 넣어요 in a real beginner sentence, then change it into want, can, cannot, and have-to forms without losing the basic meaning.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 넣어요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 넣다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 설탕을 넣어요. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 안 넣어요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 넣을 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 넣어요 feels easy, practice 넣고 싶어요, 넣을 수 있어요, and 넣어야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

Learner changes the sentence to 안 넣어요, then 넣을 수 없어요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

entries.shortExplanation: 빼다 means "to take out / to subtract" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to take out / to subtract" in Korean is 빼다 (ppaeda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 빼요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 빼다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 오이를 빼 주세요 ("Please leave out the cucumber") — then reshape the same stem into 빼고 싶어요 (desire), 뺄 수 있어요 (ability), and 뺄 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 빼요. Then practice 안 빼요 vs 뺄 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

usagePhrases.en: I do not take out / to subtract.

usagePhrases.note: 빼다 + 주세요 is how you ask for an ingredient to be removed when ordering.

examples.note: Super useful when ordering food; 에서 marks where it's removed from.

examples.en: I took my hand out of my pocket

examples.note: The idiom 살을 빼다 ('lose weight') with -려고 ('in order to').

entries.nuance: 빼다 means to take something out, remove it, leave it off, or — in math — subtract, and it's the natural transitive opposite of 넣다 ('put in'). Two collocations make it indispensable from day one: ordering food, where 빼 주세요 politely asks for an ingredient to be left out (오이 빼 주세요), and 살을 빼다, the standard idiom for 'lose weight' (literally 'take out flesh') — English speakers reaching for a 잃다-style 'lose' here sound wrong. The particle pitfall mirrors 넣다 exactly: the source takes 에서 ('out from'), so 가방에서 빼다, not 가방에 빼다. The conjugation pitfall is the contraction: the stem ends in ㅐ, and ㅐ + 어 simply merges, so the present is 빼요 (not 빼어요) and the past is 뺐어요 (not 빼었어요). Distinguish 빼다 ('remove/extract, transitive') from the intransitive 빠지다 ('fall out / drop out / be excluded'): you 빼다 a name from a list, but a name 빠지다 (goes missing) from it.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 빼다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 빼요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
The present is just 빼요 (not 빼어요) and past 뺐어요, because the ㅐ stem absorbs the 어.
Use 에서 for the source: 가방에서 책을 빼다 (take out of the bag), not 가방에 — 에 marks a destination, the opposite direction.

entries.nuance: 차다 most commonly means to kick, taking a 을/를 object for what's kicked (공을 차다), and the instrument 'with the foot' takes 로 → 발로 차다. It conjugates as a regular ㅏ-stem verb where ㅏ + 아 contracts: 차 + 아 → 차요, past 찼어요 (not 차아요). The thing to flag for learners is that 차다 is really three homophones sharing a spelling: (1) 'kick'; (2) 'be full / fill up' (방이 사람으로 가득 찼어요 'the room filled with people'); and (3) 'wear' a watch or bracelet (시계를 차다) — context disambiguates, and as a beginner you should lock in 'kick' first. There's also a high-frequency slang spin via the passive 차이다: 차다 someone = 'dump' a partner, and 차이다 = 'get dumped' (남자친구한테 차였어요), which surprises English speakers. Don't confuse 차다 ('kick') with 치다, the verb for hitting/striking (테니스를 치다, 박수를 치다) — feet 차다, hands/rackets 치다.

The present is just 차요 (not 차아요) and past 찼어요, because the ㅏ stem absorbs the 아.
Don't use 차다 for hitting with the hand or a racket — that's 치다 (박수를 치다, 테니스를 치다); 차다 is kicking with the foot.

usagePhrases.note: 밟다 = tread on something; what you step on takes 을/를.

examples.en: Sorry, I stepped on your foot
examples.note: Said after bumping someone in a crowd; pairs with 미안해요/죄송해요.

examples.en: I stepped on gum on the street
examples.note: Treading on something on the ground; the place takes 에서.

examples.en: Please don't step on the flowers
examples.note: A polite request not to tread on something.

entries.nuance: 밟다 means to step on or tread on something, taking a 을/를 object, and in daily life it shows up constantly in two settings: apologizing after stepping on someone in a crowd (발을 밟았어요 + 죄송해요) and driving, where you 밟다 the pedals — 액셀을 밟다 ('hit the gas'), 브레이크를 밟다 ('hit the brakes'). The conjugation is the classic trap: the spelling has the double final ㄼ and *looks* like it might be ㅂ-irregular, but 밟다 is fully regular — the ㅂ stays, so it's 밟 + 아요 → 밟아요 and past 밟았어요, never anything like 발워요. (Pronunciation note: the standard reading keeps the ㅂ, roughly 'bal-ba-yo'.) For meaning, keep 밟다 ('step on, with downward foot pressure') apart from 차다 ('kick', a striking motion) and from 디디다 ('plant/set your foot down', as in taking a step or gaining a foothold) — 밟다 emphasizes pressing down onto whatever is underfoot.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 밟다 becomes 밟을 수 있어요 ("can") and 밟을 거예요 ("will"). entries.shortExplanation: 세우다 means "to stop (a vehicle) / to stand up" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 세우다 (seuda) = "to stop (a vehicle) / to stand up". entries.nuance: 세우다 is the transitive 'make (something) stand / bring to a stop', and it's the causative partner of 서다 ('to stand still / come to a stop, by itself'): 서다 is what a car does on its own, 세우다 is you stopping it. The must-memorize phrase is 여기 세워 주세요 ('please stop here'), the standard way to get a taxi to pull over. Its 'make stand' core also yields the very common abstract 계획을 세우다 ('make a plan', literally 'set a plan upright'). Conjugation pitfall: the stem ends in 우, and 우 + 어 contracts to 워, so the present is 세워요 and the past 세웠어요 (not 세우어요). The transitivity pitfall is the one to drill: 세우다 takes a 을/를 object (차를 세우다 = 'stop the car'), while the intransitive 서다 doesn't (차가 섰어요 = 'the car stopped') — English uses 'stop' for both, so learners wrongly say 차가 세워요. Don't write 세우어요 — the 우 stem contracts with 어 to 워, so it's 세워요, past 세웠어요.

usagePhrases.note: The single most common collocation; Koreans 가격 비교 ('price comparison') before any purchase.

examples.en: I compare prices
examples.note: The plainest frame: object + 을/를 + 비교해요, an everyday shopping habit.

examples.ko: 사기 전에 두 제품을 비교해 봤어요
examples.romanization: sagi jeone du jepumeul bigyohae bwasseoyo
examples.en: Before buying, I compared the two products
examples.note: 사기 전에 ('before buying') + 비교해 봤어요 ('tried comparing') is exactly how a shopper talks.

examples.en: Please don't compare (your child) with others' children
examples.note: 남(의) ('other people's') + 와 + 비교하지 마세요 — a heartfelt request, the social side of this verb.

entries.nuance: 비교하다 is the Sino-Korean verb 比較(비교, 'compare-contrast') + 하다, meaning to set two or more things side by side to weigh their differences. The thing(s) compared take 을/를, and the second item of a pair takes 와/과 (formal) or 하고/랑 (casual): A를 B와 비교하다. Being a 하다 verb it conjugates to 해요 (never 하요) and 했어요. Distinguish it from 대조하다 (對照, 'contrast'), which highlights opposites for academic effect, while 비교하다 is the neutral everyday word ('compare prices, compare two phones'). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: learners copy English 'compare A to B' and say 가격에 비교해요, but the object marker must be 을/를 — 가격을 비교해요. Note too the social weight of 비교당하다 ('to be compared', passive): Koreans dislike being measured against others, so 비교하지 마 ('stop comparing me') is emotionally loaded.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 비교하다 becomes 비교할 수 있어요 ("can") and 비교할 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: Setting two or more things side by side to weigh their differences. The thing(s) compared take 을/를, and the second item of a pair takes 와/과 (formal) or 하고/랑 (casual): A를 B와 비교하다. Note too the social weight of 비교당하다 ('to be compared', passive): Koreans dislike being measured against others, so 비교하지 마 ('stop comparing me') is emotionally loaded.
Distinguish it from 대조하다 (對照, 'contrast'), which highlights opposites for academic effect, while 비교하다 is the neutral everyday word ('compare prices, compare two phones').
The Sino-Korean verb 比較 (비교, 'compare-contrast') + 하다.
Being a 하다 verb it conjugates to 해요 (never 하요) and 했어요.
The particle: learners copy English 'compare A to B' and say 가격에 비교해요, but the object marker must be 을/를 — 가격을 비교해요.

examples.en: Both are good, so it's hard to pick one
examples.note: 선택하기 어렵다 ('hard to choose') turns the verb into a noun with -기.

entries.nuance: 선택하다 is 選擇(선택, 'select-pick') + 하다 and means to pick a defined option from a presented set — menus, app settings, multiple-choice answers, life paths. It is the bookish, neutral register; in spoken everyday Korean the native verb 고르다 ('pick out') is warmer and more common ('과일을 골랐어요'). Crucially, contrast it with 결정하다 (決定, 'decide'): 선택하다 is choosing one option among several that already exist, while 결정하다 is settling a matter or reaching a conclusion ('유학을 결정했어요' = decided to study abroad). As a 하다 verb it gives 선택해요 / 선택했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the 고르다 split: say 메뉴를 선택해요 with 을/를 (not 메뉴에), and don't force 선택하다 into casual chat where a native would simply say 골라요. Also, 'choose to do X' is not 선택하다 alone — Korean prefers ~기로 하다/결심하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 선택하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 선택해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 선택하다 to translate every English 'choose', including 'I chose to stay'. For 'choose to do', Korean uses ~기로 하다: 남기로 했어요, not 남는 것을 선택했어요.
Marking the option with 에 (메뉴에 선택해요) under the influence of English. The chosen thing is a direct object: 메뉴를 선택해요.
Treating 선택하다 and 결정하다 as interchangeable. 선택하다 = pick an existing option; 결정하다 = decide/settle a matter. 'I decided' is 결정했어요.

usagePhrases.note: The core grammar: 끊기로 결심했어요 ('resolved to quit'). The -기로 is almost obligatory.

examples.en: I resolved to learn Korean
examples.note: Textbook frame: V-기로 결심했어요, a goal you set for yourself.

examples.en: I firmly resolved to exercise from the new year
examples.note: 새해부터 ('from the new year') + 굳게 — a classic resolution sentence.

examples.en: After hesitating several times, I finally made up my mind
examples.note: 망설이다가 ('hesitating and then') + 결국 ('in the end') shows the inner struggle this verb implies.

entries.nuance: 결심하다 is 決心(결심, 'decide-heart', literally 'fix the heart') + 하다, so it is not a neutral 'decide' but a determined, willpower-charged resolve — the New-Year-resolution verb. The indispensable pattern is V-기로 결심하다 ('make up one's mind to do V'): 담배를 끊기로 결심했어요. Contrast it sharply with 결정하다 (決定, 'decide-settle'): 결정하다 settles an external matter and can be about logistics or other people ('회의 날짜를 결정했어요' = decided the meeting date), whereas 결심하다 is always your own inner determination about your own action — you can't 결심하다 someone else's schedule. It is also stronger than casual 마음먹다, which feels homier. As a 하다 verb: 결심해요 / 결심했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping -기로 (saying 운동 결심했어요) and overusing 결심하다 for trivial choices; for 'I decided to have pasta tonight' Koreans just say 파스타 먹기로 했어요, reserving 결심하다 for serious resolve.

Using 결심하다 for routine decisions like picking a restaurant. It signals strong willpower; for light choices use ~기로 하다 (점심 먹기로 했어요).
Swapping it with 결정하다 when settling an external matter. 'We decided the date' is 날짜를 결정했어요, not 결심했어요 — 결심 is personal inner resolve only.

entries.explanation: 기대하다 (gidaehada) means "to expect". Start from the polite form 기대해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 기대하다. A strong first sentence is 여행을 기대하다 ("to look forward to a trip"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 기대하다 also becomes 기대하고 싶어요 (want), 기대할 수 있어요 (can), and 기대할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: to look forward to a trip
usagePhrases.note: Object + 을/를 + 기대하다 for the happy-anticipation sense.

examples.en: I'm looking forward to the weekend
examples.note: Plain frame; the hopeful, positive flavor of the verb.

examples.en: I'm really excited for this movie
examples.note: 기대돼요 (from 기대되다) describes the feeling rising in you, no object needed.

examples.en: If you expect too much, you might be disappointed
examples.note: 기대하면 ('if you expect') + 실망하다 pairs hope with its risk.

entries.nuance: 기대하다 is 期待(기대, 'period-await', i.e. 'await a hoped-for time') + 하다, and unlike English 'expect' it leans positive: it means to anticipate something good and look forward to it. The thing awaited takes 을/를 (여행을 기대해요). Its hugely common intransitive twin 기대되다/기대가 되다 ('to be exciting, to be looked forward to') describes the feeling welling up in you — 내일이 기대돼요 — and beginners must keep the two apart: you 기대하다 a thing, but a thing/situation 기대된다 to you. Contrast with 기다리다 ('wait'), which is just neutral temporal waiting with no hope ('버스를 기다려요'); and with 바라다 ('wish/hope') which is a desire without the sense of confident anticipation. As a 하다 verb: 기대해요 / 기대했어요. The pitfall: English speakers map 'expect' onto neutral or negative situations ('I expect rain', 'I expect you to be late') — Korean 기대하다 cannot carry that. For neutral prediction use 예상하다 (豫想); 기대하다 is only for things you hope will be good.

Using 기대하다 for neutral or bad predictions like 'I expect it to rain'. That is 예상하다 (비가 올 것으로 예상해요). 기대하다 is positive anticipation only.
Confusing active 기대하다 with intransitive 기대되다. You 기대하다 something (여행을 기대해요), but a thing 기대된다 to you (여행이 기대돼요) — don't say 여행을 기대돼요.
Treating it as 기다리다. 'I'm waiting for the bus' is 버스를 기다려요 (neutral waiting), whereas 기대하다 adds hopeful excitement and can't replace it.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 기대하다 becomes 기대할 수 있어요 ("can") and 기대할 거예요 ("will"). English speakers map 'expect' onto neutral or negative situations ('I expect rain', 'I expect you to be late') — Korean 기대하다 cannot carry that.

usagePhrases.note: Object + 을/를 + 상상하다; the object is a scene/picture in the mind.

entries.nuance: 상상하다 is 想像(상상, 'think-image', i.e. 'form a mental image') + 하다 — to picture in your mind something not present, from a fantasy to a hypothetical future. usagePhrases.note: Object of focus takes 에, not 을/를: 일에 집중하다, 수업에 집중하다.

examples.en: I concentrate in class
examples.note: 수업에 ('on the class') — note 에, the signature particle of this verb.

examples.en: It's noisy, so I can't concentrate on work
examples.note: 시끄러워서 ('because it's noisy') + 일에 집중하다 in a real distraction scene.

examples.en: Let's focus for just 30 minutes
examples.note: 딱 ... 만 ('exactly ... only') + 집중해 봐요, an encouraging study nudge.

entries.nuance: 집중하다 is 集中(집중, 'gather-center', i.e. 'draw to a central point') + 하다 — to gather your attention onto one thing. Its defining grammar trait is the particle: the focus target takes 에 (공부에 집중하다, 일에 집중하다), NOT 을/를, because you are 'centering toward' a point. The intransitive 집중이 되다/안 되다 ('focus comes / won't come') is essential for everyday complaints: 집중이 안 돼요. Contrast it with 몰두하다 (沒頭, 'sink the head in'), which is deeper, more absorbed immersion ('연구에 몰두하다'), and with 신경 쓰다, which is worried attention rather than productive focus. Also, English 'focus on doing X' becomes ~하는 데(에) 집중하다 (외우는 데 집중해요), not a borrowed gerund; and to tell someone to pay attention right now, the natural phrase is 집중하세요 or 집중 좀 해 ('focus, please').

entries.explanation: 인정하다 (injeonghada) means "to admit". Start from the polite form 인정해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 인정하다. Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: Object + 을/를 + 인정하다; 실수를 인정하다 ('admit a mistake') is the apology staple.

examples.en: I admit my fault
examples.note: Plain apology frame: 잘못을 인정하다, owning your error.

examples.ko: 그 사람 실력은 인정할 수밖에 없어요
examples.romanization: geu saram sillyeogeun injeonghal subakke eopseoyo
examples.en: I have no choice but to acknowledge that person's skill
examples.note: ~ㄹ 수밖에 없다 ('can only') + 인정하다 = grudging recognition.

examples.en: Honestly, I'll admit it — I was wrong
examples.note: 솔직히 ('frankly') + 인정할게요 ('I'll admit') in a candid confession.

entries.nuance: 인정하다 is 認定(인정, 'recognize-fix', i.e. 'recognize as established') + 하다, covering two linked senses: to admit/own up to something (잘못을 인정하다 = admit a fault) and to acknowledge/recognize something or someone as valid (실력을 인정하다 = recognize ability). The object takes 을/를. Its passive 인정받다 ('to be recognized') is a high-value word — earning 인정 from others is a big social currency in Korea. In texting slang, 인정 (or ㅇㅈ) alone means 'true / agreed / fair point'. Contrast with 동의하다 ('agree'), which is sharing an opinion or consenting, whereas 인정하다 is conceding a truth even one you dislike — you can 인정하다 a rival's talent without 동의하다 their views; and with 자백하다 (自白, confess a crime), which is far heavier and legal. As a 하다 verb: 인정해요 / 인정했어요. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 에 (잘못에 인정해요) — it's 을/를; and note that 'admit defeat' is the set phrase 패배를 인정하다, while a flat 인정할 수 없어요 means 'I refuse to accept that', a firm rejection, not mere doubt.

entries.nuance: 마음먹다 is a vivid native idiom: 마음 ('heart/mind') + 먹다 ('eat'), literally 'to eat the mind' — to take a decision firmly inside you, i.e. make up your mind. The signature grammar is V-기로 마음먹다 (운동하기로 마음먹었어요). Although 먹다 here is figurative, it conjugates as the ordinary verb 먹다, giving 마음먹어요 / 마음먹었어요 / 마음먹으면. Compare it with 결심하다: both mean 'resolve', but 마음먹다 is homier, more conversational and gut-level, while Sino-Korean 결심하다 is a touch more formal and goal-oriented — a New Year's 결심 looks better on a list, but a friend would say 나 운동하기로 마음먹었어. Distinguish too from 작정하다 ('to be set/determined', often with a stubborn or even negative edge: 작정하고 덤비다 = come at it with full intent). The English-speaker pitfall: keep it as one word 마음먹다 in the 'resolve' sense — splitting it into 마음을 먹다 sounds odd; and don't drop -기로, since 운동 마음먹었어요 is ungrammatical. Note the proverb-like 마음먹기에 달렸다 ('it depends on your mindset'), great for encouragement.

Dropping the -기로 connector (운동 마음먹었어요). The action resolved upon must end in -기로: 운동하기로 마음먹었어요.
Assuming the figurative 먹다 conjugates oddly. It behaves like normal 먹다: 마음먹어요 / 마음먹었어요 / 마음먹으면, not any special form.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'to eat the mind' — to take a decision firmly inside you, i.e. make up your mind. The signature grammar is V-기로 마음먹다 (운동하기로 마음먹었어요). Note the proverb-like 마음먹기에 달렸다 ('it depends on your mindset'), great for encouragement.

Compare it with 결심하다: both mean 'resolve', but 마음먹다 is homier, more conversational and gut-level, while Sino-Korean 결심하다 is a touch more formal and goal-oriented — a New Year's 결심 looks better on a list, but a friend would say 나 운동하기로 마음먹었어. Distinguish too from 작정하다 ('to be set/determined', often with a stubborn or even negative edge: 작정하고 덤비다 = come at it with full intent).
A vivid native idiom: 마음 ('heart/mind') + 먹다 ('eat').
Although 먹다 here is figurative, it conjugates as the ordinary verb 먹다, giving 마음먹어요 / 마음먹었어요 / 마음먹으면.
Keep it as one word 마음먹다 in the 'resolve' sense — splitting it into 마음을 먹다 sounds odd; and don't drop -기로, since 운동 마음먹었어요 is ungrammatical.

entries.shortExplanation: 잊어버리다 means "to forget" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to forget" in Korean is 잊어버리다 (ijeobeorida). Grow outward from one concrete line — 이름을 잊어버리다 ("to forget a name") — then reshape the same stem into 잊어버리고 싶어요 (desire), 잊어버릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 잊어버릴 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Object + 을/를 + 잊어버리다; 약속을 잊어버리다 ('forget an appointment') is a common slip.

examples.en: I forgot the password
examples.note: Everyday frame; note the past 리 + 었 → 렸: 잊어버렸어요.

examples.en: It slipped my mind and I didn't bring an umbrella
examples.note: 깜빡 잊어버리고 ('forgetting in a flash, and...') chains to the consequence.

examples.note: 잊어버리세요 ('do forget') used kindly to help someone move on.

entries.nuance: 잊어버리다 is the native compound 잊다 ('forget') + -어 버리다 (the auxiliary 버리다, 'throw away / do completely'), so it means to forget thoroughly, with the nuance that the memory is gone for good — often tinged with regret ('darn, it's gone'). Plain 잊다 states the bare fact of forgetting; 잊어버리다 adds finality and emotional color, which is why everyday speech overwhelmingly uses 잊어버리다. The object takes 을/를. Conjugation: the 리 stem contracts with 어 to 려, hence 잊어버려요 / 잊어버렸어요. The most dangerous English-speaker pitfall is the near-twin 잃어버리다 ('to lose a physical object'): 잊다 (forget, from the mind) vs 잃다 (lose, from your possession) differ by one jamo and one meaning — you 잊어버리다 a name but 잃어버리다 your wallet. Mixing them is the classic learner error. Also note: to tell someone 'don't forget', say 잊어버리지 마세요 or just 잊지 마세요; and writing the uncontracted 잊어버리었어요 is wrong — it must be 잊어버렸어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 잊어버리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 잊어버려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing it with 잃어버리다 ('lose an object'). You 잊어버리다 information (이름을 잊어버렸어요) but 잃어버리다 things (지갑을 잃어버렸어요). One jamo, totally different meaning.
Writing the uncontracted past 잊어버리었어요. The 리 + 었 contracts to 렸: 잊어버렸어요.
Thinking 잊다 and 잊어버리다 are fully interchangeable. 잊어버리다 adds 'completely/for good' and is the everyday choice; bare 잊다 is more neutral or literary.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability

entries.explanation: 생각나다 (saenggangnada) = "to come to mind". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 생각나요 plus one useful sentence like 이름이 생각나다 ("a name comes to mind"). usagePhrases.en: I do not come to mind.
I want to come to mind.
I have to come to mind.

usagePhrases.note: The recalled thing takes 이/가, not 을/를: 단어가 생각나요.

examples.en: My hometown suddenly comes to mind
examples.note: 이/가 marks what surfaces in memory; the feeling arises on its own.

examples.en: I've got a good idea!
examples.note: 생각이 나다 split by 좋은 — the everyday 'I have an idea' exclamation.

examples.ko: 아무리 해도 그 단어가 생각나지 않아요
examples.romanization: amuri haedo geu daneoga saenggangnaji anayo
examples.en: No matter what, I just can't recall that word
examples.note: 아무리 해도 ('however much I try') + 생각나지 않다 = the tip-of-the-tongue feeling.

entries.nuance: 생각나다 is 생각 ('thought') + 나다 ('arise / come out'), so it literally means 'a thought arises' — something comes to mind or you recall it spontaneously, without effort. This grammar is the heart of the word: because the memory surfaces by itself, the recalled thing is the SUBJECT and takes 이/가 (이름이 생각나요), not 을/를. Contrast it sharply with 생각하다 ('think'), which is volitional, active deliberation taking 을/를 (그 일을 생각해요 = I'm thinking about that): 생각하다 = you do the thinking; 생각나다 = a thought comes to you. Compare also 기억나다 ('a memory comes back', near-synonym, slightly more about stored memory) and 떠오르다 ('to float up', vivid for ideas/images suddenly emerging). 나다 is a regular verb: 생각나요 / 생각났어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the agency: learners translate 'I remember the name' as 이름을 생각나요 with an object, but Korean frames it as the name doing the surfacing — 이름이 생각나요. And 'I can't remember' is naturally the negative 생각이 안 나요 / 생각나지 않아요, not a 'can't' construction.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 생각나다 as a complete polite sentence.

Marking the recalled thing with 을/를: 이름을 생각나요. Because the memory arises on its own, it is the subject: 이름이 생각나요.
Confusing 생각나다 (a thought comes to you, involuntary) with 생각하다 (you actively think, volitional). 'I'm thinking about it' is 생각하고 있어요, not 생각나고 있어요.
Saying 생각할 수 없어요 for 'I can't remember'. The idiomatic form is the negative 생각이 안 나요 or 생각나지 않아요.

entries.shortExplanation: 신경 쓰다 means "to care about" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 신경 쓰다 (singyeong sseuda) means "to care about". Start from the polite form 신경 써요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 신경 쓰다. A strong first sentence is 건강에 신경 쓰다 ("to look after one's health"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 신경 쓰다 also becomes 신경 쓰고 싶어요 (want), 신경 쓸 수 있어요 (can), and 신경 쓸 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: What you mind about takes 에: 외모에 신경 쓰다, 디테일에 신경 쓰다.

examples.en: I pay attention to how I dress
examples.note: 옷차림에 ('on one's outfit') + 신경 쓰다 — note the 에 particle.

examples.en: Don't let that kind of comment bother you
examples.note: 신경 쓰지 마세요 used to comfort someone who's hurt.

examples.ko: 다른 사람 눈치까지 신경 쓰느라 피곤해요

entries.nuance: 신경 쓰다 pairs the Sino-Korean noun 神經 (신경, 'nerve') with the verb 쓰다 ('use'), literally 'to use one's nerves' — to expend mental energy minding, caring about, or worrying over something. It spans neutral attention (디테일에 신경 쓰다 = pay attention to detail) and anxious preoccupation (남 눈치에 신경 쓰다 = fret over others' reactions). The object of concern takes 에 (or 에게/한테 for a person), not 을/를. Conjugation is a key trap: 쓰다 is a ㅡ-irregular, so the ㅡ drops before 어 — 쓰 + 어 → 써, giving 신경 써요 / 신경 썼어요, never 신경 쓰어요. Contrast it with 걱정하다 ('worry'), which is pure anxiety about an outcome, whereas 신경 쓰다 is the act of devoting attention (which may or may not be worried); and with 관심 있다 ('be interested'), which is positive curiosity. The single most useful phrase is 신경 쓰지 마(세요) ('don't worry about it / never mind'), heard constantly. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 을/를 (그 일을 신경 써요) — say 그 일에 신경 써요; and don't reach for 돌보다 ('physically take care of, tend') when you mean mental attention — '나는 외모에 신경 써' is care/attention, not nursing.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 신경 쓰다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 신경 써요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the concern with 을/를 (그것을 신경 써요). 신경 쓰다 takes 에: 그것에 신경 써요 (people: 그 사람에게 신경 써요).
Ignoring the ㅡ-irregular and writing 신경 쓰어요 / 신경 쓰었어요. The ㅡ drops: 신경 써요 / 신경 썼어요.
Using 걱정하다 when you mean attentive minding. 신경 쓰다 = devote attention (possibly worried); 걱정하다 = be anxious about an outcome. 'I'm worried about the exam' is 시험이 걱정돼요.
notes: ㅡ: memorize 신경 써 and 신경 써요 together.

conjugationTips.body: 신경 쓰다 has an irregular stem (ㅡ). Memorize its polite form 신경 써요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'to use one's nerves' — to expend mental energy minding, caring about, or worrying over something. It spans neutral attention (디테일에 신경 쓰다 = pay attention to detail) and anxious preoccupation (남 눈치에 신경 쓰다 = fret over others' reactions). Pairs the Sino-Korean noun 神經 (신경, 'nerve') with the verb 쓰다 ('use').
쓰다 is a ㅡ-irregular, so the ㅡ drops before 어 — 쓰 + 어 → 써, giving 신경 써요 / 신경 썼어요, never 신경 쓰어요.
Don't use 을/를 (그 일을 신경 써요) — say 그 일에 신경 써요; and don't reach for 돌보다 ('physically take care of, tend') when you mean mental attention — '나는 외모에 신경 써' is care/attention, not nursing.

entries.nuance: 알아채다 is the native compound 알다 ('know') + 채다 ('snatch / catch quickly'), so it means to suddenly catch on to or become aware of something — often something subtle, hidden, or not openly stated (a lie, a mood shift, a hint). Contrast it with 눈치채다, an almost identical everyday synonym focused on reading social cues; the two are largely interchangeable, though 눈치채다 leans toward interpersonal/atmospheric cues. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 들어가요 the way English reuses 'come', and forgetting that 'inside here' wants 안으로/안에.

entries.nuance: 향하다 is Sino-Korean: 向 ('turn toward, face') + 하다, literally 'to do facing'. It means to head for or be oriented toward a direction/destination, which is marked with 으로/로 (집으로 향하다); when it takes 를/을 it leans toward 'to face' (바다를 향하다). The synonym line versus plain 가다: 가다 just says you move, while 향하다 spotlights the direction you are aimed at, and it reads more formal or written — in casual speech people simply say 집에 가요, not 집으로 향해요. A very common shape is the 어-form 향해 used adverbially: '…를/으로 향해 + motion verb' (출구를 향해 걸어가다). It also goes figurative — 꿈/목표를 향해 나아가다 — sounding aspirational. The English-speaker pitfall is forcing 에 ('to a place') as in '집에 향해요'; 향하다 wants 으로/로, and overusing it in everyday chat sounds stiff.

Dropping the object marker before 향해: it is 바다를 향해, not 바다 향해, when expressing 'facing the sea'.

entries.nuance: 머물다 means to stay or remain somewhere for a stretch of time — a hotel, a friend's house, a city — and figuratively for a feeling or gaze that lingers (마음에 머물다). It is a ㄹ-stem (ㄹ-탈락) verb, the trap that trips up English speakers most: the ㄹ silently drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, giving 머뭅니다 and the polite request 머무세요, while the 어-form irregularly doubles to 머물러요 / 머물렀어요. The synonym boundary: 묵다 is the close cousin specifically for lodging overnight (호텔에서 묵다) and feels a touch more colloquial for 'put up at'; 있다 ('be/stay') is what casual travel talk actually uses — 호텔에 있어요 — while 머물다 sounds a bit more composed or written. Place takes 에, and a duration like 며칠 or 일주일 sits bare with no particle. The pitfall is regularizing the conjugation: not 머물습니다 and not 머물어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 머물다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 머물러요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the formal form as 머물습니다 — the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, so it is 머뭅니다.
Forgetting the 어-form doubles: it is 머물러요 / 머물렀어요, not 머물어요 / 머물었어요.
Putting a particle on the duration: say 며칠 머물러요, not 며칠을 머물러요 — the time span stands bare.

entries.nuance: 다가오다 is 다가서다/다가- ('draw near') + 오다 (come), so it is 'to approach TOWARD the speaker' — a person, animal, or even a date getting closer. The viewpoint contrast English speakers must internalize is its mirror verb 다가가다 (… + 가다): identical meaning but opposite direction, so 다가오다 = it nears me, 다가가다 = I near it. Versus the simpler 가까워지다 ('become close', often abstract like relationships), 다가오다 keeps a sense of active motion or a looming approach. A person you approach takes 한테/에게; when time or events are the subject they take 이/가 (시험이 다가와요) and the verb becomes the go-to way to say something is 'coming up'. It can also mean 'resonate' — 마음에 다가오다. The pitfall is mixing the come/go pair, plus marking the approaching event with 를 instead of 이/가.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 다가오다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 다가와요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Mixing up direction: 다가오다 = coming toward you; for moving toward something else use 다가가다.
Marking the looming event with 를: it is 시험이 다가와요, not 시험을 다가와요 — the event is the subject.
Using the person as a 를-object: a person approached takes 한테/에게 (저한테 다가왔어요), not 저를 다가왔어요.

entries.nuance: 들어서다 is 들다 (enter) + 서다 (stand/step), so its core image is 'to step across and stand inside' — it pinpoints the moment of crossing the threshold, not the journey of entering. The contrast English speakers need is with 들어가다/들어오다: those track direction (in-away vs in-toward), whereas 들어서다 freezes the instant your foot lands inside, which is why it pairs so often with -자/-니 ('the moment I stepped in …'). It is slightly more descriptive/literary, so for plain spoken 'go in / come in' a beginner should still reach for 들어가다 and 들어오다. It also has a strong figurative life in writing: 새 시대/국면/단계에 들어서다 = to enter a new era/phase/stage, and 건물이 들어서다 = a building 'goes up/comes to stand' on a site. Place takes 에, direction 으로. The pitfall is treating it as a free synonym of 들어가다 in casual speech, where it sounds oddly narrated.

Use 들어서요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

Forcing 를 on the place: it is 방에 들어서다, not 방을 들어서다 — the location takes 에 (or 으로 for direction).

entries.nuance: 넘어가다 is 넘다 (to cross/exceed) + 가다 (go): literally to go over something — a hill, wall, or ridge — to the other side, and figuratively to 'move on' to the next page, topic, or step (다음으로 넘어가다), which makes it a fixture in lessons and meetings. The dangerous near-look-alike is 넘어지다 ('to fall over, topple') — one letter apart but a totally different action — and don't confuse it with the transitive 넘기다 ('to flip/hand over/get past'). For simply going somewhere, 가다 suffices; 넘어가다 specifically adds the 'over/across or onward' nuance. The pitfall is the 넘어가다/넘어지다 mix-up and choosing the wrong particle for obstacle vs next-step.

Mixing it with transitive 넘기다 — you 페이지를 넘기다 (flip a page) but 다음 페이지로 넘어가다 (move on to the next page).

entries.nuance: 돌다 means to turn, spin, or go around, and intransitively to circulate (소문/돈/감기가 돌다 = rumors/money/a cold going around). It is a ㄹ-stem (ㄹ-탈락) verb, which is the main hurdle: the ㄹ vanishes before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, so the formal is 돕니다 (not 돌습니다) and the polite 'please turn' for directions is 도세요 (not 돌으세요), while the 어-form is the regular 돌아요. The crucial pair English speakers must split is 돌다 vs 돌리다: 돌다 is intransitive (something turns/spins by itself — 팽이가 돌다, the wheel turns), whereas 돌리다 is transitive (you turn something — 핸들을 돌리다). Direction takes 으로 (오른쪽으로 돌다); a lap takes the counter 바퀴. The pitfall is regularizing the ㄹ-stem forms and using 돌다 where you actually act on an object, which needs 돌리다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 돌다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 돌아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the polite request as 돌으세요 — the ㄹ drops, so it is 도세요.
Saying 돌습니다 for the formal present — the ㄹ-stem rule removes the ㄹ, giving 돕니다.
Using 돌다 when you turn an object (핸들을 돌다) — that needs the transitive 돌리다 (핸들을 돌리다).
notes: ㄹ: memorize 돌아 and 돌아요 together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 돌다 becomes 돌 수 있어요 ("can") and 돌 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 돌다 has an irregular stem (ㄹ). Memorize its polite form 돌아요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

structuredNuance.t: 돌다 means to turn, spin, or go around, and intransitively to circulate (소문/돈/감기가 돌다 = rumors/money/a cold going around). Direction takes 으로 (오른쪽으로 돌다); a lap takes the counter 바퀴.

After that the endings carry the meaning — 돌리고 싶어요 for what you want, 돌릴 수 있어요 for what you can, 돌릴 수 없어요 for what you can't. entries.nuance: 돌리다 is the transitive partner of 돌다 (built with the causative -리-): you turn something — a handle, your head — or 'run' a machine like a washer or vacuum (세탁기를 돌리다). It is a regular 이-stem verb, so the 어-form is simply 돌려요 / 돌렸어요 with no ㄹ-drop drama, unlike its intransitive sibling 돌다. The clean rule English speakers need: if the thing turns by itself, use 돌다 (팽이가 돌아요); if you make something turn, use 돌리다 (팽이를 돌려요) — Korean splits self-turning vs turning-something the way English 'turn' does not. It also carries rich idioms: 마음을 돌리다 (change someone's mind / win them over), 고개를 돌리다 (turn away), 전화를 돌리다 (older: dial / route a call). The object always takes 를/을. The pitfall is reaching for 돌다 when an object is involved, and over-applying ㄹ-stem rules that simply don't apply here.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 돌리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 돌려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Mixing up 돌다 (turn by itself) and 돌리다 (turn something) — the washer is 세탁기를 돌려요 because you operate it.
Dropping the object marker: it is 고개를 돌려요, not 고개 돌려요 — 돌리다 needs a 를/을 object.
Applying the ㄹ-stem drop here: 돌리다 is regular, so it is 돌립니다, never 돕니다 — that form belongs to 돌다.

entries.english: to set out / to step forward
entries.shortExplanation: 나서다 means "to set out / to step forward" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 나서다 (naseoda) means "to set out / to step forward". Start from the polite form 나서요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 나서다. A strong first sentence is 집을 나서다 ("to set out from home"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 나서다 also becomes 나서고 싶어요 (want), 나설 수 있어요 (can), and 나설 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 나서요. Then practice 안 나서요 vs 나설 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

usagePhrases.note: 를/을 marks the place left behind; 집을 나서다 = head out to start the day.

examples.en: I set out from home early in the morning.
examples.note: Simple; 집을 나서다 takes 를/을 — leaving home to start the day.

examples.en: I stepped forward to volunteer to present.
examples.note: Everyday; 앞으로 나서다 = step up/forward to take something on.

examples.en: The neighbors took it on themselves to solve the problem.
examples.note: Real-situation, figurative; -에 나서다 = step up to undertake a task.

entries.nuance: 나서다 is 나다/나- ('come out') + 서다 (stand/step), giving two linked senses: to set out / head off (집을 나서다 = leave home to start your day; 길을 나서다 = hit the road) and to step forward — physically to the front, or figuratively to volunteer and take charge (문제 해결에 나서다 = step up to tackle a problem). The line versus plain 나가다 ('go out') matters: 나가다 just exits a space, while 나서다 carries the flavor of launching a journey or actively putting yourself forward, often with initiative or even pushiness — note 나서다 can imply meddling, as in 남의 일에 나서다 (butt into others' business). For leaving home, 집을 나서다 takes the object marker 를/을, where 나가다 would too but sounds plainer. Idioms like 발 벗고 나서다 (pitch in wholeheartedly) live here. The pitfall is treating it as a flat synonym of 나가다 and missing the 'take the initiative' nuance.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 나서다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 나서요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 나서다 (set out / step up) with 나가다 (just go out) — 나서다 implies beginning a journey or actively volunteering.
Using 에 for the place left: it is 집을 나서다 (를/을), not 집에 나서다.
Overusing 나서다 for 'help out' without noticing its 'put yourself forward' tone — 남의 일에 나서다 can sound like meddling.

entries.english: to run into / to bump into
entries.shortExplanation: 마주치다 means "to run into / to bump into" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to run into / to bump into" in Korean is 마주치다 (majuchida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 마주쳐요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 마주치다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 우연히 마주치다 ("to run into by chance") — then reshape the same stem into 마주치고 싶어요 (desire), 마주칠 수 있어요 (ability), and 마주칠 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 마주쳐요. Then practice 안 마주쳐요 vs 마주칠 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

I want to run into / to bump into.

usagePhrases.note: 우연히 (by chance) is the natural partner; underlines the unplanned meeting.

examples.en: I ran into a friend on the street.
examples.note: Simple; the person met takes 를/을, 에서 marks the place.

examples.en: I happened to run into my teacher in the elevator.
examples.note: Everyday; 우연히 (by chance) makes the accidental nature explicit.

examples.ko: 복도에서 그 사람과 눈이 마주쳐서 어색했어요.
examples.romanization: bokdoeseo geu saramgwa nuni majuchyeoseo eosaekaesseoyo.
examples.en: Our eyes met in the hallway and it was awkward.
examples.note: Real-situation; 눈이 마주치다 (subject + 이/가) + -아서 (so, as a result).

entries.nuance: 마주치다 is 마주 ('facing, head-on') + 치다 ('strike'), literally 'to strike facing each other', i.e. to run/bump into someone or something unexpectedly, by chance. The person you encounter takes 를/을 (친구를 마주치다) or the comitative 와/과 (친구와 마주치다), and it is the fixed phrase for eye contact, 눈이 마주치다 — where the eyes are the subject with 이/가, a structure English speakers often get wrong by saying 눈을 마주쳤어요. The key contrast is with 만나다 ('to meet'): 만나다 covers planned, intended meetings (친구를 만나다 = meet up with a friend on purpose), while 마주치다 is strictly accidental and momentary, hence its frequent companion 우연히 (by chance). Compare also 부딪치다, the more physical 'collide/crash into' (사람과 부딪치다 = literally bump bodies). The pitfall is using 마주치다 for an arranged get-together, and mis-marking the eye-contact phrase with 를 instead of 이/가.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 마주치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 마주쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 마주치다 for a planned meet-up — that is 만나다; 마주치다 is always by chance.
Saying 눈을 마주쳤어요 for 'eyes met' — the set phrase makes 눈 the subject: 눈이 마주쳤어요.
Confusing it with 부딪치다 (physically collide) — 마주치다 is encountering/seeing, not crashing into someone.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 마주치다 becomes 마주칠 수 있어요 ("can") and 마주칠 거예요 ("will"). entries.explanation: 데려오다 (deryeooda) = "to bring (a person)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 데려와요 plus one useful sentence like 친구를 데려오다 ("to bring a friend (here)"). entries.nuance: 데려오다 = 데리다 (to have someone in one's charge) + 오다 (to come), so it literally means 'come having someone with you' — to bring a living being TOWARD the speaker's side. The pair to learn against it is 데려가다 (take a person away from here) and 데리고 오다, which is the looser two-word version with the same meaning. The decisive split is animacy: people and animals take 데려오다/데려가다, but objects take 가져오다/가져가다 — Korean grammaticalizes 'living vs non-living' where English just says 'bring' for everything, and this is the number-one trap. Because 오다 is built in, the conjugation follows 오다: 와요/왔어요, giving 데려와요, 데려왔어요. It is neutral in register and extremely common in everyday speech: 아이를 데려오다, 친구를 데려오다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 데려오다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 데려와요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 가방을 데려와요 for 'bring a bag' — 데려오다 is only for people/animals; an inanimate bag must be 가방을 가져와요.
Marking the person with 와/과 as in 친구와 데려와요 by copying English 'come WITH a friend' — the person is the object and takes 를/을: 친구를 데려와요.
Using 데려오다 when the movement is away from you (e.g. taking your kid to grandma's); that direction is 데려가다, not 데려오다.
notes: 오다 compound: memorize 데려와 and 데려와요 together.
