entries.shortExplanation: 데려다주다 means "to take (someone) somewhere" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 데려다주다 (deryeodajuda) means "to take (someone) somewhere". Start from the polite form 데려다줘요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 데려다주다. A strong first sentence is 집까지 데려다주다 ("to take (someone) all the way home"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 데려다주다 also becomes 데려다주고 싶어요 (want), 데려다줄 수 있어요 (can), and 못 데려다줘요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 데려다주다 stacks three pieces: 데리다 (have in charge) + -다(가) (do, then) + 주다 (give/do for someone), so it means 'escort a person to a place AND it's a favor for them'. Contrast it sharply with bare 데려가다 (take someone along), which is neutral about whose benefit it is — 데려다주다 always frames the trip as a kindness done for the passenger, exactly the nuance English 'give a ride / drop off' carries. The closest synonym 바래다주다 emphasizes accompanying/seeing off (often walking), while 데려다주다 emphasizes delivering them to the destination. For objects the parallel word is 가져다주다 (bring/fetch a thing for someone), so keep the people/thing split. Conjugation rides on 주다: 줘요/줬어요 → 데려다줘요, 데려다줬어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 데려다주다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 데려다줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 데려가다 to a friend you're kindly driving home — it loses the 'for your sake' warmth; 데려다주다 is the natural offer.
Saying 가져다주다 for a person ('데려다주다' vs '가져다주다'): 가져다주다 fetches an object, so use 데려다주다 for people.
Writing the request as 데려다 주세요 with a space and treating 주다 as separate is acceptable, but learners often drop 주다 entirely (데려다세요), which is ungrammatical — keep 주다.

entries.shortExplanation: 찾아가다 means "to go visit" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to go visit" in Korean is 찾아가다 (chajagada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 찾아가요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 찾아가다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 선생님을 찾아가다 ("to go (and seek out) the teacher") — then reshape the same stem into 찾아가고 싶어요 (desire), 찾아갈 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 찾아가요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

entries.nuance: 찾아가다 = 찾다 (to look for/seek) + -아 + 가다 (to go), literally 'go seeking', so it is not plain 가다 'go' — it adds the sense of actively going TO reach a specific person or hard-to-find place, away from the speaker. Its mirror image is 찾아오다 (someone comes seeking YOU), and the direction (가 = away, 와 = toward) is the whole contrast. Beside neutral 방문하다 (Sino-Korean 訪問, 'visit', stiff/formal, used in writing and news), 찾아가다 is the warm spoken word that implies effort and intention to meet. It also has a second concrete sense: 찾아가다 = to go and collect/claim something (e.g. 택배를 찾아가다 'pick up your parcel'). It rides on 가다: 가요/갔어요 → 찾아가요, 찾아갔어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 찾아가다 as a complete polite sentence.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 찾아가다 becomes 찾아갈 수 있어요 ("can") and 찾아갈 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: 찾아가다 literally means 'go seeking', so it is not plain 가다 'go' — it adds the sense of actively going TO reach a specific person or hard-to-find place, away from the speaker. entries.nuance: 들어주다 = 듣다 (to hear/listen) + -어 + 주다 (do for someone), and crucially the ㄷ of 듣다 turns into ㄹ before a vowel (듣 → 들-), a regular ㄷ-irregular shift, giving 들어-. The 주다 adds 'as a favour for that person', so the whole verb means either (1) accept and fulfil a request/wish, or (2) listen attentively and supportively. entries.nuance: 챙기다 is one of the most useful 'caring' verbs in daily Korean, with a cluster of related senses: (1) gather/pack the things you need (짐을 챙기다), (2) make sure not to skip something, especially food (밥 챙겨 먹어 'make sure you eat'), and (3) look after a person attentively (동생 좀 챙겨 'keep an eye on your sibling'). It also contrasts with 챙겨 주다, where adding 주다 makes the care explicitly a favour for someone. Using 들다 'to lift' for 'remember to bring an umbrella' — 우산을 들어요 means physically holding it up; 'grab/take it along' is 우산을 챙겨요.
Saying 밥을 먹어 to tell someone to take care of themselves, missing the nuance — Koreans say 밥 잘 챙겨 먹어 ('make sure you eat'), where 챙기다 carries the care.
Treating 챙기다 as only 'pack objects' and never using it for people; 아이를 챙기다 / 동생을 챙기다 ('look after') is just as common.

entries.nuance: 바래다주다 = 바래다 (an old verb meaning to accompany/see off) + 주다 (do as a favour), so it means walking or going along with someone partway to send them off kindly — a small act of care, warmer than just waving goodbye at the door. Compare it with its close neighbour 데려다주다: 데려다주다 stresses DELIVERING the person to a destination (often by car, you're the one in charge), whereas 바래다주다 stresses ACCOMPANYING/seeing off, traditionally on foot and out of courtesy. The dangerous look-alike is 바라다 'to wish/hope' (바라요 'I hope') and the spelling slips 바래요 — they are unrelated verbs, so keep them apart. The 주다 ending again frames the act as for the other person's benefit. Conjugation follows 주다: 바래다줘요, 바래다줬어요.

Dropping 주다 and saying 바래다 alone in modern speech — on its own 바래다 is dated; the living form is 바래다주다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 바래다주다 becomes 바래다줄 수 있어요 ("can") and 바래다줄 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 바래다주다 means walking or going along with someone partway to send them off kindly — a small act of care, warmer than just waving goodbye at the door. The 주다 ending frames the act as for the other person's benefit.

Compare it with its close neighbour 데려다주다: 데려다주다 stresses DELIVERING the person to a destination (often by car, you're the one in charge), whereas 바래다주다 stresses ACCOMPANYING/seeing off, traditionally on foot and out of courtesy.
바래다주다 = 바래다 (an old verb meaning to accompany/see off) + 주다 (do as a favour).
Conjugation follows 주다.
The dangerous look-alike is 바라다 'to wish/hope' (바라요 'I hope') and the spelling slip 바래요 — they are unrelated verbs, so keep them apart.

entries.nuance: 인사드리다 is the humble (겸양) counterpart of 인사하다, built from 인사 (Sino-Korean 人事, literally 'person-affair', meaning a greeting/bow) + 드리다, the humble version of 주다 'to give'. 드리다 lowers the SPEAKER to raise the listener, so you use 인사드리다 when greeting someone older or higher in status (a teacher, boss, in-laws), whereas neutral 인사하다 is for peers and juniors. The sharp contrast is direction of respect: 인사하다 is plain, 인사드리다 humbles yourself, and there is NO 인사받다-style humble for receiving. English has no grammatical humility, so learners either over-use it with friends (sounds stiff/odd) or under-use it with elders (sounds rude). Note the natural particle is 께 ('to', honorific), not 에게/한테, when naming the respected person.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 인사드리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 인사드려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 인사드리다 with close friends — it sounds overly formal/servile; among equals say 인사하다 (친구한테 인사했어).
Marking the respected person with 한테/에게 (선생님한테 인사드려요) instead of the honorific 께 — say 선생님께 인사드려요.
Assuming 인사 means only 'hello'; 인사 covers bows, greetings, and paying respects, so 인사드리다 can mean 'pay one's respects', not just 'say hi'.

entries.nuance: 도와드리다 is the humble form of 도와주다 ('help (as a favour)'), where 돕다 (to help) becomes 도와- by the ㅂ-irregular (돕 + 아 → 도와), and the helper-benefit 주다 is upgraded to its humble twin 드리다. So it literally means 'humbly do the favour of helping' — you lower yourself to help someone above you: a customer, elder, or guest. Contrast the three levels you must keep straight: 돕다 (bare dictionary 'help'), 도와주다 (help someone, neutral/friendly), 도와드리다 (help a superior, humble). English flattens all of these to 'help', so the pitfall is using 도와주다 with a customer (too casual for service) or, conversely, 도와드리다 with a buddy (oddly stiff). The phrase 무엇을 도와드릴까요? is the fixed, must-know service line. Conjugation follows 드리다: 도와드려요, 도와드렸어요.

Saying 도와줄까요? to a customer or elder — it's too casual for service; the polite form is 도와드릴까요?.
Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular and writing 돕아드려요; 돕다 + 아 becomes 도와-, so it's 도와드려요.
Using 도와드리다 toward a younger friend; among peers 도와줄게 (도와주다) is natural and 도와드릴게 sounds over-formal.
notes: ㅂ irregular (돕다): memorize 도와드려 and 도와드려요 together.

entries.shortExplanation: 부탁드리다 means "to ask a favor (politely)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to ask a favor (politely)" in Korean is 부탁드리다 (butakdeurida). The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

entries.nuance: 부탁드리다 is the humble form of 부탁하다 ('to request a favour'), from 부탁 (Sino-Korean 付託, 'entrust/commit to') + 드리다, the humble 'give'. You use it to ask something of a superior, client, or anyone you want to treat with deference, while 부탁하다 is the neutral version for peers and 부탁해 the casual one for friends. The must-memorize fixed expression is 잘 부탁드립니다 / 잘 부탁드려요 — said when you begin a job, join a group, or ask for ongoing cooperation; it has no clean English equivalent ('please treat me well / I look forward to working with you'). The English pitfall is twofold: treating it as one literal 'please' (it's really 'I humbly entrust this favour to you'), and using plain 부탁하다 with a boss, which reads as too blunt. Particle: the person asked takes honorific 께. Conjugates on 드리다: 부탁드려요, 부탁드렸어요.

Translating 잘 부탁드립니다 literally as 'please do well' and misusing it — it's a fixed social greeting meaning 'I look forward to your kind help'.
Saying 부탁드려 to a close friend; casually you'd say 부탁해 / 부탁 좀 들어줘, and 부탁드려 sounds stiff.

structuredNuance.t: 부탁드리다 is the humble form of 부탁하다 ('to request a favour'). You use it to ask something of a superior, client, or anyone you want to treat with deference. The must-memorize fixed expression is 잘 부탁드립니다 / 잘 부탁드려요 — said when you begin a job, join a group, or ask for ongoing cooperation; it has no clean English equivalent ('please treat me well / I look forward to working with you'). Particle: the person asked takes honorific 께.
부탁하다 is the neutral version for peers and 부탁해 the casual one for friends.
From 부탁 (Sino-Korean 付託, 'entrust/commit to') + 드리다, the humble 'give'.
Conjugates on 드리다.
The English pitfall is twofold: treating it as one literal 'please' (it's really 'I humbly entrust this favour to you'), and using plain 부탁하다 with a boss, which reads as too blunt.

entries.nuance: 사귀다 covers BOTH platonic 'make friends' and romantic 'date / go out with', and only context (and the object) tells them apart: 친구를 사귀다 is befriending, 남자친구/여자친구를 사귀다 or just '두 사람이 사귀다' is dating. It contrasts with 만나다, which means 'meet/see' and is sometimes used loosely for dating too, but 사귀다 specifically marks an ongoing committed relationship, not a single meeting. The headline trap is spelling/conjugation: the stem ends in the vowel ㅟ, which does NOT contract in standard Korean, so the polite present is 사귀어요 — never the colloquial 사겨요 you'll hear spoken but mustn't write. The future/볼 forms do contract normally: 사귈 거예요, 사귈까요. Habitual partners: 친구를 사귀다, 오래 사귀다, 사귀자.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 사귀다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 사귀어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing or spelling the polite present as 사겨요 — the ㅟ stem doesn't contract; the correct written form is 사귀어요.
Using 만나다 when you mean a committed relationship — 만나다 can be a one-off meeting; for 'we're dating' say 사귀어요/사귀고 있어요.

Marking the partner with 와/과 like English 'date WITH' (친구와 사귀어요 is fine for 'with', but the simple object pattern 친구를 사귀어요 is the default) — learners drop the object particle and say 친구 사귀어, which is casual-only.

entries.nuance: 친해지다 = 친하다 (to be close/friendly, with 친 from Sino-Korean 親 'intimate/familial') + -어지다, the 'become' suffix that turns an adjective into a change-of-state verb. So the built-in contrast is adjective vs verb: 친하다 describes the STATE of already being close (우리는 친해요 'we're close'), while 친해지다 describes the PROCESS of becoming close (우리 친해졌어요 'we've grown close'). English uses 'close' for both, so learners wrongly say 친했어요 ('we were close') when they mean 'we became close'. Because the partner is someone you grow close WITH, the particle is 와/과 (or 하고/랑), not the object 를. Conjugation follows 지다: 친해져요, 친해졌어요. Natural partners: 빨리/금방 친해지다, 친해지고 싶다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 친해지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 친해져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 친하다 for the change and saying 친했어요 to mean 'we became close' — 친했어요 means 'we WERE close'; the becoming is 친해졌어요.
Marking the other person with 를/을 (친구를 친해져요) — 친해지다 is intransitive, so use 친구와/친구랑 친해져요.
Confusing 친해지다 with 사귀다; 친해지다 = grow closer (friends), 사귀다 = befriend or date — don't use 친해지다 for 'start dating'.

entries.shortExplanation: 어울리다 means "to hang out with" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to hang out with" in Korean is 어울리다 (eoullida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 어울려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 어울리다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 친구들과 어울리다 ("to hang out / mingle with friends") — then reshape the same stem into 어울리고 싶어요 (desire), 어울릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 어울려요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

entries.nuance: 어울리다 runs on two everyday senses you choose by context: (1) with people (와/과) it means to mingle, socialize, get along — 친구들과 어울리다; (2) with things, clothes, or colors it means to match / suit / look good together — 옷이 잘 어울려요 'that outfit suits you'. For the social sense, compare 놀다 'to play/hang out', which is more casual and child-/leisure-flavored, whereas 어울리다 adds 'blend in, get along, fit the group' and is safe in adult/formal talk. For the matching sense, its synonym is 맞다 'to fit', but 맞다 is about correct size/fit while 어울리다 is about aesthetic harmony. English keeps 'hang out' and 'suit' in totally separate words, so the pitfall is not realizing one Korean verb does both — and that the compliment 'it suits you' is 어울려요, not 좋아 보여요. Note: the subject of the 'suit' sense is the clothing, with the person in 한테/에게.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 어울리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 어울려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 놀다 in formal/adult contexts for socializing — 어울리다 sounds more mature ('mingle/get along'); 놀다 can sound childish at work.
Translating 'it suits you' as 좋아 보여요 ('looks good') and missing the idiom — Koreans say 잘 어울려요.
Marking the matching item with 를 (옷을 어울려요) — in the 'suit' sense the clothing is the subject: 옷이 어울려요.

entries.nuance: 헤어지다 means two (or more) people who were together separating and going their own ways, and it doubles as THE standard word for a romantic break-up — 남자친구와 헤어졌어요 'I broke up with my boyfriend'. It is the natural antonym of 만나다 'to meet'. Keep it apart from 떠나다 'to leave (a place/person behind)', which focuses on one person departing a location, and from 헤매다 'to wander/be lost', a similar-looking but unrelated verb. The particle for the other person is 와/과 (or 하고/랑) 'with', NOT the object 를, because both sides separate mutually — a key difference from English transitive 'I left him'. Built on -어지다, it conjugates as 헤어져요, 헤어졌어요. The everyday goodbye sense (그럼 여기서 헤어져요) is gentle and common; only context or a partner like 남자친구 signals the break-up reading.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 헤어지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 헤어져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 떠나다 for 'two people parting' — 떠나다 means leaving a place/person; mutual parting is 헤어지다.
Marking the partner with 를 (남자친구를 헤어졌어요) — say 남자친구와/남자친구랑 헤어졌어요, since the particle is 'with', not the object.
Confusing 헤어지다 with 헤매다 (to wander, be lost) because they look alike — they are unrelated verbs.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 헤어지다 becomes 헤어질 수 있어요 ("can") and 헤어질 거예요 ("will"). entries.explanation: 돌보다 (dolboda) means "to take care of". Start from the polite form 돌봐요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 돌보다. Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 돌보다 = 돌(아) + 보다 ('look around and watch over'), meaning to actively look after and nurture a person, child, patient, animal, or even plants over time — it carries responsibility and warmth, well beyond plain 보다 'to see/look'. Set it against 챙기다, which is quicker 'make sure / don't let slip' care (밥 챙겨 먹어), whereas 돌보다 is sustained nurturing (아기를 돌보다 'raise/tend a baby'). It also contrasts with the Sino-Korean 보살피다 (a near-synonym, slightly more literary/tender 'tend, look after'), and with 키우다 'to raise/bring up', which stresses growing/rearing rather than day-to-day care. The cared-for one is the direct object with 를/을. The English trap is reaching for 보다 alone ('watch the kids' → not 아이를 봐요 in writing, which can sound like merely 'see'); proper caregiving is 돌보다, and the warm request form is 돌봐 주세요. Conjugation follows 보다: 봐요/봤어요 → 돌봐요, 돌봤어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 돌보다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 돌봐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 보다 'to see' alone for caregiving — 아이를 봐요 can read as merely 'I see the child'; full caregiving is 아이를 돌봐요.
Confusing 돌보다 with 키우다; 키우다 = raise/bring up (long-term rearing), 돌보다 = look after/tend (ongoing care) — 'I'm babysitting today' is 돌봐요, not 키워요.
Forgetting it's transitive and dropping the object particle in writing (아이 돌봐요 is casual-only); standard form is 아이를 돌봐요.

entries.shortExplanation: 건네다 means "to hand over" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to hand over" in Korean is 건네다 (geonneda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 건네요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 건네다 for study notes. entries.nuance: 건네다 is the verb for the deliberate, hand-to-hand act of passing a physical object to a person who is right next to you — money, a card, a cup. Compare it with 주다 (to give): 주다 only says ownership transfers and can happen at any distance, while 건네다 foregrounds the physical gesture of the hand reaching across the gap, so a server '건네준다' a menu but a company '준다' a bonus. In real speech it usually appears as 건네주다 (건네 + 주다) when you do it as a favor: 이거 건네주세요. Note the special idiom 말을 건네다 'to strike up a conversation', which English speakers wrongly read literally as 'hand over words'. Conjugation is easy because the stem ends in the vowel ㅔ: 건네 + 어 contracts to plain 건네, so the 요-form is 건네요 (never 건네어요) and the past is 건넸어요 (never 건네었어요).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 건네다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 건네요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't write the past as 건네었어요 — a stem ending in ㅔ swallows the 어, so the correct contracted form is 건넸어요.
Don't reach for 건네다 when something is mailed or sent across a distance — that is 보내다; 건네다 needs the receiver to be within arm's reach.
Don't translate 'hand over words' literally; 말을 건네다 is an idiom for addressing/greeting someone, so use it whole rather than building it word by word.

entries.explanation: 돌려주다 (dollyeojuda) = "to give back". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 돌려줘요 plus one useful sentence like 빌린 책 돌려주세요 ("Please give back the book you borrowed"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 돌려주고 싶어요 for what you want, 돌려줄 수 있어요 for what you can, 돌려줄 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.en: Please give back the book you borrowed
usagePhrases.note: The default verb for returning anything borrowed; 빌린 + noun + 돌려주다 is the textbook pattern.

examples.en: I'll give the umbrella back tomorrow
examples.note: 반말 promise; -ㄹ게 commits the speaker to a future action for the listener's benefit.

examples.en: Who do I have to give this back to?
examples.note: Casual 한테 marks the person who should receive it back — the everyday spoken counterpart of 에게.

examples.en: The deposit is returned in full when you check out
examples.note: Real-situation honorific: to a customer you upgrade 돌려주다 → 돌려드리다 to raise the listener.

entries.nuance: 돌려주다 is the compound 돌리다 (to turn / send back) + 주다 (to give), so it literally means 'turn it back and give it' — the standard word for returning a borrowed thing, money, or even a changed situation to its rightful place. Contrast it sharply with 갚다, which is narrower and means to settle a debt or repay an obligation (빚을 갚다, 은혜를 갚다); you 돌려주다 a borrowed umbrella but you 갚다 a loan, because 갚다 carries the sense of clearing what you owe, not just physically handing an item back. When the receiver outranks you, swap 주다 for the humble 드리다 → 돌려드리다 (보증금을 돌려드립니다). Because the verb ends in 주다, every form follows 주다 exactly: 줘 → 돌려줘, 줬어요 → 돌려줬어요, 주세요 → 돌려주세요 — there are no irregular surprises.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 돌려주다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 돌려줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 갚다 for handing back a borrowed object — 갚다 is for repaying money/debt or returning a favor; a borrowed book or umbrella takes 돌려주다.
Don't say 돌려주세요 to someone you must show deference to when you are the one returning it — to a boss or elder, use 돌려드릴게요 / 돌려드립니다.
Don't split it as 돌려 주다 thinking 주다 is a separate helper here — 돌려주다 is a settled single verb meaning 'give back', so keep it together.

entries.nuance: 챙겨주다 is 챙기다 (to gather up / see to what's needed) + 주다 (to give/do for), and it radiates warmth: you thoughtfully pull together someone's belongings, meals, or wellbeing because you care about them. The dividing line with the plain 주다 is the active 'seeing-to-it' nuance — 주다 merely transfers a thing, but 챙겨주다 implies you noticed what they'd need and took the trouble to prepare it, so Koreans use it about parents, partners, and caring seniors at work. The crucial pitfall: drop the 주 and 챙기다 alone means you do it for yourself (가방을 챙기다 = pack your own bag), so only 챙겨주다 expresses doing it for another. As a 주다 compound the forms are regular: 챙겨줘요, 챙겨줬어요, 챙겨주세요, and the honorific 챙겨주세요/챙겨주셨어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 챙겨주다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 챙겨줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't drop the 주 when you mean caring for another person — 가방을 챙기다 = pack your own bag, whereas 가방을 챙겨주다 = pack it for someone else.
Don't read 챙겨주다 as only physical packing — 생일/건강/사람을 챙겨주다 means to look after a person or occasion, so 'pack' is the wrong gloss in those cases.
Don't confuse it with 챙기다's selfish reading 잇속을 챙기다 (look after one's own interests); adding 주다 flips the focus to the other person's benefit.

entries.explanation: "to carry / haul" in Korean is 나르다 (nareuda). Grow outward from one concrete line — 짐을 나르다 ("to haul luggage") — then reshape the same stem into 나르고 싶어요 (desire), 나를 수 있어요 (ability), and 나를 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. entries.nuance: 나르다 means to physically transport objects — usually heavy or numerous, like boxes, furniture, bricks, or water — from one place to another, typically over repeated trips, so it conveys effortful hauling rather than a single act. Contrast it with 들다 (to lift / hold in the hand): 들다 is just raising or holding something, while 나르다 is the whole job of relocating things across a distance, so you 들다 a single chair to look at it but 나르다 a roomful of chairs to a truck. Note also 옮기다, which simply means 'to move (something) to another place' and can be one item or one move; 나르다 specifically evokes the laborious, back-and-forth carrying. The key conjugation point is that 나르다 is a 르-irregular: before 아/어 the 르 splits and the previous syllable gains a ㄹ patchim, so 나르 + 아 → 날라, giving 날라요 and past 날랐어요. Before a consonant the stem is untouched: 나르고, 나르지, 나릅니다, and the future/potential keep it too — 나를 거예요, 나를 수 있어요.

Don't write 나르아요 / 나르었어요 — as a 르 irregular it becomes 날라요 and 날랐어요 with a doubled ㄹ.
Don't use 나르다 for lifting or holding one thing in your hand — that is 들다; 나르다 is transporting things across a distance, usually in repeated trips.
Don't confuse the future 나를 거예요 with the present — keep the bare stem 나를- before -ㄹ 거예요/-ㄹ 수 있어요 and only switch to 날라- before 아/어 endings.

usagePhrases.note: Standard restaurant/home request — fetch the thing and deliver it to me.

examples.note: 반말 everyday request; the listener fetches it and brings it back to you.

examples.note: 에게 marks the receiver; -ㄹ래요 softens it into a friendly ask.

entries.nuance: 가져다주다 is built from 가지다 (to have/take) + the connective -다(가) + 주다 (to give), literally 'take it and then give it', i.e. go fetch something and bring it to a person. The sharp contrast to learn is direction: 가져다주다 brings the item TOWARD the receiver, whereas 가져가다 (take + go) carries it AWAY from here, and 가져오다 (take + come) just means bring it here without the 'for someone' nuance — so a server 가져다준다 your water (brings and hands it to you), but a customer 가져간다 the leftovers (takes them away). It also works abstractly: 행운을/변화를 가져다주다 'to bring luck/change'. When serving someone of higher status, raise the verb to 가져다드리다 (가져다드리겠습니다). As a 주다 compound all forms are regular and predictable: 가져다줘요, 가져다줬어요, 가져다주세요, honorific 가져다주세요/가져다주셨어요.

Don't drop the 주 and say 가져오다 when you mean doing it for a person — 가져오다 just means 'bring here', while 가져다주다 adds 'and give it to them'.
Don't keep plain 주다 when serving an elder or customer — politely it becomes 가져다드릴게요 / 가져다드리겠습니다.

entries.nuance: 메다 means to carry something by slinging it on your shoulder or back with a strap — a backpack, a satchel, even a rifle. Conjugation is straightforward because the stem ends in the vowel ㅔ: 메 + 어 contracts to plain 메, so the 요-form is 메요, the past is 멨어요, and the obligation form is 메야 해요 (never 메어요 / 메었어요).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 메다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 메요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 들다 for a bag worn on the back — 들다 is hand-carrying; a shoulder or back bag with a strap takes 메다.
Don't spell it 매다 when you mean carrying — 매다 means to tie/fasten (넥타이를 매다); the strap-on-shoulder verb is 메다.
Don't write the past as 메었어요 — the ㅔ stem contracts, so it is 멨어요.

entries.nuance: 업다 means to carry a person — almost always a baby, small child, or someone who can't walk — on your back, piggyback style, and it carries a tender, caregiving warmth (hence 업어 키우다 'to raise lovingly'). Saying 어워요 is wrong. Finally keep it apart from the look-alike 엎다 'to overturn / knock over' (그릇을 엎다), which is spelled with ㅍ and means something completely different.

Don't treat 업다 as a ㅂ irregular — it stays regular, so it is 업어요 (not 어워요) and 업었어요.
Don't use 안다 when the person is on your back — 안다 is holding in your arms against the chest; the back-carry is 업다.
Don't spell it 엎다 — that ㅍ verb means to overturn/tip over (그릇을 엎다), nothing to do with carrying a person.

entries.nuance: 싣다 means to load cargo, luggage, or goods ONTO a vehicle — a car, truck, ship, train, or plane — and it implies placing things on/in a means of transport, marked by 에 (트럭에 싣다). It also extends figuratively — 기사를 싣다 'to run an article', 마음을 실어 'putting one's heart into it'. The make-or-break point is that 싣다 is a ㄷ-irregular verb: before a vowel ending the final ㄷ changes to ㄹ, so 싣 + 어 → 실어요, past 실었어요, potential 실을 수 있어요, command 실으세요. Don't use 담다 for putting things onto a vehicle — 담다 is filling a container/bowl/bag, while loading onto a truck or car is 싣다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 싣다 becomes 실을 수 있어요 ("can") and 실을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 싣다 has an irregular stem (ㄷ). Memorize its polite form 실어요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

structuredNuance.t: 싣다 means to load cargo, luggage, or goods ONTO a vehicle — a car, truck, ship, train, or plane — and it implies placing things on/in a means of transport, marked by 에 (트럭에 싣다). It also extends figuratively — 기사를 싣다 'to run an article', 마음을 실어 'putting one's heart into it'.
Contrast it with 담다 'to put into a container' (그릇에 담다, 가방에 담다): you 담다 rice into a bowl but you 싣다 boxes onto a truck, because 싣다 specifically targets transport, not ordinary containers.

싣다 is a ㄷ-irregular verb: before a vowel ending the final ㄷ changes to ㄹ, so 싣 + 어 → 실어요, past 실었어요, potential 실을 수 있어요, command 실으세요. Before a consonant the ㄷ is kept intact: 싣고, 싣지, 싣습니다. Mixing these two stems up is the classic error.

entries.shortExplanation: 나눠주다 means "to hand out / share out" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 나눠주다 (nanwojuda) means "to hand out / share out". Start from the polite form 나눠줘요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 나눠주다. A strong first sentence is 간식을 나눠주다 ("to hand out snacks"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 나눠주다 also becomes 나눠주고 싶어요 (want), 나눠줄 수 있어요 (can), and 나눠줄 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 나눠주다 is 나누다 (to divide / share / split) + 주다 (to give), so it means to break something into portions and hand one to each of several people — passing out snacks, handouts, or money to a group. The key contrast is with bare 나누다, which by itself only means 'to divide' or 'to share/have in common' (나누다 can also mean 대화를 나누다 'to share a conversation'); it lacks the explicit 'give it out to people' direction that the +주다 supplies, so 사탕을 나누다 sounds incomplete where 사탕을 나눠주다 is the natural 'hand the candy out'. Compare too 돌리다 (to pass/hand around, e.g. 떡을 돌리다 'distribute rice cakes to neighbors'), which overlaps but stresses circulating among a circle. The implied plurality of recipients is what separates 나눠주다 from one-to-one 건네다/주다. As a 주다 compound the conjugation is fully regular: 나눠줘요, 나눠줬어요, 나눠주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 나눠주다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 나눠줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use bare 나누다 when you mean handing portions out — 나누다 alone is 'divide/share'; 나눠주다 adds the crucial 'give to each person'.
Don't use 나눠주다 for giving one whole thing to one person — its built-in nuance is dividing among several; for a single recipient use 주다 or 건네다.
Don't write 나눠 주다 as two loose words here — 나눠주다 is a settled verb meaning 'hand out / distribute', so keep it joined.

entries.shortExplanation: 내밀다 means "to hold out / stick out" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to hold out / stick out" in Korean is 내밀다 (naemilda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 내밀어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 내밀다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 손을 내밀다 ("to hold out one's hand") — then reshape the same stem into 내밀고 싶어요 (desire), 내밀 수 있어요 (ability), and 내밀 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

entries.nuance: 내밀다 is 내- (out) + 밀다 (to push), literally 'to push outward', and it means to thrust or extend something forward — a hand, your head, your tongue, or an object you're presenting like a ticket or business card. The contrast to draw is with 내놓다 'to put out / set out' (음식을 내놓다, 의견을 내놓다): 내놓다 places or releases something out into the open, while 내밀다 specifically pushes it forward toward a person or through an opening, so you 손을 내밀다 (thrust your hand out to someone) but 쓰레기를 내놓다 (set the trash out). It carries a warm idiom, 도움의 손길을 내밀다 'to reach out a helping hand'. The conjugation pitfall is that 내밀다 is a ㄹ-stem verb where the ㄹ drops before ㅂ, ㄴ, and ㅅ: hence formal 내밉니다 (not 내밀습니다) and polite command 내미세요 (not 내밀으세요). Before a vowel the ㄹ stays: 내밀어요, 내밀었어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 내밀다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 내밀어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't write the polite command as 내밀으세요 — a ㄹ-stem verb drops the ㄹ before ㅅ, so it is 내미세요.
Don't say 내밀습니다 for the formal present — the ㄹ drops before ㅂ-, giving 내밉니다.
Don't swap in 내놓다 when you mean thrusting toward someone — 내놓다 is 'set/put out into the open', while 내밀다 is pushing it forward at a person or out an opening.
notes: ㄹ: memorize 내밀어 and 내밀어요 together.

entries.shortExplanation: 전해주다 means "to pass on / deliver (to someone)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 전해주다 (jeonhaejuda) = "to pass on / deliver (to someone)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 전해줘요 plus one useful sentence like 이거 친구한테 전해주세요 ("Please pass this to my friend"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 전해주고 싶어요 for what you want, 전해줄 수 있어요 for what you can, 전해줄 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: The core favor pattern — relay an object or note to a third person on the speaker's behalf.

examples.en: Pass this to mom for me
examples.note: 반말; 전해줘 asks a family member to deliver it to a third person.

examples.en: I delivered this letter to the teacher
examples.note: 께 is the honorific of 에게, raising the recipient (the teacher) you handed it to.

examples.en: I'll be sure to relay the meeting results to the CEO
examples.note: Real-situation honorific — to a superior, 전해주다 becomes the humble 전해드리다.

entries.nuance: 전해주다 is 전하다 (傳하다, 傳 'to transmit/convey') + 주다 (to give), so the Sino-Korean root literally means 'to pass something along and give it', i.e. to deliver an object, message, or feeling to someone — very often through a third person. It handles both physical things (a letter, a gift) and intangibles (안부를 전해줘요 'send my regards', 마음을 전해주다 'convey one's feelings'). The dividing line with 보내다 'to send' is distance and channel: 보내다 dispatches something across a gap (편지를 보내다 'mail a letter', 문자를 보내다 'send a text'), while 전해주다 emphasizes the item actually reaching and being handed to the recipient, frequently in person or via a go-between. To a superior, raise 주다 to the humble 드리다 → 전해드리다 (전해드리겠습니다), and use 께 for the honored recipient. As a 주다 compound the forms are regular: 전해줘요, 전해줬어요, 전해주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 전해주다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 전해줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use 보내다 when you hand/relay something so it reaches a specific person — 보내다 is 'send (across a distance)'; 전해주다 stresses it being delivered to them, often via someone.
Don't keep plain 주다 when the recipient outranks you — use the humble 전해드리다 (전해드릴게요 / 전해드리겠습니다) and mark them with 께.
Don't say 전하다 alone in casual speech for doing someone a delivery favor — everyday Korean adds 주다, so 전해주세요, not bare 전하세요, sounds natural for 'please pass it on'.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 전해주다 becomes 전해줄 수 있어요 ("can") and 전해줄 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: 전해주다 means to deliver an object, message, or feeling to someone — very often through a third person. To a superior, raise 주다 to the humble 드리다 → 전해드리다 (전해드리겠습니다), and use 께 for the honored recipient.

The dividing line with 보내다 'to send' is distance and channel: 보내다 dispatches something across a gap (편지를 보내다 'mail a letter', 문자를 보내다 'send a text'), while 전해주다 emphasizes the item actually reaching and being handed to the recipient, frequently in person or via a go-between.
전해주다 is 전하다 (傳하다, 傳 'to transmit/convey') + 주다 (to give), so the Sino-Korean root literally means 'to pass something along and give it'.
As a 주다 compound the forms are regular: 전해줘요, 전해줬어요, 전해주세요.

entries.nuance: 세수하다 means specifically to wash your face (얼굴), built from the Sino-Korean noun 세수 (洗手, literally 'wash-hands', an old word that drifted to mean washing the face) plus 하다. Don't put the negative as 안 세수해요; 하다-verbs split it as 세수 안 해요, which sounds far more natural.

entries.nuance: 샤워하다 means to take a shower, made from the English loanword 샤워 (shower) plus 하다 — so it carries no 한자. The key distinction is mode of washing: 샤워하다 is standing under running water, whereas 목욕하다 (沐浴) is soaking in a filled tub, and 씻다 is the generic 'wash up'; English 'take a bath' must NOT be rendered 샤워하다. As a 하다 verb the negative splits to 샤워 안 해요, and it collocates with 운동하고, 따뜻한/찬물로, and 매일 아침에.

entries.nuance: 정돈하다 means to put things into neat order — straightening, lining up, and arranging items so they look orderly — from the Sino-Korean 정돈 (整頓, 'arrange-settle') plus 하다. examples.note: 골고루 = 'evenly'; -아 주세요 makes it a polite request to apply it.

entries.nuance: 바르다 means to apply or spread a thin layer of something onto a surface — lotion, sunscreen, jam, ointment. Don't mark the surface with 을/를 — it's 얼굴에 크림을 바르다 (surface takes 에), not 얼굴을 바르다.
notes: 르: memorize 발라 and 발라요 together.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 바르다 becomes 바를 수 있어요 ("can") and 바를 거예요 ("will"). conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 바르다 has an irregular stem (르). Memorize its polite form 발라요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

structuredNuance.t: 바르다 means to apply or spread a thin layer of something onto a surface — lotion, sunscreen, jam, ointment. It implies deliberate, spread-out application. The two-part frame is the thing applied + 을/를 and the surface + 에 (얼굴에 로션을 발라요).

Distinguish it from neighbors: 칠하다 is to paint/coat a broad surface (벽을 칠하다 = paint a wall), and 묻히다 is to get/dab a substance onto something more loosely — 바르다 implies deliberate, spread-out application.
Conjugation is the headline grammar point: 바르다 is 르-irregular, so before -아/어 the 르 drops and an extra ㄹ appears, giving 발라요 and past 발랐어요 — never 바르어요/바르었어요.
Getting the 에 right is a frequent trap: English 'put on my face' tempts 얼굴을 바르다, but the face is the surface (에), not the object.

entries.explanation: 헹구다 (hengguda) means "to rinse". Start from the polite form 헹궈요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 헹구다. entries.nuance: 헹구다 means to rinse something with clean water to flush off soap, dirt, or residue — dishes, vegetables, laundry, or your mouth. conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.
survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.note: The person you love takes 을/를 (object marker), never 에 — 사랑하다 is a transitive verb that acts directly on a person.

examples.en: I love my family
examples.note: The neutral polite 해요 form — safe for almost any listener and the default for stating affection plainly.

examples.en: I love you
examples.note: 반말: 너를 ('you') plus bare 사랑해 marks intimacy, used only with a partner or someone very close.

examples.en: My parents loved each other their whole lives
examples.note: Honorific 시 (사랑하셨어요) raises the subject (parents), and 서로를 supplies the mutual object.

entries.nuance: 사랑하다 is the weightiest love verb in Korean, covering romantic love, family love, and devotion to a cause; it is far heavier than English 'love you', which English speakers toss off to friends and even food. The honest near-synonyms split by intensity: 좋아하다 means 'like / have a crush on' and is what you confess at the start of a relationship (너 좋아해 = 'I like you'), while 사랑하다 is reserved for committed, serious feeling — saying 사랑해 too early can feel startling. Because it is a 하다 verb, the stem 하 + 여 always contracts to 해, giving 사랑해요 and past 사랑했어요 (never 사랑하요/사랑하았어요); the future and modal forms keep 하 (사랑할 거예요, 사랑해야 해요). The object of love takes 을/를, so the classic pitfall is writing 엄마에게 사랑해요 by copying English 'love TO someone' — Korean loves the person directly: 엄마를 사랑해요. Natural partners include 진심으로 사랑하다, 죽도록 사랑하다, and the noun idiom 사랑에 빠지다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 사랑하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 사랑해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 사랑하요 instead of 사랑해요 — every 하다 verb contracts 하 + 여 to 해, so the polite form must be 사랑해요.
Marking the beloved with 에/에게 (사랑에게) by analogy with English 'love to' — the person you love is a direct object and takes 을/를: 너를 사랑해.
Using 사랑하다 for casual 'I love this food/song' — Koreans say 좋아하다 there; 사랑하다 about objects sounds melodramatic.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 사랑해요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 사랑하다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 엄마를 사랑해요. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 사랑하지 않아요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 사랑할 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 사랑해요 feels easy, practice 사랑하고 싶어요, 사랑할 수 있어요, and 사랑해야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

Teacher asks a yes/no question with 엄마를 사랑해요. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 사랑하지 않아요, then 사랑할 수 없어요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 사랑하다 becomes 사랑할 수 있어요 ("can") and 사랑할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

A 하다 verb: the stem 하 + 여 contracts to 해, so present is 사랑해요 and past 사랑했어요 (never 사랑하요 or 사랑하았어요). Future and modal forms keep 하.

entries.explanation: 미워하다 (miwohada) = "to hate". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 미워해요 plus one useful sentence like 그 사람을 미워해요 ("I hate that person"). examples.en: I don't hate anyone
examples.note: 아무도 ('nobody') must pair with the negative 하지 않아요 — Korean double-marks the negative.

examples.en: I hated my younger sibling for a while
examples.note: 한때 ('at one time') plus past 미워했어요 softens it into a feeling that has since passed.

examples.ko: 우리 이제 그만 서로 미워하지 마세요
examples.romanization: uri ije geuman seoro miwohaji maseyo
examples.en: Let's stop hating each other now
examples.note: 그만 ('stop / no more') with the polite 하지 마세요 is a gentle plea to end a feud.

entries.nuance: 미워하다 means to actively feel hatred or resentment toward a person, and it is built from the adjective 밉다 ('to be hateful / detestable') by the regular pattern 밉다 → 미워 + 하다 (the ㅂ of 밉다 softens to 워). The key boundary English speakers blur is 미워하다 vs 싫어하다: 싫어하다 is broad 'dislike' and works for things, foods, and situations (비를 싫어해요 = I dislike rain), whereas 미워하다 is a hot, personal emotion aimed almost always at a human being — you can 싫어하다 broccoli but you 미워하다 the person who hurt you. Because it is a 하다 verb, it contracts to 미워해요 / past 미워했어요 (not 미워하요), while keeping 하 in 미워할 거예요. Note that 미워하다 is often less harsh than English 'hate': Korean parents and couples use 미워! playfully to mean 'you meanie / I'm mad at you'. The pitfall is reaching for 미워하다 to translate 'I hate this weather/this job' — that needs 싫다/싫어하다; 미워하다 there sounds as if you bear the weather a grudge.

Using 미워하다 for disliking a thing ('I hate kimchi') — things take 싫어하다; 미워하다 is for resenting people.
Writing 미워하요 instead of 미워해요 — as a 하다 verb it must contract 하 + 여 to 해.
Assuming 미워해 always means strong 'hate'; between close people it is often a light, sulky 'you meanie', so don't read it as literal hatred.

entries.shortExplanation: 그리워하다 means "to miss" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 그리워하다 (geuriwohada) means "to miss". Start from the polite form 그리워해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 그리워하다. A strong first sentence is 고향을 그리워해요 ("I miss my hometown"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 그리워하다 also becomes 그리워하고 싶어요 (want), 그리워할 수 있어요 (can), and 그리워할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: A place or absent person takes 을/를 with the verb 그리워하다 (≠ the adjective 그립다, which takes 이/가).

examples.en: I miss Korean food
examples.note: Everyday line when living abroad; the food takes the object marker 을.

examples.en: He missed his old friends
examples.note: Third person + past 그리워했어요 — describing someone else's longing, which is exactly when 그리워하다 (not 그립다) is required.

examples.ko: 너무 그리워하지 마, 곧 만날 거야
examples.romanization: neomu geuriwohaji ma, gon mannal geoya
examples.en: Don't miss them too much, you'll meet soon
examples.note: 반말 comfort: 그리워하지 마 tells a friend not to pine.

entries.nuance: 그리워하다 is the action verb 'to miss / long for / yearn after', formed from the adjective 그립다 ('to be missed') via 그립다 → 그리워 + 하다. The single most important point is the adjective-vs-verb split that trips up English speakers, who have only one word 'miss': use the adjective 그립다 for your own felt state, where the missed thing is the grammatical subject (고향이 그리워요 = lit. 'my hometown is missed-to-me' = I'm homesick), and use the verb 그리워하다 when you describe someone actively missing something, taking an 을/를 object (동생이 고향을 그리워해요). The other near-synonym is 보고 싶다 ('want to see / miss'): 보고 싶다 is light, common, and aimed at people you can still meet (엄마 보고 싶어), while 그리워하다 is more literary and wistful, often for what is gone, distant, or past — you 그리워하다 your childhood, not your friend across town. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 그리워해요 / past 그리워했어요 (never 그리워하요).

Use 그리워해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 내가 고향을 그리워요 — for your own feeling use the adjective with 이/가: 고향이 그리워요; the verb 그리워하다 is for others or takes 을/를.
Treating 보고 싶다 and 그리워하다 as identical — 보고 싶다 is everyday and about people you can meet; 그리워하다 is wistful longing for what's gone or far.
Writing 그리워하요 instead of 그리워해요 — the 하다 stem must contract to 해.

entries.shortExplanation: 빌다 means "to pray" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to pray" in Korean is 빌다 (bilda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 빌어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 빌다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 소원을 빌어요 ("I make a wish") — then reshape the same stem into 빌고 싶어요 (desire), 빌 수 있어요 (ability), and 빌 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 빌어요. Then practice 빌지 않아요 vs 빌 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

usagePhrases.note: 소원을 빌다 ('wish a wish') is the set phrase for making a wish on a star, candle, or at New Year.

examples.en: I made a wish at New Year
examples.note: Past 빌었어요 — the stem 빌 keeps its ㄹ before the vowel ending 어.

examples.en: I pray for my family's health every day
examples.note: 건강을 빌다 ('pray for health') shows the 'pray for' sense aimed at a good outcome.

examples.ko: 시험 잘 보라고 행운을 빌어 줄게요
examples.romanization: siheom jal borago haenguneul bireo julgeyo
examples.en: I'll wish you luck on your exam
examples.note: 빌어 주다 ('wish on someone's behalf') + 줄게요 makes it a warm offer to a friend.

entries.nuance: 빌다 spans three related senses — to pray, to make a wish, and to plead/beg — unified by the idea of earnestly asking a higher power or another person for something (소원을 빌다 = make a wish, 행운을 빌다 = wish luck, 용서를 빌다 = beg forgiveness, 잘못을 빌다 = apologize for a wrong). entries.nuance: 키우다 is the causative of 크다 ('to be big') — literally 'to make (something) grow / get bigger' — and it stretches across raising children, keeping pets, growing plants, and figuratively building skills, dreams, businesses, even bad habits (병을 키우다 = let an illness worsen). entries.explanation: "to give birth" in Korean is 낳다 (nata). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 낳아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 낳다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 아기를 낳아요 ("to have a baby") — then reshape the same stem into 낳고 싶어요 (desire), 낳을 수 있어요 (ability), and 낳을 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: 아기를 낳다 ('give birth to a baby') — the baby takes the object marker 를.

examples.en: My older sister gave birth to a daughter
examples.note: Past 낳았어요 — the stem ㅎ is kept and ㅏ + 았 attaches normally.

examples.note: 낳다 also covers animals; 마리 is the counter for animals.

entries.nuance: 낳다 means to give birth to or bear a child or young, and it is the physical act of delivery — distinct from 키우다/기르다 (raising the child afterward). It is a regular consonant (ㅎ-final) verb, NOT the ㅎ-irregular found in some adjectives, so the ㅎ is always preserved: 낳아요, 낳았어요, 낳습니다 — never 나아요. This is the make-or-break point, because 낳다 looks and sounds almost identical to two other verbs that English speakers constantly mix up: 낫다 ('to recover from illness / be better'), which is ㅅ-irregular and drops to 나아요 (감기가 나았어요 = my cold got better), and 낮다 ('to be low'). So 'I gave birth' is 낳았어요 while 'I got better' is 나았어요 — one keeps ㅎ, the other loses ㅅ. Figuratively 낳다 can also mean 'to produce / give rise to' a result (좋은 결과를 낳다 = bring about a good result). A cultural register note: about a mother one says 낳다, but the polite, formal phrasing for giving birth is often 출산하다, used in hospitals and news; 낳다 is the plain everyday verb.

Confusing 낳다 (give birth) with 낫다 (recover) — 'I gave birth' is 낳았어요 (keeps ㅎ), 'I recovered' is 나았어요 (ㅅ drops).

usagePhrases.note: What looks good on you takes 이/가, not 을/를 — 옷이 어울려요, paired with 잘 ('well').

examples.note: A natural compliment; note 색이 (이/가), since the color is what suits.

entries.nuance: 어울리다 carries two everyday meanings bound by one idea — 'to harmonize / fit together well': (1) to suit or look good on someone (이 옷이 잘 어울려요 = this suits you), and (2) to mingle, blend in, or get along with people (친구들하고 잘 어울려요). The particle pattern is the crux for English speakers, because English 'suits you' makes 'you' the object: in Korean the thing that suits is the SUBJECT and takes 이/가 (옷이 어울려요, never 옷을 어울려요), the person it suits is unmarked or takes 한테/에게, and a matching partner or group takes 하고/와/과 (치마하고 어울리다, 사람들하고 어울리다); a setting it fits takes 에 (분위기에 어울리다). Conjugation is the regular ㅣ-vowel contraction, not an irregular: 어울리 + 어 fuses to 어울려, giving polite 어울려요 and past 어울렸어요 (not 어울리어요). A useful contrast: 어울리다 ('look good / harmonize') vs 맞다 ('fit in size / be correct') — clothes that 어울리다 flatter you, clothes that 맞다 are the right size, and the two are not the same compliment.

Writing 어울리어요 instead of the contracted 어울려요 — the stem-final ㅣ fuses with 어 to 려.
Confusing 어울리다 (look good / harmonize) with 맞다 (fit in size / be correct) — 'this suits you' is 어울려요, 'this fits (size)' is 맞아요.

entries.nuance: 분석하다 means to analyze — to break a whole down into its parts (分 'divide' + 析 'split apart') so you can understand how it works: data, a cause, a problem, or a text. The hanja itself pictures cutting something open, which is why it always implies methodical dissection, not a casual glance. As a 하다 verb it must contract to 분석해요 (never 분석하요), and the object always takes 을/를. The pitfall for English speakers is register: in English you 'analyze' anything, but 분석하다 sounds clinical and academic, so for everyday 'let me look into it' Koreans reach for 살펴보다 (look over) or 알아보다 (check / find out). The near-synonym to watch is 분석하다 vs 분류하다: 분석하다 takes one thing apart to study it, while 분류하다 sorts many things into groups — analyzing a single survey vs classifying responses by age.

Saying 데이터에 분석해요. The thing analyzed is a direct object, so it must be 데이터를 분석해요.
Using 분석하다 for a quick everyday peek; for 'let me just look into it' 살펴볼게요 or 알아볼게요 sounds far more natural.

entries.nuance: 강조하다 means to emphasize, stress, or underline that something matters (強 'strong' + 調 'tone/tune', literally 'to set a strong tone'). That 強 'strong' element is why the word belongs to lectures, presentations, and persuasive writing — you are raising the volume on one point. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 강조해요, and the point stressed takes 을/를 (중요성을 강조하다), a spot where English speakers wrongly slip in 에. The synonym boundary to keep is 강조하다 vs 주장하다: 강조하다 turns up the weight of a point everyone may already accept ('this really matters'), whereas 주장하다 pushes a contested CLAIM others might reject. So a teacher 강조한다 that review is important, but a debater 주장한다 that a policy is wrong.

entries.nuance: 제안하다 means to propose or put forward a plan, idea, or course of action, usually in a formal or business setting (提 'lift/raise up' + 案 'plan/proposal', literally 'to raise a proposal'). entries.explanation: "to oppose" in Korean is 반대하다 (bandaehada). Its clean antonym is 찬성하다 (to be in favor), which shares the same 에 frame. Keep it apart from 거부하다 (to refuse): 반대하다 is taking a stance against an idea in discussion, while 거부하다 is actively turning down a concrete request or offer.

entries.shortExplanation: 찬성하다 means "to agree / to be in favor" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 찬성하다 (chanseonghada) = "to agree / to be in favor". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 찬성해요 plus one useful sentence like 의견에 찬성하다 ("to be in favor of an opinion"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 찬성하고 싶어요 for what you want, 찬성할 수 있어요 for what you can, 찬성할 수 없어요 for what you can't. entries.nuance: 찬성하다 means to agree with, approve of, or be in favor of a proposal or opinion, especially in a vote or formal discussion (贊 'approve/assist' + 成 'accomplish', literally 'to approve and help bring about'). Like its antonym 반대하다, the thing you support takes 에 — 의견에 찬성하다 — and English speakers must resist writing 의견을 찬성해요. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 찬성해요. The key synonym contrast is 찬성하다 vs 동의하다: 찬성하다 is voting YES on a proposal or motion ('all in favor'), while 동의하다 is agreeing with a person's point or feeling in conversation. For 'I agree with you' in everyday talk, Koreans say 동의해요 or simply 맞아요, not 찬성해요, which would sound like a formal vote.

Using 찬성하다 for 'I agree with you' in chat; that is 동의해요 or 맞아요 — 찬성하다 implies a formal vote on a motion.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 찬성하다 becomes 찬성할 수 있어요 ("can") and 찬성할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: To agree with, approve of, or be in favor of a proposal or opinion, especially in a vote or formal discussion. Its antonym is 반대하다.
贊 'approve/assist' + 成 'accomplish', literally 'to approve and help bring about'.
Like its antonym 반대하다, the thing you support takes 에 — 의견에 찬성하다 — and English speakers must resist writing 의견을 찬성해요. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 찬성해요.
찬성하다 vs 동의하다: 찬성하다 is voting YES on a proposal or motion ('all in favor'), while 동의하다 is agreeing with a person's point or feeling in conversation.
For 'I agree with you' in everyday talk, Koreans say 동의해요 or simply 맞아요, not 찬성해요, which would sound like a formal vote.

entries.shortExplanation: 거부하다 means "to refuse / to reject" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 거부하다 (geobuhada) means "to refuse / to reject". Start from the polite form 거부해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 거부하다. A strong first sentence is 제안을 거부하다 ("to reject a proposal"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 거부하다 also becomes 거부하고 싶어요 (want), 거부할 수 있어요 (can), and 거부할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 거부해요. Then practice 거부하지 않아요 vs 거부할 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.
survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.en: I do not refuse / to reject.
I want to refuse / to reject.
I have to refuse / to reject.

usagePhrases.note: Object + 를 + 거부하다 = to turn down firmly. Note: 을/를, unlike 반대하다's 에.

examples.en: He refused the interview
examples.note: 인터뷰를 거부했어요 — a flat, firm refusal; object takes 를.

examples.en: The company flatly rejected his demands
examples.note: 요구를 단호히 거부했어요, the news-report register for firm rejection.

examples.en: Don't refuse a legitimate request
examples.note: 정당한 (legitimate) + 거부하지 마세요 urges against unfair refusal.

entries.nuance: 거부하다 means to refuse, reject, or decline firmly — a proposal, request, demand, or order (拒 'ward off/resist' + 否 'no/deny', literally 'to ward off with a no'). Those hanja 'resist' + 'deny' make it strong and confrontational, the word for turning something down outright, often on principle. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 거부해요, and unlike 반대하다 the object takes 을/를 (요청을 거부하다). The pitfall is the synonym pair 거부하다 vs 거절하다: 거절하다 is the polite, softer 'decline' you use for an invitation or kind offer you'd rather not accept (제안을 정중히 거절했어요), whereas 거부하다 is a blunt, principled REFUSAL — a company 거부하다 demands, a witness 거부하다 to testify. Using 거부하다 when a friend invites you to dinner sounds harshly cold.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 거부하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 거부해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 거부하요 instead of the contracted 거부해요.
Using 에 like with 반대하다 — 거부하다 takes a direct object: 요청을 거부해요, not 요청에 거부해요.
Using 거부하다 to politely turn down an invitation; that blunt tone offends — use 거절하다 for soft declines.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 거부해요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 거부하다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 제안을 거부하다. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 거부하지 않아요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 거부할 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 거부해요 feels easy, practice 거부하고 싶어요, 거부할 수 있어요, and 거부해야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

Learner changes the sentence to 거부하지 않아요, then 거부할 수 없어요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

entries.shortExplanation: 제공하다 means "to provide" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to provide" in Korean is 제공하다 (jegonghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 제공해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 제공하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 정보를 제공하다 ("to provide information") — then reshape the same stem into 제공하고 싶어요 (desire), 제공할 수 있어요 (ability), and 제공할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

examples.note: Service context; 아침 식사를 제공해요 on a hotel notice.

entries.nuance: 제공하다 means to provide, supply, or furnish something — information, services, food, resources — typically by an organization or in a formal context (提 'offer/raise up' + 供 'supply/offer', two 'give' hanja stacked for an official 'furnish'). Because both characters mean offering, the word feels institutional, the verb on hotel signs, contracts, and corporate notices. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 제공해요; the recipient takes 에게/한테 and the thing provided takes 을/를. The pitfall is register, not grammar: 제공하다 vs 주다. English 'give/provide' covers both, but 주다 is the warm everyday 'give' between people (친구가 선물을 줬어요), while 제공하다 is what a company or service does. Saying a friend 제공했어요 a gift sounds like a press release; use 줬어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 제공하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 제공해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 제공하요 instead of the contracted 제공해요.
Marking the recipient with 을/를 — it takes 에게/한테: 직원들에게 점심을 제공했어요.
Using 제공하다 for a friend giving you something; that stiff, corporate tone calls for 주다 instead.

entries.shortExplanation: 포함하다 means "to include" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 포함하다 (pohamhada) = "to include". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 포함해요 plus one useful sentence like 세금을 포함하다 ("to include tax"). Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: Active frame: the whole includes the part, which takes 을/를.

examples.en: This price includes the shipping fee
examples.note: Active 포함하다: 가격(whole) includes 배송비(part), object takes 를.

examples.en: All costs are included
examples.note: Passive 포함되어 있어요 — the part is the subject and takes 이/가.

examples.en: Including me, there are five people
examples.note: 저를 포함해서 = 'including me', the handy counting set phrase.

entries.nuance: 포함하다 means to include or contain something inside a larger whole (包 'wrap/envelop' + 含 'hold in the mouth/contain', literally 'to wrap and hold within'). The single most useful thing to learn is its passive partner 포함되다 (to be included), which flips the roles: active 가격이 세금을 포함해요 (price includes tax, part = object 을/를) vs passive 세금이 가격에 포함돼요 / 포함되어 있어요 (tax is included, part = subject 이/가). English speakers blur these and say 세금이 포함해요, which is wrong — if tax is the one being included, it must be the passive 포함되다. Also memorize the frozen phrase N을/를 포함해(서) = 'including N'.

entries.nuance: 구별하다 means to distinguish, differentiate, or tell apart two or more things by their differences (區 'divide/section' + 別 'separate/distinguish', literally 'to separate into distinct parts'). As a 하다 verb it contracts to 구별해요; the items compared join with 와/과 or 하고, and the whole takes 을/를 — 진짜와 가짜를 구별하다. The crucial synonym contrast is 구별하다 vs 구분하다 (both share 區): 구별하다 stresses perceiving the DIFFERENCE between similar things ('I can't tell the twins apart' — 구별 not possible), while 구분하다 stresses SORTING items into groups/categories ('separate the trash by type' — 쓰레기를 분리수거로 구분하다). English 'distinguish' leans toward 구별하다; if you mean 'divide into sections', reach for 구분하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 구별하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 구별해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 구별하요 instead of the contracted 구별해요.
Using 구별하다 when you mean to sort items into groups — that is 구분하다; 구별하다 is for telling similar things apart.
Marking only one item: distinguishing needs both, joined by 와/과 — 진짜와 가짜를 구별해요, not just 가짜를 구별해요.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 구별하다 becomes 구별할 수 있어요 ("can") and 구별할 거예요 ("will"). entries.shortExplanation: 비판하다 means "to criticize" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to criticize" in Korean is 비판하다 (bipanhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 비판해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 비판하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 정책을 비판하다 ("to criticize a policy") — then reshape the same stem into 비판하고 싶어요 (desire), 비판할 수 있어요 (ability), and 비판할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

entries.nuance: 비판하다 means to criticize — to weigh something and point out its faults through reasoned judgment, as of a policy, idea, or work (批 'judge/comment on' + 判 'judge/decide', literally 'to judge and pass verdict'). Both hanja mean 'judge', which is why proper 비판 is analytical, not just venting. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 비판해요, object 을/를. The pitfall is the near-twin pair 비판하다 vs 비난하다 (they look almost alike): 비판하다 is reasoned CRITIQUE that can be constructive ('this policy has these flaws'), while 비난하다 (難 'blame/reproach') is purely negative personal BLAME or condemnation ('you're terrible'). English 'criticize' covers both, so learners wrongly use 비판하다 for a personal attack; if you mean to blame or condemn a person, that is 비난하다.

Use 비판해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 비판하요 instead of the contracted 비판해요.
Using 비판하다 to personally blame or insult someone — that is 비난하다; 비판하다 is reasoned, often constructive critique.
Marking the target with 에 — it takes 을/를: 정책을 비판해요, not 정책에 비판해요.

entries.english: to occur, to happen, to arise
entries.shortExplanation: 발생하다 means "to occur, to happen, to arise" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 발생하다 (balsaenghada) = "to occur, to happen, to arise". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 발생해요 plus one useful sentence like 문제가 발생했어요. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 발생해요. Then practice 발생하지 않아요 vs 발생할 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

usagePhrases.note: The thing that occurs always takes 이/가, never 을/를 — 발생하다 cannot take an object.

examples.note: Polite 발생해요 — note 하다 contracts 하 + 어 → 해, never 발생하요.

examples.en: An error occurred during payment.
examples.note: Formal 발생했습니다 is the exact wording you see on payment screens and system error pages.

examples.en: A small mistake can turn into a big accident.
examples.note: Real-situation caution — pairs 발생할 수도 있다 (might possibly occur) with the ~(으)로 'into' marker.

entries.nuance: 발생하다 (發生, 'issue-forth + arise') is the formal, written-leaning verb for an event, problem, or phenomenon coming into existence — accidents, errors, fires, costs, side effects, diseases. The everyday near-synonym is 생기다, and the dividing line is register and scale: 문제가 생겼어요 is what you say to a friend, while 문제가 발생했어요 belongs to news, reports, manuals, and official notices. Crucially it is intransitive — the thing that occurs takes 이/가, so you can never 'occur something' (no 발생하다 with 을/를). The classic English-speaker trap is translating 'cause a problem' as 문제를 발생하다; Korean instead says 문제가 발생하다 (a problem arises) or, for an agent making it happen, 문제를 일으키다. Remember 하다 contracts to 해요 — 발생하요 is a spelling error.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 발생하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 발생해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't use it transitively — say 문제가 발생했어요 (a problem occurred), not 문제를 발생했어요; for 'cause a problem' use 문제를 일으키다.
Writing 발생하요 instead of 발생해요 — every 하다 verb contracts 하 + 어 to 해, so the polite form is 발생해요.
Using it for tiny personal events sounds robotic — say 배가 고파졌어요, not 배고픔이 발생했어요; reserve 발생하다 for incidents, errors, and reports.

entries.shortExplanation: 존재하다 means "to exist" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 존재하다 (jonjaehada) means "to exist". Start from the polite form 존재해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 존재하다. A strong first sentence is 그런 방법은 존재하지 않아요. ("Such a method doesn't exist."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 존재하다 also becomes 존재하고 싶어요 (want), 존재할 수 있어요 (can), and 존재할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 존재해요. Then practice 존재하지 않아요 vs 존재할 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.
survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.note: 존재하지 않아요 is the natural way to deny existence flatly — 'there's no such thing.'

examples.en: Does Santa Claus really exist?
examples.note: Casual 존재해? to a child or friend — the contracted 하 + 어 → 해 form.

examples.en: That problem has existed for a long time.
examples.note: 오래전부터 존재했어요 stresses a problem has 'been there' all along, not just appeared.

examples.en: Prejudice still exists in our society.
examples.note: Formal 존재합니다 with 여전히 (still) fits essays and serious discussion about society.

entries.nuance: 존재하다 (存在, 'remain + be present') means 'to exist' in an abstract, weighty, or emphatic sense — common in writing, debate, philosophy, and serious topics. Its everyday near-synonym is 있다, and the line is sharp: for 'there is / I have' you must use 있다 (책이 있어요, 질문이 있어요), never 존재하다. Reach for 존재하다 only when you want to spotlight the very fact of something's existence — a method, a being, a problem — or to deny it categorically with 존재하지 않아요. It is intransitive, so the thing that exists takes 이/가 and there is no object. The big English-speaker pitfall is mapping every English 'exist/there is' onto 존재하다: 'there's a café nearby' is 근처에 카페가 있어요, and saying 카페가 존재해요 sounds comically grand. Keep 존재하다 for the abstract and the philosophical.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 존재하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 존재해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't replace everyday 있다 with 존재하다 — 'I have a question' is 질문이 있어요, not 질문이 존재해요; 'there's a store' is 가게가 있어요.
The natural negative is 존재하지 않아요; clipping it to 존재 안 해요 sounds off-register for such an abstract verb.

entries.nuance: 발전하다 (發展, 'issue-forth + unfold/spread') means to move to a more advanced, mature, or larger stage — technology, economies, skills, companies, even relationships. The number-one trap for learners is the look-alike 발견하다 (to discover) — one syllable apart and totally unrelated, so 신약을 발전하다 wrongly means 'develop a new drug' when you meant 발견하다 (discover). entries.nuance: 향상되다 (向上, 'turn-toward + up' + 되다) literally pictures something 'turning upward,' i.e. a skill, quality, or level rising and getting better. It is the intransitive, formal cousin of the everyday 좋아지다 (to get better): 실력이 좋아졌어요 is casual, while 실력이 향상됐어요 sounds polished and is what teachers, reviews, and reports use. Use it for measurable, ratable things — 실력, 품질, 성능, 효율, 체력, 삶의 질 — rather than moods or weather. The key English-speaker pitfall is the active/passive split: 향상되다 means something improved on its own, but if YOU improved it you must use the causative 향상시키다 (실력을 향상시켰어요), never 실력을 향상됐어요. Watch the spelling too: 되어요 contracts to 돼요 and the past is 향상됐어요 — 향상되요 and 향상됬어요 are both wrong.

Don't use it transitively — say 실력이 향상됐어요 (skills improved), but 실력을 향상시켰어요 when YOU improved them (향상시키다).

entries.shortExplanation: 감소하다 means "to decrease, to decline, to drop" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 감소하다 (gamsohada) means "to decrease, to decline, to drop". Start from the polite form 감소해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 감소하다. examples.en: Fewer customers came.

examples.en: The birth rate is declining rapidly.
examples.note: Formal 감소하고 있습니다 fits news and reports about social trends.

examples.ko: 꾸준히 운동하면 질병 위험이 감소할 수 있어요.

entries.nuance: 감소하다 (減少, 'reduce + few') is the formal, statistical verb for an amount or number going down, and it lives in a fixed pair with its opposite 증가하다 (增加, to increase) — the two appear together constantly in news, reports, and graphs. Its everyday near-synonyms are 줄다 and 줄어들다: a Korean tells a friend 손님이 줄었어요, but a report says 고객 수가 감소했습니다. The dividing line is purely register and context (numbers/data → 감소하다; daily talk → 줄다). entries.nuance: 구성하다 (構成, 'construct + complete') means to put something together out of parts — a team, a menu, a program, the structure of a presentation. entries.nuance: 적용하다 (適用, 'suitable + use') means to apply a rule, discount, theory, or method so it actually takes effect — the thing applied takes 을/를 and the target takes 에/에게 (새 규칙을 직원에게 적용하다). The partner is marked with 와/과 or 하고 (옆 팀과 협력해요), it habitually pairs with 서로, 긴밀히, and 적극적으로, and the bare noun is everywhere: 국제 협력, 협력 업체, 협력 관계. entries.shortExplanation: 경쟁하다 means "to compete" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to compete" in Korean is 경쟁하다 (gyeongjaenghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 경쟁해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 경쟁하다 for study notes. usagePhrases.note: 치열하다 (fierce, cut-throat) is the signature adverb for 경쟁하다; describes tough, no-quarter rivalry.

entries.nuance: 경쟁하다 (競爭, '競 vie + 爭 contend') describes rivalry in which parties try to outdo one another for the same prize, market, or position, and its tone runs from neutral and sporty to tense and cut-throat depending on context. The boundary worth knowing: 경쟁하다 is contending against a rival, whereas 겨루다 is a more physical 'pit your skill/strength against' (used for matches and martial arts), and 다투다 leans toward quarreling or squabbling. Grammar is the trap zone here: the rival is marked with 와/과 (옆 가게와 경쟁해요), and what is at stake takes 을/를 두고, never a plain object on 경쟁 itself. It collocates with 치열하게, 심하게, and the set phrase 선의의 경쟁, and the noun saturates daily life: 경쟁률 (competition ratio), 입시 경쟁 (exam competition), 경쟁사 (a competitor), 경쟁력 (competitiveness). As a regular 하다-verb it gives 경쟁해요 / 경쟁했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 경쟁 like the English noun 'the competition' that you 'win' — Korean separates the act (경쟁) from the result, so you win 'in' the competition (경쟁에서 이기다), you don't 'beat the competition' as 경쟁을 이기다.

Marking the rival with 을/를 (친구를 경쟁해요). The opponent takes 와/과: 친구와 경쟁해요 — you compete *with/against* them, so the comitative particle is required.

entries.shortExplanation: 참여하다 means "to participate / to take part in" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 참여하다 (chamyeohada) = "to participate / to take part in". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 참여해요 plus one useful sentence like 행사에 참여하다 ("to take part in an event"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 참여하고 싶어요 for what you want, 참여할 수 있어요 for what you can, 참여 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

usagePhrases.note: 참여하다 takes 에 for the activity you join: 토론에 참여해요 = I take part in the discussion.

examples.en: I want to take part in that gathering too.
examples.note: Basic 에 marking plus 고 싶다; 참여하다 already implies you'll actually join in, not just watch.

examples.en: I actively took part in this volunteer activity.
examples.note: 적극적으로 collocates strongly; 참여하다 stresses hands-on involvement rather than mere attendance.

examples.ko: 회의에 참여는 했지만 의견은 한마디도 안 냈어요.
examples.romanization: hoeuie chamyeoneun haetjiman uigyeoneun hanmadido an naesseoyo.
examples.en: I took part in the meeting but didn't say a single word.
