entries.nuance: 참여하다 (參與, '參 take part + 與 join in') means to actively take part in and contribute to an activity, event, or process, so its core is involvement, not physical presence. The single most useful contrast for a learner: 참석하다 (出席) is simply attending — being bodily present at a meeting, wedding, or ceremony — whereas 참여하다 means you actually engage and add something. You 참석 a friend's wedding (you show up and sit there), but you 참여 a project or campaign (you roll up your sleeves); a related word 가담하다 is 'join in' with a negative slant (joining a crime or a fight). What you join is marked with 에 (행사에 참여하다), and it pairs habitually with 적극적으로 and the bare noun in 참여율 (participation rate), 시민 참여 (citizen participation), 참여형 (participatory). As a regular 하다-verb it is 참여해요 / 참여했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is using one word for both 'attend' and 'participate' the way English does — if you only mean you were physically there, say 참석했어요; save 참여했어요 for when you genuinely took part.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 참여하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 참여해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 참여하다 when you only attended without contributing: for 'I attended the ceremony' say 행사에 참석했어요; 참여하다 implies you actively engaged, which can overstate a passive presence.
Marking the activity with 을/를 (행사를 참여해요). What you join takes 에: 행사에 참여해요 — you take part *in* it, so the locative-style particle is required.
Treating 참여하다 and 참석하다 as freely interchangeable. They differ in meaning: 참석 = be present, 참여 = get involved, and picking the wrong one misstates how engaged you were.

entries.explanation: 책임지다 (chaegimjida) means "to take responsibility". Start from the polite form 책임져요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 책임지다. A strong first sentence is 끝까지 책임지다 ("to take responsibility to the very end"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 책임지다 also becomes 책임지고 싶어요 (want), 책임질 수 있어요 (can), and 책임 못 져요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: to take responsibility to the very end
usagePhrases.note: 끝까지 (all the way to the end) is the signature partner; means seeing it through, not bailing out.

examples.en: I take responsibility for my own work.
examples.note: Clean 져요 form; shows the 지다 stem contracting and the matter (일) taken as object with 을 dropped.

examples.en: Who's going to take responsibility for this accident?
examples.note: 책임지다 + 을/를: 사고를 책임지다 = be answerable for the accident; future 거예요 presses for ownership.

examples.ko: 이 일은 제가 맡았으니까 끝까지 책임지겠습니다.
examples.romanization: i ireun jega matasseunikka kkeutkkaji chaegimjigetseumnida.
examples.en: I took this on, so I'll take full responsibility to the end.
examples.note: Formal workplace pledge: 맡다 (take charge) sets it up, 책임지겠습니다 promises to own how it turns out.

entries.nuance: 책임지다 is a compound of the Sino-Korean noun 책임 (責任, '責 duty + 任 charge') plus the native verb 지다 'to carry/bear', so it literally means 'to shoulder responsibility' — to take on and own the consequences of a mistake, a task, or even the care of a person. It is heavier and more accountable than 맡다 (to take charge of / be assigned): 맡다 is accepting a duty, while 책임지다 is promising to answer for the result, good or bad. It also reaches beyond fault into provision — 가족을 책임지다 means to support and care for one's family — so it overlaps emotionally with 돌보다 (to look after) in that nurturing sense. The matter takes 을/를, it collocates with 끝까지 and 확실히, and it lives in nouns like 책임감 (sense of responsibility) and 무책임 (irresponsibility). The conjugation pitfall is the key thing for English speakers: because the stem is 지다, you must contract it to 책임져요 / 책임졌어요 / 책임져 주세요 — never the literal *책임지어요 — and negatives split the noun off as 책임 안 져요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 책임지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 책임져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Forming the casual as 책임지어요. The 지다 stem contracts, so it must be 책임져요 (and past 책임졌어요, request 책임져 주세요) — the uncontracted 지어요 sounds wrong.
Using 맡다 when the moment calls for accountability: 'I'll take responsibility for the result' is 결과를 책임질게요, not just 맡을게요 — 맡다 only says you'll handle it, not that you'll answer for how it ends.
Marking the matter with 에 (사고에 책임져요). What you take responsibility for is a direct object with 을/를: 사고를 책임져요 (or in formal writing 사고에 대해 책임지다).

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 책임져요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 책임지다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 끝까지 책임지다. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 책임 안 져요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 책임 못 져요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 책임져요 feels easy, practice 책임지고 싶어요, 책임질 수 있어요, and 책임져야 돼요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

Teacher asks a yes/no question with 끝까지 책임지다. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 책임 안 져요, then 책임 못 져요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

entries.english: to rely on / to lean on (emotionally)
entries.shortExplanation: 의지하다 means "to rely on / to lean on (emotionally)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to rely on / to lean on (emotionally)" in Korean is 의지하다 (uijihada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 의지해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 의지하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 가족에게 의지하다 ("to rely on one's family") — then reshape the same stem into 의지하고 싶어요 (desire), 의지할 수 있어요 (ability), and 의지 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.en: I rely on / to lean on (emotionally).

I want to rely on / to lean on (emotionally).
I can rely on / to lean on (emotionally).
I have to rely on / to lean on (emotionally).

usagePhrases.note: A person you lean on takes 에게/한테: 가족에게 / 친구한테 의지해요 — emotional, warm dependence.

examples.en: I rely on my older sister a lot.
examples.note: Casual 반말 with 한테; shows the everyday, intimate flavor of leaning on a close family member.

examples.ko: 힘들 때 친구에게 의지하면 마음이 편해져요.
examples.romanization: himdeul ttae chinguege uijihamyeon maeumi pyeonhaejyeoyo.
examples.en: When times are hard, leaning on a friend makes you feel better.
examples.note: 에게 marks who you lean on; 의지하다 carries warm, trusting emotional dependence, not a transaction.

examples.en: Grandmother walks slowly, leaning on a cane.
examples.note: Physical sense with 에; 의지해서 chains the support to the action of walking.

entries.nuance: 의지하다 (依支, '依 depend + 支 prop up') means to depend on or lean on someone or something for emotional, practical, or even physical support, and it almost always carries a warm, human feeling of trust rather than cold reliance. The boundary to learn: 의지하다 is leaning on someone for support and comfort, while 믿다 is believing in or trusting them, and 기대다 is the most physical/intimate 'lean against' (you can 어깨에 기대다 lean on a shoulder, and figuratively it sounds even tenderer). A crucial particle split: a person you rely on takes 에게/한테 (부모님께 의지해요), but an object you physically lean on takes 에 (벽에 의지하다). It collocates with 서로 and 많이, and the bare noun appears in 의지가 되다 (to be a source of support). The 하다-verb conjugates regularly to 의지해요 / 의지했어요. Two pitfalls for English speakers: (1) do not mark the person with 을/를 — English 'rely on someone' tempts a direct object, but Korean needs 에게/한테; and (2) the 'let's rely' (shallWe) form is unnatural, since relying isn't something two people propose doing in concert, so treat 의지할까요? as a real question ('shall I lean on you?'), not a casual suggestion.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 의지하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 의지해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the person you rely on with 을/를 (부모님을 의지해요). The supporter takes 에게/한테/께: 부모님께 의지해요 — English 'rely on X' misleads you into a direct object.
Using 에 for a person or 에게 for an object. Split them: people take 에게/한테 (친구한테 의지해요), physical props take 에 (지팡이에 의지해요).
Confusing 의지하다 with 믿다. 'I trust you' is 너를 믿어, while 'I lean on you' is 너한테 의지해 — trusting and depending-for-support are different acts.

entries.english: to respect / to look up to
entries.shortExplanation: 존경하다 means "to respect / to look up to" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 존경하다 (jongyeonghada) = "to respect / to look up to". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 존경해요 plus one useful sentence like 마음 깊이 존경하다 ("to respect from the bottom of one's heart"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 존경하고 싶어요 for what you want, 존경할 수 있어요 for what you can, 존경 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

examples.en: I look up to my grandfather.
examples.note: Plain 을/를 object; the admired person is a direct object, and the feeling is looking up to their character.

examples.ko: 저는 늘 도전하시는 그분을 진심으로 존경해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun neul dojeonhasineun geubuneul jinsimeuro jongyeonghaeyo.
examples.en: I sincerely respect that person who always takes on challenges.
examples.note: 진심으로 collocates; the honorific 도전하시는 shows you elevate someone you 존경 with 시 inside the clause.

examples.ko: 그렇게 끝까지 책임지시는 걸 보니 더 존경하게 됐어요.
examples.romanization: geureoke kkeutkkaji chaegimjisineun geol boni deo jongyeonghage dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: Seeing them stay responsible to the end, I came to respect them even more.
examples.note: 존경하게 되다 = 'come to respect', marking a shift in feeling triggered by witnessed behavior.

entries.nuance: 존경하다 (尊敬, '尊 honor + 敬 revere') is deep respect and admiration for a person's character, achievements, or values — looking up to an elder, mentor, hero, or role model. Two boundaries matter. First, it is far stronger and more upward-looking than 좋아하다 (to like): you can like a singer's songs (좋아하다) yet 존경 a person only for who they are. Second, and the classic mix-up, 존경하다 vs 존중하다 (尊重): you 존경 a *person* you admire, but you 존중 someone's *choices, opinions, or rights* — 다른 사람의 의견을 존중하다 (respect others' opinions), never 존경. The admired person takes 을/를, the modifier 존경하는 is a common formal lead-in, and the passive 존경받다 ('be respected') is everywhere. As a regular 하다-verb it is 존경해요 / 존경했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'respect' covers both senses at once, so learners overuse 존경하다 for everyday courtesy ('respect the rules', 'respect your privacy') where Korean needs 존중하다 — 규칙을 존중하다, not 규칙을 존경하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 존경하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 존경해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 존경하다 with 존중하다. You 존경 a person you admire, but you 존중 a decision, opinion, or right: 의견을 존중해요, not 의견을 존경해요.
Using 존경하다 for mere liking: 'I really like this actor' is 이 배우 정말 좋아해요; 존경하다 implies looking up to someone's character, which overshoots casual fondness.
Marking the admired person with 에게/한테 (선생님에게 존경해요). The person you look up to is a direct object with 을/를: 선생님을 존경해요.

尊敬, '尊 honor + 敬 revere'.

entries.english: to ignore / to look down on
entries.shortExplanation: 무시하다 means "to ignore / to look down on" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 무시하다 (musihada) means "to ignore / to look down on". Start from the polite form 무시해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 무시하다. A strong first sentence is 그냥 무시하다 ("to just ignore / brush off"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 무시하다 also becomes 무시하고 싶어요 (want), 무시할 수 있어요 (can), and 무시 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.en: I ignore / to look down on.
I do not ignore / to look down on.
I want to ignore / to look down on.
I can ignore / to look down on.
I have to ignore / to look down on.

usagePhrases.note: 그냥 무시해 = don't even react; standard advice for shrugging off rude comments or trolls.

examples.en: Just ignore what that person says.
examples.note: Casual 반말 advice; 무시하다 + 을/를 here is the harmless 'don't pay it any attention' sense.

examples.ko: 빨간 신호를 무시하고 길을 건너면 정말 위험해요.
examples.romanization: ppalgan sinhoreul musihago gireul geonneomyeon jeongmal wiheomhaeyo.
examples.en: It's really dangerous to ignore a red light and cross.
examples.note: Disregard-a-rule sense; 무시하고 chains the flouting to its risky consequence.

examples.ko: 돈이 없다고 사람을 무시하면 안 돼요.
examples.romanization: doni eopsdago sarameul musihamyeon an dwaeyo.
examples.en: You shouldn't look down on people just because they have no money.
examples.note: The belittle sense, which is offensive; 무시당하다 (to be looked down on) is its common passive partner.

entries.nuance: 무시하다 (無視, literally '無 without + 視 looking' — 'to not look at') carries two linked senses that context decides between: (1) to ignore or disregard something — a comment, a rule, a warning, a red light — and (2) to look down on, belittle, or disrespect a person, which is quite offensive. With an inanimate target it's the neutral first sense (신호를 무시하다 = disregard the signal); with a person it usually flips to the cutting second sense (사람을 무시하다 = treat them as inferior). Distinguish it from neighbors: 무시하다 (ignore by choice / belittle) is not 모르다 (genuinely not know) and not 외면하다 (deliberately turn one's face away, look away from a problem). The target takes 을/를, it pairs with 그냥, and the passive 무시당하다 ('be slighted') is everywhere in emotional talk. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 무시하다 just means the neutral English 'ignore' — aim it at a person and it commonly reads as 'look down on', so 나를 무시하지 마 is a forceful 'don't disrespect me', far heavier than 'don't ignore me'; if you only mean failing to notice, 무시하다 is the wrong verb entirely.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 무시하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 무시해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

Using 무시하다 for failing to notice something. 무시하다 is a deliberate disregard; if you simply didn't notice, say 못 봤어요 or 몰랐어요, not 무시했어요.

beginnerPath.body: 무시해요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 무시하다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place

beginnerPath.body: 무시 안 해요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 무시 못 해요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns

Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

entries.english: to discuss / to talk over (to decide)
entries.shortExplanation: 의논하다 means "to discuss / to talk over (to decide)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to discuss / to talk over (to decide)" in Korean is 의논하다 (uinonhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 의논해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 의논하다 for study notes. I want to discuss / to talk over (to decide).
I can discuss / to talk over (to decide).
I have to discuss / to talk over (to decide).
to talk it over with one's parents
usagePhrases.note: The person you consult takes 와/과 (or 하고): you discuss *with* them to reach a decision.

examples.en: Let's talk that over together.
examples.note: Simple 요-form invitation; 같이 marks it as a joint consultation, not a one-way report.

examples.ko: 이 문제는 부모님과 의논해 보고 결정할게요.
examples.romanization: i munjeneun bumonimgwa uinonhae bogo gyeoljeonghalgeyo.
examples.en: I'll talk this over with my parents before I decide.
examples.note: 와/과 marks who you consult; 의논해 보고 결정하다 shows the whole point is to reach a decision.

examples.en: I had a serious discussion with my teacher about my career path.
examples.note: Real-life pattern: 에 대해 (topic) + 와/과 (partner) + 진지하게 + 의논하다, the way you describe seeking advice.

entries.nuance: 의논하다 (議論, '議 deliberate + 論 discuss') is to talk something over with someone in order to reach a decision or get advice, so its essence is practical, two-way consultation, not a formal contest of ideas. Hold three neighbors apart. 의논하다 / 상의하다 both mean 'consult to decide' (상의하다 sounds a touch more formal and businesslike), so they're near-twins. 토론하다 (debate) means weighing opposing sides on an issue — public, argumentative — which 의논하다 is not. And 대화하다 (converse) is just friendly chatting with no decision at stake. The crucial particles: the person you consult takes 와/과 or 하고 (친구와 의논해요), and the topic takes 에 대해 (진로에 대해 의논해요). It pairs with 같이, 진지하게, and lives in 의논 상대 (someone to talk things over with). As a 하다-verb it is 의논해요 / 의논했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: English 'discuss it WITH my parents' tempts you toward a 'to' marker, but the consultation partner must take 와/과, never 에게/한테 — 의논하다 is mutual, not one-directional delivery.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 의논하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 의논해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the discussion partner with 에게/한테 (친구에게 의논해요). You talk things over *together*, so the partner takes 와/과 or 하고: 친구와 의논해요.
Using 의논하다 for a formal debate of opposing views; that is 토론하다. 의논하다 is consulting to decide, so a panel or classroom argument calls for 토론하다.
Treating 의논하다 as plain chatting. If there's no decision or advice at stake, 'let's talk' is 이야기해요 or 대화해요; 의논하다 specifically aims at settling something.

entries.english: to trust (firmly) / to have confidence in
entries.shortExplanation: 신뢰하다 means "to trust (firmly) / to have confidence in" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 신뢰하다 (silloehada) = "to trust (firmly) / to have confidence in". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 신뢰해요 plus one useful sentence like 서로 신뢰하다 ("to trust each other"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 신뢰하고 싶어요 for what you want, 신뢰할 수 있어요 for what you can, 신뢰 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

I want to trust (firmly) / to have confidence in.

usagePhrases.note: The trusted person/thing takes 을/를; 서로 frames it as firm, mutual confidence between parties.

examples.en: I have confidence in that person.
examples.note: Plain 을/를 object; note this sounds firmer and more formal than the everyday 믿어요.

examples.ko: 저는 그 회사를 오래전부터 신뢰해 왔어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun geu hoesareul oraejeonbuteo silloehae wasseoyo.
examples.en: I've trusted that company for a long time.
examples.note: 신뢰해 오다 (have been trusting) shows confidence built up over time, typical for brands and institutions.

examples.ko: 팀원들이 서로 신뢰해야 일이 잘 돼요.
examples.romanization: timwondeuri seoro silloehaeya iri jal dwaeyo.
examples.en: Team members have to trust one another for work to go well.
examples.note: Work register about reliability; 신뢰 here is reasoned, dependable confidence, not a fleeting hunch.

entries.nuance: 신뢰하다 (信賴, '信 believe + 賴 rely') is firm, reasoned trust or confidence in a person, organization, or system, and it sounds notably more formal and weighty than the everyday verb 믿다 (to believe/trust). The dividing line is register and grounds: you 신뢰 a colleague's competence, a company, a brand, or a system on the basis of a track record, whereas you 믿다 a friend, a rumor, a promise, or a religion more casually and on faith. (믿다 also covers 'believe that…', which 신뢰하다 never does.) The trusted target takes 을/를, and the noun 신뢰 collocates richly: 신뢰를 쌓다 (build trust), 신뢰를 잃다 (lose trust), 신뢰 관계, 신뢰감. As a regular 하다-verb it is 신뢰해요 / 신뢰했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the 'big' word in casual speech: between close friends '나 믿지?' (you trust me, right?) is natural and warm, while 나 신뢰해? sounds stiff and oddly corporate — match 신뢰하다 to formal, reasoned, often written contexts and let 믿다 carry everyday emotional trust.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 서로 신뢰하다. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 신뢰 안 해요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 신뢰 못 해요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 신뢰해요 feels easy, practice 신뢰하고 싶어요, 신뢰할 수 있어요, and 신뢰해야 돼요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

classroomScript: Teacher says: 신뢰해요. Learner repeats three times.
Teacher asks a yes/no question with 서로 신뢰하다. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 신뢰 안 해요, then 신뢰 못 해요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

miniDialogue.speaker: A
miniDialogue.en: Do you to trust each other?

miniDialogue.speaker: B
miniDialogue.en: I have confidence in that person.

miniDialogue.speaker: A
miniDialogue.en: Shall we trust (firmly) / to have confidence in?

drills.en: I do not trust (firmly) / to have confidence in.
drills.note: Change the polite present into a simple negative.

drills.en: I want to trust (firmly) / to have confidence in.
drills.note: Change the verb into a desire sentence.

drills.en: I cannot trust (firmly) / to have confidence in.
drills.note: Use this for inability or a real limitation.

selfCheck: Can you say “I trust (firmly) / to have confidence in” politely?
Can you say “I want to trust (firmly) / to have confidence in”?
Can you explain the difference between 신뢰 안 해요 and 신뢰 못 해요?

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 신뢰하다 becomes 신뢰할 수 있어요 ("can") and 신뢰할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 신뢰하다 is firm, reasoned trust or confidence in a person, organization, or system, and it sounds notably more formal and weighty than the everyday verb 믿다. The trusted target takes 을/를, and the noun 신뢰 collocates richly: 신뢰를 쌓다 (build trust), 신뢰를 잃다 (lose trust), 신뢰 관계, 신뢰감.
信賴, '信 believe + 賴 rely'.

The dividing line from 믿다 is register and grounds: you 신뢰 a colleague's competence, a company, a brand, or a system on the basis of a track record, whereas you 믿다 a friend, a rumor, a promise, or a religion more casually and on faith. (믿다 also covers 'believe that…', which 신뢰하다 never does.)
As a regular 하다-verb it is 신뢰해요 / 신뢰했어요.

Reaching for the 'big' word in casual speech: between close friends '나 믿지?' (you trust me, right?) is natural and warm, while 나 신뢰해? sounds stiff and oddly corporate — match 신뢰하다 to formal, reasoned, often written contexts and let 믿다 carry everyday emotional trust.

entries.shortExplanation: 조언하다 means "to give advice / to counsel" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 조언하다 (joeonhada) means "to give advice / to counsel". Start from the polite form 조언해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 조언하다. A strong first sentence is 후배에게 조언하다 ("to give advice to a junior"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 조언하다 also becomes 조언하고 싶어요 (want), 조언할 수 있어요 (can), and 조언 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 조언해요. Then practice 조언 안 해요 vs 조언 못 해요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.
survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.en: I do not give advice / to counsel.
I want to give advice / to counsel.
I can give advice / to counsel.
I have to give advice / to counsel.
to give advice to a junior
usagePhrases.note: The listener takes 에게/한테: 후배에게 / 친구한테 조언하다 — advice flows toward the receiver.

examples.en: I gave my friend honest advice.
examples.note: 에게 marks the receiver; 솔직하게 (honestly/frankly) is a natural adverb for candid counsel.

examples.ko: 전문가가 건강 관리에 대해 조언해 줬어요.
examples.romanization: jeonmungaga geongang gwallie daehae joeonhae jwosseoyo.
examples.en: An expert gave advice about managing your health.
examples.note: N에 대해 조언해 주다: the 주다 helper frames it as a favor; sounds informed and slightly formal.

examples.ko: 제가 조언할 입장은 아니지만 한번 들어 보세요.
examples.romanization: jega joeonhal ipjangeun anijiman hanbeon deureo boseyo.
examples.en: I'm not really in a position to advise, but hear me out.
examples.note: 조언할 입장이 아니다 (not in a position to advise) is a humble hedge before offering an opinion.

entries.nuance: 조언하다 (助言, '助 help + 言 words' — literally 'helping words') means to offer advice or counsel from knowledge or experience, and it sounds more thoughtful and a touch more formal than casually telling someone what to do. The key contrast is with 충고하다 (忠告): 조언 is helpful, supportive guidance you welcome, while 충고 carries a corrective, admonishing edge — closer to a warning or a talking-to ('너에게 충고하는데…' often precedes criticism), so they are not interchangeable in tone. It also differs from 추천하다 (recommend a specific thing) and 제안하다 (propose a course of action). Grammatically the listener takes 에게/한테 and the topic takes 에 대해; it lives as 조언해 주다 (give advice as a kindness) and the receiver's-side 조언을 구하다 (seek advice). As a 하다-verb it is 조언해요 / 조언했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the noun shape: English 'advise SOMEONE' tempts a direct object, but the person taught takes 에게/한테 (친구에게 조언해요), because what is actually 'given' is the 조언 itself — and note 조언 is uncountable-flavored, so 'a piece of advice' is 한마디 조언, not a pluralized form.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 조언하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 조언해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the advice-receiver with 을/를 (친구를 조언해요). The listener takes 에게/한테: 친구에게 조언해요 — the advice (조언) is what's given, not the person.
Using 조언하다 when you mean to warn or reproach. A corrective 'let me tell you for your own good' is 충고하다; 조언하다 is supportive guidance and softens the message.
Confusing 조언하다 with 추천하다. 'I advise you to rest' is 쉬라고 조언해요, but 'I recommend this book' is 이 책을 추천해요 — counsel versus recommending a specific item.

lesson.canDo: Use 조언해요 in a real beginner sentence, then change it into want, can, cannot, and have-to forms without losing the basic meaning.
studyFlow: Say 조언해요 first. This is the safest spoken form for most beginner situations.
Add one useful frame: 후배에게 조언하다. Read the Hangul first, then check the romanization.
Practice the contrast between 조언 안 해요 and 조언 못 해요.
Open one linked pattern and come back to this card to see the same grammar in a verb form.
lesson.teacherNote: Do not ask a beginner to memorize all 15 forms at once. Teach 조언해요 first, then add one communicative need: desire (조언하고 싶어요), possibility (조언할 수 있어요), or limitation (조언 못 해요).
lesson.pronunciationTip: 조언하다 is written joeonhada. In real sentences, compare the audio with the romanization because Korean sound changes can cross syllable blocks.

entries.shortExplanation: 토론하다 means "to debate / to discuss (formally)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to debate / to discuss (formally)" in Korean is 토론하다 (toronhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 토론해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 토론하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 환경에 대해 토론하다 ("to debate about the environment") — then reshape the same stem into 토론하고 싶어요 (desire), 토론할 수 있어요 (ability), and 토론 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 토론해요. Then practice 토론 안 해요 vs 토론 못 해요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

usagePhrases.en: I do not debate / to discuss (formally).
I want to debate / to discuss (formally).
I have to debate / to discuss (formally).

usagePhrases.note: The topic takes 에 대해 or (으)로: 그 주제로 / 환경에 대해 토론하다 = debate the issue from sides.

examples.en: Let's have a debate on that topic.
examples.note: Simple 요-form invite; (으)로 marks the topic, and 토론하다 implies weighing different sides, not chatting.

examples.en: The students debated about environmental issues.
examples.note: N에 대해 토론하다 = debate about N; presupposes presenting and weighing opposing arguments.

examples.en: Let's not fight emotionally — let's debate calmly.
examples.note: Contrasts 토론하다 (reasoned debate) with 싸우다 (quarrel); 토론 is meant to stay rational.

entries.nuance: 토론하다 (討論, '討 examine + 論 argue') is to debate or discuss an issue formally, presenting and weighing different viewpoints, so it belongs to classrooms, panels, candidate debates, and structured meetings rather than casual chitchat. Place it among its neighbors: 토론하다 (argue a question from sides, often with opposing positions) is more confrontational and structured than 의논하다/상의하다 (talk something over together to decide), and entirely distinct from 대화하다 (just converse) and 싸우다 (quarrel) — a good 토론 stays reasoned even when heated. The topic takes 에 대해 or (으)로, it collocates with 열띤, 찬반, and 활발하게, and the noun appears in 토론회 (debate forum), 토론자 (debater), 끝장 토론 (a marathon, settle-it debate). As a regular 하다-verb it is 토론해요 / 토론했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'discuss' covers everything from a chat to a formal debate, so learners overuse 토론하다 for ordinary talk — if you just want to 'talk about' your weekend or 'chat' with a friend, say 이야기하다 or 대화하다; reserve 토론하다 for a genuine, argued exchange on an issue.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 토론하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 토론해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 토론하다 for everyday chatting. For a casual 'let's talk', say 이야기해요 or 대화해요; 토론하다 implies a structured exchange of arguments on an issue.
Confusing 토론하다 with 의논하다. Deciding something together with someone is 의논하다/상의하다; 토론하다 is debating an issue from opposing sides, often in public.
Marking the topic with 을/를 (환경을 토론해요). The subject of debate takes 에 대해 or (으)로: 환경에 대해 토론해요 / 그 주제로 토론해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 좋아하다 means "to like" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 좋아하다 (joahada) = "to like". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 좋아해요 plus one useful sentence like 커피를 좋아해요 ("I like coffee"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 좋아하고 싶어요 for what you want, 좋아할 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 좋아해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 좋아해요. Then practice 안 좋아해요 vs 못 좋아해요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

usagePhrases.note: the thing liked takes the object marker 을/를, not 이/가

examples.en: I like Korean food.
examples.note: the bare polite present states a steady, ongoing preference

examples.en: Our puppy really loves walks.
examples.note: third-person liker takes 이/가 (강아지가), the liked thing still takes 을/를

examples.ko: 저는 매운 음식은 별로 안 좋아해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun maeun eumsigeun byeollo an joahaeyo.
examples.en: I don't really like spicy food.
examples.note: real refusal: 은 marks the contrast topic, 별로...안 softens the no

entries.nuance: 좋아하다 is an action verb meaning 'to like / be fond of', so it describes a person actively having a preference and takes the object marker 을/를: 커피를 좋아해요. Contrast it with the adjective 좋다 ('to be good/nice'), which describes the thing itself and takes 이/가: 커피가 좋아요 ('coffee is nice / I feel good about coffee'). The dividing line is who is in the spotlight — 좋아하다 puts the liker on stage, 좋다 puts the liked thing on stage. Be careful with 사랑하다 ('to love'): Koreans reserve it for deep romantic or familial love and rarely say it about food or hobbies, where English happily uses 'love' — so 'I love coffee' is 커피를 좋아해요, not 커피를 사랑해요. As a 하다 verb it conjugates regularly: 하다 → 해요, giving 좋아해요 / 좋아합니다 / 좋아했어요. The classic English-speaker pitfall is copying English subject logic and saying 커피가 좋아해요 with 이/가; once it is a 좋아하다 sentence, the food must take 을/를.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 좋아하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 좋아해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 커피가 좋아해요 with the subject marker — because the verb 좋아하다 needs an object, the food must take 을/를: 커피를 좋아해요.

entries.nuance: 모르다 is the standalone verb 'to not know / be unaware of', the lexical opposite of 알다, and it likewise takes the object marker 을/를: 길을 몰라요. It is a 르-irregular: when an 아/어 ending attaches, the 르 stem doubles the ㄹ and the vowel drops, so 모르 + 아요 → 몰라요 (never 모르아요) and the past is 몰랐어요. Compare 모르다 with 헷갈리다 ('to be confused / mix things up'): 모르다 is having no information at all, while 헷갈리다 is having information but getting it tangled. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation — applying a regular pattern to get 모르아요 instead of the irregular 몰라요 — and forgetting that the smooth, courteous version is 잘 모르겠어요.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 모르다 has an irregular stem (르 irregular). Memorize its polite form 몰라요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

structuredNuance.t: 모르다 is the standalone verb 'to not know / be unaware of', the lexical opposite of 알다, and it likewise takes the object marker 을/를: 길을 몰라요. The crucial register tool is 겠: 잘 모르겠어요 ('I'm not quite sure') is markedly softer and more natural than a blunt 몰라요, which can sound curt or even dismissive depending on tone, so Koreans lean on the 겠 form constantly when admitting ignorance politely.
Compare 모르다 with 헷갈리다 ('to be confused / mix things up'): 모르다 is having no information at all, while 헷갈리다 is having information but getting it tangled.

entries.nuance: 살다 means 'to live' in two senses — to reside somewhere and to be alive — and is a ㄹ-irregular verb. entries.nuance: 만들다 means 'to make / create / build' something concrete or abstract (food, objects, plans, rules) and takes the object marker 을/를: 음식을 만들어요. The English-speaker pitfall is mishandling the irregular in both directions: dropping the ㄹ before a vowel (만드러요) or keeping it before a consonant (만들습니다 instead of 만듭니다).

entries.nuance: 배우다 means 'to learn / acquire a skill or subject' and takes the object marker 을/를: 한국어를 배워요. It is a regular verb, but the stem ends in the vowel 우, so when 어요 attaches the two vowels contract into 워 — 배우 + 어요 → 배워요 (not 배우어요), past 배웠어요. So you 공부하다 for an exam at your desk but 배우다 the piano from a teacher. The English-speaker pitfall is writing the uncontracted 배우어요, and saying 학원에서 배우다 to mean 'learn from the academy' — 에서 marks where, while the human source must take 한테/에게서.

entries.nuance: 도와주다 means 'to help (for someone's benefit)' and is built from 돕다 ('to help') + 주다 ('to give'), so the 주다 already bakes in the warm sense of doing the help for another person. The base 돕다 is a ㅂ-irregular (돕 + 아요 → 도와요), which is why the compound surfaces as 도와- and the polite present is 도와줘요, past 도와줬어요. The person helped takes the object marker 을/를: 친구를 도와줘요. The most useful register fact is the request form: because 주다 is inside the verb, 'please help me' is simply 도와주세요 — adding a second giving verb to make 도와줘 주세요 is redundant and wrong. Contrast plain 돕다 (which feels more neutral/written, 어려운 이웃을 돕다 'help a struggling neighbor') with 도와주다 (the warm, conversational everyday form). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that double 주세요, plus marking the helped person with 에게 by analogy to 'give to' — but help is done to a person directly, so it is 저를 도와줘요, not 저에게 도와줘요.

entries.nuance: 시작하다 means 'to start / begin' and is a Sino-Korean 하다 verb — 시작 (始作, literally 始 'begin' + 作 'make/do', i.e. 'set in motion') plus 하다. Contrast it with the pure intransitive 시작되다 (始作되다, 'to be started/begin'), which is more formal and never takes an object — 회의가 시작됐어요 'the meeting began'. Its natural opposite is 끝나다 ('to end'). entries.nuance: 묻다 means 'to ask (a question / inquire)' and takes the object marker 을/를 for the thing asked about: 길을 물어요. It is a ㄷ-irregular verb: before a vowel ending the stem ㄷ changes to ㄹ, giving 물어요 and 물었어요 and 물을 거예요, but before consonant endings the ㄷ stays — 묻습니다, 묻고, 묻지 마세요. The person you ask takes 에게/한테, or honorific 께 for someone of higher status: 선생님께 물어요. In real speech Koreans far more often say 물어보다 ('ask and see', literally 묻다 + 보다), which sounds softer and more tentative than the bare, slightly abrupt 묻다 — so 물어보세요 ('please ask') is the natural request, not 물으세요. Two contrasts: do not confuse this 묻다 with the homograph 묻다 meaning 'to bury' (regular: 땅에 묻다), and distinguish 묻다 ('ask a question') from 부탁하다 ('to request a favor'). The English-speaker pitfall is keeping the ㄷ before a vowel to say 묻어요 (which actually reads as the 'bury' verb) instead of the irregular 물어요.

entries.nuance: 이사하다 specifically means relocating your residence — changing the home you live in — built from Sino-Korean 移徙 (移 'shift', 徙 'relocate') plus 하다. Contrast it sharply with 옮기다, which is just physically moving an object from one spot to another (책상을 옮기다 'move the desk'); you never use 옮기다 for changing homes, and you never use 이사하다 for shifting furniture. It splits into 이사 가다 (move away, focus on departure) and 이사 오다 (move in, focus on arrival near the speaker). Being a 하다-verb, the negative wraps the noun: 이사 안 해요 / 이사 못 해요, NOT 안 이사해요. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is treating it like English 'move' as a transitive verb — Koreans don't say '집을 이사해요'; the home is implied, so just 이사해요 is complete.

Saying 집을 이사해요 by direct-translating 'move house' — 이사하다 already contains the idea of home, so the object is dropped; just say 이사해요.
Using 옮기다 for relocating yourself (e.g. 서울로 옮겼어요) — 옮기다 is only for moving objects; for changing residence use 서울로 이사했어요.

entries.nuance: 빌려주다 is literally 빌려 (lend-and) + 주다 (give), so it means 'borrow-out to someone' — you give something for temporary use, expecting it back. The crucial contrast is with 빌리다, which is the SAME root from the other direction: 빌리다 = to borrow (you receive), 빌려주다 = to lend (you give). English speakers constantly swap these because casual English even uses 'borrow me your pen', but Korean keeps them strictly separate — 친구에게 책을 빌려줬어요 'I lent a book to my friend' vs 친구에게서 책을 빌렸어요 'I borrowed a book from my friend'. entries.nuance: 버리다 means to discard something as no longer wanted — to throw it out as trash or to abandon it. Don't confuse it with 던지다, which is to throw an object through the air toward a target (공을 던지다 'throw a ball'); 버리다 is about getting rid of, not about the flying motion. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 던지다 whenever they see 'throw' — but 'throw away/out' in the disposal sense is always 버리다. Also note Korea's strict 분리수거 (recycling separation) culture, so 버리다 in daily life often pairs with sorting.

Forgetting that 버리다 also means 'abandon (a person)' (애인을 버리다) — so in emotional contexts it can sound harsh; don't use it lightly about people.

entries.nuance: 줍다 means to pick up something that is lying on the ground or floor, usually by bending down — typically things that fell or litter. It contrasts with 들다 'to lift/hold up' (which is about raising weight, no fallen-object implication) and with 집다 'to grab/pinch with fingers' (a precise small grasp, e.g. with chopsticks). Crucially 줍다 is a ㅂ-irregular verb: before a vowel ending the ㅂ turns into a 우 sound, giving 주워, 주워요, 주웠어요, 주울 거예요 — but before a consonant ending the ㅂ stays, so the formal style is 줍습니다 (not 주웁니다) and 'don't' is 줍지 마세요. The classic English-speaker pitfall is regularizing it to 줍어요; that is wrong — say 주워요. Also note the place you pick it up FROM takes 에서 (바닥에서 주웠어요), since picking up is an action happening at a location.

Using 들다 (lift) for something on the floor: 바닥에서 동전을 들었어요 sounds off; for retrieving a fallen item use 줍다 → 주웠어요.

entries.nuance: 깨다 (transitive) means to break a hard, brittle thing into pieces — glass, dishes, eggs — by impact. Distinguish it from 부수다, which is to smash/demolish a larger or sturdier structure (벽을 부수다 'break down a wall'), and from 깨지다, the intransitive partner: 내가 컵을 깼어요 'I broke the cup (I did it)' vs 컵이 깨졌어요 'the cup broke (it got broken)'. The same syllable 깨다 also means to wake up from sleep (잠을 깨다 / 잠에서 깨다), and figuratively to 'break' a record, silence, or atmosphere — so context decides. The English-speaker pitfall is using 깨다 for things that don't shatter: tearing paper is 찢다, snapping a stick is 부러뜨리다, and breaking a machine so it stops working is 고장 내다 — not 깨다. Saying 고장났어요 vs 깼어요 mix-up: a broken-down phone is 고장 났어요 (stopped working), not 깼어요, which implies you physically shattered it.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 깨다 becomes 깰 수 있어요 ("can") and 깰 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 깨다 (transitive) means to break a hard, brittle thing into pieces — glass, dishes, eggs — by impact. The same syllable 깨다 also means to wake up from sleep (잠을 깨다 / 잠에서 깨다), and figuratively to 'break' a record, silence, or atmosphere — so context decides.

Distinguish it from 부수다, which is to smash/demolish a larger or sturdier structure (벽을 부수다 'break down a wall'), and from 깨지다, the intransitive partner: 내가 컵을 깼어요 'I broke the cup (I did it)' vs 컵이 깨졌어요 'the cup broke (it got broken)'.
Conjugation is regular: stem 깨- + 어 contracts to 깨, past 깼어요.
The English-speaker pitfall is using 깨다 for things that don't shatter: tearing paper is 찢다, snapping a stick is 부러뜨리다, and breaking a machine so it stops working is 고장 내다 — not 깨다.

entries.nuance: 흘리다 is the transitive 'cause to flow/drip' — to let liquid or small grains escape and run out, usually a little at a time and by accident (옷에 국을 흘렸어요 'I dribbled soup on my clothes'). Two big contrasts: first, its intransitive partner is 흐르다 'to flow' (물이 흐르다 'water flows by itself') — don't say 흘러요 when YOU spilled it; you need 흘려요. Second, against 쏟다: 쏟다 is dumping a large amount out all at once (a whole cup tipping over), while 흘리다 is a gentler, trickling spill. Beyond liquids, 흘리다 is the idiomatic verb for bodily flow — 눈물을 흘리다 'shed tears', 땀을 흘리다 'sweat', 피를 흘리다 'bleed'. The English-speaker pitfall is the 흐르다/흘리다 confusion: English 'spill' is transitive, so map it to 흘리다 (or 쏟다 for big spills), never 흐르다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 흘리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 흘려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 물을 흘러요 when you spilled it — 흐르다 ('flow') is intransitive for liquid moving on its own; if you caused the spill, use the transitive 흘려요.
Using 흘리다 for a big sudden spill: knocking over a full glass is better said 쏟다 (쏟았어요) — 흘리다 implies a small, dribbling amount.
Forgetting the body-fluid idioms: trying to say 'cry' with 울다 only — to describe tears running down, Koreans say 눈물을 흘리다, and 땀을 흘리다 for sweating.

entries.nuance: 묶다 means to tie or bind things together with string, rope, or a band so they stay fastened — boxes, hair, shoelaces, bundles. Its natural antonym is 풀다 'to untie/undo'. Distinguish it from 매다, which specifically means to fasten by knotting around something (넥타이를 매다 'tie a necktie', 안전벨트를 매다 'fasten a seatbelt') — 매다 is about securing a band to/around the body, while 묶다 is the general 'bind together' for objects and hair. Note the binding material takes 으로: 끈으로 묶다 'tie with string'. Pronunciation is a trap: the ㄲ batchim before a vowel links, so 묶어요 sounds like [무꺼요], but you must spell it 묶어요, and the formal form is 묶습니다 [묵씀니다]. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 매다 for everything 'tie' — but for hair, boxes, and bundles, the correct verb is 묶다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 묶다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 묶어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spelling by ear: writing 무꺼요 because it sounds like [무꺼요] — the stem keeps its ㄲ, so it is written 묶어요.
Using 매다 for hair or boxes: 머리를 매다 / 박스를 매다 sounds wrong — 매다 is for neckties and seatbelts (fastening around); for hair and bundles use 묶다.
Forgetting the means particle: saying 끈을 묶어요 to mean 'tie WITH string' — the tool takes 으로, so it is 끈으로 묶어요 (끈을 묶어요 would mean 'tie the string itself').

entries.nuance: 풀다 covers a wide web of meanings around 'undo/release': literally to untie or unfasten (매듭을 풀다 'undo a knot'), to solve a problem (문제를 풀다), to relieve stress or fatigue (스트레스를 풀다, 피로를 풀다), to unpack (짐을 풀다), and even to blow your nose (코를 풀다). Its literal antonym is 묶다 'to tie'. Grammatically it is a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ-dropping) verb: the stem ㄹ disappears before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ endings, so the formal present is 풉니다 (not 풀습니다) and the prohibitive is 풀지 마세요 — but the ㄹ stays before vowels (풀어요) and before 까 (풀까요?). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, regularizing the irregular to 풀습니다; second, not realizing 풀다 is the everyday word for 'solve' a question — learners often hunt for a separate 'solve' verb, but 문제를 풀다 is exactly it.

Saying 풀습니다 in formal style — 풀다 is a ㄹ-irregular, so the ㄹ drops before ㅂ: the correct form is 풉니다.
Looking for another verb to mean 'solve': for solving a problem/quiz the natural verb IS 풀다 → 문제를 풀어요, not a separate word.
Over-dropping the ㄹ before vowels: writing 푸어요 — the ㄹ only drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ; before a vowel it stays, giving 풀어요.
notes: ㄹ irregular: memorize 풀어 and 풀어요 together.

entries.nuance: 접다 means to fold something flat — cloth, paper, an umbrella — by bending it over onto itself, and by extension to close up a foldable object. Its natural antonyms are 펴다 'to unfold/spread flat' and 펼치다 'to open out/spread wide'. Distinguish 접다 from 구기다, which is to crumple/crease messily (종이를 구기다 'crumple paper into a ball') — 접다 is neat and deliberate, 구기다 is rumpling it up. Figuratively, 접다 means to give up or fold on a plan (꿈을 접다 'give up a dream', 사업을 접다 'fold a business'), much like English 'fold'. The result/shape takes 으로: 반으로 접다 'fold in half'. The English-speaker pitfall is conjugation pronunciation — 접어요 links to [저버요] and the formal 접습니다 sounds like [접씀니다], but spelling stays 접어요/접습니다; also don't confuse neat folding (접다) with accidental crumpling (구기다).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 접다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 접어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 접다 (neatly fold) with 구기다 (crumple): 종이를 접었어요 means folded tidily; if you balled it up by accident that is 구겼어요.
Using the wrong particle for 'in half': saying 반을 접어요 — the resulting shape takes 으로, so it is 반으로 접어요.
Mixing up the antonym: to 'unfold/open out' the umbrella you need 펴다 (우산을 펴다), not a negated 접다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 접다 becomes 접을 수 있어요 ("can") and 접을 거예요 ("will"). entries.explanation: 채우다 (chaeuda) = "to fill". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 채워요 plus one useful sentence like 물을 채우다 ("to fill (a container) with water"). entries.nuance: 채우다 is the causative 'make full' — to fill a space or container so it's no longer empty (컵에 물을 채우다). Its direct antonym is 비우다 'to empty out'. Note it's the causative partner of 차다 'to be/become full' (방이 사람으로 찼다 'the room filled with people'), so 차다 = get full on its own, 채우다 = someone fills it. A second, very common sense that surprises learners: 채우다 also means to fasten/do up a button, buckle, lock, or watch (단추를 채우다, 자물쇠를 채우다, 시계를 채우다) — here the antonym is 풀다 'undo'. And idiomatically 배를 채우다 'fill one's belly (eat)', 욕심을 채우다 'satisfy greed'. Particles: the container takes 를/에, the contents take 으로 (냉장고를 음식으로 채우다). The English-speaker pitfall is using 'fill' only for liquids/spaces and being thrown when a Korean says 단추를 채우다 — remember it doubles as 'fasten'.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 채우다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 채워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Mixing causative and plain: saying 컵이 물을 채웠어요 — 채우다 needs an actor; 'the cup filled (got full)' is 컵이 (물로) 찼어요, while 'I filled the cup' is 컵을 채웠어요.
Particle slip for contents: saying 냉장고를 음식을 채웠어요 — the contents take 으로, so it's 냉장고를 음식으로 채웠어요.
Not knowing the 'fasten' sense: for 'button up your shirt' learners say 단추를 잠그다; the idiomatic verb is 채우다 → 단추를 채우다 (and 풀다 to unbutton).

entries.shortExplanation: 쏟다 means "to spill" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 쏟다 (ssotda) means "to spill". Start from the polite form 쏟아요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 쏟다. A strong first sentence is 물을 쏟다 ("to spill water (a lot, at once)"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 쏟다 also becomes 쏟고 싶어요 (want), 쏟을 수 있어요 (can), and 못 쏟아요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 쏟다 means to spill or pour out a sizable amount of liquid or contents all at once, usually by knocking something over — it feels stronger and more sudden than 흘리다, which is a small trickling spill (a few drops on your shirt). So 컵을 쏟다 = the whole cup goes over, 국물을 흘리다 = you dribbled a bit of broth. Figuratively 쏟다 is 'pour out' effort or emotion: 정성을 쏟다 'pour in devotion', 노력을 쏟다 'pour in effort', 눈물을 쏟다 'burst into tears'. Its intransitive/spontaneous partner is 쏟아지다 'to gush/pour down' (비가 쏟아지다 'rain pours'), so 쏟다 = someone spills it, 쏟아지다 = it pours by itself. Particles: the spilled thing takes 를, the surface it lands on takes 에 (바닥에 쏟다). The English-speaker spelling pitfall is the ㄷ batchim — write 쏟다/쏟아요 (stem 쏟-), never 쏘다요; and don't confuse it with 쏘다 'to shoot'.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 쏟다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 쏟아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spelling the stem wrong: writing 쏟아요 as 쏘다요 or 쏟어요 — the stem is 쏟- and takes 아 (bright vowel ㅗ), giving 쏟아요, 쏟았어요.
Using 쏟다 for a tiny spill: a few drops on your clothes is better said 흘리다 (흘렸어요); 쏟다 implies a large amount poured out at once.
Confusing 쏟다 with 쏟아지다: 'the rain is pouring' is the intransitive 비가 쏟아져요, not 비가 쏟아요 (which would need an actor spilling rain).

entries.shortExplanation: 치우다 means "to clean up" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to clean up" in Korean is 치우다 (chiuda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 치워요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 치우다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 방을 치우다 ("to tidy up the room") — then reshape the same stem into 치우고 싶어요 (desire), 치울 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 치워요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

entries.nuance: 치우다 means to tidy a space by clearing things away, putting them where they belong, or moving them out of the way — the focus is on removing clutter and restoring order (방을 치우다 'tidy the room', 책상을 치우다 'clear the desk'). Contrast it with 청소하다 (Sino-Korean 淸掃, 淸 'clean' + 掃 'sweep'), which focuses on the cleaning itself — sweeping, mopping, wiping, vacuuming to remove dirt. So you 치우다 the toys (put them away) but 청소하다 the floor (mop it); a thorough clean often means doing both: 방을 치우고 청소해요. A second sense of 치우다 is simply to move/shove something out of the way (차 좀 치워 주세요 'please move your car'). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'clean up' as one word and always saying 청소하다 — but for clearing dishes, putting away laundry, or decluttering, the right verb is 치우다. Conjugation is regular: 치우- + 어 → 치워요, past 치웠어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 치우다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 치워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 청소하다 for clearing dishes/toys: 그릇을 청소했어요 sounds odd — 청소하다 is sweeping/wiping dirt; clearing and putting away is 치우다 → 그릇을 치웠어요.
Missing the 'move aside' sense: when someone's bag blocks the way, the natural request is 좀 치워 주세요 ('move it'), not just 옮기다.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 치우다 becomes 치울 수 있어요 ("can") and 치울 거예요 ("will"). entries.nuance: 만지다 is the plain verb for touching something with your hand to feel its texture, temperature, or shape; the thing touched takes 을/를 (천을 만지다). The 요-form is regular: stem 만지- + -어요 contracts 지+어 into 져, giving 만져요 / past 만졌어요. The nearest neighbor is 건드리다, but the dividing line is intent: 만지다 is neutral, even affectionate exploration ('feel, handle'), while 건드리다 carries 'mess with / disturb / poke' and often a nuisance nuance (남의 물건을 건드리다 = mess with someone's stuff). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'touch' emotionally: 'that movie touched me' is NOT 만지다 but 감동받다 / 감동적이다 — 만지다 is strictly physical contact. Also keep 만지다 (touch) apart from the look-alike 만나다 (meet); they share only the first syllable.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 만지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 만져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

Dropping the object particle and saying 천 만져요. A direct object needs 을/를: 천을 만져요 ('I touch the fabric').

entries.explanation: 보이다 (boi-da) means "to be seen". Start from the polite form 보여요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 보이다. usagePhrases.note: 잘 (well) is the habitual partner for visibility; opposite is 안 보이다.

examples.en: The sea is very visible from here.
examples.note: The thing seen takes 이/가 (바다가), not 을/를 — this is intransitive.

examples.note: 보여 주다 = 'show'; here it IS transitive because of 주다, so 표를 takes 를.

examples.note: Adjective stem 피곤하- + 보여요 = 'looks ~', a hugely common everyday use.

entries.nuance: 보이다 is the passive/spontaneous counterpart of 보다 (to look): something enters your field of vision on its own, so the thing seen takes 이/가 (산이 보여요 = 'the mountain is visible'), NOT 을/를. The 요-form contracts 보이-+-어요 → 보여요 (past 보였어요). The sharp contrast learners need is 보이다 vs 보다: 보다 is an active choice ('I look at / watch'), 보이다 is involuntary ('it is seen / comes into view'). A second, very frequent meaning is 'to look/seem' — adjective stem + 보이다 (행복해 보여요 'you look happy'; 비싸 보여요 'it looks expensive'); here English 'looks' maps cleanly. Confusing 보이다 with 보다. 'I can see it' for involuntary vision is 보여요, but 'I look at it / watch it' is 봐요 — don't use 보여요 for deliberate watching.
Forgetting the 'looks like' meaning. 'You look tired' is 피곤해 보여요, not 피곤한 것을 봐요 — adjective stem + 보이다 carries the 'seems' sense.

entries.explanation: "to be heard" in Korean is 들리다 (deulli-da). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 들려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 들리다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 잘 들리다 ("to be heard clearly") — then reshape the same stem into 들리고 싶어요 (desire), 들릴 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 들려요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. examples.en: Singing is heard from the next room.
examples.note: Source takes 에서 (옆방에서); the sound 노랫소리가 takes 가.

examples.note: -아서 gives the cause; 안 들리다 is the standard 'can't hear you' on a call.

examples.note: Adverb 이상하게 + 들리다 = 'sounded ~', mirroring English 'sounds'.

entries.nuance: 들리다 is the passive/spontaneous partner of 듣다 (to listen): a sound reaches your ears without effort, so what is heard takes 이/가 (음악이 들려요 = 'music is audible'), not 을/를. Note 들리다 is a regular -이다 derived verb, NOT the ㄷ-irregular 듣다 — the 요-form is 들려요 (듣-+-이-+-어요 → 들려요), and crucially it never becomes 들어요 (that would collide with 듣다's own form 들어요). The dividing line is 듣다 vs 들리다: 듣다 is deliberate ('I listen to / hear it on purpose'), 들리다 is involuntary ('it is heard, it comes through'). A second common sense is 'to sound (a certain way)': adverb + 들리다 (좋게 들려요 'sounds good'). With 주다 it means 'let/make someone hear' (노래를 들려 주다). Collapsing 들리다 into 들어요. 'It's audible' is 들려요; 들어요 belongs to 듣다 ('I listen'). Keep the 려 vs 어 distinction.
Missing the 'sounds ~' usage. 'That sounds weird' is 이상하게 들려요, not 이상한 것을 들어요 — use adverb + 들리다.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 들리다 becomes 들릴 수 있어요 ("can") and 들릴 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: 들리다 is the passive/spontaneous partner of 듣다 (to listen): a sound reaches your ears without effort, so what is heard takes 이/가 (음악이 들려요 = 'music is audible'), not 을/를. A second common sense is 'to sound (a certain way)': adverb + 들리다 (좋게 들려요 'sounds good'). With 주다 it means 'let/make someone hear' (노래를 들려 주다).
들리다 is a regular -이다 derived verb, NOT the ㄷ-irregular 듣다 — the 요-form is 들려요 (듣-+-이-+-어요 → 들려요), and crucially it never becomes 들어요 (that would collide with 듣다's own form 들어요).

소리를 안 들려요 uses the wrong particle; the sound is the subject, so 소리가 안 들려요.

entries.nuance: 흔들다 means to shake, wave, or rock something back and forth — a hand (손을 흔들다 'wave'), a head (고개를 흔들다 'shake one's head'), a bottle, a tree in the wind. Also remember the ㄹ-drop only before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, so 흔들지 마세요 and 흔들고 keep their ㄹ.

entries.nuance: 안다 means to hold someone or something in your arms — a hug, cradling a baby, clasping a pet to your chest; the one embraced takes 을/를 (아기를 안다). Because the stem vowel is bright ㅏ (안-), the 요-form is 안아요 (past 안았어요) and the formal is 안습니다. The trap is the spelling twins: 안다 (hug) vs 알다 (know) vs the negative adverb 안. Watch 안 안아요 — the first 안 is 'not', the second is the verb stem, so the whole thing means 'I do not hug'. A useful synonym contrast is 안다 vs 껴안다 / 끌어안다: plain 안다 is neutral 'hold in arms', while 껴안다 (꼭 껴안다) and 끌어안다 stress a tighter, more enveloping embrace ('clutch, hug close'). entries.nuance: 당기다 means to pull — to draw something toward yourself (a door, a rope, a chair). Unlike its ㄹ-irregular antonym 밀다, 당기다 is a regular ㅣ-stem verb, so the 요-form simply contracts 당기-+-어요 → 당겨요 (past 당겼어요, formal 당깁니다) with no ㄹ-drop. Its straight opposite is 밀다 'push', and together they label every Korean door (밀다 미시오 / 당기다 당기시오). A useful synonym contrast is 당기다 vs 끌다: 당기다 is a short pull toward you ('tug, draw'), while 끌다 is to drag something along the ground over distance (가방을 끌다 'drag a bag', 차를 끌다 'tow a car'). Watch a high-frequency idiom that surprises learners: 입맛이 당기다 / 음식이 당기다 means 'to crave food, feel an appetite' — the food is the subject (이/가), not the object. The English-speaker pitfall: do not force 'pull' into this idiom with 를 — it is 매운 게 당겨요 ('I'm craving something spicy'), never 매운 걸 당겨요 in that sense.

entries.nuance: 막다 means to block, obstruct, or stop something from passing — a road (길을 막다), an entrance, ears or nose (귀를 막다 'cover the ears') — and by extension to prevent or avert a problem (사고를 막다 'prevent an accident', 출혈을 막다 'stop the bleeding'). The 요-form is regular: bright ㅏ stem gives 막아요 (past 막았어요, formal 막습니다). The synonym contrast to nail is 막다 vs 닫다: 닫다 is to close a thing that has its own hinge or lid (문을 닫다 'close the door', 뚜껑을 닫다 'put the lid on'), while 막다 is to obstruct an opening or flow so nothing gets through (구멍을 막다 'plug a hole'). There is also a related passive 막히다 'to be blocked/jammed' (코가 막혔어요 'my nose is stuffed', 길이 막혀요 'traffic is jammed'). The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 닫다 for blocking a road — a road has no door to 'close', so it is 길을 막다, and traffic congestion is 길이 막히다, never 길이 닫혀요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 막다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 막아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 닫다 to block a road. 길을 닫아요 is unnatural; obstructing a road is 길을 막아요, and 'traffic is jammed' is 길이 막혀요.
Forgetting the passive 막히다 for 'be blocked/stuffed'. 'My nose is stuffed' is 코가 막혔어요, not 코를 막았어요 (which means 'I plugged my nose' on purpose).
Overlooking the 'prevent' sense. 'To prevent an accident' is 사고를 막다; learners often hunt for a separate word, but 막다 already covers averting danger.

entries.explanation: 숨다 (sum-da) means "to hide". Start from the polite form 숨어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 숨다. A strong first sentence is 뒤에 숨다 ("to hide behind"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 숨다 also becomes 숨고 싶어요 (want), 숨을 수 있어요 (can), and 못 숨어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 숨다 is INTRANSITIVE 'to hide oneself' — you make yourself unseen, so the subject is the person hiding and the hiding place takes 에/뒤에/밑에 (책상 밑에 숨어요 'I hide under the desk'); there is no direct object. The 요-form is regular: 숨어요 (past 숨었어요, formal 숨습니다). The single most important contrast is 숨다 vs 숨기다: 숨다 = 'I hide (myself)' (intransitive), while the causative 숨기다 = 'I hide SOMETHING' (transitive, takes 을/를) — 돈을 숨기다 'hide money', 비밀을 숨기다 'conceal a secret'. English 'hide' is both, which is exactly why learners stumble. A near-synonym is 피하다 'to avoid/dodge', but 피하다 is to steer clear of something (사람을 피하다 'avoid a person'), whereas 숨다 is specifically to conceal your body from view. The English-speaker pitfall: 'I hid the key' must be 열쇠를 숨겼어요 (숨기다), NOT 열쇠를 숨었어요 — using 숨다 with an object is ungrammatical.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 숨다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 숨어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Giving 숨다 a direct object. 'I hid the money' is 돈을 숨겼어요 (transitive 숨기다); 돈을 숨었어요 is wrong because 숨다 is intransitive.
Confusing 숨다 (hide oneself) with 숨기다 (hide a thing). 아이가 숨어요 = 'the child hides'; 아이를 숨겨요 = 'I hide the child away'.
Marking the hiding place with 를: 침대 밑을 숨어요 is wrong. Use 에 for the location: 침대 밑에 숨어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 빠지다 means "to fall into" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to fall into" in Korean is 빠지다 (ppaji-da). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 빠져요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 빠지다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 물에 빠지다 ("to fall into water / drown") — then reshape the same stem into 빠지고 싶어요 (desire), 빠질 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 빠져요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

entries.nuance: 빠지다 literally means to fall/drop into something — a hole, water, mud — by accident, with the place taking 에 (웅덩이에 빠지다 'fall into a puddle'). It is intransitive and spontaneous; the 요-form contracts 빠지-+-어요 → 빠져요 (past 빠졌어요). Beyond the literal sense it is enormously idiomatic, almost always with 에: 사랑에 빠지다 'fall in love', 게임에 빠지다 'get addicted to games', 살이 빠지다 'lose weight', and even 'be missing/left out' (명단에서 빠지다 'be dropped from the list'). The synonym contrast learners need is 빠지다 vs 넘어지다: 빠지다 is sinking/dropping DOWN INTO something, whereas 넘어지다 is toppling OVER, losing your balance on a flat surface (길에서 넘어지다 'fall over on the road'). The English-speaker pitfall: 'fall in love' tempts 를, but it is 사랑에 빠지다 with 에 (you fall INTO love); likewise weight loss is 살이 빠지다 (subject 이/가), never 살을 빠지다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 빠지다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 빠져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 빠지다 (fall into) with 넘어지다 (fall over). Tripping on flat ground is 넘어졌어요; dropping into a hole/water is 빠졌어요.
Using 를 in idioms. 'Fall in love' is 사랑에 빠지다 and 'lose weight' is 살이 빠지다 — both use 에 or 이/가, never 사랑을/살을 빠지다.
Forgetting the location particle 에. 'My foot fell into the hole' is 발이 구멍에 빠졌어요; 구멍을 빠졌어요 is ungrammatical.

entries.explanation: 갈아타다 (garata-da) = "to transfer". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 갈아타요 plus one useful sentence like 지하철로 갈아타다 ("to transfer to the subway"). Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off.

entries.nuance: 갈아타다 is a transparent compound of 갈다 'to change/replace' + 타다 'to ride', so it literally means 'change-ride' — you get off one vehicle and board a different one. The dividing line learners must feel is against plain 타다 (just 'to board/get on') and against 환승하다, the Sino-Korean twin (換乘, 換 'exchange' + 乘 'ride', literally 'change-ride') printed on every subway sign and announcement: 갈아타다 is the warm spoken word a friend uses ('여기서 갈아타'), while 환승하다 is the signage/official register ('환승 게이트'). The grammar trap is the particle: the vehicle you move TO takes 로/으로 (지하철로 갈아타다), the same directional 로 as 'change INTO', and the station where you do it takes 에서 — English 'transfer to the subway' tempts you to drop the particle or use 에. Because 타다 is regular, every form is regular too: the stem 타- already ends in ㅏ, so the 아 of 아요 merges in and disappears, giving 갈아타요 (not 갈아타아요), and the past is 갈아탔어요. Habitual collocations: 다른 노선으로 갈아타다, 같은 방향으로 갈아타다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 갈아타다 as a complete polite sentence.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 갈아타다 becomes 갈아탈 수 있어요 ("can") and 갈아탈 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 갈아타다 is a transparent compound of 갈다 'to change/replace' + 타다 'to ride', so it literally means 'change-ride' — you get off one vehicle and board a different one. Habitual collocations: 다른 노선으로 갈아타다, 같은 방향으로 갈아타다.

The dividing line learners must feel is against plain 타다 (just 'to board/get on') and against 환승하다, the Sino-Korean twin printed on every subway sign and announcement. 갈아타다 is the warm spoken word a friend uses ('여기서 갈아타'), while 환승하다 is the signage/official register ('환승 게이트').
환승하다 is the Sino-Korean twin: 換乘, 換 'exchange' + 乘 'ride', literally 'change-ride'.
Because 타다 is regular, every form is regular too: the stem 타- already ends in ㅏ, so the 아 of 아요 merges in and disappears, giving 갈아타요 (not 갈아타아요), and the past is 갈아탔어요.

The grammar trap is the particle: the vehicle you move TO takes 로/으로 (지하철로 갈아타다), the same directional 로 as 'change INTO', and the station where you do it takes 에서. English 'transfer to the subway' tempts you to drop the particle or use 에.

entries.nuance: 운전하다 is Sino-Korean 운전 (運轉, 'move-turn', i.e. to keep a machine running) plus the light verb 하다, and it specifically means to operate a vehicle — primarily a car. Contrast it with 타다 'to ride/board', which is what a passenger does: the driver 운전해요 while everyone else just 타요. It is neutral in register and used by everyone, but the fixed compound 음주 운전 ('drinking driving') is the serious legal phrase you'll hear in warnings and news. Natural collocations include 안전 운전 (safe driving), 운전이 서툴다 (to be a clumsy driver), and 운전대를 잡다 (lit. 'grab the steering wheel' = to drive). Because it is a 하다 verb, the polite form is the irregular-looking but standard 운전해요 (하 + 여요 → 해요), and the negative and potential SPLIT the noun from 하다: 운전 안 해요, 운전 못 해요, never 안 운전해요. The English-speaker trap is exactly that splitting — and forgetting that the destination/route takes 까지 (집까지 운전해요) or 에서 for where the driving happens, since 운전하다 itself takes no direct object.

Using 운전하다 for being a passenger. If you merely rode in a car you 탔어요 (from 타다); 운전했어요 means YOU were behind the wheel.
Attaching a direct object like 차를 운전해요 in casual speech. While grammatically possible, Koreans normally just say 운전해요 and let context supply the car; over-marking 차를 sounds like a textbook.

entries.nuance: 주차하다 comes from Sino-Korean 주차 (駐車, 'halt-vehicle', i.e. to bring a car to a stop and leave it) plus 하다, so it means parking a vehicle, not stopping briefly to let someone out — that quick stop is 정차 (停車). Keep 주차하다 distinct from 세우다 ('to stand/stop something'): you can 차를 세우다 anywhere for a second, but 주차하다 implies leaving the car in a designated spot. Register is neutral and practical. The crucial particle point is that the resting place takes 에 (locative of where something settles), NOT 에서 (which marks where an action happens) — 주차장에 주차해요, never 주차장에서. Common collocations: 주차 금지 (no parking), 주차 요금 (parking fee), 주차 자리/공간 (a spot), 발레파킹 (valet). As a 하다 verb the negative and potential split the noun off: 주차 안 해요, 주차 못 해요. The English-speaker pitfall is the 에 vs 에서 choice and over-using a direct object — Koreans simply say 주차해요 and let context name the car.

entries.nuance: 막히다 is the passive/intransitive partner of the transitive 막다 ('to block'): the -히- infix turns 'someone blocks X' into 'X gets blocked', so 막히다 is something that HAPPENS to a road, drain, or nose rather than something you do. For traffic this is the single most useful verb — 길이 막히다 / 차가 막히다 — and its opposite is 뚫리다 ('to open up/clear'), with 안 막히다 the everyday 'no traffic'. Do not confuse it with 막다 itself: 'I block the road' is 길을 막다, but 'the road is jammed' is 길이 막히다, and the particle flips from 을 to 이/가 accordingly. Register is plain and universal. Because the subject is a non-person, the polite/imperative-looking forms (막혀 주세요, 막힐까요?) are essentially never used about traffic. The big English-speaker trap is treating it as transitive: there is no 'I am blocked by traffic' with you as subject — Korean puts the ROAD in the subject slot (길이 막혀요), and you simply say 길이 막혀서 늦었어요 ('I was late because the road was jammed').

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 막히다 becomes 막힐 수 있어요 ("can") and 막힐 거예요 ("will"). entries.nuance: 넘어지다 means a standing person (or upright thing) loses balance and topples to the ground, built on 넘다 'to go over' + -어지다 'to come to be', literally 'to come to fall over'. The line to draw is against 떨어지다 ('to fall FROM a height / to drop'): a person on their feet 넘어지다, but a cup off a table or a leaf from a tree 떨어지다 — and against 쓰러지다, which is to collapse from illness/exhaustion (fainting) rather than from tripping. Register is plain and used for everyone. The place where you fall takes 에서 (action location), and the cause is usually chained with -어서: 미끄러져서 넘어졌어요. Natural collocations: 넘어져서 무릎이 까지다 (scrape a knee falling), 넘어질 뻔하다 (almost fall), 넘어지지 않게 조심하다. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 떨어지다 because English uses 'fall' for both — but 'I fell (down)' on flat ground is always 넘어지다; save 떨어지다 for dropping or falling off something.

Using 넘어지다 for fainting/collapsing from illness. That is 쓰러지다 (더위 먹고 쓰러졌어요). 넘어지다 implies a trip or loss of footing, not a medical collapse.
Marking the place with 에 instead of 에서. Falling is an action that happens somewhere, so 계단에서 넘어졌어요 (with 에서), not 계단에 넘어졌어요.

entries.nuance: 부딪치다 means to strike or collide against something — a wall, a door, another person, or vehicle to vehicle. The particle does real work here: a stationary thing you hit takes 에 (문에 부딪치다), a body part you bang takes 을/를 (머리를 부딪치다), and a mutual collision with a moving party takes 과/와 (사람과 부딪치다). Beware the near-identical 부딪히다, which is the passive ('to be struck/run into by'): 차에 부딪히다 = 'to get hit by a car', so 부딪치다 vs 부딪히다 is the active-vs-passive divide, and learners constantly swap them. Do not confuse either with 만지다 ('to touch deliberately') — 부딪치다 is sudden and unintended impact. Register is plain. Collocations: 정면으로 부딪치다 (collide head-on), 세게 부딪치다 (hit hard), and figuratively 의견이 부딪치다 (opinions clash). The English-speaker pitfall is that 'bump into a friend' in English can simply mean 'run into = meet by chance' — that social sense is 우연히 만나다, NOT 부딪치다, which keeps its literal 'physical collision' meaning.

entries.nuance: 미끄러지다 is the VERB 'to slip / slide / lose footing', describing the motion of your foot or body sliding on a slick surface. Its single most important confusion is with the look-alike ADJECTIVE 미끄럽다 ('to be slippery'): the surface IS 미끄럽다 (길이 미끄러워요 — a state, ㅂ-irregular), but a person DOES 미끄러지다 (제가 미끄러졌어요 — an event). Mixing the two is the number-one English-speaker error here. Keep it apart from 넘어지다 too: 미끄러지다 is the slide itself, 넘어지다 is hitting the ground, and they chain naturally — 미끄러져서 넘어졌어요. The slippery place takes 에서. Register is plain. Useful collocations: 발이 미끄러지다 (foot slips), 차가 미끄러지다 (a car skids), 미끄럼 주의 (the 'caution: slippery' floor sign, using the noun 미끄럼). The verb itself is regular (미끄러지다 → 미끄러져요), but its adjective cousin 미끄럽다 is ㅂ-irregular (미끄러워요), so don't carry the irregularity over.

Conjugating the verb like the ㅂ-irregular adjective: 미끄러워요 for 'I slip'. The verb 미끄러지다 is regular: 미끄러져요. Save 미끄러워요 for the adjective 미끄럽다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 미끄러지다 becomes 미끄러질 수 있어요 ("can") and 미끄러질 거예요 ("will"). structuredNuance.t: 미끄러지다 is the VERB 'to slip / slide / lose footing', describing the motion of your foot or body sliding on a slick surface. The slippery place takes 에서. Register is plain. Its single most important confusion is with the look-alike ADJECTIVE 미끄럽다 ('to be slippery'): the surface IS 미끄럽다 (길이 미끄러워요 — a state, ㅂ-irregular), but a person DOES 미끄러지다 (제가 미끄러졌어요 — an event). Mixing the two is the number-one error here.

entries.nuance: 서두르다 means to hurry / rush / get a move on, acting on yourself to do things fast because time is short. Distinguish it from 급하다, the ADJECTIVE 'to be urgent / be in a rush' (마음이 급해요 = 'I feel rushed'): 급하다 describes the pressured state, while 서두르다 is the action you take in response — you 서두르다 because something is 급하다. It is plainly conjugated speech, fine in any everyday register, and softens to a gentle 서두르지 마세요 ('don't rush') when reassuring someone. The grammar heart of this word is that it is a 르 irregular: before a vowel ending the 르 sheds its ㅡ and an extra ㄹ appears, so 서두르 + 어요 → 서둘러요, and the past is 서둘렀어요 — anchor everything on 서둘러요. The classic English-speaker mistake is regularizing it to 서두러요 (no doubled ㄹ). Collocations: 서둘러 나가다 (hurry out), 서두르다가 넘어지다 (trip from rushing), 서두를 거 없어요 (no need to rush).

entries.nuance: 헤매다 means to wander about lost, roaming without finding your way — and by extension to flounder or struggle when you can't find a solution. The contrast to nail is against 산책하다 ('to take a stroll'), which is pleasant and purposeful: a 산책 is relaxing, but 헤매다 carries frustration and being lost. Don't confuse it with the similar-sounding 헤어지다 ('to break up / part ways') — totally different meaning. Register is plain and everyday. The place or route you wander through takes the object particle 을/를 (길을 헤매다), which surprises English speakers who expect a location particle like 에서 — but here the path is treated as the thing you traverse. As a verb stem ending in ㅐ, the vowel contractions are clean: 헤매 + 어요 → 헤매요, and the past 헤매 + 었어요 → 헤맸어요 (double ㅆ). Collocations: 길을 헤매다, 정신없이 헤매다 (wander in a daze), 헤매고 다니다 (roam around lost). Pitfall: learners say 길에서 헤매다, but the idiomatic frame is 길을 헤매다.

Marking the route with 에서 instead of 을/를. The idiomatic frame treats the path as a direct object: 길을 헤맸어요, not 길에서 헤맸어요.
Writing the past as 헤매었어요 in speech. The ㅐ stem contracts: 헤매 + 었어요 → 헤맸어요 is the natural spoken/written form.

entries.nuance: 들르다 means to stop by / drop in somewhere briefly while on your way to another destination — the visit is short and incidental, not the main purpose of the trip. Contrast it with 방문하다 ('to visit', Sino-Korean 訪問), which is a planned, often formal visit you make for its own sake: you 방문하다 a client's office on purpose, but you 들르다 a convenience store because it's on the route. Register is casual and warm; 가는 길에 들러요 is exactly how a friend invites you over. The brief-visit destination takes 에 (집에 들르다). The whole difficulty is the conjugation: 들르다 is a ㅡ (eu) irregular — before a vowel ending the final ㅡ simply drops with NO doubled ㄹ (unlike 르-irregular verbs), so 들르 + 어요 → 들러요 and the past is 들렀어요. Anchor on 들러요. The biggest English-speaker trap is writing 들르어요 / 들리어요 (keeping the ㅡ) or confusing it with 들리다 ('to be heard' / 'to be audible'), a completely different verb. Collocations: 잠깐 들르다, 들렀다 가다, 가는 길에 들르다.

Use 들러요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 들르다 has an irregular stem (ㅡ (으) irregular). Memorize its polite form 들러요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

structuredNuance.t: 들르다 means to stop by / drop in somewhere briefly while on your way to another destination — the visit is short and incidental, not the main purpose of the trip. The whole difficulty is the conjugation: 들르다 is a ㅡ (eu) irregular — before a vowel ending the final ㅡ simply drops with NO doubled ㄹ (unlike 르-irregular verbs), so 들르 + 어요 → 들러요 and the past is 들렀어요. Anchor on 들러요.
