entries.nuance: 지각하다 is Sino-Korean 지각 (遲刻, 'late-moment') + 하다, meaning specifically to arrive late to an appointed place like school, work, or a meeting — it is the institutional 'tardy', the kind a teacher or boss notes. entries.nuance: 마중하다 is native Korean 마중 ('a going-out to receive an arriver') + 하다, meaning to go out and greet/pick up someone who is arriving — at a station, airport, or your door. Its exact antonym is 배웅하다 ('to see someone off' as they LEAVE): you 마중하다 an arrival and 배웅하다 a departure, and confusing the two reverses the whole scene. It carries a warm, caring connotation — going out of your way to welcome someone — and is neutral-to-warm in register. The person you greet takes 을/를 (친구를 마중하다), and the spot takes 에 or directional 으로 (공항으로 마중 가다). In real speech the standalone verb 마중하다 is actually less common than the collocations 마중 나가다 / 마중 나오다 / 마중 가다 ('go/come out to meet'), so learn those phrasal forms. As a 하다 verb the negative splits: 마중 안 해요. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the generic 만나다 ('to meet'): 만나다 is meeting on equal footing anywhere, but 마중하다 specifically means going TO the arrival point to receive someone — and don't mix it up with 마치다 ('to finish'), which only sounds similar.

Using plain 만나다 for going to receive an arriver. 공항에서 친구를 만났어요 just means 'I met my friend at the airport'; to convey 'I went to pick them up' use 마중하다 / 마중 나가다.
Forming the negative as 안 마중해요. Split the 하다 compound: 마중 안 해요 — and remember the everyday phrasing is usually 마중 나가다, not the bare verb.

entries.explanation: 좋아지다 (joajida) = "to get better". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 좋아져요 plus one useful sentence like 기분이 좋아졌어요 ("My mood got better"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 좋아지고 싶어요 for what you want, 좋아질 수 있어요 for what you can, 좋아질 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

examples.note: Simple weather change, past tense

examples.note: -고 있어요 shows the change is ongoing

entries.nuance: 좋아지다 is the adjective 좋다 (good) plus -아지다, the pattern that turns a state-word into 'become that state', so it literally means 'come to be good' — a gradual drift from worse to better, not a fixed quality. The key contrast is 좋다 vs 좋아지다: 좋다 just says something IS good right now (기분이 좋아요 = I feel good), while 좋아지다 reports a CHANGE toward good (기분이 좋아졌어요 = I feel better than before). It is warm and neutral in register, fine in both 반말 and 존댓말, and shows up constantly with 몸(body), 기분(mood), 날씨(weather), 사이(relationship), and 실력(skill). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 좋다 when you really mean a transition — 'My Korean got better' is 좋아졌어요, never 좋았어요, because 좋았어요 just means 'it was good (in the past)'. Note too that 좋아지다 means 'come to like' when the subject is a person feeling (그 사람이 좋아졌어요 = I came to like that person), so context decides between 'get better' and 'grow fond of'.

Use 좋아져요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 기분이 좋았어요 to mean 'my mood improved' — 좋았어요 only means 'I felt good (back then)' with no sense of change; for the improvement you need 좋아졌어요.
Treating 좋아지다 like a normal adjective and trying 좋아지다예요 — it is a verb (좋다 + 아지다), so the present is 좋아져요, never *좋아지다예요.

Using 좋아지다 for someone improving a thing on purpose; 좋아지다 is intransitive (it happens by itself). To say 'I improved my grades' you act on them with a different verb — 좋아지다 only describes the grades themselves getting better.

It is the adjective 좋다 (good) plus -아지다, the pattern that turns a state-word into 'become that state', so it literally means 'come to be good'.

entries.nuance: 변하다 is Sino-Korean: 變 (byeon, 'change, transform') + 하다, so it carries the feeling of something turning into a different state on its own, by nature or over time. The sharp contrast English speakers must learn is 변하다 vs 바꾸다: 변하다 is intransitive — the thing changes by itself (날씨가 변해요 = the weather changes), while 바꾸다 is transitive — somebody deliberately swaps or replaces a thing (계획을 바꿔요 = I change the plan). A related pair is 변하다 vs 바뀌다 (the passive of 바꾸다): 바뀌다 implies an external switch (신호등이 바뀌었어요 = the traffic light switched), whereas 변하다 implies inner transformation (성격이 변했어요 = his personality changed). Register is neutral and everyday. The big pitfall is using 변하다 with a direct object — you cannot say *계획을 변해요 to mean 'I change the plan'; if there is an actor doing the changing, you need 바꾸다. 변하다 only ever describes the subject itself becoming different.

The English-speaker pitfall mirrors 늘다: don't say *줄습니다 (the ㄹ drops to make 줍니다), and don't put an object with 줄다. 'I reduced my spending' needs the transitive 줄이다 (지출을 줄였어요); 'my spending decreased' uses 줄다 with the subject particle (지출이 줄었어요).

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 줄다 has an irregular stem (ㄹ). Memorize its polite form 줄어요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

structuredNuance.t: 줄다 is the exact opposite of 늘다 — it means an amount, number, or size gets smaller — and the two are learned as a pair (늘다/줄다).

The crucial synonym contrast is 줄다 vs 줄이다: 줄다 is intransitive — the thing shrinks by itself (소리가 줄었어요 = the sound got quieter on its own), while 줄이다 is the causative — you deliberately reduce something (소리를 줄였어요 = I turned the sound down). Its formal report-style synonym is 감소하다 (Sino-Korean 減少, 'reduce-decrease'), used for statistics; 줄다 is the natural conversational word.
Like 늘다 it is a ㄹ-irregular verb, so the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, giving the formal 줍니다 (not *줄습니다).

The English-speaker pitfall mirrors 늘다: don't say *줄습니다 (the ㄹ drops to make 줍니다), and don't put an object with 줄다. 'I reduced my spending' needs the transitive 줄이다 (지출을 줄였어요); 'my spending decreased' uses 줄다 with the subject particle (지출이 줄었어요).

entries.nuance: 나아지다 is built from 낫다 ('to be better / to recover') plus -아지다 ('become'), so it specifically means coming UP from a bad or sick state — recovery and relief — which gives it a more emotional, hopeful color than the neutral 좋아지다. Because the root is 낫다 (a ㅅ-irregular: 낫다 → 나아), the spelling is 나아지다 with two ㅏ vowels and NO ㅅ. entries.nuance: 긴장하다 is Sino-Korean: 緊 (gin, 'tight') + 張 (jang, 'stretch') + 하다, literally 'to be tightly stretched' — a vivid image of nerves pulled taut before a big moment. It describes performance-type nerves (tests, interviews, stages, sports), the keyed-up tension you feel when stakes are high. The key contrast is 긴장하다 vs 무섭다 vs 걱정하다: 무섭다 is 'to be scared/afraid' of a threat (귀신이 무서워요 = ghosts are scary); 걱정하다 is 'to worry' about an outcome over time (시험이 걱정돼요 = I'm worried about the exam); but 긴장하다 is the immediate bodily tension of a high-pressure moment — your heart pounds, your shoulders stiffen. Note the very common passive-feel form 긴장되다 ('to get nervous', the feeling arising in you) — 긴장돼요 often sounds more natural than 긴장해요 for 'I feel nervous right now'. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping every 'nervous' to one word: 'I'm nervous about the future' is really worry (걱정), not 긴장; reserve 긴장하다 for that taut, just-before-it-happens tension.

Forming the negative as 안 긴장해요 — with 하다 verbs built on a noun, the 안 splits inside: 긴장 안 해요 is the natural negative.

entries.nuance: 안심하다 is Sino-Korean: 安 (an, 'peace, safe') + 心 (sim, 'heart') + 하다, literally 'to make the heart peaceful' — that settling of the chest when a worry finally lifts. It is the natural pair-opposite of 걱정하다 (to worry): you 걱정하다 while the danger looms and 안심하다 once you know it's fine. The contrast you must keep clear is 안심하다 vs 안전하다, which look almost identical but differ by one syllable and one part of speech: 안심하다 is a VERB about a person's FEELING of relief (저는 안심했어요 = I felt relieved), while 안전하다 is an ADJECTIVE about a thing being SAFE (여기는 안전해요 = this place is safe). They share the 安 hanja, which is why beginners blur them. 안심하다 also commonly appears as 안심이 되다 ('to become reassured', feeling-driven) and in the warm imperative 안심하세요 ('rest assured'), which businesses and caretakers use a lot. The English-speaker pitfall is swapping in 안전하다 for the emotion — *저는 안전했어요 wrongly says 'I was safe', not 'I felt relieved'; relief is always 안심.

Forming the negative as 안 안심해요 — split the 하다: 안심 안 해요. (The doubled 안 also just sounds wrong.)
Treating 안심하다 as transitive with an object, e.g. 그것을 안심해요. It takes no object; the cause is given with a clause + -아서/-으니까 or marked with 에 (그 소식에 안심했어요).

entries.nuance: 감동하다 is Sino-Korean: 感 (gam, 'feel') + 動 (dong, 'move') + 하다, literally 'to be moved by feeling' — the heart stirred deeply by kindness, beauty, art, or a touching story. The contrast to lock in is 감동하다 vs 감사하다: 감사하다 means 'to be grateful / thank' for something done for you (도와주셔서 감사합니다 = thank you for helping), a social acknowledgment; 감동하다 is the inner emotional swell of being touched, which may bring tears, not a thank-you. They share the 感 ('feel') hanja, which is why learners conflate them. A crucial usage note: Koreans very often say 감동받다 (감동 + 받다, 'to receive deep emotion') and 감동하다 almost interchangeably for 'I was touched' — 감동받았어요 is arguably the more frequent spoken form. The cause is marked with 에 (그 말에 감동했어요 = I was moved by those words). To describe the thing itself as moving, use the adjective 감동적이다 (감동적인 영화 = a moving film), not 감동하다, which is reserved for the person feeling. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 감사하다 ('thank you') when you really mean you were emotionally moved — the two feelings are different, and Koreans keep them apart.

entries.nuance: 견디다 means to withstand and hold out against something hard, painful, or long — hardship, heat, pain, loneliness, a tough stretch of life. It conjugates as a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 견디 + 어 contracts to 견뎌, giving 견뎌요 / 견뎠어요. The contrast that matters most is 견디다 vs 참다: 참다 is to hold back or suppress a single impulse or sensation in the moment — a laugh, a sneeze, anger, the urge to pee (웃음을 참았어요 = I held in my laughter), while 견디다 is to endure a prolonged ordeal over time (외로움을 견뎠어요 = I endured the loneliness). So 참다 = suppress a momentary urge; 견디다 = weather a lasting hardship. A near-synonym for the strong, gritty 'hold out' sense is 버티다 (버텨요), which adds a flavor of stubbornly hanging on against pressure; 견디다 is a touch more neutral and can include quietly bearing pain. The English-speaker pitfall is using 견디다 for a quick, one-off suppression — 'I couldn't bear to hold my pee' is 참다 (참을 수 없었어요), not 견디다, because that's a momentary urge; reach for 견디다 only when the suffering stretches over time.

Conjugating it as 견디어요 in speech — 견디 + 어 contracts, so the natural spoken/written form is 견뎌요 (past 견뎠어요).
Dropping the object particle in set phrases. To bear a hardship you mark it with 을/를: 어려움을 견뎌요, 고통을 견뎠어요 — 견디다 is transitive and normally takes what you're enduring as its object.

entries.nuance: 걷다 means to walk on foot and is a ㄷ irregular verb: before a vowel ending the final ㄷ softens to ㄹ, so the 요-form is 걸어요 (not 걷어요) and the past is 걸었어요. Before a consonant ending the ㄷ stays put, so the formal form remains 걷습니다 and you say 걷지 마세요, 걷고 싶어요. The nearest relative is 산책하다 ('take a stroll'): 걷다 is the raw act of walking anywhere, while 산책하다 implies a leisurely walk for pleasure, so 'I walk to work' is 걸어서 출근해요, never 산책해서 출근해요. The trap for English speakers is that 걷다 doesn't take an object the way 'walk the dog' does — Korean uses 산책시키다 for that, and the path you walk takes 을/를 (공원을 걸어요), so don't reach for 에. Also remember 걸어서 ('on foot') is one fixed chunk for describing how you travel.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 걷다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 걸어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Keeping the ㄷ and saying 걷어요/걷었어요 — because 걷다 is a ㄷ irregular, the ㄷ becomes ㄹ before vowels, so the correct forms are 걸어요/걸었어요 (the ㄷ only survives before consonants, as in 걷습니다).
Saying 공원에 걸어요 to mean 'I walk in the park' — the space you walk through is the path/object and takes 을/를, so it must be 공원을 걸어요; 에 would wrongly mark a destination.
Translating 'walk the dog' literally as 개를 걸어요 — 걷다 can't take a creature as its object that way; Korean says 개를 산책시켜요 ('make the dog stroll').
notes: ㄷ irregular: memorize 걸어 and 걸어요 together.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 걸어요 feels easy, practice 걷고 싶어요, 걸을 수 있어요, and 걸어야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 걷다 becomes 걸을 수 있어요 ("can") and 걸을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㄷ → ㄹ
conjugationTips.body: 걷다 is a ㄷ-irregular verb. The final ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel ending, so it conjugates to 걸어요, never the literal ㄷ + 어요. The ㄷ stays ㄷ before a consonant ending (듣고, 듣습니다).

structuredNuance.t: 걷다 means to walk on foot. Remember 걸어서 ('on foot') is one fixed chunk for describing how you travel.

걷다 is a ㄷ irregular verb: before a vowel ending the final ㄷ softens to ㄹ, so the 요-form is 걸어요 (not 걷어요) and the past is 걸었어요. Before a consonant ending the ㄷ stays put, so the formal form remains 걷습니다 and you say 걷지 마세요, 걷고 싶어요.
걷다 doesn't take an object the way 'walk the dog' does — Korean uses 산책시키다 for that. The path you walk takes 을/를 (공원을 걸어요), so don't reach for 에.

entries.shortExplanation: 뛰다 means "to run" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to run" in Korean is 뛰다 (ttwida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 뛰어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 뛰다 for study notes. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

entries.nuance: 뛰다 is a regular verb whose stem ends in the vowel 위, so it simply adds 어 without contracting: 뛰어요, 뛰었어요. Before the formal ㅂ/ㄴ endings the stem shortens in the usual way to 뜁니다 and 뛸 거예요. Its key synonym is 달리다: 달리다 is the neutral, 'sporty' word for running over distance (마라톤을 달리다, 100미터를 달리다), while 뛰다 is the everyday word for dashing, rushing, or even jumping, so a child rushing across a room 뛰어다녀요 rather than 달려다녀요. Crucially 뛰다 also means 'to jump/leap' (제자리에서 뛰다 = jump in place; 심장이 뛰다 = the heart beats/pounds), so context decides between 'run' and 'jump'. The English-speaker pitfall is spelling: don't confuse 뛰다 (run) with 띄다 ('be visible / catch the eye', as in 눈에 띄다) — they sound close but are different verbs. Also note the polite-warning 뛰지 마세요 is the fixed phrase you'll see posted everywhere.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 뛰다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 뛰어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 뛰다 with 띄다 — 띄다 means 'to be noticeable / catch the eye' (눈에 띄다), so writing 눈에 뛰다 is wrong; keep the two verbs separate.
Assuming 뛰다 only means timed/sport running and switching to 달리다 for a quick dash — for rushing to catch a bus or train, natural Korean is 버스를 타려고 뛰었어요, not 달렸어요.
Forgetting the stem-shortening in the formal form and saying 뛰읍니다 — the correct formal present is 뜁니다 (and the future is 뛸 거예요).

entries.shortExplanation: 서다 means "to stand" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 서다 (seoda) = "to stand". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 서요 plus one useful sentence like 여기 서 주세요 ("Please stand here"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 서고 싶어요 for what you want, 설 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 서요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.

entries.nuance: 서다 means to stand or, for vehicles, to come to a stop. Because the stem already ends in 어, the 요-ending merges instead of doubling: you get 서요 and the past 섰어요, never 서어요 or 서었어요. Watch the two sister verbs: 서다 is the plain state/result 'to be standing / take a standing position', while 일어서다 ('rise to one's feet') stresses the motion of getting up from sitting — so 'please stand up (from your seat)' is 일어서 주세요, but 'please stand here' is 여기 서 주세요. For vehicles 서다 overlaps with 멈추다 ('to halt'); 멈추다 is more general and can describe machines or actions stopping, while 서다 is the everyday word for a bus or car pulling up. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: the location where you stand takes 에 (여기에 서다), not the object marker, and don't say 줄에 서다 — the idiom is 줄을 서다, treating the line as something you 'do'. Korean also has no separate verb for 'stand something up'; that meaning needs the causative 세우다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 서다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 서요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the doubled 서어요/서었어요 — since the stem ends in 어, it contracts with the ending, so the correct forms are 서요 and 섰어요.
Saying 줄에 서요 for 'stand in line' — the natural idiom treats the line as an object, so it must be 줄을 서요/줄을 섰어요.
Using 서다 to mean 'stand something upright' (e.g., 'I stood the bottle on the table') — 서다 is intransitive; for that you need the causative 세우다, as in 병을 세웠어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 눕다 means "to lie down" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 눕다 (nupda) means "to lie down". Start from the polite form 누워요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 눕다. A strong first sentence is 침대에 누워요 ("I lie down on the bed"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 눕다 also becomes 눕고 싶어요 (want), 누울 수 있어요 (can), and 못 누워요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 눕다 means to lie down and is a ㅂ irregular verb: before a vowel ending the ㅂ turns into a 우/워 sound, giving 누워요 and 누웠어요, while before a consonant the ㅂ stays, so the formal is 눕습니다 and you say 눕지 마세요, 눕고 싶어요. Don't confuse it with two neighbors: 눕다 is intransitive ('I lie down'), whereas the causative 눕히다 means 'lay someone/something down' (아기를 눕혀요 = lay the baby down), and 기대다 means 'to lean/recline' rather than fully lying flat. There's also a posture pair to keep straight: 눕다 (lie) vs 앉다 (sit) vs 서다 (stand). The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'lie down' has no object but learners still want to add 를; in Korean the surface takes 에 (침대에 눕다), and reaching for 눕어요 by analogy with regular verbs is the classic error — it must be 누워요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 눕다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 누워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Keeping the ㅂ and saying 눕어요/눕었어요 — 눕다 is ㅂ irregular, so before a vowel the ㅂ becomes 우/워, giving 누워요/누웠어요 (the ㅂ only survives before consonants, as in 눕습니다).
Using 눕다 to mean 'lay someone down' — 눕다 is intransitive; to lay a baby or object down you need the causative 눕히다, as in 아기를 침대에 눕혔어요.
Marking the surface with 를 (침대를 누워요) — the place you lie on takes 에, so it must be 침대에 누워요.
notes: ㅂ irregular: memorize 누워 and 누워요 together.

entries.nuance: 놓다 means to set an object down onto a surface, and the place where you put it takes 에 (책상에 놓다 = put it on the desk). It's a regular verb, so the ㅎ stays in writing and you add 아: 놓아요, 놓았어요; in fast speech 놓아요 routinely contracts to 놔요 and 놓았어요 to 놨어요, but the full forms are clearer to learn first. The crucial contrast is with 넣다 ('put inside / insert'): 놓다 places something ON a surface, while 넣다 puts it INTO a container (가방에 넣다 = put it in the bag) — choosing the wrong one changes the meaning entirely. Compare too 두다 ('leave/keep something in a place', often longer-term: 여기 두세요 = leave it here). 놓다 also means 'to let go / release' (손을 놓다) and appears in helpful patterns like -아 놓다 ('do and leave it done', 켜 놓다 = leave it switched on). The English-speaker pitfall: English 'put' covers both 'on' and 'in', so learners overuse 놓다 where 넣다 is needed, and they mark the surface with 를 instead of the correct 에.

entries.nuance: 입다 is a regular verb (입어요, 입었어요, 입습니다) meaning to put on or wear clothing on the torso and legs — shirts, coats, dresses, trousers, uniforms. The thing English speakers must internalize is that Korean has no single verb for 'wear'; it splits the action by body part: 입다 for body clothes, 신다 for footwear (shoes, socks), 쓰다 for things on the head/face (hats, glasses), 끼다 for snug items (gloves, rings), 차다 for things you strap on (watch, belt), and 매다 for ties/scarves you knot. So 'wear shoes' is never 신발을 입다 — it must be 신발을 신다. A second nuance is aspect: 입다 is the action of putting on, while the resulting state 'be wearing' is 입고 있다 (티셔츠를 입고 있어요 = is wearing a T-shirt). The opposite, for taking off any of these, is the single verb 벗다. The pitfall is simply over-extending 입다 to cover everything 'wear' covers in English.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 입다 as a complete polite sentence.

Using 입다 for a hat or glasses — head/face items take 쓰다, so 'wear a hat' is 모자를 써요 and 'wear glasses' is 안경을 써요, not 입다.
Saying 옷을 입고 있어요 when you mean the action of getting dressed right now — 입고 있다 is ambiguous toward the state 'am wearing'; to stress the ongoing action of dressing, context or 입는 중이에요 is clearer.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 웃다 becomes 웃을 수 있어요 ("can") and 웃을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 웃다 covers BOTH laughing and smiling; Korean doesn't force the English split. Context and adverbs do the work: 크게 웃다 / 깔깔 웃다 lean toward audible laughing, while 빙긋 웃다 / 미소를 짓다 lean toward a quiet smile. Naturally its opposite is 울다 ('to cry').

The near-synonym 미소(를) 짓다 ('make a smile', literally) is more written/formal and only means smiling, whereas plain 웃다 is the everyday word for both. A related verb to keep distinct is the causative 웃기다 ('to be funny / make someone laugh', 웃기다 ≠ 웃다): 그 사람 진짜 웃겨요 = 'that person is really funny'.
웃다 is a regular verb (the ㅅ stays): 웃어요, 웃었어요, 웃습니다.

The pitfall is twofold: (1) hunting for a separate verb for 'smile' when 웃다 already does it — 웃어 주세요 is the photo phrase, not 미소해 주세요; and (2) spelling/meaning confusion with 울다 (cry), which differs by a single jamo.

entries.nuance: 울다 means to cry and is a ㄹ irregular verb: the stem ㄹ drops before endings starting with ㅂ, ㄴ, or ㅅ, so the formal present is 웁니다 (not 울습니다) and the honorific is 우세요; before a plain vowel the ㄹ stays, giving 울어요 and 울었어요, and the future keeps it too in 울 거예요. The crier is the subject and takes 이/가 (아기가 울어요), unlike English where 'cry' can feel transitive. Its natural opposite is 웃다 (laugh), and its near-synonyms split by intensity and register: 눈물을 흘리다 ('shed tears', literally, more composed/quiet) describes tears running down without sobbing, while 흐느끼다 ('to sob') is heavier and more literary; plain 울다 is the everyday all-purpose word, often boosted by mimetics like 펑펑 울다 (bawl) or 엉엉 울다. Note 울다 also describes animals making their cry/call (새가 울다 = a bird sings/cries) and even a phone or alarm 'ringing/sounding'. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation — writing 울습니다 by habit when the ㄹ must drop to 웁니다 — plus confusing 울다 with 웃다, which differ by a single jamo.

Confusing 울다 (cry) with 웃다 (laugh) — they differ by one jamo, so 울었어요 means 'cried' while 웃었어요 means 'laughed'.
Marking the crier with 을/를 (아기를 울어요) — 울다 is intransitive, so the one crying is the subject: 아기가 울어요 (to MAKE someone cry, use the causative 울리다, as in 동생을 울렸어요).

entries.nuance: 켜다 means to bring a device, screen, or flame to life by supplying power, and it is the exact opposite of 끄다 (to turn off) — the two are always taught as a pair. The biggest pitfall: English 'turn ON' tempts learners toward 돌리다 (to spin/turn) — but there is no rotating image here, so 돌리다 is wrong. Habitual collocations are 불을 켜다, 텔레비전·컴퓨터를 켜다, 에어컨·히터를 켜다, and 촛불을 켜다.

Writing 켜어요 for the polite form — the 여 already contains the ㅓ sound, so it contracts to 켜요, never 켜어요.
Using 돌리다 because English says 'turn on' — 돌리다 means to rotate, which has no place here; the correct verb is 켜다.

entries.nuance: 끄다 is the direct opposite of 켜다 and means to cut the power to a device or to extinguish a flame, so the same verb that turns off a lamp also 'puts out' a fire (불을 끄다 covers both). Register is neutral — 불 꺼 to a friend, 불을 꺼 주시겠어요? to a superior. A subtler point: to merely silence a phone, Koreans say 무음으로 하다 or 진동으로 하다, not 끄다, because 끄다 means the screen goes fully dark. Using 끄다 to mean 'put the phone on silent' — fully turning it off is 끄다, but silencing is 무음으로 하다 or 진동으로 하다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 끄다 becomes 끌 수 있어요 ("can") and 끌 거예요 ("will"). conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㅡ drop
conjugationTips.body: 끄다 loses its ㅡ vowel before 아/어, giving 꺼요 (the same drop turns 바쁘다 into 바빠요). The ㅡ never takes its own 어요, so don't add 어요 to the bare ㅡ.

structuredNuance.t: 끄다 is the direct opposite of 켜다 and means to cut the power to a device or to extinguish a flame, so the same verb that turns off a lamp also 'puts out' a fire (불을 끄다 covers both). Register is neutral — 불 꺼 to a friend, 불을 꺼 주시겠어요? to a superior. Natural collocations: 불·전등을 끄다, 핸드폰·컴퓨터를 끄다, 에어컨·히터를 끄다, 촛불을 끄다.

The conjugation is the key trap: 끄다 is a ㅡ-dropping (으 불규칙) verb, so when you add 아/어, the bare ㅡ vowel disappears and the ㅓ of the ending takes over — giving 꺼요 and past 껐어요, never 끄어요.
English speakers confuse 끄다 with 닫다 (to close): you 닫다 a door or app window, but you 끄다 the power; saying 컴퓨터를 닫다 wrongly means 'close the laptop lid', not 'shut it down'.

entries.nuance: 닦다 is a hands-on cleaning verb that means to rub a surface to make it clean, dry, or shiny, and crucially it is the normal Korean word for brushing teeth — 이를 닦다 — even though English uses 'brush', not 'wipe'. The sharp contrast learners need is 닦다 vs 씻다: 씻다 means to wash with running water (손을 씻다, 얼굴을 씻다), so you 씻다 your hands but 닦다 your teeth, a table, or a window; mixing them up (이를 씻다) sounds odd to natives. 닦다 also differs from 청소하다, which is 'to clean a whole room/space' as a chore — you 청소하다 the house but 닦다 one specific surface. It is a plain native verb, neutral in register. Note the spelling: the stem ends in the double consonant ㄲ, so the present is 닦아요 (the ㄲ stays) and the formal is 닦습니다. Pitfall: do not import English 'clean' as one verb — Korean splits it into 닦다 (wipe/scrub a surface), 씻다 (wash with water), and 청소하다 (tidy a space). Common collocations: 이를 닦다, 창문·바닥을 닦다, 눈물·땀을 닦다, 구두를 닦다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 닦다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 닦아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 이를 씻다 for 'brush teeth' — 씻다 is to wash with water; teeth are brushed/wiped, so the correct phrase is 이를 닦다.
Using 청소하다 for wiping one surface — 청소하다 means to clean a whole space; for a single window or table use 닦다.
Spelling the present as 닦어요 — after the stem 닦, the ㅏ ending is used, giving 닦아요, not 닦어요.

entries.explanation: 팔다 (palda) means "to sell". Start from the polite form 팔아요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 팔다. entries.nuance: 팔다 means to sell — to hand over goods in exchange for money — and it is the natural opposite of 사다 (to buy), so the two are learned as a pair. The conjugation is the headline feature: 팔다 is a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ 탈락) verb, meaning the stem-final ㄹ drops out before endings beginning with ㅂ, ㄴ, or ㅅ. That is why the formal present is 팝니다 (not 팔습니다) and the 'shall we' form is 팔까요? while ㄹ survives before vowels (팔아요, 팔았어요). The contrast to watch is 팔다 vs 판매하다: 판매하다 (販賣하다, 'sell-trade-do') is the Sino-Korean, formal/business equivalent you see on signs and in retail (온라인 판매), whereas 팔다 is the everyday spoken word. Register is neutral and native. A common English-speaker pitfall is the particle: the thing sold takes 을/를 (빵을 팔다), and you do not need a 'to'-phrase unless naming the buyer, who then takes 에게/한테. Do not confuse 팔다 with 팔리다, the passive 'to be sold / to sell well' (이 책이 잘 팔려요). Habitual collocations: 표·물건을 팔다, 싸게·비싸게 팔다, 중고로 팔다, 다 팔다(sell out).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 팔다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 팔아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 팔습니다 for the formal present — 팔다 is ㄹ-irregular, so ㄹ drops before -습니다 and the form becomes 팝니다.
Confusing 팔다 (to sell, active) with 팔리다 (to be sold / sell well) — say 책을 팔아요 to sell it, but 책이 잘 팔려요 for 'the book sells well'.
Marking the goods with the wrong particle — the item sold takes 을/를 (빵을 팔다); only the buyer takes 에게/한테.
notes: ㄹ irregular: memorize 팔아 and 팔아요 together.

entries.explanation: "to borrow" in Korean is 빌리다 (billida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 빌려요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 빌리다 for study notes. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

entries.nuance: 빌리다 means to borrow — to take something with the understanding that you will return it (or, for money, repay it) — so it always implies a temporary, give-it-back relationship. The single biggest English-speaker trap is direction: 빌리다 is only 'borrow' (the thing comes TO you), while lending (giving it OUT to someone) is the separate verb 빌려주다, literally '빌리다 + 주다 (give)'. So '친구한테 책을 빌렸어요' = I borrowed a book from a friend, but '친구한테 책을 빌려줬어요' = I lent a book to a friend — the same 한테 changes meaning entirely depending on the verb. English 'borrow' and 'lend' are two words too, but learners reflexively use 빌리다 for both. The conjugation is regular (stem 빌리- + 어 → 빌려, past 빌렸어요). Watch the particles: the borrowed item takes 을/를, and the source takes 에서 for places (도서관에서) or 한테(서)/에게(서) for people. Register is neutral and native. Note also 빌리다 ≠ 임대하다/대여하다, the formal Sino-Korean for commercial renting (차를 대여하다). Common collocations: 책·돈·차를 빌리다, 도서관에서 빌리다, 빌려주다, 빌려 가다/오다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 빌리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 빌려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 빌리다 to mean 'lend' — 빌리다 is only to borrow (it comes to you); to lend (give it out) you must say 빌려주다.
Marking the lender wrong — the person you borrow from takes 한테(서)/에게(서), as in 친구한테(서) 빌리다, not 친구를 빌리다.
Saying 빌려요 when you mean lending — to ask someone to lend you something, say 빌려주세요, not 빌리세요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 빌리다 becomes 빌릴 수 있어요 ("can") and 빌릴 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 빌리다 means to borrow — to take something with the understanding that you will return it (or, for money, repay it) — so it always implies a temporary, give-it-back relationship. Register is neutral and native. Common collocations: 책·돈·차를 빌리다, 도서관에서 빌리다, 빌려주다, 빌려 가다/오다.
Note also 빌리다 ≠ 임대하다/대여하다, the formal Sino-Korean for commercial renting (차를 대여하다).
The conjugation is regular (stem 빌리- + 어 → 빌려, past 빌렸어요). Watch the particles: the borrowed item takes 을/를, and the source takes 에서 for places (도서관에서) or 한테(서)/에게(서) for people.

The single biggest English-speaker trap is direction: 빌리다 is only 'borrow' (the thing comes TO you), while lending (giving it OUT to someone) is the separate verb 빌려주다, literally '빌리다 + 주다 (give)'. So '친구한테 책을 빌렸어요' = I borrowed a book from a friend, but '친구한테 책을 빌려줬어요' = I lent a book to a friend — the same 한테 changes meaning entirely depending on the verb. English 'borrow' and 'lend' are two words too, but learners reflexively use 빌리다 for both.

entries.shortExplanation: 잡다 means "to grab" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 잡다 (japda) = "to grab". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 잡아요 plus one useful sentence like 손을 잡다 ("to hold hands"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 잡고 싶어요 for what you want, 잡을 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 잡아요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 잡아요. Then practice 안 잡아요 vs 못 잡아요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.
survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.note: Physically grasp a hand; 손을 꼭 잡다 = hold tightly.

examples.en: Hold my hand.
examples.note: Simple physical action; fixed phrase 손을 잡다.

examples.en: It's hard to catch a taxi on the street.
examples.note: Everyday difficulty; -기가 어렵다 = it is hard to.

examples.en: We set the meeting date for next week.
examples.note: Real situation; figurative 날짜를 잡다 = fix a date.

entries.nuance: 잡다 starts from the physical idea of closing your hand firmly around something — to grab, grasp, or hold — and from there fans out into many idioms Koreans use daily. The contrast to learn is 잡다 vs 들다: 들다 is to LIFT something up off a surface (가방을 들다 = pick up a bag), whereas 잡다 is to take HOLD of it without necessarily lifting (손잡이를 잡다 = grip the strap). It also differs from 쥐다, which is to clench in a fist (주먹을 쥐다); 잡다 is the broad everyday grip. Beyond the body, 잡다 means to CATCH (택시를 잡다 hail a cab, 도둑을 잡다 catch a thief, 물고기를 잡다 catch fish) and to SET/FIX a plan (약속을 잡다, 날짜를 잡다). The English pitfall is assuming 'grab' is purely physical and reaching for 가지다/들다 in the idioms — but 'catch a taxi' and 'set a date' both require 잡다 in Korean. It is a plain native verb, regular (잡아요, 잡았어요, formal 잡습니다), neutral register. Note the passive 잡히다 (be caught): 택시가 안 잡혀요. Common collocations: 손·손잡이를 잡다, 택시를 잡다, 약속·날짜를 잡다, 기회를 잡다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 잡다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 잡아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 들다 (to lift) when you mean grip — 가방을 들다 is to lift a bag, but to hold a strap or hand you say 잡다 (손잡이를 잡다).
Translating 'catch a taxi' literally with a different verb — Korean fixes this as 택시를 잡다; saying 택시를 받다/가지다 is wrong.
Forgetting 잡다 for plans — 'set up an appointment' is 약속을 잡다, not 약속을 만들다, which sounds unnatural here.

lesson.canDo: Use 잡아요 in a real beginner sentence, then change it into want, can, cannot, and have-to forms without losing the basic meaning.
studyFlow: Say 잡아요 first. This is the safest spoken form for most beginner situations.
Add one useful frame: 손을 잡다. Read the Hangul first, then check the romanization.
Practice the contrast between 안 잡아요 and 못 잡아요.

lesson.teacherNote: Do not ask a beginner to memorize all 15 forms at once. Teach 잡아요 first, then add one communicative need: desire (잡고 싶어요), possibility (잡을 수 있어요), or limitation (못 잡아요).

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 잡아요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 잡다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 손을 잡다. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 안 잡아요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 못 잡아요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 잡아요 feels easy, practice 잡고 싶어요, 잡을 수 있어요, and 잡아야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

classroomScript: Teacher says: 잡아요. Learner repeats three times.
Teacher asks a yes/no question with 손을 잡다. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 안 잡아요, then 못 잡아요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

drills.note: Change the polite present into a simple negative.
Change the verb into a desire sentence.
Use this for inability or a real limitation.

selfCheck: Can you say “I grab” politely?
Can you say “I want to grab”?
Can you explain the difference between 안 잡아요 and 못 잡아요?

entries.shortExplanation: 보내다 means "to send" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 보내다 (bonaeda) means "to send". Start from the polite form 보내요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 보내다. A strong first sentence is 문자를 보내다 ("to send a text message"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 보내다 also becomes 보내고 싶어요 (want), 보낼 수 있어요 (can), and 못 보내요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 보내요. Then practice 안 보내요 vs 못 보내요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

examples.en: I send a text to my friend.
examples.note: Simple action; 에게 marks the recipient.

examples.en: Please send me the address via KakaoTalk.

examples.en: I spent the vacation at my grandmother's in the countryside.
examples.note: Real situation; the 'spend time' sense of 보내다.

entries.nuance: 보내다 means to send something or someone away from you toward another place or person — a message, a parcel, even a child to school — and it also carries the everyday idiom 시간을 보내다, 'to spend/pass time'. The sharp contrast is 보내다 vs 주다: 주다 (to give) is a face-to-face hand-over where giver and receiver are together, while 보내다 implies distance — the thing travels to reach the other person. So you 줘요 a gift you hand over now, but 보내요 a gift you mail; using 주다 for a text or parcel sounds like you are physically handing it across. The recipient particle is 에게/한테 (and honorific 께): 부모님께 보내다. For the 'spend time' sense, English speakers wrongly reach for 쓰다 (to use/spend money) — but time is 보내다, not 쓰다: 좋은 시간 보내세요! is the standard 'have a good time'. It is a plain native verb, regular (stem 보내- + 어 contracts to 보내, past 보냈어요), neutral register. The means/channel takes 으로 (이메일로, 택배로). Common collocations: 문자·이메일을 보내다, 소포·택배를 보내다, 시간·세월을 보내다, 사람을 보내다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 보내다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 보내요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 주다 for things sent over a distance — 주다 is a hand-to-hand give; for a text or parcel that travels, use 보내다 (소포를 보내다).
Saying 시간을 쓰다 for 'spend time' — 쓰다 is for spending money/using things; spending time is 시간을 보내다.
Marking the recipient with 을/를 — the person you send to takes 에게/한테/께 (친구에게 보내다), while the thing sent takes 을/를.

entries.shortExplanation: 들어가다 means "to go in" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to go in" in Korean is 들어가다 (deureogada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 들어가요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 들어가다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 방에 들어가다 ("to go into the room") — then reshape the same stem into 들어가고 싶어요 (desire), 들어갈 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 들어가요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Enter an enclosed space; the place entered takes 에 or 안에.

examples.en: Go inside.
examples.note: Simple direction; 안으로 = toward the inside.

examples.en: It's cold, so let's go inside quickly.
examples.note: Everyday suggestion; -읍시다 'let's'.

examples.ko: 저는 보통 열한 시쯤 집에 들어가요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun botong yeolhan sijjeum jibe deureogayo.
examples.en: I usually get home around eleven.
examples.note: Real routine; the 'get home' idiom of 들어가다.

entries.nuance: 들어가다 combines 들다 (to enter) + 가다 (to go), so it literally means 'enter-and-go' — to move into an enclosed space in a direction AWAY from where the speaker stands. The crucial paired contrast is 들어가다 vs 들어오다: 들어오다 ('enter-and-come') is the same entering motion but TOWARD the speaker. So if you are inside a room and want someone to come in, you say 들어오세요 (come in), but if you are heading into a room over there, you 들어가요. English 'go in / come in' splits the same way, yet learners default to 들어가다 for both and tell a guest at their own door 들어가세요, which oddly means 'go away in / head on home'. Beyond the literal, 들어가다 idiomatically means to get home (집에 들어가다), to enter a school or job (대학·회사에 들어가다), and even 'to fit' (이 옷이 가방에 안 들어가요). It is a plain native compound, regular, neutral register. The destination takes 에 or 안에 (방에/방 안에 들어가다). Common collocations: 방·집에 들어가다, 학교·회사에 들어가다, 안으로 들어가다, 잘 안 들어가다(won't fit).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 들어가다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 들어가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Telling a visitor at your door 들어가세요 — that means 'go on in (away from me) / head home'; to welcome them in toward you, say 들어오세요.
Using a 'to' particle like 으로 for the room — the space entered takes 에 (방에 들어가다); 으로 marks only a direction (안으로).
Forgetting the idioms — 'get home' is 집에 들어가다 and 'get into university' is 대학에 들어가다, not 집에 가다 / 대학에 가다 alone, which lose the 'enter' nuance.

entries.nuance: 나가다 is 나다/나- (to exit, come out) + 가다 (to go), literally 'exit-and-go' — to move from an inside space OUT, in a direction away from the speaker. entries.nuance: 올라가다 is 오르다/올라- (to rise, ascend) + 가다 (to go), literally 'rise-and-go' — to move UPWARD in a direction away from the speaker. entries.nuance: 내려가다 is 내리다/내려- (to descend, lower) + 가다 (to go), literally 'descend-and-go' — to move DOWNWARD in a direction away from the speaker. usagePhrases.note: Return to a place toward the speaker; 에 marks the place.

examples.en: I come back home.
examples.note: Simple action; 에 marks the destination of return.

examples.en: I came back from a business trip yesterday.
examples.note: Everyday past; 에서 marks where you returned from.

examples.en: I'll come straight back home when work is done.
examples.note: Real situation; -을게요 promise to the listener.

entries.nuance: 돌아오다 is 돌다/돌아- (to turn, circle back) + 오다 (to come), literally 'turn-and-come' — to come BACK to a place, in a direction TOWARD the speaker or the home base. Its mirror is 돌아가다 ('turn-and-go'), returning AWAY from the speaker, and this is the central trap: if you are at home and tell family you'll be back, you say 집에 돌아올게요 (I'll come back here), but speaking of returning to your faraway hometown you say 고향에 돌아가다 (go back there, away). English 'come back / go back' splits the same way, yet learners overuse 돌아오다. The destination of return takes 에 (집에 돌아오다), while the place you return FROM takes 에서 (여행에서 돌아오다). 돌아오다 also has the gentle idiom of things coming round again — 봄이 돌아오다 (spring returns), 기회가 돌아오다 (a chance comes back around). It is a plain native compound; the stem 돌아오- + 아 contracts to 돌아와, past 돌아왔어요, neutral register. Note 돌아오다 ≠ 다시 오다 exactly: 다시 오다 is just 'come again', while 돌아오다 implies returning to where you started. Common collocations: 집에 돌아오다, 여행·출장에서 돌아오다, 다시 돌아오다, 봄이 돌아오다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 돌아오다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 돌아와요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 돌아오다 for returning to a faraway place — if the return is away from the speaker (e.g., back to your hometown), it must be 돌아가다, not 돌아오다.
Marking the origin with 을/를 — the place you return FROM takes 에서 (여행에서 돌아오다); the place you return TO takes 에 (집에 돌아오다).
Writing 돌아오아요 — the stem ends in 오, so 오 + 아 contracts to 와, giving 돌아와요 (past 돌아왔어요), never 돌아오아요.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 돌아와요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 돌아오다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 집에 돌아오다. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 안 돌아와요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 못 돌아와요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 돌아와요 feels easy, practice 돌아오고 싶어요, 돌아올 수 있어요, and 돌아와야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

Learner changes the sentence to 안 돌아와요, then 못 돌아와요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 돌아오다 becomes 돌아올 수 있어요 ("can") and 돌아올 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

entries.shortExplanation: 생각하다 means "to think" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 생각하다 (saenggakada) means "to think". Start from the polite form 생각해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 생각하다. A strong first sentence is 저도 그렇게 생각해요. ("I think so too."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 생각하다 also becomes 생각하고 싶어요 (want), 생각할 수 있어요 (can), and 생각 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: 그렇게 (like that) + 생각하다 is the everyday way to agree with an opinion.

examples.en: What are you thinking about?
examples.note: Casual 해; drop the object and Koreans understand 'about what'.

examples.en: I think this movie is fun.
examples.note: To report an opinion, attach -다고 to the plain form (재미있다 → 재미있다고).

examples.en: When I think of my family, I get strength.
examples.note: 생각하면 (when/if I think) + emotion — thinking 'of' a person, not just an idea.

entries.nuance: 생각하다 (a native verb 생각 'thought' + 하다, not Sino-Korean) covers two jobs English splits apart: holding an opinion ('I think it's good') and mentally pondering or picturing ('I'm thinking about it / about you'). The near-synonym 믿다 means to believe with conviction, and 알다 means to know as fact; 생각하다 stays softer and more subjective, so use it for personal views. To report what you think, the partner pattern is -다고 생각하다 (좋다고 생각해요 = I think it's good); this is THE pitfall — English speakers say 생각해요 그것은 좋다 word-for-word, but Korean must embed the clause with -다고 before 생각하다. As a 하다 verb it splits in the negative (생각 안 해요, 생각 못 해요), and the polite stem is 생각해요, never 생각하어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 생각하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 생각해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying '생각해요 이거 좋다' to mean 'I think this is good.' Korean needs the quoted clause first: 이거 좋다고 생각해요. The -다고 ending is what carries 'that…'.
Using 알다 (know) for an opinion, as in '좋은 영화라고 알아요.' 알다 is for facts you know; for a view use 생각하다 → 좋은 영화라고 생각해요.
Forming the negative as '안 생각해요.' Because 생각하다 is noun+하다, the 안 goes inside: 생각 안 해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 느끼다 means "to feel" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to feel" in Korean is 느끼다 (neukkida). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 느껴요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 느끼다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 행복을 느껴요. ("I feel happiness.") — then reshape the same stem into 느끼고 싶어요 (desire), 느낄 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 느껴요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

usagePhrases.note: Emotion-noun + 을/를 + 느끼다; the feeling is the object, not an adjective.

examples.en: Are you cold? (lit. do you feel cold?)
examples.note: For bodily cold/hot Korean uses the adjective 춥다, NOT 느끼다 — a key boundary.

examples.en: I was moved by those words (lit. felt being moved).
examples.note: Past 느꼈어요; 감동을 느끼다 is a set collocation for being touched.

examples.en: I feel a lot of warmth/connection in Korea.
examples.note: 정 is an untranslatable Korean affection; 정을 느끼다 is how you say you sense it.

entries.nuance: 느끼다 (a native verb, no 한자) means to become aware of something through the senses or the heart — an emotion (행복을 느끼다), a physical sensation (통증을 느끼다 = feel pain), or an abstract impression (차이·분위기를 느끼다). The contrast with 생각하다 is sharp: 느끼다 is what your body and heart register, 생각하다 is what your mind concludes. The big English-speaker pitfall is over-using it for states: 'I feel cold/sick/tired' in natural Korean is usually the plain adjective — 추워요, 아파요, 피곤해요 — not 추움을 느껴요. Reserve 느끼다 for when you're consciously naming the sensation as an object (감동을 느끼다, 책임감을 느끼다). Conjugation: the stem 느끼 + -어 contracts to 느껴 (느껴요, 느꼈어요), never the spelled-out 느끼어요.

Use 느껴요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying '나는 추움을 느껴요' for 'I feel cold.' Natural Korean uses the adjective directly: 추워요. 느끼다 here sounds like a clinical translation.
Writing 느끼어요 / 느끼었어요. The vowel stem contracts: 느껴요 / 느꼈어요.
Using 느끼다 for 'I feel that we should go.' That sense of 'feel = opinion' is 생각하다 in Korean: 가야 한다고 생각해요, not 느껴요.

entries.nuance: 기억하다 comes from the 한자 記憶 (記 'record' + 憶 'recollect'), literally 'record-and-recollect,' so it spans both keeping something in memory and calling it back up. The crucial contrast is with 외우다: 외우다 means to memorize by effort (study a list, learn lines), while 기억하다 is simply having or retrieving a memory — you 외우다 a phone number so you can later 기억하다 it. Its opposite is 잊다 (forget). A very natural alternative for spontaneous recall is the idiom 기억이 나다 ('a memory arises'): Koreans say 기억이 안 나요 far more than 기억 못 해요 for 'I can't recall it right now.' Pitfall for English speakers: don't use 기억하다 where English 'memorize' is meant (cramming for a test is 외우다), and remember it's a 하다 verb, so the negative is 기억 안 해요 / 기억 못 해요, with 안 inside.

Use 기억해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 기억하다 for 'memorize this vocabulary.' Active memorization is 외우다: 이 단어를 외우세요, not 기억하세요.
Saying '기억 못 해요' for a name that just slipped your mind. Native speakers prefer the idiom 기억이 안 나요 ('it won't come to me') in that moment.
Confusing it with 생각나다. 생각나다 = something pops into mind / I just thought of it; 기억하다 = I hold it in memory. They overlap but aren't interchangeable in writing.

entries.nuance: 잊다 (native verb) means something disappears from your memory — a password, a promise, a person. Its dead-opposite is 기억하다. The number-one English-speaker trap is the look-alike 잃다 'to lose (a physical object)': you 잃다 your wallet but 잊다 your password. They even sound close (잊다 [읻따] vs 잃다 [일타]), yet swapping them changes the meaning entirely. Koreans very often attach the auxiliary -어버리다 to make 잊어버리다, which adds a nuance of 'it's completely, irretrievably gone,' frequently with a tinge of relief or regret (다 잊어버렸어요). Note the consonant stem conjugates plainly: 잊어요, 잊었어요, and the formal is 잊습니다. For 'don't forget,' the fixed warning form is 잊지 마세요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 잊다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 잊어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 잃다 (lose an object) for forgetting information: '비밀번호를 잃었어요' is wrong for a forgotten password — use 잊었어요. Save 잃다 for losing your phone or keys.
Saying 'I forgot my umbrella at the shop' as 우산을 잊었어요 only. If you physically left it behind, Koreans say 우산을 (가게에) 두고 왔어요 or add 잊어버렸어요 — 잊다 alone covers the mind, not the leaving.
Treating 잊어버리다 as a separate, harder word. It's just 잊다 + -어버리다; use it freely for 'totally forgot.'

entries.nuance: 결정하다 is built on the 한자 決定 (決 'resolve, cut through' + 定 'fix, settle'), so it literally means 'cut through and settle' — reaching a firm choice after deliberation. Three near-synonyms divide the space: 정하다 is the everyday, lighter 'set/decide' (그냥 정해요 = let's just settle it); 선택하다 (選擇) is 'select' from given options; 고르다 is the casual 'pick' (고르다 a fruit, a color). Use 결정하다 for consequential, considered decisions (a job, a move, a date) — for which thing to pick off a shelf, 고르다 or 선택하다 fits better. To decide to DO an action, the partner pattern is -기로 결정하다 (가기로 결정했어요); English speakers often forget the -기로 and say 결정했어요 가다. As a 하다 verb the negative splits: 결정 안 해요, 결정 못 해요. The heavier idiom 결정을 내리다 frames it as 'handing down' a decision.

Forgetting -기로 when deciding to do something: '결정했어요 한국에 가다' is ungrammatical. Embed it: 한국에 가기로 결정했어요.
Forming the negative as 안 결정해요. Inside the 하다 verb: 결정 안 해요 (or 아직 결정 못 했어요 for 'haven't decided yet').

examples.note: Casual; 밥 stands in for 'a meal' generally.

entries.nuance: 준비하다 comes from 한자 準備 (準 'standard, level' + 備 'provide, equip'), literally 'get equipped to standard' — to ready things or yourself beforehand. It naturally collocates with events and outcomes: 시험을 준비하다, 여행을 준비하다, 저녁을 준비하다, 마음의 준비. Compare 마련하다 ('arrange/procure' funds or a place — 집을 마련하다) and 챙기다 ('gather up, pack' your own belongings — 여권 챙겼어? = did you grab your passport?); 준비하다 is the broad 'prepare,' while 챙기다 zooms in on not forgetting items. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'prepare FOR the exam' tempts 시험에 준비하다, but Korean treats the exam as a direct object — 시험을 준비하다. Also don't reach for 만들다 'make' when you only mean getting ready. As a 하다 verb, negate inside (준비 안 해요), and its passive 준비되다 ('be ready') is everywhere: 준비됐어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 준비하다 as a complete polite sentence.

Wrong particle: '시험에 준비해요' for 'prepare for the exam.' Korean uses the object marker: 시험을 준비해요.
Using 만들다 (make) for getting ready: 'dinner is being prepared' is 저녁을 준비해요, not 저녁을 만들어요 unless you stress the cooking itself.
Saying '준비해요' to answer 'Are you ready?' The state 'I'm ready' is the passive 준비됐어요 / 준비됐어; 준비해요 means the act of preparing.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 준비하다 becomes 준비할 수 있어요 ("can") and 준비할 거예요 ("will"). entries.nuance: 사용하다 is the 한자 使用 (使 'employ, make use of' + 用 'use') + 하다 — to put a tool, service, or facility to use. Its everyday native twin is 쓰다, which means the exact same 'use' but sounds more casual and conversational (이거 써도 돼? vs the more formal 이거 사용해도 돼요?). A third relative, 이용하다 (利用), leans toward using a service or system (지하철을 이용하다 = use the subway, 시설을 이용하다 = use the facilities). Rule of thumb: speech and casual notes → 쓰다; signs, manuals, and polite requests → 사용하다; services and transport → 이용하다. The pitfall is over-formalizing chat: a friend asks to borrow your pen and 사용해도 돼? sounds stiff — say 써도 돼? Also beware that 쓰다 is a homonym meaning 'write' and 'wear (on the head/face),' so context disambiguates. As a 하다 verb, negate inside: 사용 안 해요, 사용 못 해요.

Using 입다 (wear clothes) for 'use': you don't 입다 an app or a card. Tools and services take 사용하다/쓰다.
Saying 안 사용해요. Inside the 하다 verb: 사용 안 해요. And for transport/services, 이용하다 often sounds more idiomatic (버스를 이용해요).

entries.nuance: 여행하다 is 한자 旅行 (旅 'journey, sojourn' + 行 'go') + 하다 — to travel, typically for leisure or sightseeing. Here's the natural-usage point most textbooks bury: Koreans far more often say 여행(을) 가다 'go on a trip' or 여행(을) 하다 with the noun split out than the bare verb 여행하다. A destination then takes 으로/로 ('toward') in 부산으로 여행 가다, or 을/를 when you 여행하다 a place you tour around (유럽을 여행하다). Compare 관광하다 (觀光, 'sightsee' — the tourist act of viewing attractions) and plain 가다 'go'; 여행하다 implies the whole trip, not a single going. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: (1) saying just 가다 ('I went to Busan' = 부산에 갔어요) when you mean a vacation — add 여행; (2) attaching 에 to 여행하다 (제주도에 여행해요) — for the verb 여행하다 the place is the object (제주도를 여행해요), while with 가다 you use 으로/에. As a 하다 verb, negate inside: 여행 안 해요.

Wrong particle with the verb: '제주도에 여행해요' is off — 여행하다 takes the place as object: 제주도를 여행해요. (With 가다 it's 제주도로/에 여행 가요.)

entries.nuance: 청소하다 is 한자 淸掃 (淸 'clear, pure' + 掃 'sweep') + 하다 — literally 'sweep clean,' i.e. tidy up a room or space. Using 청소하다 for wiping one surface or brushing teeth: the table is 닦아요, teeth are 이를 닦아요, not 청소해요. 청소하다 is for whole spaces.

entries.nuance: 노래하다 joins the native noun 노래 'a song' with 하다 to mean 'to sing,' but here's the catch that surprises learners: Koreans usually prefer 노래(를) 부르다 ('call out a song') for the act of singing, especially singing a particular song — 노래를 불러 주세요 sounds far more natural than 노래해 주세요. Bare 노래하다 leans poetic or general ('the birds are singing'), while 노래를 부르다 is the everyday choice at a 노래방 (karaoke room). For 'I'm a good singer,' the set phrase is 노래를 잘하다 (do songs well). The big pitfall: there is no verb 춤하다 — dancing does NOT take 하다 the way 노래(하다) or 운동(하다) do, because 추다 is its dedicated verb; saying 춤해요 is a classic beginner slip. Conjugation: the stem 추 + -어 contracts to 춰 (춰요, 춤췄어요, 춤출 거예요), and in the negative the noun separates so 안/못 land before the verb: 춤 안 춰요, 춤 못 춰요. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 대답하다 also becomes 대답하고 싶어요 (want), 대답할 수 있어요 (can), and 대답 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 대답해요. Then practice 대답 안 해요 vs 대답 못 해요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.
essential.example: Use the polite form with staff, teachers, strangers, and most adults.

conversation.meaning: Forms for time, desire, ability, and inability.
conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

survival.meaning: Forms for rules, permission, requests, and suggestions.

usagePhrases.note: The thing answered takes 에, not 을: 질문에 대답해요, never 질문을 대답해요

examples.en: I answered, "Yes."
examples.note: Simple: the bare reply 네 plus 대답하다 — this is how you report what someone said back

examples.en: I answered the teacher's question right away.
examples.note: Everyday: note 질문에 (에, the question you reply TO) and 바로 = right away

examples.en: In the interview, don't panic — answer calmly.
examples.note: Real situation: 차분하게 대답하다 is the set phrase for composed, measured replies

entries.nuance: 대답하다 is 對答(대답)하다, the hanja 對 'facing' + 答 'reply', so it literally means to 'reply facing' a question — you give a verbal response back to something someone asked. The key boundary is against 답하다 and 응답하다: 대답하다 is the everyday spoken word (a child 대답해요 when called), 답하다 is more clipped and written (편지에 답하다 'reply to a letter'), and 응답하다 is formal/technical (서버가 응답하다 'the server responds'). The single biggest English-speaker trap is the particle: in English you 'answer the question' (direct object), but in Korean the question is the target you reply toward, so it MUST be 질문에 대답하다 with 에 — 질문을 대답하다 sounds clearly wrong to natives. Also note this is a 하다 verb, so every form is regular: 대답 + 해요, and the negative cleanly splits the noun off as 대답 안 해요 / 대답 못 해요. Do not stretch it to phones (use 전화를 받다) or to 'responding to email,' which Koreans handle with 답장하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 대답하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 대답해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 질문을 대답해요 by copying English 'answer the question.' The question is what you reply toward, so use 에: 질문에 대답해요.
Using 대답하다 for answering the phone (전화를 대답해요). A ringing phone is 받다 — say 전화를 받아요.
Confusing 대답하다 (give an answer) with 질문하다 (pose a question) — they are opposite roles in a Q&A.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 질문에 대답하다. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 대답 안 해요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 대답 못 해요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 대답해요 feels easy, practice 대답하고 싶어요, 대답할 수 있어요, and 대답해야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

entries.explanation: "to ask a favor" in Korean is 부탁하다 (butakada). entries.nuance: 부탁하다 is 付託(부탁)하다, hanja 付 'hand over' + 託 'entrust', so the image is entrusting a task into someone's hands — you are asking them to do something FOR you, leaning on their goodwill. Contrast it sharply with 요청하다 and 시키다: 부탁하다 is personal and humble (you owe a thank-you), 요청하다 is formal/institutional (자료를 요청하다 'request documents'), and 시키다 is to MAKE/order someone do it from a position of authority — never use 시키다 with someone older or you sound bossy. The famous phrase 잘 부탁합니다 has no clean English equivalent; it pre-thanks someone for the cooperation you're about to receive and is near-mandatory in introductions. English speakers misfire two ways: they try to use 부탁하다 to order food or goods (that is 주문하다), and they attach the favor with the wrong particle — the person is 에게/한테, and the favor itself, if stated, is the object: 친구에게 부탁을 했어요. As a 하다 verb it is fully regular, negating as 부탁 안 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 부탁하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 부탁해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 부탁하다 to order at a restaurant or shop (커피를 부탁해요). Ordering goods is 주문하다 — say 커피를 주문할게요.
Marking the person with 을/를 (친구를 부탁해요 meaning 'ask the friend'). The person asked is 에게/한테: 친구에게 부탁해요. (친구를 부탁해요 instead means 'please look after my friend.')
Swapping in 시키다 to be polite. 시키다 means to order/make someone do it and sounds bossy to elders; humble requests use 부탁하다.

entries.explanation: 약속하다 (yaksokada) = "to promise". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 약속해요 plus one useful sentence like 친구와 약속하다 ("make plans with a friend"). usagePhrases.note: 와/하고 marks the other party; here 약속 means an appointment to meet

examples.en: I'll definitely come. I promise!
examples.note: Simple: standalone 약속해! as an emphatic vow between friends

examples.en: We promised to meet again next time.
examples.note: Everyday: -기로 약속하다 is the pattern for promising an action

examples.romanization: naeil du sie yaksogi isseoseo mot gayo.
examples.en: I have an appointment at two tomorrow, so I can't go.
examples.note: Real situation: here the noun 약속 means a scheduled meet-up, not a vow

entries.nuance: 약속하다 is 約束(약속)하다, hanja 約 'bind/pact' + 束 'tie up' — literally to 'bind and tie,' a vivid image of two people lashing their word together. The crucial thing for learners is that the noun 약속 carries TWO meanings that English splits: a 'promise' (a vow) and an 'appointment/plans' (a scheduled meeting). 친구와 약속이 있어요 means 'I have plans with a friend,' not 'I made a vow.' Contrast 약속하다 with 예약하다: 약속하다 is a person-to-person agreement to meet or to do something, while 예약하다 is to RESERVE a slot from a business (식당을 예약하다 'book a restaurant') — never say 식당을 약속하다. To promise an action, Koreans don't use the infinitive as in English ('promise to come'); they nominalize with -기로: 오기로 약속했어요. The verb honoring it is 지키다 (지키다, 'guard'), and breaking it is 어기다, so memorize 약속을 지키다/어기다 as a fixed pair. It is a regular 하다 verb (약속 + 해요), negating as 약속 안 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 약속하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 약속해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 약속하다 to reserve a table or hotel (식당을 약속해요). Booking a business slot is 예약하다 — say 식당을 예약했어요.
Copying English 'promise to come' as 오는 것을 약속해요. Korean nominalizes the action with -기로: 오기로 약속했어요.
Saying 약속을 지지 않다 or inventing a verb for 'break a promise.' Keep means 지키다, break means 어기다: 약속을 어겼어요.

conversation.example: These answer questions like what happened, what you will do, and what you can do.

usagePhrases.note: The person introduced is 을/를; the recipient is 에게/한테

examples.en: This is my friend. Let me introduce you.
examples.note: Simple: 소개할게요 (I'll introduce) used at the moment of presenting someone

examples.en: I introduced my boyfriend to my parents.
examples.note: Everyday: 을/를 for the person shown, 께 (honorific) for the parents who receive

examples.ko: 좋은 책 좀 소개해 주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: joeun chaek jom sogaehae jusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: Could you recommend a good book?
examples.note: Real situation: 소개하다 stretched to 'recommend' — common for books, shops, apps

entries.nuance: 소개하다 is 紹介(소개)하다, hanja 紹 'connect/join' + 介 'go between', so the core sense is acting as a go-between who connects two parties — you present a person to someone else, or by extension present a place/product to an audience (recommend it). Watch the dual particle frame: the person or thing introduced takes 을/를, and the recipient takes 에게/한테 (honorific 께): 친구를 선생님께 소개했어요. Contrast 소개하다 with 추천하다: when recommending, 소개하다 means 'let me present/show you this option' (neutral introduction), while 추천하다 carries a stronger personal endorsement ('I vouch for it'). For introducing yourself, do not say 저를 소개해요 — Korean uses the set noun 자기소개를 하다. A culturally loaded offshoot is 소개팅 (소개 + meeting), being set up on a blind date by a mutual friend. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it onto 'meet' or 'greet': you 소개하다 (present) someone, but you 만나다 (meet) them and 인사하다 (greet) them — three different verbs. Regular 하다 verb: 소개 + 해요, negative 소개 안 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 소개하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 소개해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 저를 소개할게요 for 'I'll introduce myself.' Use the fixed noun: 자기소개를 할게요 or 제 소개를 할게요.
Dropping the recipient particle or using 을/를 on both. The recipient is 에게/한테/께: 친구를 부모님께 소개했어요.
Confusing 소개하다 (present someone) with 만나다 (meet) or 인사하다 (greet) — introducing is not the same as meeting or saying hello.

lesson.canDo: Use 소개해요 in a real beginner sentence, then change it into want, can, cannot, and have-to forms without losing the basic meaning.
studyFlow: Say 소개해요 first. This is the safest spoken form for most beginner situations.
Add one useful frame: A를 B에게 소개하다. Read the Hangul first, then check the romanization.
Practice the contrast between 소개 안 해요 and 소개 못 해요.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 소개해요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 소개하다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like A를 B에게 소개하다. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 소개 안 해요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 소개 못 해요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 소개해요 feels easy, practice 소개하고 싶어요, 소개할 수 있어요, and 소개해야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

classroomScript: Teacher says: 소개해요. Learner repeats three times.
Teacher asks a yes/no question with A를 B에게 소개하다. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 소개 안 해요, then 소개 못 해요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 소개하다 becomes 소개할 수 있어요 ("can") and 소개할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

소개하다 is 紹介(소개)하다, hanja 紹 'connect/join' + 介 'go between'.

entries.shortExplanation: 설명하다 means "to explain" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to explain" in Korean is 설명하다 (seolmyeonghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 설명해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 설명하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 이유를 설명하다 ("explain the reason") — then reshape the same stem into 설명하고 싶어요 (desire), 설명할 수 있어요 (ability), and 설명 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 설명해요. Then practice 설명 안 해요 vs 설명 못 해요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

entries.nuance: 설명하다 is 說明(설명)하다, hanja 說 'speak' + 明 'bright/clear', so it literally means to 'speak something into clarity' — you talk about a thing so the listener understands it. The dividing line against 설득하다 and 말하다 matters: 설명하다 is to make something UNDERSTOOD (neutral, informational), 설득하다 is to PERSUADE (change someone's mind), and 말하다 is just to 'say/tell' without the goal of clarifying. So '설명해 주세요' = 'help me understand,' which is far more specific than '말해 주세요' = 'just tell me.' The thing explained takes 을/를 (이유를 설명하다), and for a broad topic Koreans add -에 대해(서): 그 사건에 대해 설명했어요. Natural adverbs are 자세히 (in detail), 쉽게 (simply), 간단히 (briefly). The English-speaker pitfall is the construction 'explain me' / 'explain to me' — Korean attaches the listener with 에게/한테, not the object slot, and very often just uses 설명해 주다 (explain as a favor) to imply the listener. It is a regular 하다 verb: 설명 + 해요, negating as 설명 안 해요 / 설명 못 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 설명하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 설명해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Mapping 'explain me' onto 저를 설명해요 (which means 'describe me as a person'). To explain TO me, use 저에게 설명해 주세요 or just 설명해 주세요.
Using 말하다 when you mean make-it-clear. 말하다 is merely 'say'; to clarify so someone understands, use 설명하다.
Confusing 설명하다 (explain) with 설득하다 (persuade) — explaining shares information; persuading changes a decision.

entries.explanation: 이야기하다 (iyagihada) = "to talk". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 이야기해요 plus one useful sentence like 친구와 이야기하다 ("talk with a friend"). entries.nuance: 이야기하다 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) built from the noun 이야기 'a story/talk' + 하다, so at heart it means to exchange talk — to chat, converse, or tell about something. The contrast with 말하다 and 대화하다 is the thing to internalize: 말하다 is one-directional 'to say/tell' (a single utterance), 이야기하다 is the relaxed back-and-forth of chatting or recounting (often longer, with a partner marked by 와/하고), and 대화하다 is the more formal, neutral 'to converse/hold a dialogue.' So 친구와 이야기해요 feels friendly and chatty, while 대화해요 feels almost clinical. Massively important for sounding natural: in actual speech 이야기 contracts to 얘기 nearly every time — 얘기 좀 하자, 얘기해 줘. For talking ABOUT a topic, add -에 대해(서): 영화에 대해 이야기했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like one-shot 'tell me' — for a quick fact use 말해 줘, but for 'let's discuss / tell me the whole thing' use 이야기해 줘. It is a regular 하다 verb, negating as 이야기 안 해요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 이야기하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 이야기해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Never contracting it. Real spoken Korean uses 얘기 (얘기하다), so 이야기 in casual speech can sound stiff — say 얘기해.
Using 이야기하다 for a one-line factual statement. A single 'tell me X' is 말하다; 이야기하다 implies a fuller chat or account.
Marking the partner with 을/를 (친구를 이야기해요). The conversation partner is 와/하고: 친구하고 이야기해요.

entries.shortExplanation: 인사하다 means "to greet" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 인사하다 (insahada) means "to greet". Start from the polite form 인사해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 인사하다. A strong first sentence is 선생님께 인사하다 ("greet/bow to the teacher"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 인사하다 also becomes 인사하고 싶어요 (want), 인사할 수 있어요 (can), and 인사 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 인사하다 is 人事(인사)하다, hanja 人 'person' + 事 'affair' — literally 'the affairs between people,' which tells you it is broader than English 'greet': it covers saying hello, bowing, saying goodbye, and even paying one's formal respects. Crucial cultural point baked into the verb: Korean greeting is physical and hierarchical — a younger person bows the head (고개를 숙이다) to an elder, and failing to 인사하다 first when meeting someone senior reads as rude. Contrast 인사하다 with 소개하다: greeting is the bow/hello you perform yourself, whereas introducing is presenting a third party. Note that the noun 인사 also means 'personnel/HR affairs' (인사부 = HR department) — same hanja, different sphere. The English-speaker pitfall is leaving out the bow-culture and treating it as a casual 'hi,' and also confusing it with the literal greeting words: 안녕하세요 is WHAT you say, 인사하다 is the act of greeting. entries.nuance: 사과하다 is 謝過(사과)하다, hanja 謝 'express thanks/apology' + 過 'fault/error', so it literally means to 'acknowledge one's fault' — you take responsibility for a mistake to the person you wronged, who is marked with 에게/한테 or honorific 께. The boundary against 미안하다 and 변명하다 is essential: 미안하다 is the adjective/feeling 'to be sorry' (an emotional state — 미안해요), while 사과하다 is the ACT of formally apologizing (you can 사과하다 even publicly or in writing); and 변명하다 is the opposite move, to 'make excuses.' So you might 사과하다 instead of merely feeling 미안하다. The cause of the apology attaches with -아서: 늦어서 사과했어요. A notorious trap is the homograph: 사과 also means 'apple' (native-Korean noun), so context disambiguates 사과를 했어요 'apologized' from 사과를 먹었어요 'ate an apple' — they share spelling but are unrelated words. English speakers also wrongly say '~에 대해 미안해요' as if 'sorry' were a verb taking objects; to apologize FOR something, use 사과하다 with -아서 or -에 대해. Regular 하다 verb: 사과 + 해요, negative 사과 안 해요.

Marking the wronged person with 을/를 (친구를 사과해요). Use 에게/한테/께: 친구에게 사과해요.
Confusing the homograph 사과 (apology) with 사과 (apple), or mixing up 사과하다 (apologize) with 변명하다 (make excuses) — opposite intentions.

entries.nuance: 초대하다 is 招待(초대)하다, hanja 招 'beckon/summon' + 待 'receive/treat', so the image is beckoning someone over AND hosting them — inviting a guest to an event or your home with the intent to welcome and entertain them. The guest takes 을/를 and the event/place takes 에: 친구를 파티에 초대했어요. The sharp contrast is with 부르다: 초대하다 is a warm, planned invitation to a social occasion (you'll host them), whereas 부르다 is simply to 'call' someone over (call their name, summon them) with no hosting connotation — so 친구를 불렀어요 just means 'I called my friend over,' not 'I invited them to an event.' Using 부르다 where you mean a gracious invite sounds abrupt. Note the related noun 초대장 (invitation card) and the host's courtesy verb 모시다 for elevating an honored guest. The English-speaker pitfall is using 초대하다 for 'invite' in the loose sense of 'ask someone to come along casually' (that's closer to 같이 가자/오라고 하다), and forgetting that the EVENT is 에 while the guest is 을/를. Regular 하다 verb: 초대 + 해요, negative 초대 안 해요.

Putting the event in the object slot (파티를 초대해요). The guest is 을/를 and the event is 에: 친구를 파티에 초대해요.

entries.explanation: 칭찬하다 (chingchanhada) means "to praise". Start from the polite form 칭찬해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 칭찬하다. A strong first sentence is 아이를 칭찬하다 ("praise a child"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 칭찬하다 also becomes 칭찬하고 싶어요 (want), 칭찬할 수 있어요 (can), and 칭찬 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

usagePhrases.note: The person praised takes 을/를: 아이를 칭찬했어요

examples.en: Well done! I praised them, saying they did great.
examples.note: Simple: -다고 reports the praising words

examples.en: The teacher praised my presentation.
examples.note: Everyday: 을/를 for what's praised, -아 주시다 marks it as kindness from a senior

examples.note: Real situation: passive 칭찬을 받다 + -ㄹ수록 'the more...'

entries.nuance: 칭찬하다 is 稱讚(칭찬)하다, hanja 稱 'state/declare' + 讚 'extol', so it means to openly declare someone's merit — to praise or commend a person for good work, effort, or behavior, with the person taking 을/를. The vital contrast is against 자랑하다: 칭찬하다 is praising SOMEONE ELSE for THEIR good qualities (외부를 향한 칭찬), whereas 자랑하다 is boasting about YOURSELF or your own things (자기 자랑). English 'praise' can blur into 'show off,' but in Korean these are firmly separate verbs — mixing them up reverses who's being celebrated. A second near-synonym is 칭찬 vs 격려하다 (encourage): 칭찬하다 rewards results already achieved, 격려하다 cheers someone on toward something. The passive 'to be praised' is 칭찬을 받다, not a verb ending. entries.nuance: 거짓말하다 is a native Korean compound: 거짓 'false' + 말 'speech/words' = 'false words,' plus 하다 — so it transparently means 'to do false-speech,' i.e. to tell a lie. It is built on the noun 거짓말, which is why the negative and the 못 form split the noun cleanly off the verb: 거짓말 안 해요, 거짓말 못 해요. The person lied to takes 에게/한테. Contrast it with 속이다 and 농담하다: 거짓말하다 is the act of stating an untruth (the words themselves are false), 속이다 is 'to deceive/trick' (to fool someone, broader than just words — you can 속이다 with actions), and 농담하다 is 'to joke,' which is harmless and not meant to be believed. Calling a joke a 거짓말 sounds like an accusation. A natural intensifier is 새빨간 거짓말 ('a bright-red lie' = a barefaced lie). The English-speaker pitfall is the reflex 'lie about something' — Korean doesn't take 'about' here; you simply 거짓말하다 and add context separately, or use 거짓말로 ... 하다. Also note English 'lie' looks intransitive but Korean often makes the lie an explicit object: 거짓말을 하다. It is a regular 하다 verb.
