entries.nuance: 질문하다 is 質問(질문)하다, hanja 質 'inquire into substance' + 問 'ask', so it means to pose a question in order to obtain information — and the person asked takes 에게/한테 or honorific 께: 선생님께 질문했어요. The boundary against 묻다 is the one to nail: 질문하다 and 묻다 both mean 'ask,' but 질문하다 is the heavier Sino-Korean word for a deliberate, often public question (in class, a meeting, a Q&A), while 묻다 is the plain everyday verb for asking a quick thing ('let me ask you something' = 뭐 좀 물어볼게요). entries.nuance: 돌아가다 is literally 돌아(turn around) + 가다(go), so it paints you turning back and heading AWAY from the listener toward your origin — home, your country, a former state. It also means revert: 원래대로 돌아가다 (go back to normal), even 돌아가시다 is the gentle euphemism for passing away, so tread carefully. As a 가다 compound it conjugates regularly and the 가 + 아 contracts to 가요. The English-speaker trap: do not force 에서 on the destination — you return TO a place with 에/로, never 집에서 돌아가요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 돌아가다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 돌아가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 집에 돌아와요 when you're talking to someone back home about flying home — from your current spot the motion goes away, so it must be 돌아가요; 돌아오다 is only for motion toward where you are now.
Writing 돌아가아요 by adding the full 아요 ending — the 가 stem already ends in ㅏ, so it contracts to 돌아가요.
Using 에서 for the place you return to (집에서 돌아가요). Return destinations take 에 or 로; 에서 would mean you start FROM the house.

entries.nuance: 출발하다 is Sino-Korean 出發(출발: 出 go out + 發 set off/shoot) plus 하다, the crisp word for a journey or vehicle SETTING OFF from a starting line. commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 출발하다 as a complete polite sentence.

Saying 출발하지 않아요 / 출발해 안 해요 awkwardly — the clean short negative of a 하다 verb is 출발 안 해요, splitting the noun from 해요.
Treating it as emotional 'leave' for people (친구를 출발했어요). To leave a person or place behind you need 떠나다; 출발하다 is for setting off on a route or schedule.

entries.nuance: 도착하다 is Sino-Korean 到着(도착: 到 reach + 着 attach/touch down) plus 하다 — the moment of REACHING and touching a destination. Its mirror is 출발하다(depart), and the key is the particle: you arrive AT a place with 에 (호텔에 도착해요), whereas 출발하다 leaves FROM a place with 에서. Don't confuse it with 들어가다/들어오다(enter): 도착하다 is reaching the destination's threshold, not stepping inside a building. As a 하다 verb, 하 + 아 fuses to 해 (도착해요) and the short negative and inability split the noun off: 도착 안 해요, 도착 못 해요. The classic English-speaker error is copying 'arrive at' as 에서 — 'at' here is the static endpoint 에, so 공항에 도착해요, and 공항에서 도착해요 is wrong.

Mixing it up with 들어가다 (enter) — 도착하다 means you've reached the place, not that you've walked inside. To go in through the door, use 들어가다.
Forming inability as 못 도착해요 in this set — the natural split-negative for the 하다 verb is 도착 못 해요, keeping 못 right before 해요.

entries.nuance: 떠나다 means to LEAVE a place, person, or situation behind, and unlike neutral 출발하다(depart) it carries feeling — separation, finality, the pull of moving on, which is why songs and goodbyes use it (곁을 떠나다 leave someone's side). The dividing line with 출발하다: a train 출발해요 (sets off on schedule) but a person 고향을 떠나요 (leaves home, emotionally). The thing left behind takes the object particle 을/를, not 에서 — this is the big surprise for English speakers, since you'd expect 'leave from'. So it's 한국을 떠나요 (I leave Korea), and 여행을 떠나다 idiomatically means to embark on a trip. It's a native verb; 나 + 아 contracts to 나, giving 떠나요 and past 떠났어요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 떠나다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 떠나요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

Swapping in 출발하다 for an emotional or final leaving (가족을 출발했어요). Leaving family/home/a person behind needs 떠나다; 출발하다 is only setting off on a route.
Writing 떠나아요 with the full 아요 ending — the stem 떠나 already ends in ㅏ, so it stays 떠나요 and the past is 떠났어요.

entries.nuance: 멈추다 means coming to a HALT — ceasing motion that was underway — and it covers a person freezing, a car braking, the rain letting up, even a clock stopping (시계가 멈췄어요). entries.nuance: 움직이다 is the broad word for MOVING or shifting position, and its range is wide: your own body (몸을 움직이다), a crowd inching forward, an object that budges, even an abstract heart being moved (마음이 움직이다 = to be swayed). Contrast it with 이사하다(move house), the Sino-Korean 移徙 word reserved for relocating your home — English 'move' covers both, but Korean splits them, so 'I'm moving next month' is 이사해요, never 움직여요. It also differs from 옮기다(transfer/relocate a thing), which is transitive and deliberate (책상을 옮기다, shift the desk). 움직이다 itself works both intransitively (안 움직여요, it won't move) and transitively (몸을 움직여요). It's a regular 이-stem verb: 이 + 어 fuses to 여, giving 움직여요 and 움직였어요. Pitfall: don't use it for changing residence.

entries.nuance: 건너다 means crossing FROM one side TO the other — a street, a river, a bridge, the sea — picturing the whole traverse from edge to edge. The road or water you cross takes the object particle 을/를 (길을 건너요), which surprises English speakers who expect 'across' to be adverbial. The sharp contrast is with 넘다(go over): 넘다 stresses surmounting a high obstacle or boundary, going OVER a mountain pass, a wall, even a limit (산을 넘다, 한계를 넘다), whereas 건너다 is the flat side-to-side passage of a road or river. There's also the compound 건너가다/건너오다 when you want to add the go/come direction. It's a native verb whose stem 건너 ends in ㅓ, so 너 + 어 contracts to 너, giving 건너요 and past 건넜어요. Pitfall: don't use 넘다 for an ordinary crosswalk.

Using 넘다 for crossing a flat street (길을 넘어요). 넘다 means going over a height or limit; an ordinary road or river is 건너다.
Writing 건너어요 with the full ending — the ㅓ-final stem contracts, so the present is 건너요 and the past is 건넜어요.

survival.example: Use request forms only when it is natural to ask someone else to do that action.

usagePhrases.en: I pass in front of the bank.
usagePhrases.note: 앞을 지나가다 = pass in front of, with 을

examples.en: The bus just went by.
examples.note: 지나가 + 았 → 지나갔어요; 가 stem contracts.

examples.en: Excuse me, please let me through.
examples.note: 지나가 주세요 politely asks for room to pass.

examples.en: Go past this alley and you'll hit the market.
examples.note: 면 = if/when; handy for directions.

entries.nuance: 지나가다 is 지나(pass) + 가다(go) — moving PAST a point and continuing on, AWAY from the listener, without stopping; a bus goes by, you slip past someone, a season passes (여름이 지나가다). Distinguish it from plain 지나다, which leans toward time ELAPSING (3년이 지났어요, three years passed) and is less about physical motion through space. Its pair 지나오다 adds the come-this-way direction. The place you pass takes 을/를, often with 앞을 (은행 앞을 지나가요, pass in front of the bank). Figuratively 지나가는 말 means an offhand remark made in passing. As a 가다 compound it's regular and 가 + 았 contracts to 갔, giving past 지나갔어요. Pitfall: for 'three years have passed' don't say 지나가다; that physical-motion verb sounds odd for elapsed time — use 지나다 (지났어요).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 지나가다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 지나가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 지나가다 for elapsed time (3년이 지나갔어요 to mean 'three years passed'). For time passing, the natural verb is 지나다: 3년이 지났어요.
Marking the place passed with 에서 (가게에서 지나가요). The spot you go past takes 을/를, frequently 앞을: 가게 앞을 지나가요.
Confusing direction with 지나오다 — 지나가다 moves past and away from you; if something passed and is now coming toward you, use 지나오다.

lesson.canDo: Use 지나가요 in a real beginner sentence, then change it into want, can, cannot, and have-to forms without losing the basic meaning.
studyFlow: Say 지나가요 first. This is the safest spoken form for most beginner situations.
Add one useful frame: 은행 앞을 지나가요. Read the Hangul first, then check the romanization.
Practice the contrast between 안 지나가요 and 못 지나가요.

lesson.teacherNote: Do not ask a beginner to memorize all 15 forms at once. Teach 지나가요 first, then add one communicative need: desire (지나가고 싶어요), possibility (지나갈 수 있어요), or limitation (못 지나가요).
lesson.pronunciationTip: 지나가다 is written jinaga-da. In real sentences, compare the audio with the romanization because Korean sound changes can cross syllable blocks.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 지나가요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 지나가다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 은행 앞을 지나가요. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 안 지나가요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 못 지나가요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 지나가요 feels easy, practice 지나가고 싶어요, 지나갈 수 있어요, and 지나가야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

classroomScript: Teacher says: 지나가요. Learner repeats three times.
Teacher asks a yes/no question with 은행 앞을 지나가요. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 안 지나가요, then 못 지나가요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 지나가다 becomes 지나갈 수 있어요 ("can") and 지나갈 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 지나가다 is 지나(pass) + 가다(go) — moving PAST a point and continuing on, AWAY from the listener, without stopping; a bus goes by, you slip past someone, a season passes (여름이 지나가다). The place you pass takes 을/를, often with 앞을 (은행 앞을 지나가요, pass in front of the bank). Figuratively 지나가는 말 means an offhand remark made in passing.
Distinguish it from plain 지나다, which leans toward time ELAPSING (3년이 지났어요, three years passed) and is less about physical motion through space. Its pair 지나오다 adds the come-this-way direction.
As a 가다 compound it's regular and 가 + 았 contracts to 갔, giving past 지나갔어요.
For 'three years have passed' don't say 지나가다; that physical-motion verb sounds odd for elapsed time — use 지나다 (지났어요).

entries.shortExplanation: 따라가다 means "to follow" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 따라가다 (ttaraga-da) = "to follow". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 따라가요 plus one useful sentence like 가이드를 따라가요 ("I follow the guide."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 따라가고 싶어요 for what you want, 따라갈 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 따라가요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 따라가요. Then practice 안 따라가요 vs 못 따라가요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

examples.en: My leg hurts, so I can't keep up.
examples.note: 못 따라가다 = can't keep pace, literal or figurative.

entries.nuance: 따라가다 is 따라(along/following) + 가다(go) — going ALONG behind someone or something, moving in the same direction AWAY from the listener; you trail a guide, tag after a friend, or figuratively 'keep up' (못 따라가요, can't keep pace). Its essential pair is 따라오다(come along/follow toward me): a leader walking ahead says 따라오세요 (follow me, toward where I'm going), but you describing yourself trailing them say 따라가요. The person or thing followed takes 을/를, not 에게 — a frequent English-speaker slip, since 'follow' feels like motion 'to' someone. Note 따라가다 is a 가다 compound, so despite the 라 it is NOT a 르-irregular; it conjugates regularly and 가 + 아 contracts to 가, giving 따라가요. It can also mean to copy/imitate (잘 따라 하다). Pitfall: don't mark the followed person with 에게.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 따라가다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 따라가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the person followed with 에게/한테 (친구에게 따라가요). The one you follow is a direct object: 친구를 따라가요.
Saying 따라오세요 when you mean to tell someone you'll go after them — from your viewpoint you move away, so it's 제가 따라갈게요; 따라오다 is for motion toward the speaker.
Over-applying 르 irregular logic to the 라 (expecting 따랄라 forms). 따라가다 is a compound of 가다 and conjugates regularly: 따라가요, 따라갔어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 데려가다 means "to take a person" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 데려가다 (deryeoga-da) means "to take a person". Start from the polite form 데려가요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 데려가다. A strong first sentence is 아이를 데려가요 ("I take the child along."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 데려가다 also becomes 데려가고 싶어요 (want), 데려갈 수 있어요 (can), and 못 데려가요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then bend it.

examples.ko: 저도 그 식당에 좀 데려가 주세요.
examples.romanization: jeodo geu sikdange jom deryeoga juseyo.
examples.en: Please take me to that restaurant too.
examples.note: 데려가 주세요 asks to be brought along; 에 marks where.

examples.en: I take my child to school.
examples.note: Person 아이 takes 를, destination 학교 takes 에.

examples.en: I want to take my parents to the sea this weekend.
examples.note: 데려가다 for people; 가져가다 would be wrong here.

entries.nuance: 데려가다 is 데리다(accompany) + 가다(go) — taking a PERSON or animal along with you, moving AWAY from the listener to another place; you take a child to school, a friend to a restaurant, a dog to the vet. The crucial split is animacy: 데려가다 is ONLY for living beings, while 가져가다 is for objects — English 'take' blurs them, so 'take the kids' is 아이들을 데려가요 but 'take the bags' is 가방을 가져가요. Its directional pair is 데려오다(bring a person toward me). For someone older or deserving respect, the politer 모시고 가다 is used instead of 데려가다 (할머니를 모시고 가요). The person takes 을/를 and the destination 에. As a 가다 compound it conjugates regularly (데려가요, 데려갔어요). Related 데려다주다 means to escort/drop someone off. Pitfall: never use 데려가다 for things.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 데려가다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 데려가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 데려가다 for objects (우산을 데려가요). Living beings use 데려가다; for an umbrella or any thing use 가져가다.
Saying 데려가다 about an elder you respect (할아버지를 데려갔어요) can sound too plain or even rude. For seniors, use the honorific 모시고 가다: 할아버지를 모시고 갔어요.
Picking 데려오다 when the motion is away from you — taking someone elsewhere from here is 데려가요; 데려오다 is bringing a person toward your location.

entries.shortExplanation: 가져가다 means "to take a thing" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to take a thing" in Korean is 가져가다 (gajyeoga-da). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 가져가요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 가져가다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 우산을 가져가요 ("I take an umbrella.") — then reshape the same stem into 가져가고 싶어요 (desire), 가져갈 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 가져가요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 가져가요. Then practice 안 가져가요 vs 못 가져가요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.

entries.nuance: 가져가다 is 가지다(have/hold) + 가다(go) — taking an OBJECT away with you to another place, moving AWAY from the listener; you take an umbrella, a passport, leftovers. The animacy split is the heart of it: 가져가다 is strictly for things, while 데려가다 is for people and animals — since English 'take' covers both, learners wrongly say 가져가다 about a child. Its directional pair is 가져오다(bring a thing toward me): leaving the house you 우산을 가져가요, but asking a waiter you say 메뉴판 가져와 주세요. The object takes 을/를 and the destination 에. As a 가다 compound it's regular: 가 + 아 contracts, giving 가져가요 and 가져갔어요. Casual speech often shortens 가지고 to 갖고, and 가지고 가다 = 가져가다. Pitfall: don't use it for people, and don't flip the direction with 가져오다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 가져가다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 가져가요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 가져가다 for a person or pet (동생을 가져가요). Things use 가져가다; people and animals use 데려가다: 동생을 데려가요.
Choosing 가져오다 when the motion is away from you — carrying something off from here is 가져가요; 가져오다 brings a thing toward where you are.
Writing it long as 가지어 가요 — the contracted compound is 가져가다 (가져가요), and the casual variant is 갖고 가요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 가져가다 becomes 가져갈 수 있어요 ("can") and 가져갈 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: 가져가다 is 가지다(have/hold) + 가다(go) — taking an OBJECT away with you to another place, moving AWAY from the listener; you take an umbrella, a passport, leftovers. The object takes 을/를 and the destination 에.

The animacy split is the heart of it: 가져가다 is strictly for things, while 데려가다 is for people and animals. Its directional pair is 가져오다(bring a thing toward me): leaving the house you 우산을 가져가요, but asking a waiter you say 메뉴판 가져와 주세요.
As a 가다 compound it's regular: 가 + 아 contracts, giving 가져가요 and 가져갔어요. Casual speech often shortens 가지고 to 갖고, and 가지고 가다 = 가져가다.
Since English 'take' covers both, learners wrongly say 가져가다 about a child. Don't use it for people, and don't flip the direction with 가져오다.

entries.shortExplanation: 가져오다 means "to bring a thing" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 가져오다 (gajyeoo-da) = "to bring a thing". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 가져와요 plus one useful sentence like 물 좀 가져와요 ("Bring some water."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 가져오고 싶어요 for what you want, 가져올 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 가져와요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help.

entries.nuance: 가져오다 is 가지다(have/hold) + 오다(come) — bringing an OBJECT TOWARD the speaker's location, the mirror image of 가져가다(take away): here it points HERE, there it points away, exactly like English bring vs take keyed to where 'here' is. So in a restaurant you ask 메뉴판 가져와 주세요 (bring it to me), but leaving home you say 우산을 가져가요 (take it with me, away). The animacy rule still holds: things use 가져오다, whereas bringing a PERSON toward you is 데려오다 (아이를 데려와요). Figuratively it means to bring about (변화를 가져오다, bring about change). The object takes 을/를, often dropped in casual speech. As an 오다 compound it's regular and 오 + 아 fuses to 와, giving 가져와요 and 가져왔어요. Pitfall: don't aim the direction wrong with 가져가다, and don't use it for people.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 가져오다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 가져와요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 가져가다 when something should come toward you — asking a waiter for water is 물 가져와 주세요 (bring it here); 가져가다 would send it away.
Using 가져오다 for a person (친구를 가져왔어요). Bringing a living being toward you is 데려오다: 친구를 데려왔어요.
Writing 가져오아요 with the full ending — the 오 stem plus 아 fuses to 와, so the present is 가져와요 and the past is 가져왔어요.

entries.shortExplanation: 이해하다 means "to understand" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 이해하다 (ihaehada) means "to understand". Start from the polite form 이해해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 이해하다. entries.nuance: 이해하다 is Sino-Korean: 理解 means 'untie/loosen (解) the logic (理)', so it pictures a tangled idea coming apart in your head — it covers both intellectual comprehension AND emotional sympathy ('I understand how you feel'). The dividing line versus 알다 is crucial: 알다 is to KNOW a fact ('I know his name', 이름을 알아요), while 이해하다 is to make sense of WHY or HOW something works. As a 하다-verb it conjugates regularly (이해해요, past 이해했어요). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle in the negative: 'I don't understand' is almost always 이해가 안 돼요 (subject 가 + 되다, lit. 'understanding doesn't form'), not the literal 이해를 안 해요, which sounds like you're refusing to understand on purpose. Also resist translating 'understand my feelings' as 내 감정 — Koreans say 내 마음을 이해하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 이해하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 이해해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 알아요 when you mean 'I grasp/follow it' — 알다 is to know a fact, 이해하다 is to comprehend the reasoning; for 'I get why' use 이해해요.
Translating 'I don't understand' literally as 이해를 안 해요. That implies willful refusal. The natural form is 이해가 안 돼요 with 가, treating understanding as something that fails to occur.
Saying 내 감정을 이해해 주세요 for 'understand my feelings'. The idiomatic collocation is 마음 (heart): 내 마음을 이해해 주세요.

entries.nuance: 믿다 is a single native word that spans two English verbs at once: to BELIEVE a fact/claim (그 말을 믿어요 'I believe that') and to TRUST a person (친구를 믿어요 'I trust my friend') — context, not a different word, tells them apart. The closest relatives are 믿음 (the noun, 'faith/trust') and the compound 신뢰하다 (信賴, the formal 'to have confidence in', used in business or writing); 믿다 is the warm, everyday spoken choice. Crucially, 믿다 keeps its ㄷ in the stem (믿어요, 믿었어요) — it is NOT a ㄷ-irregular like 듣다→들어요, so it never becomes *밀어요. Watch the homophone trap: that wrong *밀어요 collides head-on with the real verb 밀다 'to push' (밀어요), so one careless slip doesn't just misconjugate — it accidentally says 'push' instead of 'believe'. English 'believe in (a god/religion)' transfers fine: 신을 믿어요, 종교를 믿어요.

entries.nuance: 바라다 is to HOPE or WISH FOR something, especially good things for other people, which gives it a warmer, more selfless feel than 원하다 ('to want' for yourself). The sharp contrast learners need: 바라다 leans toward outcomes beyond your control that you wish would happen (평화를 바라요 'I hope for peace'), while 원하다 names a concrete desire you intend to get (돈을 원해요 'I want money'). Its signature grammar is verb-기를 바라다 ('I hope that ~ happens'): 합격하기를 바라요. THE famous pitfall: the present polite form is 바라요, but almost every Korean accidentally says/writes 바래요 — that 바래다 actually means 'to fade in color'! The textbook-correct form is 바라요 / past 바랐어요, even though 바래요 dominates casual texting. Don't confuse 바라다 (hope) with 바라보다 (to gaze at).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 바라다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 바라요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the polite form as 바래요. That belongs to 바래다 'to fade/discolor'. The standard form of 바라다 is 바라요, and the past is 바랐어요, not 바랬어요.
Using 바라다 for a selfish concrete want like 'I want this phone'. For tangible personal desires use 원하다 (이 폰을 원해요); 바라다 fits wishes for good outcomes, often for others.
Forgetting the 기를 frame for events: saying 빨리 낫고 바라요. The correct nominalizer is 낫기를 바라요 ('I hope you get well').

beginnerPath.body: 바라요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 바라다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 행복을 바라요. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 안 바라요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 바랄 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 바라요 feels easy, practice 바라고 싶어요, 바랄 수 있어요, and 바라야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 바라다 becomes 바랄 수 있어요 ("can") and 바랄 거예요 ("will"). entries.shortExplanation: 원하다 means "to want" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 원하다 (wonhada) means "to want". Start from the polite form 원해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 원하다. A strong first sentence is 뭘 원해요? Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 원하다 is Sino-Korean (願 'wish/desire' + 하다) and means to WANT a thing or outcome — it takes a NOUN object (커피를 원해요 'I want coffee'). The critical contrast for English speakers is with -고 싶다: to want to DO an action, you cannot use 원하다, you must use the verb stem + 고 싶다 (가고 싶어요 'I want to go'), never 가는 것을 원해요, which sounds stiff and translated. Compared with 바라다 ('hope'), 원하다 is more direct, concrete, and self-centered — a desire you mean to fulfill, not a gentle wish. It also feels a touch more formal and forceful than 갖고 싶다 ('want to have'); a waiter or a contract uses 원하다. Pitfall: English 'I want to eat' tempts you to reach for 원하다, but the natural Korean is 먹고 싶어요. Reserve 원하다 for noun objects.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 원하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 원해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 원하다 to want an ACTION: 가는 것을 원해요 for 'I want to go'. Korean uses verb + 고 싶다 instead: 가고 싶어요.
Treating 원하다 like gentle 바라다. 원하다 is a firm, concrete desire (돈을 원해요); for warm wishes toward others use 바라다 (행복을 바라요).
Dropping the object particle in writing: 저는 휴식 원해요. In full sentences attach 를: 휴식을 원해요 (the 를 may drop only in very casual speech).

entries.shortExplanation: 걱정하다 means "to worry" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to worry" in Korean is 걱정하다 (geokjeonghada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 걱정해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 걱정하다 for study notes. entries.nuance: 걱정하다 (걱정 = 'worry/anxiety' + 하다) is the everyday verb for being anxious or concerned about someone or something. Distinguish it sharply from 고민하다: 걱정하다 is feeling ANXIOUS about how things will turn out ('I'm worried about my grades'), whereas 고민하다 is actively DELIBERATING over a hard choice ('I'm agonizing over which job to take'). As a 하다-verb it splits in the negative — 걱정 안 해요 (separating the noun) or 걱정하지 않아요 — and the favor form 걱정해 주다 means 'to worry on someone's behalf', a kind gesture. The natural way to say 'I feel worried' is 걱정이 돼요 (걱정 + 이 + 되다), not 걱정을 해요, which sounds like deliberate worrying. The single most useful phrase in the whole language family is 걱정하지 마세요 ('don't worry') — memorize it. English 'I'm worried about you' is 네가 걱정돼 or 너를 걱정해, not 너에 대해 걱정해.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 걱정하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 걱정해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 걱정을 해요 for the feeling 'I'm worried'. Korean prefers 걱정이 돼요 (worry arises) for the spontaneous emotion.
Confusing 걱정하다 (anxious feeling) with 고민하다 (mulling over a decision). 'Worried about the result' = 결과를 걱정해요; 'agonizing over the choice' = 선택을 고민해요.
Over-attaching ~에 대해: 너에 대해 걱정해요. Natural Korean is 너를 걱정해요 or 네가 걱정돼요.

usagePhrases.note: 깜짝 is the mimetic adverb for a sudden jolt of shock

examples.en: I was surprised to hear the news
examples.note: -고 links the trigger (hearing) to the reaction

examples.note: Casual; 놀랐잖아 nudges 'see, you made me jump'

entries.nuance: 놀라다 is to BE SURPRISED, STARTLED, or SHOCKED — a sudden involuntary reaction, so it lives mostly in the past tense (놀랐어요 'I was surprised') because by the time you speak, the jolt already happened. Although it ends in 라, it is NOT a 르-irregular like 빠르다→빨라요; it conjugates straightforwardly: 놀라 + 았어요 → 놀랐어요. The cause of the surprise takes the particle 에 (가격에 놀랐어요 'surprised at the price') or the connector -고 (듣고 놀랐어요 'heard and was surprised'). Distinguish it from 놀다 'to play' — one extra ㄹ-syllable apart but utterly different. Its constant companion is the mimetic word 깜짝 ('with a start'): 깜짝 놀랐어요 is the default phrase. To say something IS surprising/amazing, switch to the adjective 놀랍다 (놀라워요). English speakers wrongly mark the cause with 를; remember the trigger gets 에, not the object particle.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 놀라다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 놀라요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the cause with 를: 가격을 놀랐어요. The thing that surprises you takes 에 — 가격에 놀랐어요 — because 놀라다 is intransitive.
Using the present 놀라요 for a past shock. Since surprise is instantaneous, use the past: 놀랐어요 ('I was surprised').
Mixing up 놀라다 (be surprised, 놀라요) with 놀다 (to play, 놀아요). To say something is amazing, use the adjective 놀랍다 → 놀라워요.

A very useful construction is 즐겨 + verb, meaning 'to habitually do X with pleasure': 즐겨 보다 ('enjoy watching, watch regularly'), 즐겨 듣다 ('enjoy listening to'). Also note 즐기다 takes a noun object with 를, so 'enjoy reading' becomes 독서를 즐기다 or 책 읽는 걸 즐기다, not a bare verb.

entries.explanation: "to regret" in Korean is 후회하다 (huhoehada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 후회해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 후회하다 for study notes. entries.nuance: 후회하다 is Sino-Korean — 後悔 literally stacks 後 'after' + 悔 'regret/remorse', i.e. the regret that comes AFTER the deed — and names the painful wish that you had chosen differently. It typically points backward (그 결정을 후회해요 'I regret that decision') and frequently pairs with a reason clause in -아서/어서 or with a past-action nominalizer -(으)ㄴ 걸: 그렇게 말한 걸 후회해. Distinguish it from 아쉽다, which is a milder 'it's a shame / I wish it were a bit different' about things often outside your control, whereas 후회하다 carries genuine self-reproach over your own past action. Also separate it from 미안하다 ('to be sorry' TO someone) — 후회하다 is regret felt inside, not an apology directed at another person. Pitfall: 'I regret to inform you' has no 후회하다 equivalent; that polite-letter formula becomes 안타깝게도 or 죄송하지만. Keep the object with 를, and remember the negative splits as 후회 안 해요.

Confusing it with mild 아쉽다. 'It's a shame the trip ended' = 여행이 끝나서 아쉬워요; deep self-blame over your decision = 그 결정을 후회해요.
Saying 후회를 안 해요 awkwardly in speech — fine, but the more idiomatic split is 후회 안 해요, and 'I'll regret it' is 후회할 거예요, not 후회겠어요.

entries.nuance: 고민하다 is Sino-Korean: 苦悶 fuses 苦 'bitter/painful' + 悶 'anguish/stuffiness', so it literally paints a bitter, stuffy churning in the chest — it means to AGONIZE OVER or deeply DELIBERATE a hard problem or choice, heavier than plain 생각하다 ('to think'). The key contrast is with 걱정하다: 걱정하다 is anxious WORRY about an uncertain outcome, while 고민하다 is wrestling with a DECISION or a problem you're trying to solve (어느 대학에 갈지 고민해요 'I'm agonizing over which university to attend'). It also outweighs 생각하다, which is neutral thinking; 고민하다 implies the matter weighs on you. As a noun, 고민 means 'a worry/dilemma' (고민이 있어요 'I have something troubling me'), and 고민 중이에요 is the natural 'I'm still deciding'. Pitfall: don't use 고민하다 for light, pleasant pondering like daydreaming — that's just 생각하다. And it's a problem you mull, not a person.

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: To AGONIZE OVER or deeply DELIBERATE a hard problem or choice, heavier than plain 생각하다 ('to think'). As a noun, 고민 means 'a worry/dilemma' (고민이 있어요 'I have something troubling me'), and 고민 중이에요 is the natural 'I'm still deciding'.

The key contrast is with 걱정하다: 걱정하다 is anxious WORRY about an uncertain outcome, while 고민하다 is wrestling with a DECISION or a problem you're trying to solve (어느 대학에 갈지 고민해요). It also outweighs 생각하다, which is neutral thinking; 고민하다 implies the matter weighs on you.
Sino-Korean: 苦悶 fuses 苦 'bitter/painful' + 悶 'anguish/stuffiness', so it literally paints a bitter, stuffy churning in the chest.
Don't use 고민하다 for light, pleasant pondering like daydreaming — that's just 생각하다. And it's a problem you mull, not a person.

entries.shortExplanation: 참다 means "to endure" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 참다 (chamda) means "to endure". Start from the polite form 참아요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 참다. A strong first sentence is 조금만 참아요 ("Hold on just a little"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 참다 also becomes 참고 싶어요 (want), 참을 수 있어요 (can), and 참을 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 참아요. Then practice 안 참아요 vs 참을 수 없어요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about basic everyday communication. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

entries.nuance: 참다 is a native verb meaning to ENDURE, BEAR, or HOLD BACK — both physical discomfort (아픔을 참다 'endure pain') and inner urges you suppress (화를 참다 'hold back anger', 눈물을 참다 'hold back tears', 웃음을 참다 'stifle a laugh'). The stem ends in ㅁ, so it is a REGULAR verb: add 아 → 참아요, past 참았어요 — never 참어요 (the bright ㅏ vowel governs the ending). Contrast it with 견디다, which is to withstand a prolonged hardship or pressure over time (고통을 견디다 'endure suffering', 더위를 견디다 'bear the heat'); 참다 leans toward actively restraining a momentary impulse, while 견디다 leans toward holding up under sustained strain. 참다 carries cultural weight — patience and self-restraint (참을성) are prized virtues. Pitfall: choose 참아요 not 참어요, and for an ongoing battle against hardship 견디다 often fits better than 참다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 참다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 참아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Conjugating it as 참어요. The stem vowel ㅏ is bright, so it takes 아: 참아요, past 참았어요.
Using 참다 for long-term withstanding: 일 년 동안 참았어요 for 'endured for a year' is better as 견뎠어요. 참다 = restrain a momentary urge; 견디다 = hold up under sustained hardship.
Forgetting 못 for the 'can't bear it' meaning: saying 안 참아요 ('I choose not to endure') when you mean 못 참아요 ('I can't endure it'). 못 marks inability.

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 참아요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 참다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 조금만 참아요. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 안 참아요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 참을 수 없어요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 참아요 feels easy, practice 참고 싶어요, 참을 수 있어요, and 참아야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

classroomScript: Teacher says: 참아요. Learner repeats three times.

Learner changes the sentence to 안 참아요, then 참을 수 없어요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

entries.shortExplanation: 화내다 means "to get angry" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to get angry" in Korean is 화내다 (hwanaeda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 화내요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 화내다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 화내지 마세요 ("Please don't be angry") — then reshape the same stem into 화내고 싶어요 (desire), 화낼 수 있어요 (ability), and 화낼 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.

entries.nuance: 화내다 literally combines 화 (火, Sino-Korean 'fire' = anger) + 내다 ('to put out, let out'), so it pictures LETTING THE FIRE OUT — to OUTWARDLY SHOW or express anger (raising your voice, scolding). The essential contrast is with 화나다 (화 + 나다 'to arise'): 화나다 is the anger RISING inside you, an involuntary feeling ('I'm angry / I got mad', 화났어요), while 화내다 is the active VENTING of it toward someone ('he got angry at me', 나한테 화냈어요). So 화났어요 = 'I feel angry' (inner state), but 화냈어요 = 'I lashed out' (outward act). The target of 화내다 takes 한테/에게 (나한테 화내다), and the trigger takes 에 (작은 일에 화내다). Pitfall: English 'I'm angry' is the feeling — use 화났어요, NOT 화냈어요, which would mean you displayed anger at someone. Keep 내다 (let out) and 나다 (arise) straight; one letter flips agent vs experiencer.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 화내다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 화내요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 화냈어요 for 'I am/was angry' (the feeling). The feeling rising in you is 화나다 → 화났어요; 화내다 (화냈어요) means you actively vented anger at someone.
Marking the person you're mad at with 를: 너를 화내요. The target takes 한테/에게 — 너한테 화내요.
Confusing 내다 (let out) and 나다 (arise): 화내다 = show anger outward; 화나다 = anger wells up inside. Mixing the stems reverses who is doing what.

entries.explanation: 무서워하다 (museowohada) = "to be afraid of". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 무서워해요 plus one useful sentence like 무서워하지 마세요 ("Don't be scared"). entries.nuance: 무서워하다 is the VERB form built from the adjective 무섭다 ('scary/frightening') plus -어하다, the suffix that turns a feeling-adjective into 'to show/display that feeling'. This is the heart of the matter for English speakers: 무섭다 describes the OBJECT — 'X is scary' (개가 무서워요 'dogs are scary TO ME', expressing the speaker's own fear) — whereas 무서워하다 describes a PERSON outwardly being afraid of something and takes a 를-object: 개를 무서워해요 ('he is afraid of dogs'). Korean grammar reserves bare adjectives like 무섭다 mainly for the speaker's own felt state, so to report a THIRD person's fear you must use 무서워하다 (동생이 개를 무서워해요), not 동생이 개가 무서워요. The same -어하다 pattern drives 좋아하다 (from 좋다), 싫어하다 (from 싫다), 예뻐하다 (from 예쁘다). Pitfall: don't put 를 on 무섭다 (개를 무서워요 is wrong) — 무섭다 takes 가 for the scary thing; only 무서워하다 takes 를.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 무서워하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 무서워해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 동생이 개가 무서워요 to mean 'my sibling is afraid of dogs'. Bare 무섭다 expresses the speaker's OWN fear; for a third person's fear use the verb: 동생이 개를 무서워해요.
Putting 를 on the adjective: 개를 무서워요. 무섭다 takes 가 (개가 무서워요 'dogs are scary'); only the verb 무서워하다 takes the 를-object.
Forgetting the -어하다 logic across feelings: by the same rule, a third person 'likes/dislikes' uses 좋아하다/싫어하다, not bare 좋다/싫다.

entries.nuance: 요리하다 (料理하다, 料 'handle/measure' + 理 'arrange/manage') means to actually prepare a dish — chopping, seasoning, applying heat — so it carries a sense of real cooking, not just touching the stove. Contrast it with 끓이다 ('boil', e.g. 라면을 끓이다 for instant noodles) and 데우다 ('reheat'): a Korean would say 라면을 끓여요, not 라면을 요리해요, because boiling ramyeon barely counts as 요리. As a 하다-verb the stem 요리하 + 여요 contracts to 요리해요, and because 요리 is a separable noun the negative and 못 wedge between the two parts: 요리 안 해요, 요리 못 해요. The English-speaker trap is mirroring 'I cook dinner' as 저녁을 요리해요 (fine) but then saying 저녁 안 요리해요 — wrong; it must be 저녁 요리 안 해요 or 저녁을 안 만들어요. Saying 못 요리해요 for 'I can't cook' — 요리하다 is noun(요리)+하다, so 못 must go right before 하다: 요리 못 해요.
Using 요리하다 for boiling ramyeon or just reheating soup — Koreans use 끓이다 or 데우다; 요리하다 implies actually making a dish.
Writing the negative as 안 요리해요 — the standard split form is 요리 안 해요 (the noun, then 안, then 해요).

entries.nuance: 빨래하다 specifically means to wash clothes/fabric, and the noun 빨래 doubly refers to both the act and the pile of clothes themselves (빨래가 많아요 = 'there's a lot of laundry'). Don't confuse it with neighbors that all touch 'wash': 씻다 is washing your body or hands (손을 씻다), 설거지하다 is washing dishes, and 빨다 is the raw verb 'to scrub/wash (cloth)' from which 빨래 derives — so 양말을 빨다 ('wash socks') and 빨래하다 overlap, but 빨래하다 names the whole chore. As a noun+하다 compound, 안 and 못 insert before 하다: 빨래 안 해요, 빨래 못 해요. The classic English-speaker error is reaching for 씻다 because English says 'wash my clothes' the same way as 'wash my hands' — but 옷을 씻다 sounds wrong to Koreans; say 옷을 빨다 or 빨래해요. Habitual collocations: 빨래를 하다 → 널다(hang) → 개다(fold).

Using 접다 to 'fold laundry' — paper is 접다, but clothes and blankets are 개다: 빨래를 개요.
Putting 못 first as 못 빨래해요 — the correct split is 빨래 못 해요 because 빨래+하다 is a separable compound.

entries.explanation: 고치다 (gochida) = "to fix". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 고쳐요 plus one useful sentence like 고장 난 것을 고치다 ("to fix something broken"). examples.note: Plain object + verb; stem 고치 + 어요 → 고쳐요 (이+어 contracts to 여)

examples.note: 고장 난 is the past-modifier 'broken'; 고쳤어요 is the past tense

entries.nuance: 고치다 is wonderfully broad: it repairs broken objects (자전거를 고치다), corrects mistakes (답을 고치다), reforms bad habits (버릇을 고치다), and even cures illness (병을 고치다) — the unifying idea is 'restore something faulty to a good state'. The sharp line to learn is 고치다 vs 바꾸다: 고치다 keeps the SAME thing and makes it work again, while 바꾸다 swaps it for a DIFFERENT one. If your phone is buggy, 핸드폰을 고쳐요 means repair this phone, but 핸드폰을 바꿔요 means get a new phone. A more formal/technical synonym is 수리하다 (修理, used for appliances/cars on signs and receipts: 수리 센터), and for software/policy you'll hear 수정하다 (修正, 'revise'). The verb is regular: 고치 + 어요 → 고쳐요, past 고쳤어요. English-speaker pitfall: don't overextend the English 'fix' meaning 'arrange/decide' (as in 'fix a date') — that's 정하다, not 고치다. 날짜를 고치다 would mean 'change the already-set date', a different idea.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 고치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 고쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 고치다 when you mean replacing with a new one — 'I'll get a new laptop' is 노트북을 바꿔요, not 고쳐요 (고치다 = repair the same item).
Saying 약속을 고치다 for 'set up an appointment' — to decide/arrange use 정하다; 고치다 would imply altering one already set.
Confusing it with the formal 수리하다 in casual speech is fine, but on official repair contexts (car, appliance) Koreans default to 수리하다, so recognize both.

entries.nuance: 바꾸다 means to replace one thing with another, or to alter something into a different state — money (돈을 바꾸다), seats (자리를 바꾸다), plans (계획을 바꾸다), even your mind (마음을 바꾸다). The dividing line from 고치다 is essential: 바꾸다 ends with a DIFFERENT thing, 고치다 keeps the SAME thing repaired. Returning a defective shirt for a new one is 옷을 바꾸다; mending the torn seam is 옷을 고치다. The destination of the change takes the particle -(으)로: 작은 걸로 바꿔 주세요 ('change it for the small one'). Note also 바뀌다, the intransitive twin: 바꾸다 is 'I change X' (transitive, takes 을/를), while 바뀌다 is 'X changes by itself' (신호등이 바뀌었어요 = 'the light changed') — mixing these up is a frequent error. Conjugation is regular: 바꾸 + 어요 → 바꿔요, past 바꿨어요. English-speaker pitfall: 'change my mind' is 마음을 바꾸다, not 생각을 고치다, and 'change clothes (get dressed)' is 옷을 갈아입다, not 옷을 바꾸다.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 바꾸다 becomes 바꿀 수 있어요 ("can") and 바꿀 거예요 ("will"). entries.nuance: 부르다 chiefly means to call/summon someone to come (택시를 부르다, 친구를 부르다), to call out a name (이름을 부르다), and — a key idiom — to sing (노래를 부르다, the standard phrase, not 노래를 하다). Also note honorific contexts: to summon a superior you'd soften with 모시다 ('escort/bring respectfully') rather than bluntly 부르다.

entries.nuance: 고르다 means to choose by picking one (or some) out of a concrete set of options laid before you — clothes on a rack, gifts in a shop, items on a menu. The fine line versus 선택하다 (選擇, a Sino-Korean synonym) is register and abstraction: 고르다 is everyday and hands-on ('grab that one'), while 선택하다 is more formal/written and fits weighty or abstract choices (진로를 선택하다, 'choose a career path'). It also differs from 정하다/결정하다 ('decide, settle'): you 골라요 among visible things, but you 정해요 a date or a plan. As a 르-irregular, before 아/어 the ㅡ drops and ㄹ doubles: 고르 + 아요 → 골라요, past 골랐어요; before consonants it's intact (고르고, 고를게요, 고릅니다). The headline pitfall is 고르아요 (wrong) for 골라요. Also, English 'choose to do something' (a course of action) is NOT 고르다 — say -기로 하다/결정하다; 고르다 needs a tangible thing as its object.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 고르다 becomes 고를 수 있어요 ("can") and 고를 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 고르다 has an irregular stem (르 irregular). Memorize its polite form 골라요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

structuredNuance.t: To choose by picking one (or some) out of a concrete set of options laid before you — clothes on a rack, gifts in a shop, items on a menu.

The fine line versus 선택하다 (選擇, a Sino-Korean synonym) is register and abstraction: 고르다 is everyday and hands-on ('grab that one'), while 선택하다 is more formal/written and fits weighty or abstract choices (진로를 선택하다, 'choose a career path'). It also differs from 정하다/결정하다 ('decide, settle'): you 골라요 among visible things, but you 정해요 a date or a plan.
As a 르-irregular, before 아/어 the ㅡ drops and ㄹ doubles: 고르 + 아요 → 골라요, past 골랐어요; before consonants it's intact (고르고, 고를게요, 고릅니다).
The headline pitfall is 고르아요 (wrong) for 골라요. Also, English 'choose to do something' (a course of action) is NOT 고르다 — say -기로 하다/결정하다; 고르다 needs a tangible thing as its object.

entries.shortExplanation: 자르다 means "to cut" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: "to cut" in Korean is 자르다 (jareuda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 잘라요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 자르다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 머리를 자르다 ("to cut/get a haircut") — then reshape the same stem into 자르고 싶어요 (desire), 자를 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 잘라요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. entries.nuance: 자르다 means to cut THROUGH and separate something with a blade or scissors — paper, hair, cake, rope, nails — i.e. to sever into pieces. Distinguish it from 썰다, which is 'to slice' food into many pieces on a board (양파를 썰다, 'chop an onion'), and from 끊다, which is 'to cut off / break' a connection, line, or supply (전화를 끊다 'hang up', 담배를 끊다 'quit smoking') — note 머리를 자르다 (cut hair) but never 머리를 끊다. There's also 깎다 for shaving/peeling/paring (사과를 깎다 'peel an apple', 수염을 깎다 'shave'). It's a 르-irregular: 자르 + 아요 → 잘라요 (ㅡ drops, ㄹ doubles), past 잘랐어요, but consonant endings keep it whole (자르고, 자를게요, 자릅니다). The big pitfall is 자르아요 (wrong) instead of 잘라요. Also, English 'cut prices' or 'cut down' does not map to 자르다 — reducing an amount is 줄이다, and cutting off a service is 끊다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 자르다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 잘라요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 자르아요 — being 르-irregular it becomes 잘라요 (ㅡ drops, ㄹ doubles), past 잘랐어요.
Using 자르다 for 'hang up the phone' or 'quit smoking' — severing a connection/habit is 끊다 (전화를 끊다, 담배를 끊다), not 자르다.
Confusing 자르다 with 썰다 when chopping food — slicing veggies on a board is 썰다 (양파를 썰다); 자르다 is a single cut-through.
notes: 르 irregular: memorize 잘라 and 잘라요 together.

usagePhrases.note: 정하다 fixes a concrete arrangement; 날짜를 정해요 ('let's decide the date')

examples.en: I set the time.
examples.note: Single 하다-verb (no separable noun), so it's regular: 정하 + 여요 → 정해요

examples.en: Let's decide our meeting time first.
examples.note: 먼저 ('first') sequences the action; 만날 is the future-modifier 'to meet'

examples.en: I haven't been able to decide my vacation dates yet.
examples.note: 아직 + past = 'not yet'; 못 정했어요 ('couldn't decide')

entries.nuance: 정하다 (定하다, 定 'fix/settle') means to settle on and pin down a choice — a date, place, rule, or one's own mind — turning something open into something fixed. Its close synonym 결정하다 (決定, 'decide') leans more formal and weightier (회의에서 결정했어요, 'we decided in the meeting'), whereas 정하다 is the lighter everyday word for arranging plans (시간 정하자, 'let's set a time'). Don't confuse it with 고르다/선택하다 ('choose'): you 골라요 one item from several visible options, but you 정해요 an arrangement or commitment. Unlike the separable noun+하다 verbs (요리하다 → 요리 안 해요), here 정 is bound, so 안/못 go in FRONT: 안 정해요, 못 정해요 — saying 정 안 해요 is wrong. Conjugation: 정하 + 여요 → 정해요, past 정했어요. English-speaker pitfall: 'decide TO do something' is best rendered with -기로 하다 (가기로 했어요, 'decided to go'), not 정하다 alone; 정하다 wants a noun object like 날짜를/장소를.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 정하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 정해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Splitting it as 정 안 해요 — unlike 요리하다, the 정 in 정하다 is a bound Sino-root, so the negative is 안 정해요 and 못 정해요.
Using 정하다 for 'choose an item' — picking one of several is 고르다/선택하다; 정하다 is for settling an arrangement (date, place, plan).
Saying 가기를 정했어요 for 'I decided to go' — the natural form is 가기로 했어요 (-기로 하다); 정하다 takes a noun, not this clause.

entries.explanation: 신청하다 (sincheonghada) means "to apply for". Start from the polite form 신청해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 신청하다. Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.

entries.nuance: 신청하다 (申請하다, 申 'state/report' + 請 'request') means to formally apply, sign up, or put in a request through a proper channel — a class, a card, a scholarship, a subsidy — usually involving a form (신청서) or an online system. Distinguish it carefully from 부탁하다 ('ask a personal favor', 친구한테 부탁해요) and from 지원하다 (志願/支援): 지원하다 is 'apply' for a job or school admission (회사에 지원하다, 'apply to a company'), with a sense of volunteering yourself, whereas 신청하다 is 'apply for / request' a service, slot, or benefit that's offered. As a separable noun+하다 verb, 안/못 wedge before 하다: 신청 안 해요, 신청 못 해요. Conjugation is regular: 신청하 + 여요 → 신청해요, past 신청했어요. English-speaker pitfall: don't use 신청하다 for applying to a job/university — Koreans say 지원하다 there; and don't confuse the everyday 'ask someone to do me a favor' (부탁하다) with the institutional 신청하다.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 신청하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 신청해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 신청하다 for a job or college application — that's 지원하다 (회사에 지원해요); 신청하다 is for services, classes, cards, benefits.
Confusing it with 부탁하다 — asking a friend for a favor is 부탁하다; 신청하다 is a formal request through a system or form.
Saying 못 신청해요 — as a noun+하다 compound the negative is 신청 못 해요 / 신청 안 해요 (the split goes before 하다).

structuredNuance.t: To formally apply, sign up, or put in a request through a proper channel — a class, a card, a scholarship, a subsidy — usually involving a form (신청서) or an online system.

usagePhrases.note: 확인하다 = verify/confirm the content; 이메일을 확인해요

examples.en: I check my email.

entries.nuance: 확인하다 (確認하다, 確 'certain/firm' + 認 'recognize') means to check, verify, or confirm that something is correct or true — facts, times, reservations, messages — making sure reality matches what you expect. The crucial contrast is with 찾다, which English 'check' can blur: 찾다 is 'to look FOR / search' something not yet located (열쇠를 찾다, 'look for the keys'), whereas 확인하다 is 'to verify' something you can already see (열쇠가 있는지 확인하다, 'check whether the keys are there'). It also differs from 알아보다 ('look into/inquire to find out', 가격을 알아보다). It's a regular noun+하다 verb: 확인하 + 여요 → 확인해요, past 확인했어요, with 안/못 splitting before 하다 (확인 안 해요, 확인 못 해요). Saying 확인하다 for 'check (tick) a box' — that's 체크하다/표시하다; 확인하다 means confirm/verify, not mark.
Splitting as 못 확인해요 — the standard negative for a noun+하다 verb is 확인 못 해요 / 확인 안 해요.

entries.nuance: 취소하다 (取消하다, 取 'take' + 消 'extinguish/erase') means to cancel — to call off or undo something already arranged: a reservation, an order, an appointment, a plan. The neat way to remember it: it's the natural opposite of 예약하다/신청하다 (book/apply). Distinguish it from 그만두다, which is 'to quit/stop' an ongoing activity or job (회사를 그만두다, 'quit the company'; 운동을 그만두다, 'stop exercising'): you 취소해요 a future arrangement, but you 그만둬요 something already in progress. It also differs from 미루다 ('postpone', 약속을 미루다, push the appointment later rather than scrap it) — canceling removes it, postponing reschedules it. As a noun+하다 verb it's regular: 취소하 + 여요 → 취소해요, past 취소했어요, with 안/못 before 하다 (취소 안 해요, 취소 못 해요). English-speaker pitfall: 'cancel my subscription / unsubscribe' is more often 해지하다 (解止, end a contract) than 취소하다, and don't use 취소하다 for 'quit a job' — that's 그만두다.

entries.nuance: 출근하다 is Sino-Korean 出勤 — 出 'go out' + 勤 'duty/diligence' — so literally 'go out to your duty', i.e. physically travel to your workplace and start your shift. Its exact opposite is 퇴근하다 (退勤, leave work). Do not confuse 출근하다 with plain 일하다 'to work': 출근하다 is the act of arriving/clocking in, while 일하다 is the doing of work itself — 회사에 출근해서 여덟 시간 일해요 (I go in and then work eight hours). Because it is a noun(출근) + 하다 verb, every form built off the 하다 part: dictionary 출근하다, 요-form 출근해요 (하 + 여 contracts to 해), past 출근했어요, formal 출근합니다. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, the negative and impossible forms split the noun off — 출근 안 해요 and 출근 못 해요, never 안 출근해요; second, the place takes 에 (destination) not 에서, so 회사에 출근해요 is right and 회사에서 출근해요 (which would mean leaving from the company) is wrong.

conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 출근하다 becomes 출근할 수 있어요 ("can") and 출근할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

structuredNuance.t: Physically travel to your workplace and start your shift. The act of arriving/clocking in, not the work itself.

Its exact opposite is 퇴근하다 (退勤, leave work). Do not confuse 출근하다 with plain 일하다 'to work': 출근하다 is arriving/clocking in, while 일하다 is the doing of work itself — 회사에 출근해서 여덟 시간 일해요 (I go in and then work eight hours).
Sino-Korean 出勤 — 出 'go out' + 勤 'duty/diligence' — so literally 'go out to your duty'.
Because it is a noun (출근) + 하다 verb, every form builds off the 하다 part: dictionary 출근하다, 요-form 출근해요 (하 + 여 contracts to 해), past 출근했어요, formal 출근합니다.

Twofold. First, the negative and impossible forms split the noun off — 출근 안 해요 and 출근 못 해요, never 안 출근해요. Second, the place takes 에 (destination) not 에서, so 회사에 출근해요 is right and 회사에서 출근해요 (which would mean leaving from the company) is wrong.

entries.nuance: 졸업하다 is Sino-Korean 卒業 — 卒 'finish/complete' + 業 'studies/work' — so 'complete one's studies' and receive a diploma. Note Koreans very often state it in the past about themselves — 저 작년에 졸업했어요 — because graduating is a completed life event; the present 졸업해요 usually means a scheduled near-future ('I graduate this year').

entries.nuance: 합격하다 is Sino-Korean 合格 — 合 'meet/match' + 格 'standard' — literally 'meet the standard', i.e. clear a cut-off and pass a test, interview, or admissions screen. entries.nuance: 외우다 is a NATIVE Korean verb (no hanja), meaning to commit something to memory deliberately — to get it 'by heart' through effort. Contrast it sharply with 기억하다 (記憶, 'remember/recall'): 외우다 is the act of putting info IN ('I'll memorize these words tonight'), while 기억하다 is having or pulling it back OUT ('Do you remember my number?'). Mixing them is the #1 English-speaker error, because English 'remember' blurs both. A near-synonym 암기하다 (暗記) means the same as 외우다 but sounds more bookish/formal. Crucially, because 외우다 is native (not noun+하다), its conjugation differs from every other verb on this list: the stem 외우- meets 어요 and the 우 + 어 fuse to 워 → 외워요, past 외웠어요; the negative is the simple 안 외워요 and impossible 못 외워요 — there is NO noun to split off. Common collocations: 단어를 외우다, 통째로 외우다, 줄줄 외우다.

Mis-contracting the 요-form as 외우어요 or 외우요 — the 우 + 어 must fuse to 워: 외워요, past 외웠어요.
Splitting the negative like a 하다 verb (외우 안 해요) — 외우다 is one native verb, so it's simply 안 외워요 / 못 외워요.

entries.nuance: 복습하다 is Sino-Korean 復習 — 復 'again/repeat' + 習 'study' — literally 'study again', i.e. go back over material you've already learned to lock it in. Its mirror-image partner is 예습하다 (豫習, 豫 'in advance' + 習 'study'), meaning to study a lesson BEFORE class; Koreans habitually pair them as 예습과 복습. Don't confuse 복습하다 with 연습하다 (練習): both end in 습(習), but 복습하다 is re-studying KNOWLEDGE you covered, while 연습하다 is drilling a SKILL by repetition — you 복습해 yesterday's grammar but 연습해 your pronunciation. Note the 復 here is read 복 (not 부 as in 부활); the whole word is pronounced [복씁하다] with a tensed ㅆ. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates entirely on 하다 (복습해요, 복습했어요, formal 복습합니다); the negative and impossible forms split the noun (복습 안 해요, 복습 못 해요), never 안 복습해요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 복습하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 복습해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Confusing 복습하다 (review what's already learned) with 예습하다 (study ahead before class) — they are opposites: 복습 = after, 예습 = before.
Using 복습하다 for drilling a skill — re-studying knowledge is 복습하다, but repeated skill practice is 연습하다 (e.g. 발음을 연습하다, not 복습하다).
Writing the negative as 안 복습해요 — split the noun: 복습 안 해요 (impossible = 복습 못 해요).

entries.nuance: 발표하다 is Sino-Korean 發表 — 發 'issue/emit' + 表 'express/show outwardly' — so 'issue something into the open'. It has two senses: (1) give a presentation/talk in front of an audience (수업에서 발표하다), and (2) officially announce/release information (정부가 결과를 발표하다 — the government announced the results). Contrast it with 설명하다 (說明, 'explain'): 설명하다 is clarifying so someone understands a point, while 발표하다 is the public act of presenting or announcing as a whole. Also distinguish 발표하다 from 말하다 'to say' — 발표하다 implies prepared, formal, to-an-audience delivery. A particle nuance: in the 'present' sense the location uses 에서 (수업에서), but the content shown is an object (자료를 발표하다). As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (발표해요, 발표했어요, formal 발표합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (발표 안 해요, 발표 못 해요).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 발표하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 발표해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 설명하다 when you mean giving a presentation — 설명하다 = explain a point for understanding; the public/prepared delivery is 발표하다.
Marking the venue with 에 instead of 에서 in the 'present' sense — an action you perform IN a place uses 에서: 수업에서 발표해요.
Forming the negative as 안 발표해요 — split it: 발표 안 해요 (impossible = 발표 못 해요).

entries.explanation: 제출하다 (jechulhada) means "to submit". Start from the polite form 제출해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 제출하다. entries.nuance: 제출하다 is Sino-Korean 提出 — 提 'lift/raise up' + 出 'out' — so 'put forward, hand out', i.e. formally submit a document, application, or assignment to an authority. Its register is the key point: 제출하다 is the formal, official word, while everyday speech often just uses 내다 'to put out/hand in' — students say 숙제를 냈어요 casually but write 과제를 제출했습니다 formally. The opposite side of the transaction is 받다 'to receive'/접수하다 'to accept (a submission)'. The English-speaker pitfall: 'submit TO the office' tempts an English-style structure, but the destination simply takes 에 (사무실에 제출하다) and the document is a direct object (서류를 제출하다). As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (제출해요, 제출했어요, formal 제출합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (제출 안 해요, 제출 못 해요). Note pronunciation [제출하다] is straightforward, but watch the polite request form 제출해 주세요.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 제출하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 제출해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 제출하다 in casual chat where it sounds stiff — among friends, handing in homework is naturally 숙제 냈어? 제출하다 is the formal/written register.
Confusing it with 받다 (receive) — you 제출하다 (submit) papers TO an office, which then 받다/접수하다 (receives) them; they are opposite ends.
Writing the negative as 안 제출해요 — split it: 제출 안 해요 (impossible = 제출 못 해요).

entries.nuance: 참석하다 is Sino-Korean 參席 — 參 'take part' + 席 'seat' — literally 'take one's seat (and take part)', i.e. attend a formal event like a meeting, ceremony, or banquet. Its register is more formal than just 가다 'to go'; you 결혼식에 가요 casually but 결혼식에 참석합니다 in polite/written contexts. Distinguish it from its close cousin 참가하다 (參加, 'participate/enter'): 참석하다 emphasizes being PRESENT and seated at a gathering, while 참가하다 emphasizes actively TAKING PART (참가하다 fits a contest, race, or program — 대회에 참가하다). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: English 'attend THE meeting' (object) drives learners to 회의를 참석하다, but Korean uses 에 — 회의에 참석하다 — because you 'join INTO' the event. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (참석해요, 참석했어요, formal 참석합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (참석 안 해요, 참석 못 해요).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 참석하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 참석해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 회의를 참석해요 because English makes the meeting an object — Korean marks the event with 에: 회의에 참석해요.
Using 참석하다 for a contest or competition — being present at a gathering is 참석하다, but actively competing/taking part is 참가하다: 대회에 참가하다.
Forming the negative as 안 참석해요 — split it: 참석 안 해요 (impossible = 참석 못 해요).

beginnerPath.title: 1. Memorize the safe sentence first
beginnerPath.body: 참석해요 is the everyday polite form. A beginner can use it with staff, teachers, adult classmates, and strangers. Do not start from 참석하다 when speaking.

beginnerPath.title: 2. Add one real-life noun or place
beginnerPath.body: Practice the verb inside a useful frame like 회의에 참석하다. Korean words become usable only when you know what particle or place phrase usually sits beside them.

beginnerPath.title: 3. Separate choice from inability
beginnerPath.body: 참석 안 해요 means you do not do it or are not doing it. 참석 못 해요 means you cannot do it because of time, ability, rules, health, or circumstances.

beginnerPath.title: 4. Recycle the same verb through patterns
beginnerPath.body: Once 참석해요 feels easy, practice 참석하고 싶어요, 참석할 수 있어요, and 참석해야 해요. This is how one verb becomes many real sentences.

classroomScript: Teacher says: 참석해요. Learner repeats three times.
Teacher asks a yes/no question with 회의에 참석하다. Learner answers with 네 or 아니요.
Learner changes the sentence to 참석 안 해요, then 참석 못 해요.
Learner says one personal sentence using today, tomorrow, here, or together.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 참석하다 becomes 참석할 수 있어요 ("can") and 참석할 거예요 ("will"). entries.shortExplanation: 취직하다 means "to get a job" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
entries.explanation: 취직하다 (chwijikada) = "to get a job". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 취직해요 plus one useful sentence like 회사에 취직하다 ("to get a job at a company"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 취직하고 싶어요 for what you want, 취직할 수 있어요 for what you can, 취직 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations.
entries.learnerPriority: First master 취직해요. Then practice 취직 안 해요 vs 취직 못 해요, because that contrast appears constantly in beginner conversations.
entries.contextHint: Use this verb when talking about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations. Start with one complete sentence and then substitute the noun, place, or time phrase.

essential.meaning: The base forms you need before building longer sentences.

entries.nuance: 취직하다 is Sino-Korean 就職 — 就 'take up/settle into' + 職 'a post/position' — literally 'take up a post', i.e. get hired and start a job. It nearly overlaps with 취업하다 (就業, 'take up work'): in daily speech they're interchangeable, but 취직 leans toward landing a specific job/post at a company, while 취업 is the broader 'entering employment' (you'll see 취업률 'employment rate', 취업 준비생 'job seeker'). Don't confuse 취직하다 with 일하다 'to work': 취직하다 is the one-time event of GETTING the job, while 일하다 is the ongoing doing of work — 좋은 데 취직해서 열심히 일해요 (I got a good job and work hard). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'get a job AT a company' makes learners write 회사를 취직하다, but the employer takes 에 — 회사에 취직하다. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (취직해요, 취직했어요, formal 취직합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (취직 안 해요, 취직 못 해요).
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 취직하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 취직해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 회사를 취직했어요 because English uses 'a company' as an object — the employer takes 에: 회사에 취직했어요.
Using 취직하다 for the act of working day-to-day — getting hired is 취직하다 (a one-time event), but doing the work is 일하다.
Forming the negative as 안 취직해요 — split the noun: 취직 안 해요 (impossible = 취직 못 해요).
